Lula and his Workers' Party have cast this election as a "battle for democracy", arguing that Jair Bolsonaro's conviction for coup-plotting is evidence that "Bolsonarismo" constitutes a threat to Brazil's democratic institutions.
During Lula's latest term in office, relations with Trump have been rocky.
Lula has insisted that Brazil "does not fit into anyone's backyard", an apparent reference to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with.
Bolsonaro, on the other hand, argues that working with Washington to combat powerful criminal gangs - which wield immense power in parts of Brazil - will restore the state's sovereignty to gang-controlled areas.
He has also been labelling the Workers' Party as corrupt, reminding voters of the massive financial scandals which plagued the party for years and which have turned many voters against it.
Lula plans to be in São Paulo to watch the results on Sunday evening while Bolsonaro is set to be in the capital Brasília - which is also where his father is under house arrest.

Major LPG distributors' federations have opposed a proposed protest in Delhi and an indefinite strike, favouring dialogue with state-run oil marketing companies (OMCs) and the Petroleum Ministry to resolve demands for higher commissions and relief from operational and commercial pressures.
The Federation of LPG Distributors of India (FLDI) and All India LPG Distributors Federation (AILDF) — the two main bodies that claim membership of most LPG distributors in the country — distanced themselves from the proposed protest and strike call given by a smaller splinter group.
While FLDI said it did not support the proposed agitation, maintaining that distributors' concerns should be addressed through constructive engagement and concrete decisions, AILDF said it is not participating in the proposed protest announced in Delhi on October 26.
AILDF said it "believes in solutions through meaningful discussions" and that its "member distributors assure uninterrupted LPG home delivery, whatever the challenge."
"When the nation needs us, we have always delivered. Every home, every crisis, every time," AILDF said.
Commission paid to LPG distributors for sale of domestic cooking gas has remained unchanged for the last five years despite a rise in cost.
Distributor associations have been engaged with the oil marketing companies (OMCs) as well as the Petroleum Ministry for raising the commission.
A splinter group has however, given a strike call to press for the issue.
The LPG Distributors Association of India (LDAI) has called for a day-long dharna on October 26 in Delhi.
"The AILDF has once again met with the Directors (Marketing) and senior LPG officials at the head offices of PSU oil marketing companies, continuing its sustained dialogue with the oil companies, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, and GAIL/IGL officials," it said. "Since March 2026, followed by April, June, August, September and now October 2026, AILDF has consistently taken up the concerns of LPG distributors at various levels. Sometimes due to the world energy crisis, decisions take time. Hope for better outcomes for the distributor network."
FLDI said it, along with AILDF, "jointly raised fair commission, distributor viability & operational concerns before OMC leadership. This dialogue is a positive first step. FLDI will pursue these issues with OMCs & MoPNG until resolution."
Stating that it does not support the proposed protest and indefinite strike, FLDI said it continues to favour dialogue with OMCs and the Ministry for the "just demands" of LPG distributors.
"FLDI & AILDF jointly sought no indent changes without distributor consent and no push sales of non-fuel products, NDNE or FTL. Business must be demand-led. OMCs assured consideration of these concerns to promote ethical practices," it said.
The All India HP Gas Distributors Association (AIHPGDA) also said the federations were in regular dialogue with the oil companies and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, adding that solutions should emerge through discussions rather than direct action.
The federations' position follows a meeting on October 21 at Indian Oil Corporation Ltd's headquarters in Mumbai, attended by directors (marketing), executive directors and senior officials of Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL), along with representatives of the All India LPG Distributors Federation (AILDF) and FLDI.
The associations have sought a revision in distributor commissions, an end to pressure to take up non-fuel products, protection against changes to refill indents without distributors' consent, and written standard operating procedures (SOPs) to improve relations between distributors and OMC field officials.
AIHPGDA said distributors had highlighted financial distress, operational difficulties and commercial pressures at the meeting. The association said digital reforms had improved transparency, but refill sales had declined in several markets while expenses continued to rise. Restrictions on new connections, unpaid work and unsold commercial stock were adding to working-capital pressures, it said.
On distributor commissions, AIHPGDA said OMC management had informed the meeting that proposals for a revision had already been submitted to the petroleum ministry. The directors also agreed to jointly recommend an interim increase within a definite time frame, although ministry approval remained pending, according to the association.
The federations have been raising distributors' concerns at various levels since March, with further engagements in April, June, August, September, and October, AILDF said in social media posts.
A commission increase would offer distributors some relief from rising operating costs, although the extent of the benefit would depend on the size and timing of any revision.
The associations also raised concerns over what they described as pressure to take up non-fuel products and other sales categories, including DNDE and FTL. They argued that business should be driven by genuine demand rather than targets imposed on distributors.
FLDI said the associations had jointly sought an assurance that refill indents — orders placed for LPG supplies — should not be changed without distributors' consent. The federation said OMC officials had assured them that the concerns would be considered to promote ethical business practices.
AIHPGDA said the directors had expressed concern over deteriorating relations between distributors and field officials and assured action on issues within OMC authority relating to the forced upliftment of non-fuel products, DNDE and FTL.
The associations also sought written SOPs, recorded consent for commercial indents, digital audit trails and an independent grievance-escalation mechanism. They called for reconciliation of OMC records with invoices and GST returns, stronger supply-chain accountability, consumer-safety safeguards and a five-year roadmap for the LPG distribution network.
Restrictions on new LPG connections were another concern raised by distributors. AIHPGDA said the management had reviewed the matter at the highest level and that work was under way, while seeking early operational relief when the geopolitical situation improves.
The federations, meanwhile, have reiterated their commitment to maintaining uninterrupted household LPG deliveries despite the challenges facing distributors.
AILDF said it had consistently raised distributors' concerns with oil companies, the Petroleum Ministry and gas-sector officials, while continuing to assure consumers of reliable home delivery. The federations have stressed that resolving distributors' financial and operational difficulties is important to maintaining a viable last-mile distribution network.
OMC management acknowledged distributors' dedication and staff efforts during the recent crisis, while indicating that a complete return to normal operations would take time, AIHPGDA said.

1 person rescued from collapsed building in Kenya as others remain missing
A person has been rescued from the rubble of a collapsed building in Nairobi more than 24 hours after the incident
NAIROBI, Kenya -- One person was rescued from the rubble of a building that collapsed in the capital, Nairobi, more than 24 hours after its floors pancaked, police said Saturday.
The building was under construction on a busy commercial street in the Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents. Police said more than 10 stories were under construction.
Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen said Friday that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped in the rubble.
The man was rescued Saturday and taken to a hospital.
Government spokesman Charles Owino said the registered owner of the building was deceased, and his family and another party were in charge.
Vincent Ochieng, a disaster officer with the Kenya Red Cross, said the organization had recorded 31 missing persons but was still verifying the reports. Some workers may have left the site before the building collapsed, he said.
Rescuers used sniffer dogs and thermal sensors to locate people trapped in the rubble.
Businesses in buildings near the collapsed structure remained closed as business owners counted their losses and blamed the local government for failing to enforce building regulations.

Firefighters battled on Saturday to put out flames that tore through Adolf Hitler’s “Eagle’s Nest” mountain retreat while police detained a suspect who investigators said may have psychiatric problems.

No one has entered the building because of fears it could collapse, Brandl added.

In September 2026, high school and university students, along with teachers, launched massive protests in France demanding reforms in the education system and increased funding for schools. Joined by ordinary citizens, farmers, and workers frustrated by the rising cost of living and an economic crisis, the demonstrations escalated into a nationwide, violent movement by the third week of October. These protests resulted in severe property damage, the burning of buildings, and thousands of arrests. As the unrest turned increasingly violent, the French government imposed partial curfews across several cities.
In this context, a video (here and here) is being shared online claiming to show protesters in France attacking security forces, who were seen defending themselves with riot shields. Let’s verify the claim made in the posts.
Claim: Video of protesters in France attacking security forces, who were seen defending themselves with riot shields in October 2026.
Fact: Although protesters in France did clash with security forces, the viral video is unrelated to those events. The video actually shows individuals throwing rocks at police during a protest in Medan, Indonesia, on 29 August 2025. Hence, the claim in the post is Misleading.
We first noted the word ‘POLISI’ written on the riot shields in the viral video and identified it as the Indonesian translation of the word ‘Police’. We then conducted a reverse image search of the video and found the same visuals had been uploaded by several media outlets (here, here & here) in August 2025.
According to the media reports, the video shows people throwing rocks and sticks at police during a protest in Medan, Indonesia, on 29 August 2025. The demonstration took place after the death of a delivery rider in clashes between riot police and students who were protesting against lawmakers’ allowances.
A comparison of the surroundings in the video with Google Streetview imagery of the parliament building’s surroundings confirms that the location is in Indonesia, not France. We previously debunked this video in September 2025 when it was linked to protests in Nepal.
To sum it up, an old video from Indonesia is being falsely shared as footage of protesters attacking security forces in France.

When millions of voters fill out their ballots in November, they won’t just be choosing elected representatives. Many states are offering the chance to impact conservation and wildlife as well, through ballot measures focused on things like dedicating more money to habitat protection or mitigating the impacts of climate change. One could even reshape wildlife management in one of the country’s most picturesque mountain states — and also lead to the indiscriminate deaths of all kinds of wild animals.
Wild animals can’t vote. Here’s where they’re on the ballot anyway.
The midterms are packed with ballot measures that could dramatically affect natural spaces.
And while ballot measures might seem like small potatoes in the grand scheme of electoral politics, they could have an outsized impact this year. The Trump administration has been systematically rolling back protections for endangered species, taking a hammer to longstanding pillars of climate regulation, and cutting funding to agencies like the National Park Service and National Forest Service, both of which oversee vast stretches of wildlife habitats. In many cases, states have had to step up, putting more resources into conserving the habitats and species within their borders, and ballot measures can help shape those decisions.
Here are the seven ballot measures that could transform ecosystems across the country this election:
California — Proposition 45: Cutting pesky environmental reviews, also maybe cutting habitats
This ballot measure would shorten environmental review periods for “essential projects” like housing, water systems, clean energy, and medical facilities, among others. In a state that’s been struggling to build what it needs fast enough, this could help speed essential clean energy projects that could help slow climate change. On the other hand, reducing California Environmental Quality Act review time, as this proposition would do, could also lead to increased habitat destruction, leading advocacy organizations like the Sierra Club to oppose it.
Georgia — Amendment 1: Tax breaks for conservation land (maybe)
This amendment might seem a little in the weeds — and mostly in the interest of farmers and ranchers looking for tax breaks. But it would double (from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres) the amount of land an owner can get tax breaks from if they protect it under the state’s Conservation Use Valuation Assessment program. As Yanshu Li, an Associate Professor of Forest Economics at the University of Georgia, told me, the amendment could incentivize landowners to set aside larger tracts of their property for wildlife habitat conservation, which would benefit species like the nine-banded armadillo and the northern bobwhite quail that call these habitats home.
Massachusetts — Question 6: A fund for nature
Question 6 would create a “Nature for All Fund,” routing existing taxes on sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and money spent at golf courses to conservation. That fund could then be used on natural resource conservation, making it the first time the state has a dedicated funding source for conservation projects.
Colorado — Proposition 137: More money for restoration and wildfire prevention
This proposition, similar to Massachusetts’, would direct existing sales taxes on sporting goods to a state fund dedicated to conservation and wildfire prevention. In a state where wildfires have torn through more than 2 million acres in the past decade, dozens of conservation groups are supporting this measure to protect habitats and species.
Arkansas — Issue 4: Waterworks and waterways
Here, voters are being asked to approve up to $500 million in bonds that can be used to fund water-related infrastructure projects like water treatment, waste disposal, and wetlands infrastructure. A boost to wetlands under the Arkansas proposal could help animals that live in those habitats, which are often overlooked in this region.
Rhode Island — Question 5: New money for climate resilience and habitat protection
This measure would allow for $55 million in bonds to fund environmental and recreational projects. The largest chunk of this change — $25 million — would go to helping to protect the state from the impacts of climate change. Another $7 would be devoted to protecting Narragansett Bay and its watersheds, which would include funding to “restore natural habitats and control invasive aquatic plants,” according to the Rhode Island Current.
These ballot measures are all relatively straightforward so far, but there’s one question up to voters this fall that puts wild animals front-and-center — and is splitting hunters and anglers down an ethical centerline. Which takes us back to Colorado:
Colorado — Amendment 83: A constitutional right to hunt…traditionally
On its surface, this amendment seems fairly innocuous. It asks voters to enshrine “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” in the state’s constitution. Hunting and fishing are already big in Colorado, and they’re protected by statute, so this may not seem like a major change. But, as Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, speaking for herself, told me, neither the text of the bill nor its proponents define what “traditional methods” of hunting and fishing would be allowed under this amendment.
“Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Niemiec said. Many of these practices injure or maim animals, including ones that aren’t targeted: Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf, and a lynx. All of these practices have been outlawed in Colorado over the years, either through other ballot measures or regulatory changes; in 1992, for example, Coloradans voted to ban hunting bears using bait and hounds, and four years later they banned leg-hold traps and snares.
The new amendment also continues on to propose: “establishing hunting and fishing as the preferred means of managing fish and wildlife populations.” This would leave far less room for wildlife agencies like CPW to make nuanced decisions or roll out alternative programs, like birth control or animal relocation. It also reduces their ability to take into account the preferences of people who value wildlife for reasons other than hunting.
“Biological science can inform decisions about how many animals can be killed without threatening a population,” Niemiec said. “But it can’t tell us what hunting practices are ethical, or how to balance hunting opportunities with the public’s desire to see wildlife alive — and protected from unnecessary suffering.”
The push for these constitutional protections, Niemiec told me, is part of a larger backlash against conservation groups. But in this case, it’s not as simple as hunter vs. non-hunter: Plenty of hunters and anglers support taking ethical considerations into account when making decisions about how to manage wildlife, and some hunting groups in Colorado have publicly spoken out against the amendment.
“If we’re going to enshrine anything in the Constitution, it should say we should be balancing the diversity of public interest in wildlife in all of our management decisions,” Niemiec said. “We need innovative methods, not traditional methods, if we’re going to deal with the complex challenges that our wildlife is facing moving forward in the state and throughout the country.”

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.
In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.
“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

Drought, fire and high diesel prices 'addin' up tough' for Oregon ranchers
HARNEY COUNTY, ORE. - Late bloomin' rabbitbrush – wads of swaying ochre – stud the roadsides and steep eroded-basalt buttes rising up from the basin floor outside of Hines, Oregon.
In a broad open field, horses munch standing hay as Katie Baltzor watches her black angus cattle on this fall day.
We've ridden out here in a side-by-side vehicle – it's like an overgrown golf cart with a pickup bed in the back made for rough ranch work.
All the animals are quiet. Happy. With their heads down grazing.
"You see that horse, how he's got speckled colors?" said Baltzor with a smile in her voice. "Looks like country gravy, I guess that's why they called him Gravy."
Diesel prices remain near record highs, despite recent actions by President Trump as the mid-term elections get closer.
The high prices are adding to pain for cattle ranchers in western states, who were already struggling with persistent drought. And in Harney County, where bovines outnumber the people – by a lot - there's many mouths to feed.
'Everything has gone up'
"Fuel costs, parts costs, everything has gone up," Baltzor said. "People say that prices have gone up, but calf prices (paid to ranchers) have (too).
"But calf prices still have not kept up with inflation – and so that's what makes it tough for ranchers to keep in business. If everything else goes up and cattle prices don't, you're just spinning your wheels a bit – you better like what you do."
Baltzor's face shows a life spent working in the desert sun. Her long ponytail glints a bit reddish in the afternoon light.
Baltzor and her husband Keith, had just finished riding a bunch of about 150 hundred head of their cattle down Highway 205 on horseback from another pasture.
"Sometimes it is dicey," she said. "There were cars starting to come through our bunch of cows … unfortunately a woman opened up her door and jumped out. And those cows would not go near her. It scared them, they wanted to come back anyway. Then she got out again and still was stopped. People just don't understand, they don't know. When you see a herd of cows and they're coming towards you, don't stop, just keep coming through them."
Baltzor was moving the cattle so they could work them closer to home. They are going preg-check the mother cows to make sure they're carrying new babies, and give all the cattle and calves vaccinations and dewormer.
Wildfires brought them home
But for Baltzor, this year is already addin' up tough. The places where Baltzor typically ranges her cattle in the mountains were ravaged by record-size wildfires this summer, robbing them of the grass the herds usually eat. Baltzor, and hired riders, had to hoof it through heavy smoke into the mountains to extract their cattle from the path of the fires.
"So all our cows, instead of coming home the second week of September, we had to bring them home the third week in July," Baltzor said. "Other folks had to do the same. And some people had to start feeding – we didn't, we had the rakebrunch."
Rakebunching means just raking pasture hay into piles, and leaving it in the field for animals.
Now, it's gonna take time 'til the mountain grass comes back. In some areas where her neighbors' ground has been burned over, it's taken years for them to be able to return their animals to graze, Baltzor said.
"Where are we gonna run cows?" she said. "Some of those fields that burned, the allotments you can't go back on them for a couple of years. And because so many acres burned in Harney County, it's not just my husband and myself that have this issue."
With no grass, ranchers need hay to feed their cattle. But the drought that set the stage for the fires has dried up Baltzor's hay meadows, too.
"So, the meadows were very short," Baltzor said. "Some of them got some water and you were able to cut a little bit. Some of them didn't even get water and you couldn't even cut some of the fields."
Rakebunch
Here's where the high diesel prices add up tough – what little hay there is, is a lot more expensive to harvest.
"The tractors, you know everything is diesel, and it's expensive and it costs a lot to keep them running," she said.
Haying typically takes several passes with a tractor – you have to cut it, turn the windrows to sun dry, and then bale them and stack them. Each time they fill the tractor with diesel now, it's about $300.
"And so just like this year when we were trying to decide, 'Should we try to run and bale some of this hay? Or it's not very good, it's very light, should we just rakebunch it?" she said. "Part of that was looking at the cost of diesel."
Rakebunching means going over it fewer times with the tractor. They also rakebunched because they feared more wildfire would force them back to their homeplace with the drought. Rakebunching is a good solution for the late summer and fall, but it will leave them short of hay later.
"But the bigger problem becomes next year," Baltzor said. "If we don't get the precipitation, then we don't have the irrigation water and then we'd be looking at purchasing hay."
Purchasing hay can mean driving long distances to get it, or having it delivered, in big trucks that burn a lot of diesel.
Baltzor drives her side-by-side through grass the color of a flaxen palomino.
'You keep a heifer'
This year's high diesel prices come at a time when the price of beef in the supermarket is also way up. Ranchers can sell their calves now for pretty good money. But, "It's not something you just do," Baltzor said. "You keep a heifer."
Heifers are young females, ranchers like to keep some or all of the ones born every year, so they can produce more calves, and replace cows that are too old for that. It's a longer term investment.
"It's two years [for a heifer to be bred and] before you have a calf," she said. "You know, a product. It's not that they're going to have a calf right away. And sometimes people don't understand that."
Break point and winter
Baltzor said she and her husband and ranch partner have switched to gas pickups to try to save a little on diesel. But she said every ranch here has a different break point
"Do you have vehicle loans?" Baltzor said. "Do you have cow loans? Do you have land loans?"
Baltzor said she and her husband worked outside jobs for years to be able to build their herd and accumulate land.
"It will pencil for us," Baltzor said. "Because we're lucky we worked really hard not to have debt. But not everyone's that lucky. And when we first started out we had a lot of debt …. Nobody gave it to us. We had to find places to rent, and we had to buy cattle. And we had to take out loans to do all of that."
On the way out of the pasture, a metal gate squawks a lot as it's closed and then clanks shut, held fast by a rope.
"There's different ways to get into the cattle business, and ours wasn't the easiest way," Baltzor said. "But I think it's very worthwhile. Because you appreciate what you have."
But times are lean for many in southeast Oregon, and now – here comes winter.

Severe flooding in the Four Corners region prompts evacuations and rooftop rescues
Heavy rain flooded dozens of homes in Utah, while tornadoes in Arizona tore off roofs, knocked trees onto structures, and brought down power lines

Severe flooding across Colorado and New Mexico left hundreds without power and forced evacuations, with emergency crews carrying out overnight rescues and key roads and bridges remaining closed on Saturday across the Four Corners region.
Officials anticipated further precipitation on Saturday where the borders of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah meet.
Two months of heavy rains had already broken a summer drought, delivering 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain from Wednesday through Friday onto saturated soil, with an additional 1 inch (2.5 centimeters) possible on Saturday.
"We may see some floodwaters receding, but there will be more rain, and the rivers are expected to rise again," San Juan County, New Mexico, Emergency Management warned in a Facebook post Saturday.
Emergency responders staged 20 rescues near Farmington and Shiprock, New Mexico.
Officials advised residents of 600 homes to evacuate, while local power companies reported around 1,500 people were left without electricity.
The New Mexico Department of Transportation closed a 2-mile (3.2-kilometer) section of U.S. Highway 64 west of Shiprock due to water on the road.
Flooding over a bridge on the San Juan River also shut down a four-mile stretch of New Mexico 371 south of Farmington, the region's main population center with approximately 46,000 residents.
The inundation follows a week of stormy weather across the region.
Heavy rain flooded dozens of homes in Utah, while tornadoes in Arizona tore off roofs, knocked trees onto structures, and brought down power lines.
During a Friday news conference, Farmington Police Chief Steve Hebbe referred to the flooding as a "once in a generation" event.
In southern Colorado, flood levels exceeded predictions, cresting 3 feet (1 meter) higher than a 100-year flood event on the San Juan River just a year ago.
While parts of the Southwest are rocky, sparsely vegetated, and naturally prone to flash flooding, recent rainfall had thoroughly soaked the ground, making widespread flooding far more likely.
Forecasters attributed the intense moisture to the remnants of Pacific tropical weather systems pushing inland.

A large clinical trial testing a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of disease recurrence in patients with melanoma by 42% compared to a standard treatment, STAT tells us. The results are an important advance because patients lived significantly longer without cancer returning. The vaccine may also usher in a new wave of treatments for other types of cancer, though experts are debating how broadly applicable the technology could be. Merck and Moderna announced its success in August, but details including the magnitude of benefit were being withheld until a scheduled presentation Saturday at the annual meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology. But an oncology news website published some of the data on Thursday, breaking the conference embargo.
A U.S. judge granted a request by the Pharmaceutical Research & Manufacturers of America and three drug makers to intervene in a lawsuit over a government rebate pilot program, pivoting from a previous decision denying their involvement, Bloomberg Law notes. The order will allow the trade group, AbbVie, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Boehringer Ingelheim to step into a fresh legal battle over the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program slated to go into effect Jan. 1. Hospitals filed a challenge earlier this month seeking to block the U.S. Health Resources & Services Administration from allowing drugmakers to provide rebates instead of upfront discounts for medicines purchased through the 340B Drug Discount Program.

Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.
The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.
The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.
Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.
All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.
America PAC declined to comment.
Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”
The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error.
The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him.
Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine. In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”

Chelsea: Cole Palmer red card, Mike Penders howler and 'out-coached' by Roberto De Zerbi on horror night for Xabi Alonso
Tottenham won at Stamford Bridge for just the second time in 36 visits in the Premier League; Chelsea created very little in the defeat with Gary Neville calling them 'awful'; Cole Palmer was described as 'petulant' following his red card; Mike Penders made a 'monumental' error
Saturday 24 October 2026 21:42, UK
They say bad things come in threes. That was certainly the case for Chelsea on a miserable evening at Stamford Bridge as they lost 2-0 to Tottenham in a game where they were described as "awful" by Gary Neville.
Spurs had won only one of their previous 36 league visits to Chelsea but dominated Xabi Alonso's side from start to finish, with an own goal from Mike Penders and a stunning late strike from Mathys Tel securing a well-deserved win for Roberto De Zerbi's side.

To add to their woes, on an evening where the dismal weather matched their performance, Cole Palmer was sent off for a second bookable offence after already escaping a straight red card earlier in the game, having barged into Spurs midfielder Mateus Fernandes.
"Tottenham outplayed Chelsea. Out-coached, everything. None of us expected Tottenham to come here and win today, but after 10-15 mins, that confidence did start to grow," Gary Neville said while on commentary duty, in a game that was also described as the worst performance of Xabi Alonso's short tenure so far.
"Chelsea have been awful, really. On the ball, they've been well short. Nowhere near the level. I am stunned."
Chelsea started the game without a recognised striker due to the surprise absence of regular starter Joao Pedro.
Both Danny Welbeck, who started as the striker in the 3-0 loss to Brentford when Joao Pedro was also absent, and Estevao were on the bench. Welbeck was not introduced until the 88th minute, when Chelsea were 2-0 down.
Neville added: "Welbeck must be thinking 'how do I get a game here?' Disciplinary problems have cost him [Alonso] today, but I don't think that's the biggest problem.
"The biggest problem is that Tottenham have come and outplayed them. They've made them look really ordinary.
"Where Tottenham have absolutely battered Chelsea is in midfield. Cole Palmer, [Morgan] Rogers, [Jordan] Henderson and [Moises] Caicedo have been able to get nowhere near. Spurs' midfield has run the game.
"They absolutely bossed the game. I usually say when it's bad weather and teams are getting pressed, knock it long. I think it's mad.
"But you could just see that Chelsea wouldn't be able to keep that pressure on. Tottenham's combinations and patterns in midfield were really good."
'Petulant' Palmer and Chelsea's overall frustration
The frustrations for Chelsea - and Palmer specifically - were clear to see throughout. After being stopped in his tracks on the counter by a deliberate handball from Fernandes, Palmer confronted the Spurs midfielder when the whistle had blown.
The England international then barged into Fernandes, sparking a melee between the two sides. Sky Sports News understands the incident was checked and cleared by official John Brooks on VAR.
"I think that could be a red. If this wasn't at Stamford Bridge, I think it's a red," Neville said at the time of the incident, which ended in a first yellow for Palmer.
Jamie Redknapp said the reaction was "petulant" and out of character for a player who is usually known for his cool and composed nature.
Just three minutes after Penders' own goal, the forward then caught Conor Gallagher late and was swiftly shown a second yellow by referee Chris Kavanagh.
"They started to lose their heads. It was frustration as they couldn't get near them," Redknapp continued. And that spread across the team as a whole, not just with their talisman Palmer.
Morgan Rogers was also booked after catching Gallagher, the same player who was on the receiving end of Palmer's second tackle, in an incident which Neville believed could have reduced Chelsea to nine men.
"I think that's a red. I do," Neville added. "He's absolutely wellied him with no intent. That's ludicrous from Rogers. They have lost it. Xabi Alonso needs to get them off."
'Monumental' error from Penders - but he's their only option
The howler from Penders, tipping the ball into his own net after failing to claim a corner, came in his first start in place of the injured Emiliano Martinez.
After going 1-0 down, Chelsea unravelled. But with Martinez set to be sidelined for the foreseeable future after undergoing facial surgery having fractured his jaw against Everton, the goalkeeper will need to bounce back quickly ahead of facing Liverpool in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports.
"He made a monumental mistake; it's as simple as that. The ball comes in and where he goes wrong is that he comes with no authority," Redknapp said.
"He, to a certain extent, gets bullied. There is hesitation. It's hard. It has to become character building for him. He has to fight within himself.
"They will need to put their arm round him; he is going to play again next week.
"Of course you will make mistakes but it is how you handle it. He has to get on with it and show some character."
Chelsea sanctioned the loan move of Robert Sanchez to Como following the arrival of Martinez from Aston Villa in the summer.
Their other option in goal in the match-day squad against Spurs was 23-year-old Teddy Sharman-Lowe, who spent last season on loan at Bolton and has not made a competitive senior appearance for the Blues.
Gabriel Slonina remains at the club but has not been named in the squad since pre-season.
The stats behind Chelsea's horror-show vs Spurs
- Spurs gained just their second away win in 35 attempts against Chelsea in the Premier League (D11 L22) and their first since April 2018 (3-1).
- Spurs have beaten Chelsea in all competitions at Stamford Bridge while keeping a clean sheet for the first time since December 1986 (also 2-0).
- Chelsea failed to score at home in a Premier League London derby for just the second time in their last 17 such games, after a 0-0 draw with Crystal Palace on MD1 last season.
- Chelsea's Mike Penders (21yrs 85d) is the second-youngest goalkeeper to score an own goal in the Premier League, after Illan Meslier (20yrs 354d) for Leeds against Wolves in February 2021.
- Chelsea have conceded eight goals from set pieces in the Premier League this season, double the amount of any other side.
- Cole Palmer's sending-off was the 100th red card Chelsea have been shown in the Premier League (excluding rescinded cards), becoming the third team to reach this milestone after Everton (113) and Arsenal (110).
- Mike Penders became just the second Chelsea goalkeeper to score an own goal in a Premier League match, after Petr Cech against Everton in December 2009.
- Chelsea had just seven attempts against Spurs, their fewest in a Premier League game this season and their fewest at home in the competition since January against Brentford (6).

Indonesia gas supply cut unlikely to have much impact on Singapore electricity prices in short term: Tan See Leng
Global gas prices are a bigger factor in costs, says Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng.
SINGAPORE: Electricity prices in the short term are unlikely to be affected by Indonesia cutting natural gas exports to Singapore, said Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng on Sunday (Oct 25).
Speaking to reporters after the People’s Action Party (PAP) conference, Dr Tan reiterated that the reduction amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas needs.
"In the short term, the prices would not really affect that much. In fact, if anything at all, we should be looking at the world prices because a lot of our gas, the unit price is actually pegged to the movement of some of the key global index itself," he said.
"We have always looked at energy as a very critical part of our entire country's economy, sustainability, and also our survival. Energy is existential for all of us, so we have put in place contingency measures, insurance measures, to ensure that our energy supply is diversified."
Indonesia on Saturday began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.
In response to media queries, an Energy Market Authority (EMA) spokesperson said on Saturday the total reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to 17 British thermal units per day over a period of 18 days.
Dr Tan added that Singapore has multiple layers of defence in place, including diversifying sources of natural gas, maintaining its standby liquefied natural gas (LNG) facility, and ensuring that Singapore GasCo is ready to import more LNG whenever required.
"I would like to urge all of our fellow Singaporeans: keep calm and carry on. We have dealt seamlessly with such reductions in the past without any incident, and the government will continue to ensure the reliability and the resilience of Singapore's energy supply," he said.
Beyond gas, Singapore is also exploring alternative energy sources, including biomethane, geothermal and solar. It is also studying the possible use of nuclear energy, although no decision has been made on that yet.
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at the conference on Sunday that Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial gas contracts to “honour their commitments”.
He added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.
Singapore imports natural gas through pipelines from Indonesia and Malaysia, as well as LNG shipped in from international suppliers. In 2025, piped natural gas accounted for 43 per cent of Singapore's total gas imports, while LNG made up the remaining 57 per cent.
Dr Tan added that Singapore has very good relations with Indonesia at the highest level of government, particularly between President Prabowo Subianto and Mr Wong.
This was built through "many, many decades of very good, solid partnerships", said Dr Tan.
"We understand that they may have some domestic supply needs and bottlenecks, which we can understand," he added.
"The exact details moving forward, I think these are still early days, and we will continue to monitor the situation very closely."

Arignar Anna Zoological Park in Vandalur will not be allowing visitors on October 22 and 23 as a precautionary measure following confirmation of H5N1 avian influenza infection in water birds by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, on October 2, 2026.
According to Forest Department officials, seven water birds in the zoo had died between October 3 and 7. Of them four were painted storks, one grey pelican, one grey heron and one oriental darter. As soon as the first bird died on October 3, the zoo officials cordoned off the area.
Immediate preventive measures, including disinfection, sanitisation, and strict implementation of biosecurity protocols, were undertaken in accordance with the Government of India’s guidelines, officials said. However, the zoo remained open as no further bird mortality or sickness has been reported since October 9.
Now that the confirmation has come, the zoo management has to follow the protocols laid out by the Centre and so the zoo would remain closed on Thursday and Friday, officials said.
This temporary measure is intended to facilitate intensive sanitisation, strengthen biosecurity measures, and ensure close monitoring of the situation. The public are requested to cooperate with the precautionary measures, a press release from the zoo said.
According to the protocol, as soon H7 avian influenza is confirmed, visitors’ entry needs to be stopped forthwith.
The movement of the vets and labourers should be restricted and in no case they should move from infected pens to healthy pens. The management of the healthy sheds should be done by a separate team. Maximum possible number of birds is to be sampled, while sampling a water body, birds arriving at different locations be taken into consideration, it should be ensured that different species are proportionately represented.
In addition to sampling of birds, environment samples like water, soil are to be collected and sent for testing, the guidelines state. The control actions to be initiated are same as for domestic poultry. However, endangered and precious captive birds confirmed as non-infected could be exempted from culling, say officials.
Sampling has to be repeated every 15 days for at least four times and if consecutive two samplings from the last positive result are found negative then the opening of the zoo for public could be considered by the competent authority, according to the action plan for prevention, control and containment of avian influenza.

Ukraine and Russia eye new peace talks — and Melania Trump's mission — but steep obstacles remain
Ukraine and Russia have signaled willingness to resume peace talks and back a humanitarian mission led by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, but deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees underscore obstacles to ending the war
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine and Russia have signaled their willingness to resume U.S.-brokered peace talks and are backing a humanitarian mission led by First Lady Melania Trump. But deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees that re-emerged this week underscore obstacles to ending the war. The new diplomatic push comes after more than 4½ years of fighting, bringing with it a surprise announcement on Friday: Kyiv and Moscow have agreed to a local ceasefire to allow aid next week into a stranded town in Ukraine's southern war-divided region of Kherson, following secret consultations between Melania Trump and civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine. While the initiative raised hopes of similar humanitarian missions in the future, there were few indications that any of the key positions have shifted. Russia continues to demand Ukrainian territory it does not fully control, while Kyiv insists any agreement must include ironclad guarantees against another invasion. Within hours of Russian President Vladimir Putin saying he agreed “in principle” to restart talks, Russia launched a deadly barrage of ballistic missiles and drones on Kyiv. Moscow on the same day said it had destroyed more than 800 Ukrainian drones heading toward its cities.
Here’s a look at where the two countries stand as potential negotiations loom.
U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff secured the latest commitment to talks after shuttling between Oslo, Norway, and St. Petersburg, Russia, this week to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin.
A new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, following the most recent round in Geneva in February.
A Kremlin spokesman said that the next round of talks is likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, around mid-November. Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s ties with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, have sunk to a new low. Moscow has been bolstered by Trump’s deal for Russia to supply the U.S. with diesel and his recent rejection of new Russia sanctions.
Kyiv has been undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones after rejecting a call by the U.S. president to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Ukrainian leaders fear the moves will embolden Putin, giving him little incentive to compromise at the negotiating table.
As Trump increased pressure on Zelenskyy, accusing him of being an obstacle to peace, Witkoff secured the release of an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. The envoy described the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” at their meeting in St. Petersburg — a remark met with consternation in Ukraine.
While both sides back calls for new talks, Russia and Ukraine are still far apart on their terms for a settlement, while their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes.
Central to Russia’s demands is full control of four Ukrainian regions it illegally annexed months after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022: Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, in addition to Crimea, which Moscow seized in 2014.
Russia currently occupies about 20% of Ukraine but has failed to capture all the territory in the regions over which it claims sovereignty.
In a long list of demands, Moscow also wants Ukraine to withdraw forces from all four annexed regions, renounce its bid to join NATO, reduce the size of its military and drop restrictions against the Russian language and a Moscow-affiliated branch of the Orthodox Church.
Speaking on state television late Thursday, Putin said Moscow remains "ready to negotiate and seek solutions to this difficult, complex situation,” before adding: “But if some prefer a different path, so be it. In any case, all the objectives of the special military operation will be achieved.”
Zelenskyy — who for months has publicly advocated for peace talks — argues that giving up land would leave Ukraine more vulnerable to future attacks. Kyiv views security guarantees as essential to prevent Russia from restarting the war in the future.
The Ukrainian president has reaffirmed support for a ceasefire that would freeze front-line positions, followed by talks on conditions for ending the war. Moscow has rejected a break in hostilities until a comprehensive agreement on its terms is reached.
While Kyiv and Moscow have maintained limited contact to organize prisoner exchanges and the return of fallen soldiers, previous talks have made no progress on the security arrangements needed to sustain a peace deal.
Ukraine believes security guarantees backed by Western allies are essential to any future settlement, ideally in the form of NATO membership — an option Vladimir Putin has rejected. Ukraine expects to heavily rely on its own army as the main security guarantee with financial backing from its allies.
Other elements of security guarantees being discussed range from NATO membership, which the U.S. administration has currently ruled out, direct guarantees from the United States in what Zelenskyy has described as an “Article 5-like format” and backing by the European-led 30-country alliance known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Article 5 of the NATO charter contains the alliance's mutual-defense guarantee, which establishes that an attack on one is an attack on all.
“All of these guarantees are possible on the basis of a strong Ukrainian army — in terms of both numbers and quality — with clear funding, and not a small amount. Our colleagues in Europe and America know this,” Zelenskyy told reporters Thursday at a briefing.
Following the massive attacks on Kyiv and other cities this week, he argued that only increased Western pressure on Moscow would change its calculations about future peace talks.
“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post. “But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps — steps toward ending the killing.”

Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year.
A South Korean government source told the Yonhap news agency that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.
Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.
The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.
Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

Obama unloads on Trump over the Iran war and mocks the president’s diplomatic strategy
Obama bashed Trump for causing fuel prices to surge and what he saw as the unnecessary deaths of service members in a war that has raged on for nearly eight months

Former Democratic President Barack Obama has unloaded on Donald Trump for the Iran war, mocking the Republican president’s diplomatic strategy.
“These are not serious people. They’re not serious people. And the problem is you end up having to pay the price for their lack of seriousness,” Obama said Saturday while stumping for Democrats in Ohio.
The U.S., alongside Israel, started launching strikes against Iran in late February, with Trump claiming that Americans were in imminent danger over the Middle Eastern country’s nuclear ambitions.
But Obama argued that the issue had already been dealt with under his administration — until Trump unraveled it.
“Let’s think about this Iran war. The original rationale was, we’re going to go in there and get them to give up their nuclear program, their nuclear weapons,” Obama said. “Now, the thing was, Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons, because I put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged — kept them from getting nukes. And I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it; I just had to engage in diplomacy.”
Obama was referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, commonly called the Iran Nuclear Deal, which the Middle Eastern country signed in 2015 and Trump withdrew from during his first term.
The deal restricted Iran’s nuclear program to ensure it was only using those materials for peaceful purposes in exchange for sanctions relief.
But Trump argued when withdrawing from the deal in 2018 that it “allowed Iran to continue enriching uranium and — over time — reach the brink of a nuclear breakout.”
Trump has insisted throughout the war that it would be a quick operation, but it has now dragged on for nearly eight months. Soon after the strikes began, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, blocking oil tankers from passing through the vital passageway and causing fuel prices to skyrocket.
A total of 21 American service members have been killed and 865 wounded in operations related to the war, according to the Pentagon.
“So seven months later, how’s that war going?” Obama asked.
“Our allies and our bases have been attacked; Americans have been killed; hundreds of Americans have been wounded; we have, we’ve run down our stock of missiles,” the former president said, though Trump has denied reports of munitions shortages. “And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to the world market.
“This is the reason why the price of oil is up. Nobody disputes that. This is reason the price diesel is up. This is why the reason the just about everything is up.”
Trump is hosting daily rallies across the country to boost Republicans’ chances of keeping control of Congress in November’s midterm elections — all while dealing with his deeply unpopular war.
Forty-seven percent of Democrat voters and 56 percent of Republican voters think ending the war in Iran should be one of the highest priorities for the next Congress, according to a new AP/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
Obama was in Cleveland Saturday to support Amy Acton, who is running for Ohio governor against Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Senator Jon Husted.
Ramaswamy saw his betting odds plummet over a controversial ad using his opponent’s mother, whom Acton has accused of abuse, to call her a “liar” and urge Ohians not to vote for her.
Acton has an 83 percent chance of winning the race compared to Ramaswamy’s 18 percent on the prediction market Polymarket as of Saturday evening.
Ramaswamy was also trailing Acton by seven points in a traditional poll. Acton had 50 percent of support among likely Ohio voters compared to Ramaswamy’s 43 percent, according to a recent survey conducted by Marist Poll before the campaign ad was released.
In that same poll, Brown was up four points with 48 percent of voter support compared to Husted’s 44 percent.

More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
Dad shift: Men now file majority of paid family leave claims in key states
Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.
On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.
Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.
It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.
"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.
"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.
"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"
Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.
In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.
There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.
"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.
California's program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.
Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.
" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."
Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"
Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.
Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.
In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.
States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.
In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.
In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.
"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.
"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.
"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"
While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.
A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.
One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.
President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.
"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey.
According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.
"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."
The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.

Katie Miller, the wife of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, has warned about Democrats who want to go after President Donald Trump’s staffers who commit crimes.
Democratic lawmakers have constantly sounded the alarm over Trump administration policies that they consider to be illegal, such as the president’s massive deportation agenda, his war in Iran and his sweeping tariffs — most of which the Supreme Court already struck down.
Miller has now warned that the Trump administration should believe Democrats when they say they will go after those who have committed crimes.
In an X post Saturday, Miller referred to comments made by Sen. Brian Schatz from Hawaii, who Punchbowl News said secured support from a majority of Democrats to become their next whip once Dick Durbin retires next year.
“There is some pretty significant corruption at the deputy assistant secretary level,” Schatz recently told The Bulwark’s Sam Stein. “There should be a message across the government—not that we’re going to punish anyone who worked for the Trump administration—but that we are a country of laws and not of men.
“And if you committed an actual federal crime, that as long as the statute of limitations has not run, you should probably get a lawyer.”
Miller cautioned on X: “When Democrats say they are going to prosecute and go after junior Trump staffers, we should believe them.”
The Independent has reached out to the White House for comment.
Miller previously worked as an aide for Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, early in the president’s second term. Headed by tech billionaire Elon Musk, DOGE gutted federal agencies to reduce what the Trump administration saw as government waste.
Democrats have also viewed DOGE’s actions as unlawful, and members of the party who serve on the House Oversight Committee are reportedly looking to target Musk, depending on whether November’s midterm elections go in their favor.
“Our committees need to be doing oversight both into the Trump administration, but I think even more importantly or equally importantly into the corporations and ultra-rich people who have tried to corrupt our government,” Representative Greg Casar from Texas told Politico’s flagship newsletter Playbook.
“And, of course, Elon Musk is on that list because it takes two to tango.”
Miller’s warning comes as White House attorneys are weighing whether to issue mass pardons to junior staffers, according to a new report from The Washington Sun.
A pardon for all junior officials in the Trump administration seems unlikely, a source familiar with the matter said. But the publication noted that Trump could give blanket pardons for those involved in policy areas such as immigration, war or trade.

During her Oct. 13 debut, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia answered three questions from outlets typically friendly to U.S. President Donald Trump, stumbling over parts of those answers, and ended the press conference after just 14 minutes.
Many social media users mocked Zacharia's performance afterward. Some posts included a video of a young beauty pageant contestant (archived), supposedly Zacharia, struggling to answer a question.
The video, along with the claim that it showed Zacharia, was shared in several popular X posts (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent emails wondering if the video really was of Zacharia.
The woman in the video was not Zacharia, but instead a 2007 Miss Teen USA contestant, Caitlin Upton. Therefore, we've rated this claim miscaptioned.
The video has gone viral before, as the internet culture website Know Your Meme has documented, and many of those who shared it with a caption identifying the woman as Zacharia appeared to have done so jokingly. However, responses to the posts indicated that at least some people unfamiliar with the video believed the captions were serious.
The question Upton, who was Miss South Carolina Teen USA that year, struggled to answer was about a large number of Americans being unable to identify the U.S. on a world map. She didn't really answer the question; Upton stumbled over her words while referencing people in the U.S. who didn't have maps, education, South Africa, Asian countries and building up the future.
Video of Upton's attempt to answer the question has been available on YouTube (archived) since Aug. 24, 2007, the date of the competition.
A few days later, Upton appeared on the "Today" show and said she was overwhelmed when she was asked the question and made a mistake. While on the show, she gave a more focused answer to the question she was originally asked during the contest:
Personally, my friends and I, we know exactly where the United States is on a map. I don't know anyone else who doesn't. If the statistics are correct, I believe there should be more emphasis on geography in our education so people will learn how to read maps better.
Several years later, Upton spoke publicly about how Upton struggled following the viral fame of her appearance in the Miss Teen USA contest. In 2015, she told Teen Vogue that she suffered from depression and even suicidal thoughts due to bullying, harassment and hate directed her way both online and offline.
In 2024, Vice President JD Vance, then a candidate for the office, posted the clip again to X to mock then-Vice President Kamala Harris for her performance in a CNN interview. At that time, Vance was criticized for bringing attention back to a moment that had Upton contemplating suicide for a time, according to Vanity Fair.
At the time Upton competed in the pageant, she was 18 years old.
In 2007, Zacharia was graduating from Pepperdine University, putting her outside the age range of the Miss Teen USA contest for that year.
