As reported by Music Business Worldwide, Spotify appears to be stepping up enforcement of existing policies regarding Family and Duo subscription plans by requiring users to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager’s device in order to maintain access to it. Those who fail to scan the address verification QR code within seven days will see their account demoted to the free tier and be barred from joining any other Duo or Family plan for 12 months.
Spotify’s support documentation verifies the policy after users on Reddit began posting reports of receiving the QR prompt. The enforcement stems from Spotify’s requirement that family plan members reside at the same address—a seemingly reasonable policy in concept. But what if you have a child away in college, a spouse who works on the road, or any number of other circumstances that might see families separated by physical distance? The policy could extend beyond friend groups looking to save a buck, affecting actual families who thought they were using the program as intended.
Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On report, made available by HITS Daily Double, estimate that “a meaningful share of family plan users are not actual household members, but rather friends sharing a plan to reduce costs.” The report goes on to add, “We see additional monetization upside from tightening household verification on multi-user plans. Most family plans require members to reside at the same address, but enforcement has been minimal in practice.”

Evidence from photojournalists on the scene confirms Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of the new White House ballroom and saluting officials visible far behind and to the left side of the helicopter.
In mid-to-late October, a video spread purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump waving to and saluting nobody on the White House South Lawn prior to boarding his helicopter, Marine One.
For example, Democratic commentator Harry Sisson said the footage (archived) highlights how Trump is experiencing increasing "mental decline."
The clip shows Trump walking toward Marine One — the call sign officials use when a president flies on a special fleet of helicopters — waving toward his left, continuing to walk and then waving, saluting and waving again in a slightly different direction, also off to his left. At the end of the clip, he salutes a Marine and boards the aircraft.
Numerous social media users and other left-leaning commentators shared the video and iterations of the rumor, including former cable news hosts Don Lemon and Joy Reid, as well as fellow progressive voice Adam Mockler. All three have prominent presences on YouTube.
Similarly, The New Republic initially reported, "Trump, 80, Wanders Off While Waving and Saluting to No One." The publication displayed that headline as an image on social media.
In sum, while the clip is authentic, meaning it displays no signs of artificial-intelligence manipulation, evidence shows Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of his new White House ballroom, which has replaced the demolished White House East Wing. He was also saluting and throwing smaller waves to other darkly-dressed officials positioned far behind and to the left side of the helicopter. Therefore, the above social media posts miscaptioned the video.
Fox News broadcast the same live moment leading up to the moment in question, helping to confirm the date this occurred, Oct. 19, as well as providing a clearer look at two or more darkly-dressed individuals standing next to a white fence whom the president appeared to salute (pictured below, to the left of Trump).
(Fox News)
Snopes contacted Lemon, Reid and Mockler to ask if they wished to address this matter but did not receive responses prior to publication. The New Republic declined to comment, but said it updated its report to include a new headline and other updated information. We also emailed the White House to ask if a spokesperson wished to respond to people sharing the false claim. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Reputable media-licensing website Getty Images hosts several photos with text captions providing more information about the moment in question. For example, a picture of Trump waving (shown at the top of this article) is captioned, "U.S. President Donald Trump waves to people working on building the new ballroom as he departs the White House on October 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C." Other photographs show the ballroom construction happening behind Trump and people working on the project both on the ground and up high.
(Brendan Smialowski via Getty Images)
One of Getty's captions says the picture below shows a construction worker giving Trump a thumbs-up sign as Marine One prepared for takeoff.
(Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images)
The Associated Press' image-licensing website also provides more data, including a photo of the ballroom construction from the White House South Lawn, a glimpse of both the White House and ballroom construction from the Washington Monument, a view of Marine One flying over the work zone on the same day, and Trump giving a similar acknowledgement to workers with a fist sign last week.
For further reading, we previously reported on whether Trump took a 2.5% contractor fee on the construction of the new ballroom.

A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money. I can say that personal finance wasn’t dinner table conversation in my house, and even as I went off to college and started fending for myself, it was almost a taboo subject. When it came to money, people either had it or they didn’t, and you definitely didn’t talk about it.
Should you let a chatbot manage your money?
ChatGPT can give decent financial advice — to the people who need it the least.
Maybe this is why the average American isn’t exactly fluent in personal finance, and the situation is getting worse. Americans can only answer about 50 percent of basic questions about borrowing, savings, and risk on a financial literacy survey, according to a 2026 study by TIAA, a retirement services company. About a third of those surveyed said they have a hard time making ends meet and are debt-constrained. These figures have remained relatively unchanged for nearly a decade, but dropped to their lowest level in this year’s study.
It makes sense: It’s hard to learn about money when it’s not taught in schools, and it’s such an intensely private topic. It’s also hard to make good financial decisions when you’re one of the growing number of American households struggling to pay bills, repay debts, and save for the future — and feeling very stressed about it.
In a perfect world, each of us could sit down with a financial adviser to get help — but most of us can’t afford that. Instead, average Americans tend to find personal finance tips on TikTok, in Reddit threads, by watching Suze Orman on YouTube or How to Get Rich on Netflix, or by Googling their questions.
Now we have AI tools, too.
With access to an internet’s worth of information and financial advice, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI chatbots can answer any question you ask. They can help you put together a basic budget or, armed with your bank statements and the details of your student loans and your retirement accounts, tailor solutions to your specific situation. Or, at least, that’s the promise.
Key takeaways
- More people are turning to AI for financial advice: One in five Americans have used AI to help manage their money, and some experts think chatbots could be better than the status quo.
- AI works best if you know what questions to ask: Those with basic financial literacy will be able to make the most of these tools, while those without it — who might need help the most — could be led astray.
- Better advice comes with greater risks: Sharing your financial information with a chatbot helps personalize its recommendations. This raises privacy concerns, so you might want to delete your data when you’re done.
- Think of AI as a financially savvy friend: Chatbots can answer money questions you might be embarrassed to ask someone else and use that context to help build your budget.
AI could create a more utopian, more equitable future, where reliable, hyper-personalized advice is just a prompt or two away for people who can’t afford to meet with an expert in real life. But machines are built by people, and there’s good reason to be concerned that these machines will simply replicate the biases and disparities built into our current system.
Here’s what experts say about how to make the most of these tools — and how to think about all of the inherent risks of uploading a lot of personal financial information to a chatbot or, worse, giving an AI agent the keys to your bank account.
The steep rise, risks, and rewards of AI financial advisers
Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used AI tools like ChatGPT for financial advice, and close to 25 percent for Gen Z adults and millennials have tried it, according to an August Gallup poll. These numbers could tick up too: In October, OpenAI started rolling out a dedicated personal finance tool to its ChatGPT Free and Go users in the United States, which effectively means anyone can try it. ChatGPT Finances lets you securely connect your bank account to the tool using a platform called Plaid, and then you can basically have a conversation with the chatbot about your real-time finances down to the penny. It’s like an AI-powered Mint (RIP) that you can talk to directly.
Regardless of where you encounter a chatbot or how much data you give it, experts say these tools could genuinely help improve financial literacy. You can talk to them about money problems you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family, or ask questions and receive actionable, personalized information. There are real upsides to using AI this way.
Taha Choukhmane, an associate professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management, has been studying outcomes when people turn to chatbots for financial advice. In general, these AI tools give pretty good advice, and that advice gets better as people become more practiced in asking the right question, according to research he published earlier this year.
“We were actually quite surprised that relative to the status quo, the average American would be better off if they were to follow the advice,” Choukhmane told me. But he added a caveat: “Just following the advice without understanding the advice puts you at risk of not fully understanding the risk.”
But you shouldn’t trust everything a chatbot tells you and should verify everything before making any decisions.
Chatbot advice has some significant limitations. First, it’s not impartial. The finance industry has a vested interest in steering you toward certain ways of managing your money, and that typically means selling you products, like loans. If you’ve ever searched for personal finance tips on Google, you’ve probably noticed that a lot of the top results come from banks and other financial institutions. This is by design, according to John Campbell, an economics professor at Harvard. But because AI is aggregating all of that advice, the specific influences and possible bias is less obvious.
“AI is very promising for providing low-cost financial advice in plain English that will arguably be better than what many people would be able to do on their own,” said Campbell, who’s also the co-author of Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone. “One caveat is that chatbot advice is quite likely — unless a model has been carefully trained — to reflect the average of whatever’s being posted on the internet, and that may or may not be first-rate advice.”
An example Campbell gives is the question of when to start taking Social Security benefits. While you’re eligible at age 62, many economists agree that you should delay your benefits, which, based on the way the government calculates your monthly payouts, will allow you to enjoy much higher benefits later in life. But paid financial advisers can recommend starting as early as possible, since waiting longer reduces the amount of money that needs to be managed, which reduces the adviser’s fees. That means there’s a lot of conflicting advice online, much of it supplied by the finance industry. And that’s the information used to train AI models.
“The advice is much more mixed,” Campbell said. “And so if a chatbot is learning from that, it may not actually give the best advice.”
It can be hard to recognize bad advice anywhere in life, but especially when you’re talking to a machine that’s programmed to please you. A chatbot could encourage you to consider a balance transfer, to lean in on credit card rewards, or to refinance your mortgage — all decisions with upsides and downsides for you, but definite upsides for banks — without you realizing how much of its training data comes from the finance industry selling these products. What’s worse is that if you do end up taking bad advice, it might be years before you realize it. You won’t know that you refinanced a mortgage at a bad time until a better time comes along.
That leads me to the other major issue with using chatbots for money advice: People who lack financial literacy are the most likely to fall for bad advice, because they simply don’t recognize it as such. They also tend to be less wealthy, which means they can’t afford big mistakes.
One way to mitigate risk, oddly enough, is to give the AI chatbot more personal information. The more details about your situation it has to consider, the more it can offer personalized advice. More context also means better advice, according to Choukhmane.
“There’s a trade-off there,” Choukhmane said. “There’s real risk around privacy, and so I think everyone needs to find their level of control.”
Don’t assume your data is safe
Any time you’re talking to a chatbot, you’re putting a lot of trust in tech companies to take care of the personal details you’re sharing. Sending sensitive financial data is an especially risky proposition. While tech companies, including OpenAI, promise to keep your data secure, there’s already a long list of breaches, leaks, and privacy violations that serve as cautionary tales.
It’s also impossible to know what tech companies might do with your data in the future. Most of them will use it to train their models, unless you tell them not to. Some of them will use the data to serve you personalized ads.
Then there’s the risk of bad actors getting into your ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini account. If you’ve been using a chatbot for financial advice and uploading your bank statements, a hacker could gain access to a stunning amount of information that could enable them to do all kinds of terrible things to your life.
“They could steal your identity and open accounts and then quickly bankrupt a person,” said Delicia Reynolds Hand, a senior director at Consumer Reports. “It’s not even so much the primary underlying accounts that could be at risk, it’s more just access to this information.”
The steady march of AI progress is making this situation even more complicated. The previous era of chatbots offering financial advice is quickly bleeding into a new phase of AI agents logging into bank accounts on users’ behalf. If you’re using a tool like Claude Cowork or even an AI assistant like Muse, you can give an agent the login credentials to your bank account, and because the agent is operating its own computer, it can actually make transfers, apply for loans, or really do anything in your account. This is reportedly driving major banks wild, since they don’t know which logins are coming from humans and which are agents. And because we know that AI agents are unpredictable, it’s hard to know how that access might go wrong.
Beyond data security and privacy, you should also be aware of the simple fact that nobody’s really at fault if you end up losing money using these tools. Chatbots are not regulated in the way that human financial advisers, who have a fiduciary duty to act in your best interest, are.
“If I get bad tax advice from H&R Block or a tax adviser, there are a clear set of rules and guardrails in place to manage what I can expect in that relationship and where the service they use has liability and where that liability ends,” Hand said. “Currently, that’s not the case for these tools.”
Trust but verify — and then delete your data
In the final years of the Cold War, Ronald Reagan popularized an old Russian proverb: Trust, but verify. The phrase is somewhat nonsensical, since trusting someone implies that you don’t need to verify what they’re saying, and verifying what’s said implies you didn’t trust them in the first place. But if you are willing to shoulder a bit of risk, consider approaching AI this way, especially when your life savings are on the line. I’d also suggest adding a coda to the phrase: And then delete your data.
Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you.
The great paradox with tools like ChatGPT and Claude is that they’re very good at generating truthy text. It sounds authoritative and looks correct — and usually is. Except when it isn’t. AI is famously unpredictable and prone to hallucinations. You can ask the same question twice and get two different answers. That doesn’t mean these tools are useless. It just means you have to approach them with caution. You have to interrogate these chatbots, challenge whatever advice they give you, and then crosscheck that with other, more reputable, sources.
“If you’ve never used these tools, I would not encourage you to just change all your financial plans based on your first conversation,” Choukhmane said. “You want to be quite careful. Start using these tools, start understanding, ask a lot of follow-up questions.”
When it comes to mitigating risk, consider giving ballpark figures for your income or spending when you’re talking to a chatbot about your finances. Uploading financial documents, even if they’re redacted, is inevitably filling a tech company’s vault with your sensitive information without necessarily knowing what will happen to it next. You should also dig into your privacy and security settings to make sure you’ve turned on multi-factor authentication and that your personal data is not being used to train AI models and gets deleted after 30 days.
Ethan Bloch, the product lead for ChatGPT for Financial Services, made a similar set of recommendations when I talked to him recently. Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you. They’re designed to inform and help you think through complex topics.
“You should liken it to just talking to a friend who has some very informed opinions about finance,” Bloch told me. “But if you’re actually making some large financial decision — your portfolio or retirement — you still need to seek out the help.”
Regardless of how experienced you are with chatbots or how much data you’re prepared to hand over, remember what Campbell, the Harvard professor, said. If your financial literacy isn’t great, AI chatbots can be trouble. And if you’re like most Americans, you could probably stand to learn a little bit more about things like mortgages and interest rates.
Yes, Chatbots can be a good way to brush up on financial literacy. You can ask them the money questions you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family. But you can also learn about money the old-fashioned way: Reading books and websites written by reputable, independent sources. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has a portal of financial education resources, including games and quizzes. Khan Academy has a course that covers everything from credit scores to college savings. There’s a personal finance subreddit that I joined years ago and read almost daily. There are budgeting apps, like YNAB which has its own huge Reddit presence.
Whatever you do to learn more about personal finance, simply doing something is progress. Talking about personal finance isn’t the taboo it once was in the US, and it’s even a required course in the vast majority of American high schools now. And while AI won’t magically solve your money problems, it can help get you started. Just be careful. Your livelihood could be on the line.

Since the news about Christina Applegate’s multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis was released, texts from friends in disbelief have been popping up on my phone. “How could this happen?” they asked. “I wonder what else it could be?” they questioned. Because it took so long to receive my multiple sclerosis diagnosis, they assume that I might be wondering if I, too, could be misdiagnosed. “I’m not surprised,” I responded each time someone reached out. “MS can be difficult to diagnose.”
“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations — you don’t have MS,’” Applegate shared on a recent episode of her podcast, “MeSsy.” While the doctor thought this was positive news, Applegate told her listeners that she was not happy at all. “You don’t get misdiagnosed, and all of the sudden I’m better,” she said. I felt her disappointment as if it were my own — because not long ago, it was.
I’ll never forget when my neurologist said the words, “I think what we’re dealing with here is MS.” It was 2017. He’d mentioned the possibility at previous appointments, and I’d already been living with debilitating weakness, pain, and fatigue for 13 years, so I wasn’t completely shocked. But I was scared, and also relieved.
On that day, those two letters — MS — were so much more than a couple of symbols from the alphabet. They held the weight of 13 years of repeated lab work and office visits. They carried the anger of being told I was exaggerating and the hopelessness of feeling as though there was no solution to the weakness preventing me from walking. They provided the validation I deserved for waking up every day for 13 years and choosing to keep searching despite being told I may never receive an answer. Those letters were definitively spoken after all other possibilities had been ruled out. But what happens when every other possible disease isn’t considered first? Perhaps a misdiagnosis.
Across the country, news programs are interviewing doctors to understand how such a critical mistake can be made — and asking what else could be causing her debilitating symptoms. But Applegate is not alone. While data appear to be limited, recent publications from specialized MS centers suggest that around 30% of those originally referred for MS were eventually diagnosed with another disease.
There is no one test to confirm MS. It doesn’t yet have a measurable numerical value like high blood pressure or elevated cholesterol does. The McDonald Criteria for diagnosing MS were recently revised to prevent misdiagnoses from occurring. They didn’t provide clarity in my case even as I begged for an answer.
Other diseases that cause similar symptoms and findings include lupus, Lyme disease, fibromyalgia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and less common conditions like neuromyelitis optica and MOG antibody disease. During my diagnostic journey, I was tested for these conditions and other, much rarer — and only newly discovered — antibodies that cause diseases of the nervous system. And researchers continue to discover novel antibodies that cause similar neurological autoimmune diseases, so some people diagnosed with MS today could potentially learn they have a disease that falls outside of the MS umbrella in the future.
Ongoing research is focusing on finding measurable MS biomarkers that would make diagnosis much clearer. Ultimately, if symptoms continue to worsen on treatment, as they did for Applegate, a new medication or diagnosis should be considered.
While some autoimmune conditions — like Sjögren’s, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and rheumatoid arthritis — have antibodies that can be measured in the blood and used to confirm diagnosis, MS does not yet have a known antibody. Diagnosis relies solely on symptoms, MRI, and spinal tap findings. But other conditions can present with similar findings and symptoms. Essentially, MS is a diagnosis of exclusion.
For years, I was misdiagnosed with fibromyalgia, but I always felt there was more going on. My MRI findings were nonspecific, meaning they could stem from other causes, and they were initially blamed on migraines. But ultimately, my spinal tap showed oligoclonal bands (proteins found in the spinal fluid) and white blood cells, confirming an autoimmune, inflammatory neurological diagnosis. By that point — more than a decade after my symptoms began — other diseases that mimic MS had been ruled out, but only because I was forced to inquire about them after doctors had wrongly written off MS early in my diagnostic search. Perhaps the one — and only — perk of a delayed diagnosis is an eventual definitive one.
Michael Levy, a neuroimmunologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, told Boston 25 News it was likely Applegate’s age (diagnosed in her 40s rather than mid-20s) and her lack of response to treatment that prompted doctors to reconsider. But as I texted with friends about her setback, I found myself questioning that reasoning. “Without presenting a new diagnosis, I don’t understand how they can rule out MS,” I contested. If they’d pinpointed a new diagnosis via a measurable marker, one that better explained her symptoms, that would make more sense. But without another clear answer, and already having met the criteria for an MS diagnosis initially, I wasn’t sure how they could discount it completely.
I was yearning for more information: What did her MRI show? Was a spinal tap performed? Did she, too, have oligoclonal bands? What medication had she been taking as her symptoms progressed? Did she try another? Internally, I returned to my darkest days as I struggled to stand while doctors failed to help. From one once-undiagnosed patient to another, I wanted to ease her despair of learning she’s once again facing a disease with no name.
In my case, so much was ruled out, there was nothing left but MS. And my MS treatment has drastically changed my life, restoring strength and allowing me to return to many activities I was unable to do while undiagnosed and untreated.
Applegate feels as though her reason for pushing onward has been taken from her. “It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down. It’s this weird feeling of like I became this, you and I, the poster children for MS. All that I did, everything that I was doing, I had a f—ing reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason,” she said on her podcast.
But Applegate is no longer solely impacting the MS community. Through her honesty, she’s also helping those who may soon realize they don’t have MS and every person struggling to find a diagnosis. I hope she realizes that her reason has not been erased — it has multiplied.
Lindsay Karp is a freelance writer and essayist with clips in the Washington Post, Boston Globe, Time, USA Today, and other outlets.

A 35-year-old firecracker manufacturing unit owner was arrested by Anaicut police in Vellore after an explosion in the unit killed two workers.
The arrested person was identified as Hari Prasad, who runs a cracker unit in Chinna Anaicut village, that comes under Anaicut Panchayat Union in the district. He was nabbed by a special team from his hideout in Jawadhu Hills. A case was registered and he was lodged at Central Prison in Vellore.
On Wednesday, R. Gayathri, 41, a worker, was killed on the spot after an explosion occured in the firecracker unit. Another worker U. Sangeetha, 45, sustained 96 per cent burns in the incident. Both workers belong to Kottaiyur village near the unit.
The workers were packing firecrackers in the unit when the explosion occurred. The building was razed to the ground.
The injured worker, Sangeetha was admitted at Government Medical College Hospital in Vellore where she succumbed to burn injuries on Friday. Collector P.S. Leela Alex handed over ₹4 lakh ex-gratia from Chief Minister’s Public Relief Fund to family members of the deceased workers. Based on orders of Ms. Alex, license of the firecracker manufacturing unit was cancelled, and the unit was sealed by revenue officials.

Since five members of the American Diabetes Association were ejected from its scientific session in New Orleans on June 5, the professional organization has released two explanations, one apology, one summary of its review of the events, and one notice of further review. Members have protested through petitions and an 1,100-member boycott. The flagship journal has stopped accepting manuscripts and grant reviews, fundraisers, and educational activities have ceased.
On Friday, the ADA posted a news release about the long-awaited review, three days after it disclosed without explanation the departure of Rita Kalyani, its chief medical and scientific officer.
The post offers background for the evictions, citing a “written threat that there would be protest and disruption,” but also backs off from previous explanations, noting that the “ADA’s code of conduct didn’t explicitly state that distributing materials inside the convention center was prohibited.”

YouTuber arrested after popular Indian finance influencer's suicide
- Published
A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.
V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.
In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria.
Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".
BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denied wrongdoing in a post on X.
The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.
Account was taken down
Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.
Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".
He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.
The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.
The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.
But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.
A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others.
A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them.
According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external.
The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.
Police complaint
Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.
Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.
This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life.
"We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.
A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case".
"[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.
Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.
In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".
He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish.
"I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity.
"I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.
If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Capcom confirms data breach that affected 11.7 million users
Capcom ID is still available to use, but users may see more phishing scam emails.
Capcom ID users should be on the lookout for phishing scam emails after Capcom confirmed a massive data breach that affected more than 11.7 million of its users. Earlier this week, the video game company said its online membership service was hit with "unauthorized access by a third party."
According to Capcom's statement, the data breach included millions of account emails, but also the birth date, gender, country or region and nicknames of 43 accounts, as well as unauthorized changes to 196 account passwords. However, the company noted that customer credit card information was not included in this data breach.
Capcom said the incident began on October 19 when it "detected suspicious activity indicating potential unauthorized access" to Capcom ID. Capcom said it blocked access immediately and started investigating the cause and scope of the incident, but also confirmed that the unauthorized access already happened. Afterwards, Capcom reported the incident to local police and its external advisory board for security oversight.
Capcom confirmed that it "identified and addressed the attack method in this incident," and that any service that uses Capcom ID is still available, including games like Street Fighter 6 that require it for online play. However, the company warned that users should be wary of any suspicious emails since the leaked info could be used to send scam emails that impersonate Capcom. Capcom isn't the only major gaming company to be hit with a data breach recently, as Rockstar Games confirmed in April that it was hit by a "third-party data breach."

Foodtech major Swiggy’s shares plunged as much as 17.23% to a 52-week low of ₹174.90 on the BSE today, a day after its Q2 FY27 results showed widening losses at quick commerce arm Instamart. The stock pared some losses to trade at ₹181.50, down 14.10%, at 11:21 IST. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹50,099.69 Cr (about $5.2 Bn) at that time. Several brokerages lowered their price targets following the results, citing higher-than-expected quick commerce losses and concerns over Instamart’s growth and execution. However, most retained their existing ratings. Swiggy’s consolidated net loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr in Q2 FY27 but widened 17% from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss increased to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1 FY27, offsetting an improvement in food delivery profitability. Brokerages Lower Price Targets Citi retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹330. It highlighted 18% YoY growth in food delivery gross order value (GOV), alongside margin improvements of 60 basis points YoY and 30 basis points QoQ. However, Instamart’s net order value (NOV) grew around 13% sequentially, below its estimate of 16%, while losses exceeded expectations. CLSA retained its ‘Outperform’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹262. It said Instamart’s 13.4% sequential NOV growth fell short of expectations, while losses were higher than anticipated. The brokerage flagged a widening gap between Swiggy and Eternal in growth and profitability, adding that Instamart needs to deliver consistent improvements to rebuild investor confidence. Nomura retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹300. It expects Swiggy’s food delivery business to generate ₹1,300 Cr to ₹1,900 Cr in EBITDA across FY27 and FY28. However, it said quick commerce execution continued to disappoint. The brokerage values food delivery at 40 times its estimated FY28 EBITDA and assigns no value to quick commerce or Swiggy’s cash balances. Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹330. While food delivery revenue and EBITDA met expectations, it said reducing quick commerce losses remains critical. UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating and ₹375 target price despite describing the results as weaker than expected. Food delivery performed in line with estimates, but quick commerce losses exceeded expectations. It nevertheless noted early signs of a recovery in growth. HSBC maintained its ‘Hold’ rating but cut its target price to ₹240 from ₹315. It said improvements in Instamart’s operating metrics were insufficient to build confidence in Swiggy’s long-term plans, while flagging food delivery market share losses and intensifying competition. Macquarie maintained its ‘Underperform’ rating with a target price of ₹230, citing negative cash flow and intense competition. It said continued spending on pricing and network expansion, alongside monetisation pressures, could delay profitability. Bank of America retained its ‘Neutral’ rating but cut its target price to ₹245 from ₹275. It noted that Swiggy’s food delivery GOV grew 18% YoY, compared with Zomato’s 21.5%. The brokerage also flagged potential cannibalisation of Swiggy’s main food delivery business by its affordable-meals offering Toing, adding that Blinkit’s performance was increasing pressure on Instamart to demonstrate a path to profitability. Instamart’s Profitability Roadmap Instamart reported operating revenue of ₹1,306 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 33% YoY and 6% QoQ. Its segment loss widened to ₹764 Cr from ₹739 Cr a year earlier and ₹651 Cr in the preceding quarter. Despite the increase in absolute adjusted EBITDA losses, its adjusted EBITDA margin improved marginally to -9.7% of GOV from -9.8% in Q1 FY27. Swiggy said it believes Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27. It expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 FY27, alongside an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin. Instamart added 1.3 Mn average monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking the total to 14.8 Mn. Orders rose 29% YoY to 130.3 Mn, while net average order value increased 4% to ₹506. The platform added 69 dark stores, expanding its network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities. Swiggy also plans to begin shifting Instamart to an inventory-led model by mid-Q3 FY27, with the transition expected to take two to three quarters. Under this model, the business will own the inventory it sells. Swiggy expects the transition to improve Instamart’s contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten its working capital cycle by eight to 10 days. Meanwhile, food delivery operating revenue rose 22% YoY to ₹2,338 Cr, while segment profit increased 39% to ₹349 Cr. “Our food delivery business delivered its highest ever profits and margins while we continue to unlock new category growth through Toing, our standalone offering for affordable meals,” Swiggy cofounder, MD and group CEO Sriharsha Majety said.

India’s baby care market is growing, and so is the challenge of finding products parents can genuinely trust. When it comes to baby care, Indian parents often look for the same thing: products that are made well, priced for the value they deliver, and worth bringing home. Ahmedabad-based Kunal and Kinjal Popat found themselves at the centre of this dilemma when they became parents in 2011. The couple began searching for a safer alternative, but that search opened another can of worms: finding a product that was safe, well-designed and priced right. Their hunt for safer alternatives soon hit a snag. While there was no shortage of baby products in the market, very few offered the combination of safety, thoughtful design and transparent pricing the couple was looking for. Instead of compromising, the Popats decided to build what they could not find. Kunal brought over a decade of experience across engineering, marketing and sales, while Kinjal, trained in design, brought a different lens to the problem. Together, they set out to make baby products that put safety first with the right price tag. And that is how R for Rabbit came into being in 2014. The couple started with around ₹40 Lakh of their own savings, designing products in-house and working with established, safety-certified manufacturers. “I used to visit factories before finalising any partnerships to ensure quality control, testing and certification standards remain as we want for the brand,” said Kinjal. Initially, R for Rabbit started with three baby-gear products, led by strollers. From there, the company began expanding its portfolio and distribution. Today, the brand controls more than 450 SKUs across categories such as car seats, baby apparel, personal care, feeding ranges, and ride-on toys. R for Rabbit expanded into kids' personal care by launching the Biomimic baby skin care range in August this year and entered the baby clothing segment with its apparel range in September. As it continues to grow its product portfolio and distribution, getting products to customers efficiently became an increasingly important part of its growth strategy. The company’s partnership with Shadowfax in 2026 reflects this shift, with last-mile delivery becoming a key consideration as the brand scales across markets. Building A Full-Stack Baby Care Brand At the outset, R for Rabbit relied heavily on word of mouth to build trust. Mothers who discovered the brand began recommending its products through WhatsApp groups and personal networks because of the brand’s focus on quality and international standards of safety. This grassroots buzz helped the duo build early sales without leaning heavily on traditional advertising. Thanks to this organic growth, the brand’s portfolio grew to around 25 products by 2016. “Over time, as our range grew, we put a much clearer framework around how we developed our products. We built everything around four pillars: safety, quality, innovation and customer support. For us, the highest quality and international standards are the floor, rather than the ceiling,” Kunal told Inc42. The founders’ focus was clear: the brand’s products should be designed around everyday realities of Indian parents. Strollers, for instance, were designed to fold with one hand, making them easier to manoeuvre in India’s often cramped lifts and busy urban spaces. Similarly, the founders focused on plug-and-play assemblies for parents to set up products without a complicated installation process. They also designed convertible high chairs that could double up as toddler desks. R for Rabbit also began developing and patenting more of its own products instead of selling products already available in the market. This helped the brand carve out a space between expensive imported brands and cheaper local alternatives. By 2019, R for Rabbit built a base of nearly 1.5 Mn parents. From Growth To A More Complex Fulfilment Model The key change for R for Rabbit came when it moved beyond products that parents bought only occasionally. It entered toys with ‘Orapple Toys’ in 2020 and then launched Feather Diapers in 2022. The expansion into new categories also began to show up in R for Rabbit’s business numbers. The company raised its first institutional round in October 2021, and by FY23, its revenue reached ₹128 Cr. It crossed ₹250 Cr in FY25, helped by a wider product portfolio that grew by more than 100 products during this period. Diapers, in particular, emerged as one of the company’s fastest-growing categories, giving the business a more consistent revenue stream. The 2025-26 phase brought further expansion. In August 2025, R for Rabbit raised $27 Mn in Series B funding, led by Filter Capital and 3one4 Capital. In the following year, the company added BioMimic, a biomimicry-based kids’ personal care range, and launched its first apparel line. In 2026, R for Rabbit’s offline reach crossed 3,000 retail touchpoints, while quick commerce emerged as another important channel. As the company added more products, repeat purchases and customers across more markets, fulfilment became a bigger part of the equation. The challenge was no longer just having the right products, but getting them to customers quickly while keeping delivery costs in check. This also meant rethinking how it stored and moved inventory. R for Rabbit eventually moved from a single warehouse to a regional third-party logistics model, bringing inventory closer to customers across different markets. The company partnered with Shadowfax in 2026 to strengthen its last-mile network and offer same-day and next-day deliveries. The primary aim of the partnership was to improve delivery speed and coverage as the brand continues to grow across categories and markets. “We wanted to build a logistics network that could keep pace with our growth and get products to customers faster. As we expand across categories and markets, being closer to the customer becomes increasingly important. Our partnership with Shadowfax helps us strengthen that last-mile capability and improve both delivery speed and coverage,” says Kunal. Shadowfax’s same-day and next-day delivery capabilities have helped the brand reach more pincodes and improve delivery timelines. According to Kunal, the partnership has brought tangible improvement in its turnaround times and greater operational flexibility. As volumes increase, the company expects better logistics efficiency and wider coverage to help it grow revenue while keeping fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies under control. Faster delivery and broader coverage could also help reduce delivery-related drop-offs and improve the customer experience. Scaling The Next Mile For R for Rabbit, the next stage of growth will extend beyond its existing footprint. The company is looking to deepen its presence in Tier II, Tier III and other emerging markets while continuing to grow in metros. This expansion will bring more customers, higher order volumes and greater demand for faster deliveries, making fulfilment an increasingly important part of the customer experience. “As we work towards becoming a ₹1,000 Cr business, we know that our ability to serve customers across more locations will be critical. Partnering with Shadowfax lets us hold that promise on delivery too, with faster, more reliable fulfilment as we reach deeper into Tier II and Tier III India,” said Kunal. That makes logistics more than just an operational function. Faster same-day and next-day deliveries can improve the customer experience, while better reverse logistics can make returns and exchanges easier. R for Rabbit maintains an overall NPS of 80+, reflecting the word-of-mouth loyalty that has helped build the brand. As the company expands, maintaining that trust will depend on delivering a consistent experience beyond the product itself. By partnering with Shadowfax, R for Rabbit is strengthening its last-mile capabilities to support faster deliveries and wider coverage as it expands into new markets. At the same time, expanding into new markets means R for Rabbit needs to bring inventory closer to customers without allowing fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies to rise. From three baby-gear products in 2014 to a portfolio spanning everyday parenting needs, R for Rabbit has come a long way. But as the company enters its next phase, the challenge now is to make sure that its products reach customers quickly, reliably and efficiently.

Activist Amit Bhatnagar ends 27-day protest against Ken-Betwa link project on Madhya Pradesh Congress leader's request

Activist Amit Bhatnagar on Saturday ended his 27-day protest against the Ken-Betwa Link Project after senior Madhya Pradesh Congress leader Umang Singhar visited Panna and assured him of the opposition party's support.
Bhatnagar ended his stir by having coconut water at the request of Singhar, the leader of Opposition in the Madhya Pradesh Assembly.
Tribal farmers and villagers affected by the Ken-Betwa Link Project, under the leadership of Bhatnagar, have been staging a protest for the past 42 days demanding compensation and rehabilitation, among other demands. Taking part in the 'Save the Constitution, Save Democracy' march organised by the project-affected people, who submitted a memorandum at the Collectorate, Singhar said the Congress will always lend strong support in their fight for rights, justice, dignity, and fair compensation.
"The BJP government, which considers tribals, Dalits and farmers as orphans, should remember that the Congress is still alive. The Congress will continue to fight for the rights and justice of the affected families, from the streets to Parliament. No family should be subjected to injustice in the name of development," he said.
Singhar said he had raised the demands of the protesters in the assembly after visiting them on July 14.
"Chief Minister Mohan Yadav had directed a resurvey of the affected families and an investigation into the status of compensation. But no concrete action has been taken by the government so far. "The Congress stands with the tribal farmers, villagers, and displaced families affected by the Ken-Betwa Link Project. The party will continue to raise its voice until the affected families receive justice, adequate compensation, and dignified rehabilitation," he said.

PAP votes in top decision-making body, Jeffrey Siow and Jasmin Lau nominated but not voted in
Sunday’s ballot was the first for secretary-general Lawrence Wong since he led the party through his first General Election as prime minister last year.
SINGAPORE: The People’s Action Party (PAP) has elected its next central executive committee (CEC), as cadres voted in a renewed leadership slate at the party’s conference on Sunday (Oct 25).
First-term Members of Parliament Jeffrey Siow and Jasmin Lau made the nomination list for the party’s top decision-making body, but were not voted in.
Sunday’s ballot was the first for secretary-general Lawrence Wong since he led the party through his first General Election as prime minister last year. The PAP conference takes place every two years.
In no particular order, the PAP’s 39th CEC comprises:
1) Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong
2) Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong
3) Minister for Education Desmond Lee
4) Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence Chan Chun Sing 
5) Minister for Social and Family Development Masagos Zulkifli
6) Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs K Shanmugam
7) Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu
8) Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat
9) Minister for Law Edwin Tong
10) Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah
11) Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health Ong Ye Kung
12) Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan 
These 12 members were elected from a secret ballot of 19 candidates earlier in the morning.
Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng and Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs Zaqy Mohamad were then co-opted into the CEC with the 13th and 14th highest number of votes among party cadres. The PAP’s constitution allows for up to six members to be co-opted.
Party insiders told CNA that the other five candidates on the ballot were: Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC MP Alex Yam, Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau, Minister for Transport Jeffrey Siow, Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo, Second Minister for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs Sim Ann.
First-term minister David Neo was not on the list of nominees.
CNA understands that Mr Wong, Mr Lee Hsien Loong, Mr Desmond Lee, Mr Chan, Mr Masagos, Mr Shanmugam and Ms Fu were identified as the core leaders of this team.
Other co-opted members, as well as specific appointments within the committee – such as chairman, secretary-general, treasurer and organising secretaries – will be announced in the weeks ahead.
The timing for this has varied in the past. It took 10 days in 2024, 20 days in 2022, and 11 days in 2020.
At Sunday’s conference, Mr Wong said the party cannot expect younger Singaporeans to feel the same bond with it simply for its past work, and must connect with them on their own terms.
“The strong mandate we received at the last election does not guarantee continued support,” he said. “We must continue to earn the trust of Singaporeans through what we deliver, how we conduct ourselves, and how well we serve Singaporeans.”
He called for the party to have the courage to make difficult decisions and the determination to see them through, and to remain a party for Singaporeans across generations, communities and all walks of life.
“The world around us may be growing darker. But together, we will keep our little red dot shining brightly. Together, we will secure a brighter future for all Singaporeans,” said Mr Wong.

The iPhone Duo is finally here. Apple's first folding smartphone arrives seven years after Samsung pioneered the category with the Galaxy Fold. That gave Apple plenty of time to refine the hardware behind closed doors rather than in public view—and the results show: The Duo is a pretty dang good foldable.
Whether your Duo just landed on your doorstep or you're still weighing that $1,999 price, here's what you need to know before unfolding it.
Apps Aren’t Optimized—Yet
The iPhone Duo is a new shape and size for Apple, so many of your apps likely aren't optimized to show up properly on the unique 5.4-inch outer screen or the 7.6-inch inner display. Apple also changed how navigational elements appear on the Duo, aligning them on the right rail instead of centering them on the bottom like every other iPhone.
Apple apps, redesigned for the Duo, look great. Many third-party apps look like the Google Home app in the picture above: a strip down the middle with thick, black bars on the sides. Several major app developers have already optimized their apps for iOS 27.1—Slack, Instagram, DoorDash, and WhatsApp, for example—but I've noticed that even some optimized apps like Instagram can still have broken user-interface elements. It will take time for every app in your library to work perfectly across these new screens.
It might be a good thing that the Duo is back-ordered for several weeks. By the time you snag yours, app developers will likely have caught up to the new device, and you might enjoy a richer folding experience.
Say Goodbye to Face ID
Nearly a decade ago, Apple introduced Face ID as the future of the iPhone, eventually replacing the fingerprint-based Touch ID. So it might be confusing to hear that Apple's first folding phone doesn't have Face ID at all and instead relies on the older biometric authentication method. (Likely because Face ID tech takes up too much space in the thin iPhone Duo.) Touch ID never disappeared—Apple has used it on the iPhone SE and still features it on iPads and MacBooks—but this is the first time it has returned on a flagship iPhone.
Using your thumb again will take some getting used to, but it's not a deal-breaker. Some folks will miss the convenience and speed of Face ID, where all you needed to do was stare at the screen, instead of now reaching for the Touch ID sensor on the right side. Others who hated facial authentication might actually like the return of the fingerprint sensor.
Apple also introduced the Dynamic Island a few years ago—the pill-shaped island around the Face ID camera sensors that shows live app activities, like the next turn on your navigation or music currently playing, giving a second job to the camera cutout. Without Face ID, Dynamic Island hasn't disappeared from the iPhone Duo. Instead, Apple moved it to the top-right edge around the outer selfie camera; on the inner display, it appears at the top-right edge when a live activity is in progress.
You Need a New MagSafe Wallet
The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe just like the rest of the iPhone lineup, so you can magnetically stick your favorite phone grip on the back, or attach the phone to a magnetic car dock, bike mount, or wireless charger. One thing to note: If you unfold the Duo and attach it to a car dock or tripod, the phone will tip to one side because the magnet can’t keep it held straight given the uneven weight distribution. Third-party accessory makers could address this with anti-rotation magnets, but it might mean upgrading your current accessories.
Wallets, unfortunately, are the one accessory that won't really play well with the Duo. Yes, you can still attach a MagSafe wallet, but because the Duo is shorter than other iPhones, the wallet sticks out awkwardly past the lower edge. Apple doesn't have an official solution, so if you want to use a magnetic wallet with your iPhone, you'll have to look at third-party accessories.
Use the Rear Camera for Selfies
Everyone knows the rear cameras on your smartphone are better than the selfie camera on the front. One of the best features on a folding phone is the ability to take a selfie with those superior rear cameras and still be able to see a preview with the outer screen.
Don't confuse this with “Duo Preview” as I did, though. That's a feature that lets you show the person you're photographing the camera's viewfinder, so they can make sure they look picture-perfect before you tap the shutter. The setting to enable this is on the left edge of the camera app, where you can also turn on “Kids Cue” to have Snoopy animations play on the outer screen to get the attention of a kid for the perfect photo.
But if you're taking a selfie yourself and want the camera controls on the front screen, all you need to do is launch the camera and flip the phone around—you'll see a slider that says, “Slide to show camera.” Slide it, and the full camera app will show up on the outer screen, so you can switch modes and access Photographic Styles right there and enjoy the higher-quality results from the superior cameras. Doing this also crucially disables the inner screen, so your fingers won't accidentally switch modes.
You Can Create App Pairs
Filling the inner 7.6-inch screen with two different apps running side by side is incredibly handy and one of the cornerstone features of any folding phone. Whether you're on a phone call and want to pull up a confirmation email, or want to browse two different Safari webpages, you can drag an app from the bottom and pull it to the left or right side to enter the split-screen state.
One trick that isn't immediately obvious is that you can create app pairs. Just tap the middle bar between the two apps once, and it'll glow white, meaning that those two apps are now locked and can be accessed at any moment from the Recent apps menu. You can't save that as an app icon combo, though. This is still very handy if you know you'll always want to open two apps simultaneously on the big screen.
Be Careful of the Inner Screen
I get it, you're going to want to protect the fragile screens of your $1,999 iPhone. A case is smart—folding phone cases aren't like normal cases, as they usually come in two shells that attach to each side of the phone. You can also totally add a screen protector to the outer 5.4-inch screen.
But for the 7.6-inch matte inner screen, exercise some caution. You might see chatter online that you can “remove” the Duo's nano-texture finish, but it's an “integral” component of the inner display—as Apple says on this support page. “Don't attempt to remove it,” Apple writes. (Apple also has a page on cleaning the nano-texture display properly here.) Attempting to remove the finish is likely a surefire way to void your warranty. Apple doesn't say anything about using third-party screen protectors, but using one could compromise the display performance.
If you scratch or damage the nano-texture finish, Apple says you can take it to any Apple Store or an Apple Authorized Service Provider and have it replaced for $19 (or $49 if the phone is out of warranty). That's not the same as if there's an actual crack in the inner display—that'll run you a cool $999 if you don't have AppleCare+.
You Can Split the Keyboard
The iPhone Duo is a wide phone. If you've complained about the size of modern smartphones and how it's hard to reach the top of the screen, well, you might still have some issues reaching the sides of the Duo. There's some good news, though. Apple lets you split the keyboard to make typing on the inner display a little easier.
Later this year, Apple will also issue a software update bringing Reachability to the Duo. On other iPhones, this brings the top of an app down, making it easier to reach. On the Duo, it will move an app to the left or right so you won't have to stretch those fingers as much.
Apple Pencil Support Is Coming
Have you always wanted to use a stylus on an iPhone? Soon! Steve Jobs is probably rolling in his grave.
Apple will bring support for the USB-C Apple Pencil (and only that Apple Pencil model, not others) in a software update later this year. Paired with the 7.6-inch screen's nano-texture finish, it should make writing and drawing on the iPhone Duo feel paper-like. Sadly, there's no place to store the stylus on the iPhone like you can on an iPad. I'm sure someone will make an accessory for it.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

No panic for England but Mitchell issues PWR warning
- Published
Before England's three-match series against Canada, few would have predicted this outcome.
A 2-0 series defeat for the Red Roses; their record 39-match winning streak and 41-match unbeaten run – stretching back nearly four years – ended; and consecutive losses for the first time since 2016.
Over the past 13 months, Canada have turned a 33-13 defeat in the World Cup final into a statement 31-22 win in Ottawa. And three years out from the 2029 World Cup, they have laid down an early marker of their title credentials.
More than that, they have proved England are not invincible – a reality which should hearten New Zealand and perennial Women's Six Nations bridesmaids France because both have beaten giant-killers Canada in the past 12 months.
For the second time in eight days, England captain Meg Jones has been called upon to take stock of a defeat. Once again, she opted for a message of defiance.
"It was a hell of a contest. We're not broken, we just need to grow," said Jones. "Do it together, use the lessons. We're playing the best teams, getting the best punches thrown at us.
"I genuinely believe we've got the best players in the world. When we're firing, generally we're unstoppable. We don't dwell on the past, we're not anxious about the future, we're focused on the present."
- Canada inflict back-to-back losses on England 
  - Published5 hours ago
- How have Canada closed gap to world champions England? 
  - Published4 days ago
It's true, this is far from panic stations. In 2016, England were the defending world champions when they lost to France and beaten finalists Canada. Since then, they've been imperious, winning a second World Cup, reaching the final in 2017 and 2022, and lifting nine of the past 10 Six Nations titles.
This is only their third defeat in 74 matches, so perspective is required.
But England's performances throughout the WXV Global Series highlighted areas for improvement.
They have lacked their usual clinical edge in attack. In Ottawa, Sarah Bern was held up over the line and England conceded a turnover less than five metres out as they failed to make their dominance pay before the break.
Tellingly, they opted to kick a penalty early in the second half to close the deficit – perhaps a lesson learned from last month's 26-26 draw in Exeter, where they turned down a shot at goal to snatch the win in the dying moments.
In defence, they have conceded 18 tries across their past five matches in the WXV, compared to eight in six at the World Cup. They have trailed at the break three times, something they hadn't experienced since 2020.
Last week, ill-discipline repeatedly gifted Canada field position before a late handling error, which put a clearing kick under pressure, opened the door for the hosts' winning try.
On Friday night, Gabrielle Senft picked off a bouncing ball from a missed pass to set up Canada's second try. Minutes later, England were lucky not to concede a similar try when a pass bisected Jess Breach and Jones, who pounced on the ball just before Lizzie Gibson got to it.
"We were riding the waves, building phases, scrum, set piece, we were very strong. Sometimes it's the bounce of the ball or it doesn't swing your way. We couldn't execute when we got in their 22, that's a big one to reflect on for sure," said Jones.
England 'will suffer' if young players don't get PWR game time
Canada does not have a professional women's domestic league and their players had to launch a crowd-funding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.
It's unsurprising, therefore, that many of Canada's top talents play domestically in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, which offers a level of training and match experience they cannot find elsewhere.
Twenty-five Canadian players are contracted for the 2026-27 season, with 11 featuring in July's PWR final between Saracens and Trailfinders. Three Canadian coaches, including head coach Kevin Rouet at Saracens, are also involved in English domestic rugby.
PWR squads must have a minimum of 13 England qualified players in a matchday squad.
But England head coach John Mitchell has warned that too many overseas players in the PWR could be detrimental for future Red Roses sides.
"I think it's necessary to make sure that young English girls are getting enough PWR time," Mitchell said. "It's a critical pathway because Sevens is definitely gone. For players aged between 19 and 23, it's critical.
"We're just going to make sure we don't erode our depth as a result of [overseas involvement]. It's not so much about now. It will be the future that will suffer if we're not smart in that area."
Mitchell has been forced to call upon England's squad depth on multiple occasions in 2026 with Abby Dow and Emily Scarratt retiring after the World Cup, four players absent through pregnancy, and several big names – including Hannah Botterman, Alex Matthews, and Amy Cokayne – spending time on the sidelines because of injury.
He's handed out more than half a dozen debuts this year, with hooker Bryony Field particularly impressing during September's home internationals, played the likes of Abi Burton and Ellie Kildunne out of position, and brought Liz Crake back into the fold after several years away.

Defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh gets one-year extension in Centre's big move
Since May 31 this year, Singh has also held additional charge as secretary, Department of Defence Research and Development, and chairman of the DRDO.
The Narendra Modi government has extended defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh's tenure by one more year, until October 31, 2027. Saturday's decision came a week before he was due to complete his two-year fixed tenure on October 31.
Singh, a 1989-batch IAS officer of the Kerala cadre, has been given the unprecedented extension of one year due to his work in promoting "Aatmanirbhar Bharat" in the defence sector and pushing reforms in the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) in order to make India more self-reliant.
A quiet yet firm taskmaster, Singh has pushed the defence ministry and the DRDO into speedier decision-making and opening the conventional missile manufacturing into private sector.
He took charge as the 40th defence secretary on November 1, 2024, succeeding Giridhar Aramane. When he was appointed to the post in August 2024, his service was extended beyond superannuation—up to October-end this year.
Since May 31 this year, Singh has also held additional charge as secretary, Department of Defence Research and Development, and chairman of DRDO.
An Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC)'s order in May gave him the charge when Samir V Kamat completed his tenure. Kamat had headed DRDO since August 25, 2022. That arrangement was to last until a regular incumbent was appointed or until further orders. No regular DRDO chief has been named since.
Of Singh's predecessors under the present government, Ajay Kumar and Giridhar Aramane left office on superannuation. RK Mathur and G Mohan Kumar continued beyond their normal retirement age to complete fixed two-year terms. Sanjay Mitra received a three-month extension in 2019, beyond his two-year tenure. None was kept on for as long as Singh now will be.
Before joining the defence ministry, Singh was secretary of the department for promotion of industry and internal trade from April 2023 to August 2024. Before that, he was secretary of the department of animal husbandry and dairying. In the Kerala government, he served as secretary, urban development, and later as finance secretary.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): The Madhya Pradesh government has constituted a five-member committee to investigate claims that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district, officials said on Sunday.
The panel will submit its report within 15 days, they said. Ujjain divisional commissioner constituted the committee after conflicting claims over the deaths. Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16.
The district administration had earlier dismissed the claims as false and misleading. It later said viscera samples of two deceased persons have been sent to a forensic science laboratory (FSL) for examination. The cause of death would become clear after the reports are received, it added.
The administration said 10 persons died in Chandana village between October 1 and 15, but denied that any of the deaths was caused by spurious liquor. It attributed the deaths to old age, common illnesses, brain haemorrhage and "deterioration of health due to excessive alcohol consumption".
Ujjain Additional District Magistrate Pratham Kaushik will head the probe committee, which includes Mandsaur Additional Superintendent of Police Ramsanehi Mishra, Ratlam Sub-Divisional Police Officer Lekhraj Meena, Ujjain divisional flying squad Deputy Excise Commissioner Harshvardhan Rai and Regional Director of Public Health and Medical Education Dr Deepak Kumar Pippal.
The panel will conduct a detailed and impartial inquiry into the causes and circumstances of the deaths, along with the related technical and administrative aspects, and submit a factual report within 15 days, according to the Ujjain divisional commissioner's order.
Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari has claimed that 22 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Chandana, Binjana and adjoining areas over the past month, while at least 40 people suffered damage to their eyesight.

Himesh Reshammiya recently had a conversation with Komal Nahta and revealed why he flatly refuses to compose music for films that don't have a situation for a romantic song.
