Authorities investigating whether first Kenyan and Nigerian Ebola cases crossed paths
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.
Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.
She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.
Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.
Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.
The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.
Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.
Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."
Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

No two mattresses are the same, and what’s happening beneath the sheets has a lot to do with why. Memory foam contours to your body, latex has a springier feel, and hybrid mattresses combine foam or latex layers with a supportive coil system for the best of both worlds.
As a product reviewer who has been testing mattresses and writing about sleep products since 2022, I’ve spent the past four years getting up close and personal with mattress construction. I’ve learned how everything from the fabric covering the mattress to a few extra inches of foam can change the feel of an entire bed. I’ve also spent a fair amount of time lying down in the name of research, which is a pretty great job perk.
Consider this a primer on the five main types of mattresses—hybrid, innerspring, memory foam, latex, and even smart beds—so you can figure out which one best suits your sleep style and gives you the best excuse to hit snooze. To help us explain these materials even more, we asked John Merwin, CEO of 3Z Brands (parent company of Helix, Birch, Bear, Nolah, and Leesa) and founder of Brooklyn Bedding, to weigh in as well. —Nicole Kinning
Updated October 2026: We've rewritten portions of this guide, added a fresh introduction, updated FAQs on mattress buying, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Our Favorite Mattresses We’ve Tested
How to Choose the Right Mattress Type
Knowing your memory foam from your latex is a good start, but how do you actually put that knowledge into practice and choose a bed you’ll be excited to climb into every night? A few factors can help narrow down your options:
Feel preference: Do you like sinking into your mattress or feeling like you’re sleeping on top of it? Memory foam tends to closely contour to your body, and latex feels springier and makes it easier to change positions. Hybrids can go either way, depending on comfort layers and coil system.
Sleeping position: Side sleepers typically benefit from mattresses that have enough cushioning to relieve pressure around the shoulders and hips. Back sleepers usually need a balance of cushioning and support, while stomach sleepers often prefer a firmer surface that keeps their midsection from sinking into the bed.
How hot you sleep: If you’re a sweaty sleeper, consider a latex or hybrid mattress. Both offer more airflow than memory foam, which tends to trap heat. That said, cooling features can help, too; some memory foam mattresses use gel infusions or phase-change fabrics that are designed to pull heat away from the body.
Bed sharing: If you or your sleeping partner toss and turn, proper motion isolation should be at the top of your wish list. Memory foam absorbs movement well, so sleeping partners won’t disturb each other. Pocketed coils have a bit more bounce without wiggling the entire mattress. Innerspring, on the other hand, tends to be the bounciest of the bunch. And then there’s firmness: If you and your partner disagree on this crucial mattress characteristic, a split or adjustable mattress may work best.
Hybrid
Traditional coil mattresses have evolved into hybrids, which is what you will likely encounter on today’s mattress market (aside from latex and foam options). Hybrid mattresses are highly customizable, allowing you to pick and choose what you want in your bed, whether that’s a combination of foam and coils, latex and coils, or even a mix of the three. Many mattress reviews will use the phrase “best of both worlds” to describe hybrids, as this mattress lets you sample the design aspects of the materials involved. You can get the pressure relief you need from memory foam or latex on top, but ample support from the coil core (not to mention the aforementioned responsiveness from coil inclusion).
Speaking of coils and harking back to traditional mattress design, the type of coil used in hybrid mattresses matters too, as it improves upon the design of the Bonnell coil. The keywords to look for are “pocketed coils” or “individually wrapped coils,” which make up the main support mechanism of a mattress. Instead of being interconnected, each coil stays in its own lane (pocket, really) and will compress uninhibited by the other coils around it. In other words, where there is more weight, the bed will feel firmer.
This is especially applicable for areas where body weight is centralized when you’re lying down, particularly around the hips and shoulders. Pocketed coils are also meant to outperform traditional ones in the motion isolation arena, meaning that when you move around, the individual coil takes the heat motion-wise and stops the bed from reenacting a small earthquake. With the interconnectivity of traditional coils, it doesn’t take much for the feeling of movement to travel along the entire surface of the bed.
Fun fact: You do not need a box spring with a hybrid mattress. This is a recurring question I see, and pocketed coils in hybrids eliminate the need for one. Box springs were designed to give more support and elevate performance to traditional coil beds, which would align certain sections of coils to yield more support. Nowadays, you may actually void your warranty if you use a box spring with a hybrid mattress—be sure to check that fine print.
Our favorite hybrid we've tested is the Helix Midnight Luxe, which happens to be our top overall pick in our Best Mattresses guide. It also utilizes pressure-relieving foams and pocketed coils to provide targeted lumbar support.
Another awesome hybrid mattress, the Nolah Evolution, seamlessly puts together some superb memory foam and pocketed coils, both of which counteract tension buildup for pressure points. I love it as an option for side sleepers for this reason, but it also works for back and stomach sleepers. The coils also make it easy to move around on, which is helpful for co-sleepers.
Innerspring
This is as much a history lesson as a type of mattress you want to shop for. “Traditional” innerspring mattresses are the firm-feeling beds you probably have early memories of, given that the makeup is just innerspring coils wrapped in a cover. It’s just as squeaky as you probably remember, too, as the coil type used involves connecting every coil so they work as one unit.
These are Bonnell coils, and they connect both laterally and vertically. When you lie down, and your weight is pressed into the mattress, all those coils act as “one for all and all for one” and simultaneously compress. It’s not going to work wonders for pressure relief like modern hybrids will, but it is highly responsive, which means it’ll pop back into its original shape as you move around. So if you’re a sleeper who moves around between sleeping positions, coils are a good feature to have, so you’re getting near-instantaneous support.
Why aren't traditional coils in the works with mattresses nowadays? According to Merwin, upgraded pocketed coils far outperform traditional ones. “Unlike traditional coils that are wired together and move as a unit, pocketed coils are encased individually, which allows each coil to respond independently to movement and pressure," he said. "This design minimizes motion transfer, so when one person moves or gets out of bed, their partner feels far less disruption. It also provides more targeted support, contouring to the body in a way that improves spinal alignment and overall comfort.” While you can still find innerspring mattresses with traditional coils out there, they're typically getting phased out in favor of hybrids. I've only tested a handful of these over the years.
The Saatva Classic is one of the rare modern beds that rely on traditional coils in the secondary coil layer on the very bottom of the bed. This is to help with overall durability and support, which WIRED tester Nena Farrell has mentioned could be beneficial for those with back pain.
Memory Foam
We actually have NASA to thank for this one. If you Google search images of those early space missions, it’s no wonder that something was needed to keep astronauts from being jostled around inside rockets; hence, memory foam was born. It’s evolved quite a bit from those initial iterations, especially when Tempur-Pedic came onto the scene in the ’80s with a vision for it to become the basis of sleep products. Today, memory foam stands in a league of its own when it comes to the unique, compressive feel.
Memory foam is an umbrella term for all the iterations mattress brands have come up with today, but let's refer to the mattress manufacturing expert for this one.
"Memory foam is produced by combining liquid polyurethane with various chemicals, like polyols and isocyanates, to enhance its viscosity and density," says Merwin. Without whipping out the periodic table of elements and giving you a science lesson in the chemical components of this material, here’s the need-to-know: These compounds form a malleable foam that holds teeny-tiny bubbles within it. How it works is, as you lie on it, your body imparts heat onto the surface, flowing into these air pockets, which in turn allows it to become softer to contour around your body.
“The key ingredient is a polymer that creates an open-cell structure, which allows the material to respond to heat and pressure. This is what gives memory foam its signature contouring or ‘hugging’ feel," Merwin says. "During the manufacturing process, the liquid foam mixture is poured onto a moving line, where it expands and solidifies into large foam blocks, which we call ‘buns.' At a high level, it’s a blend of chemistry and precision that transforms raw materials into a high-quality product.”
To say it's a natural fit for those who need pressure relief from their mattress may be a bit too on-the-nose, but it's the standout feature of this material. It also lessens the feeling of movement for the most restless of sleepers, which also makes it an attractive option for couples. Arguably, the biggest issue that plagues memory foam is heat retention, since once the heat enters these air chambers, it turns into something akin to microscopic saunas that can make the overall mattress into a nightmare for those who sleep warm. This is where the various iterations of foam come into play, as some brands infuse elements like graphite, copper, gel, or more advanced cooling technology like phase-change materials into the foams that they use.
Three layers of foam make up the Bear Original, but its certifications and cooling cover are here to help dispel any rumors that circulate about the downsides of memory foam. You won't find any eyebrow-raising chemicals here thanks to CertiPur-US and GreenGuard Gold certifications. Plus, you can add on a Celliant cover for a cooler feel.
The Nectar Premier is another memory foam option we've tested and liked, especially for side sleepers. Its foam layers are stacked so that you feel more pressure relief on top, but get more than enough support via a firmer foam layer at the bottom.
Latex
The same stuff that goes into tires, balloons, and sports equipment can also be used for mattresses—and it’s the good stuff, too. Latex acts similarly to memory foam when it comes to pressure relief, but is far more reactive to you moving around. Think of a rubber band snapping back into shape when released; it’s pretty dang close to that. Many brands rely on organic rubber sap to create latex as we know it, and there are two categories of latex foam you’ll usually find with mattresses: Dunlop and Talalay. These names refer to the production process and resulting product, as liquid rubber is poured into molds, torched at high temperatures (called “vulcanization” and yes, I have to resist doing Spock’s “live long and prosper” hand signal every time), and flash-frozen to retain the feel. Dunlop is a firmer latex foam, and hence, has a firmer feel. Talalay yields a more plush feel. Latex is generally pretty even-keeled when it comes to temperature, too, keeping heat from accumulating within your mattress to maintain a nice, room-temperature feel.
WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson has applauded the organic latex construction of the Birch Luxe Natural, citing great support for the lower back region and good temperature regulation.
Smart Beds
Smart mattresses offer the ability to adjust their firmness level with the press of a button. They do this via internal air chambers or sensors that adjust coil firmness. To make your bed softer or firmer, you use a remote control or the brand's accompanying app.
That's not the only thing that sets this mattress type apart. Some are also outfitted with tech features such as sleep trackers and massage settings, as in the case of the Bryte Balance Pro. Smart beds are becoming more refined as sleep tech evolves.
Smart beds often employ adjustable bases, which allow the head and foot of the bed to move up and down. This is an important consideration in the purchase—you should budget for the cost of the base, as this type of bed can't inherently achieve this level of flexibility on its own.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is It Better to Get a Boxed Mattress or a Fully Set-Up Mattress?
One of the biggest arguments I see in the mattress world isn't what the best type of mattress material is—it's how the mattress is delivered to you. Some will argue that mattresses compressed into boxes compromise the materials' long-term durability and performance. The thought is that you won't get as much support because of this, which is why some brands insist on bringing a fully inflated, set-up mattress to you via white-glove delivery.
On the other hand, manufacturers that specialize in boxed mattresses will tell you that these materials are resilient and compressing them doesn't damage them. As long as you set the bed up within the prescribed delivery window (usually within 30 days of delivery), the mattress itself inflates and operates just fine.
My take is that one is not better than the other; it simply comes down to the manufacturer. Some brands, like Saatva or certain Tempur-Pedic models, shouldn't be compressed because of how the materials were developed. Hence, they will be delivered ready to go upon arrival. 3Z's brands, including Nolah, Leesa, and Helix, can be compressed because their foam and coil components can withstand this pressure. The beds are compressed, boxed, and promptly shipped out within a few days. Upon arrival, they should be unboxed immediately, but it's not the end of the world if you don't get to it right away. Make sure not to exceed the maximum time range (usually a month), and let the bed inflate for at least 24 hours after unboxing. This will allow the materials time to “breathe” as they inflate, ensuring they reach their full height and support potential.
What Does Off-Gassing Mean?
When a boxed mattress is first opened, there may be a noticeable chemical odor. What you’re smelling are volatile organic compounds (VOCs) coming from the layers of foam, especially memory foam, and from the adhesives used to glue the layers together. You’ll want to look for certifications like CertiPUR-US and GreenGuard Gold to ensure that emission levels are low and that they don’t contain noxious chemicals like formaldehyde. Even then, it’s a good idea to air out the mattress for a day or two in a well-ventilated room before you sleep on it. If a bed contains memory foam and is not CertiPur-US certified, you don’t want it in your home.
How Long Does It Take a Mattress to Expand After Unboxing?
This depends on the mattress’s construction and unboxing instructions. Many mattresses can be used shortly after unboxing, while others can take up to a few hours or days to fully expand.
Do I Need a Box Spring for My Mattress?
Most modern mattresses, including hybrid and memory foam mattresses, are designed to sit on a solid platform bed, slatted bed frame, or adjustable base. A traditional box spring is meant for older innerspring mattresses and has actual springs inside it. Always check your mattress manufacturer’s requirements, because using the wrong foundation can affect the mattress’s performance or warranty.
How Long Does a Mattress Typically Last?
With the right care, a mattress typically lasts around seven to 10 years. Lifespan can depend on its construction, materials, and how much use it gets.
How Do I Know When It’s Time to Replace My Mattress?
If you notice visible sagging, lumps, or permanent indentations in a mattress, it may be time for a new one. Or if you find that you’re waking up with new aches and pains, these could be signs your mattress is wearing down and it’s time to get a replacement.
What’s the Best Type of Mattress for Couples With Different Preferences?
Some mattresses offer split firmness, allowing each side of the bed to have a different feel, while adjustable smart beds allow sleepers to customize their firmness independently. Mattresses with good movement isolation are also great if one partner moves around throughout the night.
What’s a Mattress Topper, and When Should I Use One?
A mattress topper is a thick layer of cushioning you can put on top of a mattress to make it softer or firmer. It's worth considering if your mattress is still in good condition but needs a little adjustment—check out our guide for recommendations.
How Often Should I Flip or Rotate My Mattress?
It depends on your mattress. Many modern mattresses actually shouldn’t be flipped because they’re designed with specific layers that need to stay in a particular order. Rotating a mattress 180 degrees from head to foot can help distribute wear, but not every mattress needs it. Check the manufacturer’s instructions for a suggested rotation and flipping schedule.
Do All Mattresses Work With an Adjustable Bed Frame?
No. A mattress needs to be flexible enough to bend safely with an adjustable base, and not every model is designed for that. Check the manufacturer’s guidelines before using a mattress on an adjustable base.
So, Now What?
Congratulations, if you made it to this part of this article, you’ve passed your mattress-type crash course. Hopefully it’s a bit less overwhelming to kick off your mattress research when you better understand what each product actually is. And to further your mattress education, we are actively testing beds to put into our mattress guides. These picks are not only what material works in what instance, but specific models we’ve tested that best exemplify what the material has to offer.
There is always the option to try these mattress types in person to better discern what the bounciness of latex feels like, or the pressure relief of memory foam. But if you aren't all for a field trip to the mattress store, online brands offer sleep trials so that you can comfortably try out their products without leaving your house. Now comes the next part of our course: becoming a mattress tester yourself!

Logitech MX Keypad Design and Appearance: Compact and Well Built
The Logitech MX Keypad has a two-piece design. One is the keypad itself, and the other is a detachable stand; you can prop it up using the stand, or you can place the keypad itself directly on the surface, where its slightly slanted design makes it easy to access. It also comes with a slanted surface that makes it easy to interact with. It also comes in two colors; I received the Graphite color. There is also a Pale Grey variant that looks best if you have a premium desktop setup.
The base has a rubber finish so it won’t slip off smooth tables and stays firmly in one place, and the keypad itself is slim and lightweight and connects to Mac or Windows via a USB-C cable. The same cable powers the device, so you don’t need a separate power source, though I wish it had wireless connectivity and a built-in battery. But since it uses only one USB cable, you can tuck it to the back and keep the setup clean. Both are solidly built.
The Keypad comes with nine customizable keys with their own individual LCD displays, along with two left and right navigation controls in the button array, aligned to the left, and with a Logi logo to the right. On the back, the USB-C cable connects to the device and is also removable. The buttons have a glossy, smooth finish; they aren’t tactile, but I like the soft, jelly-like click when pressed.
The LCD button displays are sharp; the icons and the action text are sharp and easy to read, even in brightly lit desktop setups. They are also full-color displays, so you can choose different themes based on your needs and preferences. And at just 91.7 × 77.9 × 25.5 mm, it also doesn’t take up much space on your desk.
Logitech MX Keypad Specs and Features: Nine Keys That Do a Lot More
The Logitech MX Keypad has nine physical LCD buttons, where each button can be assigned a different action or shortcut. But you are not limited to just nine shortcuts. You can set up 15 individual pages for each app, which allows you to set up 135 shortcuts for each app and switch between them using the switch arrows below.
For most users, this setup should be enough to perform frequently used shortcuts and actions, and the Logi Options+ app also lets you create and assign multiple shortcuts for each app, so you have set up multiple shortcuts and switch between them daily.
In my testing, I didn’t notice any latency between pressing the button and seeing the action happen on your Mac. Since it’s designed for developers, it also shows live actions, including the running status of your AI model.
For instance, when using Claude, the Keypad shows the live running status of the AI model. You can also stop the task directly from the keyboard with a single press; you can also create a new chat; approve Claude to perform actions with a single click, which is the most common in AI agents where you need to manually click Allow every time the model needs your permission to perform a task if you set it to manual approval.
If you don’t want to use these controls, you can customize the buttons and assign completely different tasks that suit your workflow. In addition, the Logi Options+ app supports various system shortcuts, including clipboard shortcuts such as pasting copied text, clearing the clipboard, formatting text, and other useful actions like making text title case, and more. You can also control volume, use automation to run multiple actions with a single click, and more. Even without AI tools, you can set up automations for everyday tasks.
Logitech MX Keypad Everyday Use: The Little Things Make It Work
Devices like the Logitech MX Keypad should make your work easier rather than adding extra burden. If the team behind this hasn’t thought about these tiny interactions, using the device becomes a burden for the user.
First, it automatically switches profiles based on which app you are using. Even if you set multiple custom profiles, the app instantly switches to the app you are using without having to manually switch between different sets of shortcuts.
In my testing, it works, and the keypad instantly switches to the shortcuts I set for each app, even for the app I custom-built. It also works with other apps and software, including the latest AI applications like VS Code, Claude Code, your browser like Chrome, or the usual shortcuts you can use on the Mac’s home screen.
Another thing that I initially thought would be extra work is manually turning off the device if I shut down my Mac. Thankfully, Logitech has thought of that too: the Keypad automatically powers off when you shut down your computer and turns back on automatically when you start. Although they may seem like tiny details, these thoughtful interactions make the Logitech MX Keypad easy to use instead of adding to your workload.
Logitech MX Keypad Interface and App: Reliable and Easy to Customize
The app also offers plenty of customization options, which I cover in detail in this section, but one handy feature is the ability to adjust key brightness, which can come in handy if you are working in dark environments.
Although many people say Logitech device companion apps are buggy and unreliable, that hasn’t been my experience with the Logi Options+ app I installed on my Mac. The app worked for me without any issues throughout my testing and was surprisingly reliable.
It also has one of the cleanest UI experiences for an accessories provider. The app lets you completely customize your Logitech MX Keypad. By default, you have a general profile that appears when you turn on your Mac and are on the home screen. You can also create multiple general profiles and switch between them too.
You can also create and customize profiles for each individual app. Logitech already offers popular shortcuts for some popular and most-used apps like Google Chrome, Slack, and more. So you don’t need to set everything from scratch. If you cannot find the action you are looking for, you can create your own shortcut and add it to an app profile.
There is also a dedicated Logitech Marketplace that lets you access various shortcuts created for apps by the community. AI apps like Claude and ChatGPT aren’t available by default, but they are available in the Logi Marketplace. Even if an app isn’t available in the marketplace, you can build your own plugins and custom profiles using the Logi Actions SDK. Logitech also partnered with GitHub to offer 3 months of a GitHub Copilot Pro+ subscription for free and include all shortcuts for the VS Code app.
And since you have everything under your control, you can create custom profiles for the personal applications you have created on your device.
This level of flexibility makes the device stand out, even for power users who want to perform everyday tasks with just a button instead of constantly switching between apps, navigating menus, and repeating the same steps.
Logitech MX Keypad Compatibility: Mac and Windows Only, with Some Setup Required
And for those wondering whether it works with Android, iPhone, or even iPads, no, it doesn’t. To use it, you need the Logi Options+ app installed on the device, which is currently limited to Windows and Mac. You also need to download an additional file, such as a .crx extension, to work in Chrome and go through multiple steps to set it up for the first time. Once setup is done, it works flawlessly. But if you are a developer, you can also technically build a workaround to control an Android app or other devices.
Logitech MX Keypad Review Verdict: Worth It if It Fits Your Workflow
Overall, the Logitech MX Keypad is a well-crafted device that makes a lot of sense for people who spend much of their day with AI tools, whether they are developers, students, or creative professionals.
It is not just about triggering shortcuts with a single press but also about tiny details that make it easy to use. Also, at $99.99, it can be a neat and useful addition to your desktop that is genuinely useful. Remember that it will take a bit of time to get used to its input style, and sometimes you will even forget it’s there if you don’t make it part of your workflow. At $99.99 (INR 15,999), it’s a worthwhile addition to your desktop.

President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday that he is considering shifting the White House press corps to a new area.
Trump rejected a report claiming he intended to tear down the current press briefing room to bring back a historic swimming pool, stating he had never "even thought to do such a stupid thing,” Trump said on social media.
Still, he noted that moving reporters out of their existing White House space remains a possibility.
"I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location," Trump wrote in his post.
The New York Times reported Tuesday that Trump had suggested to then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August that news briefings be moved outside the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, though the plan was not enacted.
That report claimed the president expressed a preference for the indoor therapy pool originally built during Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency. The Nixon administration later replaced that pool with the current press room.
Trump has consistently criticized U.S. media outlets, accusing them of biased coverage regarding his administration.
During a Tuesday press gaggle, Trump repeatedly snapped at Andrew Feinberg, The Independent’s White House correspondent, ordering him to pipe down, warning him to “be careful” and labeling him a “sick person.”
“Wait, wait, wait, wait. Quiet, quiet!” Trump said while seated behind the Resolute Desk. “What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”
Last month, he temporarily prohibited journalists representing CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from entering White House grounds, warning other organizations could face similar measures.
Advocates for free expression argued the decision violated First Amendment rights.
Their credentials were restored following a federal judge's ruling that the ban was likely unconstitutional, though the Trump administration remains in court fighting the case.

Most parents worry about exposing their kids to too much screen time, but it can be tough to find alternatives that children find entertaining and that might be beneficial. Enter Qubitunes, a screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. Content comes in wooden cartridges that you slot in the top, and kids can place wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays.
This seemingly simple design allows for interactive stories that change based on the characters and spots your kids choose, music that can be layered up with different instruments, and themed games and quizzes. I’m a huge fan of Qubitunes, and it has a deserving place in my guides to the best STEM toys and speakers for kids. As Black Friday and gifting season approaches, the Qubitunes starter kit is one toy to keep an eye on for discounts.
I played with Qubitunes for hours when it arrived and really enjoyed it. The stereo speakers are decent, there's a headphone port, and it can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. It has since gone into my wife’s classroom, and it’s usually the first thing picked when kids have finished their work and it’s choosing time. It’s very popular with 7- and 8-year-olds, but kids aged 3 years and up (all the way up to adults) will potentially get a kick out of this.
There is a caveat: the need to purchase content separately. These add-ons cost between $10 and $20 each. Stories, games, and other options come in wooden blocks that slot into the device so you can download the content. You need a Wi-Fi connection for the initial content download and firmware updates, but then you can play offline. They usually come with three or four character blocks and a labelled bag to keep them in.
My top pick is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. There are also stories about quirky characters, such as The Groblies ($20), a fun cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients, and various themed soundscapes and quizzes. I prefer activities where there’s some creativity or a learning game involved, but the stories and soundscapes are good for very young kids. The interactive nature of these sets elevates the experience beyond passive listening and provides replay value, as kids experiment to discover what happens when they move and replace pieces on the stage.
Qubs has also recently released a Maestro expansion ($10) with four new composers, a Jurassic Sounds Dinosaur Game ($20) with facts and T-Rex roars, and versions of Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel & Gretel, among many others. If you like the idea of sustainable, screen-free toys, the maker Qubs also made a clever wooden car STEM toy called Cody Block ($70) that introduces kids to basic coding concepts, and it’s on sale right now, down from $100.

When is Premier League 'sacking season' - and who should be worried?
- Published
Premier League managers beware.
It's the last thing Manchester United boss Michael Carrick will want to read - as pressure piles on his future after Wednesday's Champions League humiliation in Como - but sacking season is just around the corner.
He won't be the only one looking anxiously over his shoulder, though.
Last season those Premier League managers - or head coaches, as a majority of top-flight bosses are now officially titled - who vacated their roles had been in charge for an average of 310 days.
Is 10 months long enough for a coach to implement their vision, sign the players they want and connect with the fanbase?
During the course of 2025-26, 11 bosses parted company with their clubs, with only Enzo Maresca's resignation at Chelsea happening of his own accord.
So far in this campaign, all 20 remain in situ. But when is the Premier League's 'sacking season'? And who is at risk even at this early stage of proceedings?
When do managers get sacked?
It doesn't make for good reading for those struggling managers.
The most popular months for in-season managerial departures are November and December, with almost a third of all manager exits happening in these two months alone.
Over the course of the competition's 34 completed seasons, there is a clear pattern of club boards opting for change around the autumn international breaks, and before Christmas and, crucially, the winter transfer window, which was introduced in England in 2003.
Perhaps most ruthlessly of all, Charlton Athletic's Les Reed was dismissed on Christmas Eve in 2006, having won only one of his seven league games in charge, amassing four points.
Reed's 40-day tenure was the shortest in Premier League history for almost two decades, until Sam Allardyce took that record in 2022-23 with a 30-day spell at Leeds United that ended in relegation. Ange Postecoglou lasted 39 days with Nottingham Forest last year.
Among the high-profile managers to be shown the door in November are Chelsea's Roberto di Matteo in 2012, Mauricio Pochettino at Spurs in 2019 and Manchester United playing legend Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2021.
Di Matteo had spectacularly guided the Blues to FA Cup and Champions League success as caretaker boss six months earlier, but paid the price for a poor start in the defence of their European title.
December has accounted for Jose Mourinho twice. In 2015 he departed reigning league champions Chelsea by mutual consent and in 2018 he was sacked by Manchester United.
How long do managers get now?
Last season's average tenure of 310 days for departing managers was the second lowest on record in Premier League history. Only 1994-95 was lower, with an average of 154.
Over the decades the patience of club owners has ebbed and flowed, with a notable dearth of sackings in 1995-96 and a more recent peak in longevity in 2021-22 that can largely be attributed to the pandemic.
Since then, however, that patience seems to be wearing thin, with the average length of managerial reigns steadily plummeting.
Postecoglou's brief stint at Forest last autumn was followed by a similarly short spell at Spurs for Igor Tudor, who picked up one point from five league games before being shown the door after 44 days.
A record nine clubs entered this season with new permanent managers. Five of them are currently in the bottom half of the Premier League.
With the grave financial consequences of relegation – and social media noise seemingly inescapable – clubs are showing no mercy when it comes to making big decisions.
Who should be worried?
While no top-flight manager has been dismissed this season, there are several who will be looking over their shoulder before November's international break.
The scrutiny on Carrick has only intensified after the chastening 4-1 defeat by Como at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia.
Following Lisandro Martinez's critique of the club's hierarchy last week, club captain Bruno Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick's tactics in Como, suggesting all is not well in the Old Trafford dressing room.
Asked about Carrick's future after the coach cut an isolated figure as he applauded the away fans alone at full-time, Match of the Day pundit Nedum Onuoha said: "Bruno Fernandes thinks the tactics were essentially wrong in this game, while Michael Carrick thinks the players weren't running enough for the tactics to work out.
"When you find those sorts of splits it can be very hard within a dressing room to maintain that sort of energy behind the manager.
"So I think for Carrick himself to go and see those fans... he knows how bad this game was in particular."
Tudor's successor at Spurs, Roberto de Zerbi, has eased any pressure on him after successive wins moved them to 12th in the Premier League, while Fulham's Alvaro Arbeloa has also moved the heat away from his future for now with back-to-back 1-0 wins.
But new Forest boss Oliver Glasner, and Sunderland's Regis le Bris - whose side are juggling Europa League football - will be feeling a little bit anxious at the moment.
Marco Rose, another newcomer to English football, hasn't had the most convincing domestic start with Bournemouth, who face Carrick's United at Old Trafford on Sunday. But surely the midweek win against AC Milan, which extended their perfect Europa League start, is enough to keep the pressure off him for now?
Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage apologised to fans after the 5-0 battering by Brighton on Sunday and faces a fight to keep his job only four months after joining from Lens. His side entertain Newcastle on Sunday, another side who's new boss, Matthias Jaissle, could do with a positive result quickly.
It may feel early to talk about managers feel the pressure, but history tells us that it might not be long before someone is on their way out.

A team from Haryana’s BPS Government Medical College (BPSGMC) for Women in Khanpur Kalan has won the IMU-Ron Harden Innovation in Medical Education (IMU-RHIME) Award 2026, the first time the award has been won by an Indian college. The award was for BPS Government Medical College for Women’s student leadership programme ‘Network of Student Leaders’ (NEST).
The award was presented at the 19th International Medical Education Conference, held at IMU University in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and was received by Dr. Sumita Sethi, Professor of Ophthalmology at BPSGMC. Dr. Sethi presented the winning work on behalf of the college team, which also includes Dr. Renu Garg and Dr. Ruchi Agarwal.
The award is aimed at encouraging innovations in medical education and recognising innovations by academics, “which otherwise might go unnoticed,” the official document on the award says.
“Humbled and delighted to share that our initiative on student leadership, NEST (Network of Student Leaders) received the IMU-Ron Harden Innovation in Medical Education (IMU-RHIME) Award 2026 at the 19th International Medical Education Conference at IMU University, Kuala Lumpur,” Dr. Sethi posted on social media.
“This is the first time since the award was instituted in 2008 that the rolling trophy has come to India,” she added.
The award, instituted in 2008, has previously been won by medical colleges in Hong Kong, Malaysia, the U.K., the U.S. and Pakistan.
Under the NEST programme, 278 medical students from 11 colleges across India received leadership training and went on to lead 63 projects addressing community health issues, including menstrual hygiene, cervical cancer awareness, child marriage and drug abuse.
“None of this would have been possible without the core faculty of NEST, Dr. Renu Garg and Ruchi Agarwal,” Dr. Sethi added.
The Director congratulated the team on its achievement, describing it as a matter of pride not only for Haryana but also for the Indian medical fraternity.

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

Parents of spinal muscular atrophy(SMA)-afflicted children coming to the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital had been counselled several times about the government introducing the generic version of Risdiplam, instead of the Evrysdi brand by Roche, said V.H. Shankar, Head of the Department of Medical Genetics, who is also in charge of the treatment of children with rare diseases at the hospital, here on Friday.
Dr. Shankar, who attended a press conference along with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, said several meetings had been held with the parents of SMA-afflicted children, during which time all their queries on the efficacy of the generic drug were clarified.
He was answering queries on whether the parents had been told about the introduction of the generic drug for SMA and whether their concerns had been assuaged adequately by the authorities.
Dr. Shanker said he himself had spoken at several of the meetings with the parents. He added that the new generic drug Natsmart was given to six children and the parents were clearly told that the drug being dispensed was not the same brand (Evrysdi) that used to be dispensed earlier.
He said the technical committee had evaluated the decision to shift from Evrysdi to Natsmart several times. The purchase procedure was initiated in February 2026 itself.
Chairperson of the technical committee and Director of Medical Education K.V. Viswanath said the medicine bottles bore the sticker “Physicians’ sample/ for clinical trials”, which is just an indication that the bottles were not for open sale.
The SAT Superintendent had earlier clarified that they were awaiting the government supply of Natsmart, when on Monday, patients had arrived at the SMA clinic seeking the medicine. He had also clarified that rather than asking them to come another day, the hospital had contacted Natco and secured some samples from them to be given to the SMA patients.
The government supply arrived on Tuesday evening itself, but by which time, the campaign that clinical trial medicines were being given to SMA patients was already raging.
Former Health Minister, Veena George, had demanded on Thursday at a press conference that the government should explain how “drugs meant for clinical trials” had been supplied through the hospital. She also alleged that after the controversy broke, the parents had been “threatened” into returning the medicine bottles by the SAT Hospital authorities.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the authorities took back the medicines and replaced it with the lot from the government supply to put the controversy and concerns at rest. He said the doctors at SAT Hospital had spoken to the parents and explained everything and the so-called “concerns” were the creation of some news channels. He said it was also possible that the controversy was deliberately raked up by some along with pharma majors.
He said the government intended to purchase only the generic version of Risdiplam so that the treatment can be provided to more patients.
Meanwhile, many public health experts have expressed concern over the manner in which the issue is being politicised by the Opposition, which has continued to perpetuate the concerns and misgivings of parents of SMA patients by raising the allegation that “clinical trial drugs” were distributed to children.

Nigeria and Kenya Ebola patients may have crossed paths at Uganda airport, officials say
- Published
Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.
Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October, and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.
Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.
Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.
The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry confirmed to Reuters news agency. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.
The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.
She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.
Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.

The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death in the current outbreak.
Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.
"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.
The WHO said it was too early to determine where the Nigerian woman became infected.
"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.
He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.
Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.
"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.
Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.
However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.
Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.
Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.
"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.
"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.
Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.
In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.
Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.
He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.
The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.
Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.
The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.
Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.
The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.
Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

Arsenal draw level with Manchester City at the top of the table, only behind on goal difference, with a scrappy 2-0 win over Everton at the Emirates on Saturday.

Mikel Arteta was forced to make changes to his starting lineup, having played a tough match in the midweek against Bayern Munich and an injury pileup with Bukayo Saka and Christos Tzolis both out of contention.

LUDHIANA: A 28-year-old woman in Ludhiana has alleged that her husband assaulted her over his demand for a vehicle.
The woman, identified as Twinkle, submitted the CCTV footage to the Jagatpuri police post, alleging that her husband first demanded a Thar SUV and later a motorcycle.
According to her complaint, her husband questioned why she could not buy him a vehicle when she "earned more than him" through her salon at Samrala Chowk.
The dispute escalated when Twinkle fled to a neighbour’s house for help, she alleged. Her husband followed her and assaulted her on the road, according to the complaint. Neighbours intervened after hearing her screams.
Twinkle said an earlier dispute over the vehicle demand had been settled through a mediator, but the issue resurfaced when her husband allegedly demanded a motorcycle.
The couple married in November 2025. Twinkle has a seven-year-old son from her previous marriage, according to the complaint.
Inspector Jasvir Singh, station house officer of Haibowal police station, said police were awaiting Twinkle’s medico-legal report (MLR). 
A case would be registered in connection with the complaint, he said.

The story so far
An initiative launched by Keralam government to make the treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) accessible to more patients is now courting controversy.
SMA is a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function. While a complete cure remains elusive, the launch of Risdiplam, marketed as Evrysdi by Roche Pharmaceuticals, the first at-home, oral treatment for SMA, gave hope to thousands of SMA patients. Risdiplam was found to have a significant effect on the progression of the disease, by slowing down motor degeneration, improving physical milestones and stabilising respiratory function.
Risdiplam was launched in India in July 2021, making it the first and only approved drug in the country to manage SMA. But the drug’s astronomical cost made it inaccessible to most families.
Keralam, which has been giving Risdiplam free of cost to eligible children since 2022, made a switch to the less expensive generic version of the drug in October this year . But since then, a section of parents of children living with SMA children have urged the government to switch back to the expensive, branded version.
Last week, when the generic drug was dispensed for the first time at SAT hospital, a Centre of Excellence for Rare Diseases in Thiruvananthapuram, a sticker on the bottle which said “Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials” reopened the branded versus generic debate and a new allegation, that drugs meant for clinical trials were being used on children
How Keralam began SMA treatment
Keralam was the first State to give Risdiplam free of cost through government hospitals in 2022 and an SMA clinic was subsequently opened at SAT hospital. Though initially Risdiplam was given free only to children under 12, in 2026 the government announced an extension of coverage to genetically confirmed SMA Type 2 patients up to age 25, with ₹30 crore allocated in the State budget for this. However, as of now, 109 Type 1 and 2 children with SMA below the age of 12 are being given Risdiplam, free.
Risdiplam, under its trade name Evrysdi, used to cost ₹6.3 lakh for a bottle (current price ₹4.44 lakhs), which the State was getting at a negotiated price of ₹5.4 lakh per bottle. Under the patient assistance programme, Roche used to give 11 bottles free of cost to the State for every four bottles it purchased. The State’s annual requirement was estimated at around 2,500 bottles and the annual financial commitment was around ₹23 crore. The State, therefore, was up against enormous cumulative expenditure as more children became eligible and existing patients required continued treatment.
The decision to switch to generic
A technical experts committee in Keralam met several times to evaluate if the generic alternative, Natsmart, which has all regulatory approvals, and which was ready for commercial distribution in October 2025, could replace Roche’s Evrysdi. Natco Pharma, through a historic Delhi High Court verdict, had won the right to marker the generic alternative of Risdiplam at a dramatically reduced price of ₹15,900 per bottle, against Roche’s Rs. 6.3 lakhs per bottle.
A bottle of Evrysdi on which Roche holds a patent, typically lasts 12 days, meaning the annual maintenance cost for a patient would amount to a crushing ₹60-70 lakh. With Natsmart, the generic alternative, the cost would be under ₹5 lakh. In February 2026, the Keralam government gave the go ahead for Natsmart, and purchase processes were initiated.
What are parents’ concerns?
Parents and advocacy groups including the Cure SMA Foundation of India claim that the branded medication, Evrysdi, has a proven, long-term track record of safety and efficacy, while the new generic version lacks dedicated human bioequivalence or long-term clinical studies specific to paediatric patients. They claim that a sudden switch to an unverified or less effective generic formula could reverse the critical motor and survival progress already achieved by children who are currently stable on the original drug. They have been continuously petitioning the government asking that their children be allowed to continue on Evrysdi.
What do doctors say?
Public health experts have hailed the government’s decision to switch to the generic drug. They say that arguments challenging the efficacy of the generic formulation and alleging a lack of ‘bioavailability’ are entirely unscientific and baseless.
Bioavailability denotes the rate and extent to which an administered pharmaceutical substance enters systemic circulation through the digestive tract. A bioequivalence study normally compares the rate and extent of absorption of the generic with the reference product. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises this as an important way to establish interchangeability. However, bioequivalence studies are not required for every generic medicine. The WHO’s guidance on generic medicines explicitly recognises circumstances in which equivalence studies can be waived. One such circumstance is when the generic and reference products are pharmaceutically equivalent oral solutions containing the same active ingredient at the same molar concentration, subject to the applicable requirements for excipients.
In this case, both products contain Risdiplam. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Natsmart and the regulator’s position is that a bioequivalence study is not required for this particular oral solution. Public health experts also say that the absence of a conventional bioequivalence study does not necessarily mean the regulator approved the drug without adequate evidence. A regulator may accept a scientifically-justified waiver.
Doctors also point out that Natsmart is being prescribed by many premier teaching hospitals in the country and several patients are already using it in Keralam too, for the last five months, without any complaints.
Public health is about maximising access to people, and unless credible scientific evidence demonstrates that the approved generic is less safe or less effective than the original molecule, regulatory approval should remain the primary basis for procurement decisions in publicly-funded health programmes, experts have argued.
The current controversy
The current controversy centres around an alarm raised by parents of children with SMA, after they pointed out that the bottle of Natsmart dispensed to them was labelled, ‘Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials’. Though the authorities clarified later that these were drug sample bottles they were forced to source directly from Natco and not part of the government supply (which was delayed), the issue has become something for Opposition parties, particularly the CPI(M), to latch on to. It has also served to perpetuate fears and misgivings about the generic drug among SMA families.
What is happening at present?
SAT Hospital authorities, who are responsible for the SMA clinic, have now decided to hold a meeting of families to assuage their concerns. They say that several meetings had been held earlier too, to reassure parents about the switch from Evrysdi to Natsmart. However, the new controversy over ‘clinical trial’ drugs may have undone some of the previous work. The labelling issue is clearly separate from the concerns about the switch to generic medicine and the families’ demand for scientific evidence and transparent communication is valid, authorities admit.

Ukraine’s Starlink speeds restored after week of frontline disruption
Questions persist about who ordered the interruptions to the satellite internet system that Kyiv’s forces rely on to counter Russian attacks
Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.
“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said on social media, adding that restoration began overnight and was sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.

Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc reasons why Ferrari went from US GP pole favourites to behind Kimi Antonelli, Red Bulls on grid
Ferrari had topped all three practice sessions but went on to qualify fourth and fifth; Both drivers hope race distance offers chance to move forward; watch the United States GP live on Sky Sports F1 and Sky Sports Main Event at 8pm on Sunday, with build up from 6.30pm
Sunday 25 October 2026 01:55, UK
Ferrari's wait for a first Grand Prix pole position since August 2025 continued in the United States on Saturday as Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton qualified outside the top three in a session they had been widely tipped as favourites for.
For the first time this season, Ferrari went into qualifying having Ferrari topped all three practice sessions in Austin, on a weekend their car features the team's final significant upgrade of the season.
Leclerc finished second fastest to McLaren's Lando Norris in Q1, but only after the McLaren driver took a second run to do so, and then was then back at the head of the field in Q2.
But the Scuderia found themselves on the back foot immediately from the start of Q3 with Leclerc holding a provisional fourth and Hamilton sixth after the first runs of the decisive final phase.
Hamilton improved one place to fifth on his final run, but Leclerc stayed where he was, to leave the Ferraris behind the two Red Bull drivers and Mercedes polesitter Kimi Antonelli for the start of Sunday's 56-lap race.
Team principal Frederic Vasseur told Sky Sports F1: "Bit of mixed feelings for sure. The potential was there over the weekend. We had good pace in free practice.
"Until the last corner we are fighting for pole but it is like it is."
So where did Ferrari's pace go?
On team radio after ending up fifth, 0.276s away from pole, a bemused Hamilton said: "These guys must be turning up for that last Q3 because where did that time go?"
Speaking to Sky Sports F1 afterwards, Hamilton said that his car's handling had felt consistent through all three sessions, instead suspecting that the team's straight-line speed deficit had again played a central role.
"We did a really good job overnight. The car felt really good in FP3 - competitive," said Hamilton, who had topped that final practice session.
"Q1 and Q2 both felt pretty strong. It felt like we were right there in the fight and the car was just as good as.. we didn't make any changes, the car didn't flip upside down in Q3. It was a really good lap.
"Those guys just somehow took another step. I don't know what it is. Ultimately we do lose, I think we are a few tenths off on the straight as we usually are, but a great lap by Kimi and the power deficit to the Red Bull and Mercedes is still significant.
"Our car is clearly as good as theirs through the corners but we lose that down the straights."
Leclerc, though, offered a different suggestion, believing that the increase in cloud cover, and therefore a small drop in temperatures, for the start of Q3 had made a pivotal difference to their competitiveness.
Asked if it was again a case of rivals finding something extra to them at the end of qualifying, Leclerc replied: "This time I think it's slightly different in that I don't think the others have changed anything from Q2 to Q3. Where we have lost is on ourselves and that is mostly the tyres.
"The out lap was extremely difficult. There was a bit more cloud in Q3. We lost one or two degrees of track temp and, for us, it was night and day different and already from the out lap I felt I was having lots of difficulties.
"It's a shame that it happened in Q3 because I strongly believe that we had the pace to be fighting in front but unfortunately not today again."
Why Ferrari are not out out of victory hunt yet
All is not yet lost, however, for Ferrari in terms of fighting at the front on a track where overtaking is possible and tyre degradation is predicted to be high.
Leclerc felt they could even still repeat his Austin victory from the same starting berth two years ago.
"Yeah [Ferrari can still win the race]. The last time I think I started from fourth here I won so I hope we can do the same," he said.
"Just a good start and then where you position your car and trying to anticipate what is going to happen [is key] because there are many different scenarios that can happen in such a turn one with very wide entry.
"Then if you are doing the right choices you can get a lot more than any other track, so I'm looking forward to that."
Hamilton was staying cautious, but hoped Ferrari would have the pace over the longer distance.
"Starting position isn't everything. You have to have really good pace to overtake," he added.
"It's a long race. There was more degradation than anticipated on Friday on the long runs. Our car will hopefully be decent and we will do the best job we can to apply pressure.
"To beat the Red Bulls and Mercedes will be challenging, for sure, but we will give it absolutely everything."

Ravi Singh, Railways’ hard-hitting willow-wielder, is quite new to the rigours of First-Class cricket.
The 25-year-old — who has a penchant for striking big in the shorter formats — hasn’t taken long to adjust to the longest discipline, averaging a creditable 58.2 after seven Ranji Trophy innings.
Ravi, who works as a ticket collector in Howrah, had to bide his time before finding his place in the Railways team.
He shifted from Varanasi to Lucknow to hone his skills under coach Saurabh Dubey, though he couldn’t quite break into the senior Uttar Pradesh set-up.
But once he landed a Railways job, Ravi’s career finally stoked some steam.
“After playing well for the under-23 side, I was called to the National Cricket Academy [now Centre of Excellence]. My Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy and Vijay Hazare Trophy tournaments went quite well. Some of those matches were broadcast, and the selectors at a higher level watch them. I was called for IPL trials, and, after seven or eight years of not playing anything [significant], things suddenly started falling my way,” Ravi said at the MAC Stadium on Saturday, two days ahead of the Ranji game against Tamil Nadu.
Ravi was picked up by Rajasthan Royals for 95 lakh in the IPL 2026 auction. Whether it be being mentally prepared to face the wrath of Jofra Archer in the nets or learning the skill sets required to succeed at the highest level, Ravi never backed down.

Flat-track bullies Celtic continue descent into European irrelevance
- Published
When Mika Baur scored early in the second half against Celta Vigo, so much in Celtic's garden was rosy.
The team had an intensity now that they didn't have before. They had momentum. Belief. They had a Liam Scales header hopping off the top of the crossbar. The La Liga visitors were under the pump.
It was easy to conclude in those naively optimistic moments that Celta Vigo were all passing and no penetration. They passed it to death and got pretty much nowhere.
More than 350 passes in the opening half and one attempt on target. All very pretty. All very technical. All very tippy-tappy.
The question that Celtic fans will be asking now, some with pitchforks in hand, is what the hell happened in the last half-an-hour of this game. Particularly, what happened from minutes 68 to 71.
From three points to no points. From building on the hiding dished out to Hearts to another loss and getting shunted back to bitterness and rancour.
Celtic stopped playing and stopped believing. They were hit with a bit of adversity and they were bowled over by it. Knocked to the ground, never to rise up again.
They'll complain - as they already have - about a foul on Camilo Duran that wasn't picked up just before the equaliser, but there is no talking to the errors they made thereafter.
The inability to deal with a free-kick, the failure to pick up the goalscorer in the first instance and then multiple calamities in the concession of the second goal. How many chances does one side need to get a ball away to safety?
Long before the end, Celtic were gone. Psychologically spent. This is nothing new. Something new would have been the sight of them kicking on at 1-0, but in Europe such strength is a dying art form in this team.
A third straight loss in Europe, 35th out of 36 teams in the Europa League table, only a side from Armenia keeping them off rock bottom. This is their place in the grand scheme now.
Domestic football proves lousy barometer
Chris Sutton calls them flat-track bullies. How many Celtic fans would disagree with that depiction? Not many.
Thursday was yet another example of domestic football being a lousy barometer of Celtic's capacity to win - or even draw - games in Europe.
In the wake of the 7-1 trouncing of Hearts, some Celtic folk with desperately short memories rounded on a few commentators who were critical of Martin O'Neill, his players and this Celtic board following their losses to Rangers and their failures against LASK, Ferencvaros and Benfica.
As if beating up Hearts made it all better. The message, after the goal deluge, was 'what are you saying to it now?' The answer: Exactly as we were saying before.
O'Neill said on Thursday that there are still loads of points to play for - and there are. But it was a claim made from a position of serious weakness. Desperation, almost.
Even at their best in recent decades, Celtic have struggled awfully to win European games on the road. Right now, that looks way beyond them. Winning at home is too much for them these days, too.
So, yes, there are enough points on offer for Celtic to fight their way out of their Europa League dungeon and into the play-off, but in their current state it's more a philosophical thought than an attainable reality.
If you have lost three out of three, have scored three goals and have conceded nine, then banging on about points you might win down the line is an exercise in wishful thinking.
In the here and now, Celtic's standards are plummeting. That's on everybody.
It's on O'Neill and his players, though it's easy to have some sympathy for the manager when he not only has to field questions about the stuff he's responsible for but also come up with answers about stuff that he has no responsibility for - the ongoing circus that is Celtic's relationship with large elements of their own support.
And the blame is also, in greater part, on a board who are happy to have O'Neill and - when he's not around - Shaun Maloney, talking about the disconnect between fans and club, as was the case on Wednesday.
No chief executive, no chairman, no major shareholder and no major shareholder's son are anywhere to be seen when those issues are raised at news conferences. Just a manager or an assistant who, let's face it, have a few other things on their mind.
Do Celtic have vision to make it better?
Just after the television coverage ended on Thursday there was a programme of highlights of big Celtic Park Champions League nights. Remember them?
Celtic beating the Manchester United of Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs, Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney; Celtic beating the AC Milan of Alessandro Nesta, Andrea Pirlo, Clarence Seedorf and Kaka; Celtic beating the Barcelona of Jordi Alba, Xavi, Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
A stadium literally shaking to its very foundations. Packed solid. Deafening. Unforgettable.
Look at it now. Empty seats and people leaving early. A game against the eighth best team in Spain, in a second-tier European competition - defeat and apathy. How they have fallen.
Of course, it might seem a little tiresome looking back at how things were 20 years ago, so let's not. Let's look at how things were in February last year.
Bayern Munich versus Celtic. Ninety-three minutes gone in the second leg in Germany and it's 2-2 on aggregate.
Bayern have started with a front four of Michael Olise, Jamal Musiala, Serge Gnabry and Harry Kane. Thomas Muller has replaced Musiala, Leroy Sane has come on for Gnabry, Kingsley Coman for Kane.
It took Bayern until the fourth minute of added time to see Celtic off. From there to here is some descent into European mediocrity and irrelevance.
O'Neill said that he "can't ask anything more" from his players. He can - and he must.
More must be asked of O'Neill and more - much, much more - must be asked of the board. Bringing in new players and a new manager is easily done, if they so wish. Whether it's the right players and the right manager is a different story, but it can be done in a heartbeat.
Changing a board, and a way of thinking, is a whole lot harder. There's little doubt all of these people want success for Celtic. They might get more of it domestically. They might win another league, another cup, maybe two. That is all highly possible, if not probable.
This question has been asked so many times now - and it's grim that it still has to be asked. What do Celtic stand for? Flat-track bullydom or something more, something more adventurous, something in keeping with the 'great European story' they so often talk about.
Because of the Lisbon Lions it is and always will be the greatest of all Scottish football stories. Nothing is ever likely to surpass it.
But there are other stories, in the present day, that are tiresome for Celtic folk, stories that are playing out now, almost on a loop. From Champions League to Europa League. What's next? Conference League. And after that?
Everyone in power at the club cannot look at that 36-team table and not feel an enormous sense of embarrassment. If they don't, they're really not in the right job.
The question is - do they have any kind of vision to make it better? Many observers of the club might see that as a rhetorical question.
