When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

What is the cheapest new gaming console you can buy in 2026?
The lowest upfront price doesn't necessarily mean the most affordable when you factor in the cost of games.
Gaming has become an even more expensive hobby in the past couple of years due to import tariffs and surging memory prices. For example, the PlayStation 5 Pro debuted in 2024 for $700. Today, the same system has a sticker price of $900, and resellers like GameStop are charging upwards of $1,400. If you want the best way of playing Grand Theft Auto VI at launch, you might need to take out a loan.
But let's say you just want to play good games and don't necessarily need the newest system or latest titles. Relatively affordable new consoles are available, but you may need to make compromises on graphical fidelity or form factor to keep prices within the realm of sanity. Also, as we'll discuss, an initially cheap system can end up being more expensive in the long run if you never get a break on game prices.
For the purposes of this discussion, we're going to skip over niche consoles like the Playdate or Analogue 3D, as well as the multitude of generic Android devices that exist. Some of these might be exactly what you're after, but they're not what most people think of when they want a mainstream gaming console.
The cheapest console upfront
You can immediately ignore anything from Sony or Microsoft. Following price hikes, the discless PlayStation 5 Digital Edition is $600, and even the scaled-down all-digital Xbox Series S is $500. You might be interested in one of the two for their game libraries, but most people wouldn't consider $500 cheap, especially when there's no way of buying used games for either console.
Without disc drives, you're limited to whatever discounts appear on Sony and Microsoft's online stores. Major releases are usually $60 or $70, with GTA VI coming in hot at $80. Game Pass or PlayStation Plus can provide savings if you play a lot of games, but the additional $10 to $23/month might not be feasible if you're looking to minimize spending.
A slightly better deal is the Nintendo Switch 2. That also starts at $500, but you can at least buy some used Switch games on physical cartridges, rather than getting everything digitally via the Nintendo eShop. If you're willing to spend a little bit more, you can also get the console bundled with Mario Kart World or Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, giving you something to play from the jump.
For the lowest initial cost, the winner is another Nintendo product: the Switch Lite. It's just $230, putting in the same pricing bracket as a lot of those generic Android devices. Keep in mind that the Switch Lite is a variation of the original 2017 Switch, meaning it can't play Switch 2 exclusives. It also lacks the ability to dock with your TV. But if you're okay with this, there's an incredible game catalog available. Apart from major first-party titles like Super Mario Odyssey and Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, there's a wealth of third-party and indie standouts like Hades, Portal and Undertale.
Why you might want a handheld PC instead
Compared to the above options, a handheld PC can be shockingly expensive. Valve's Steam Deck OLED starts at $789, and a higher-powered product like the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X is a whopping $1,000. There are cheaper options, but you're probably not going to find anything worth buying below the $600 mark unless it's used. None of these devices have access to games on card or disc, either, unless you count retro ROMs you copy onto an SD card.
The way they beat conventional consoles is in offering affordable game downloads. While Sony and Microsoft are decent at offering discounts on older releases, the deals are amped up significantly on PC storefronts like GOG and Steam. Those have access to decades' worth of content, frequently reduced to just a few dollars, and new releases tend to get discounts within just a few months. Conversely, Nintendo will barely budge (if at all) on games that are a decade old. If you want to build a large collection of major releases, the Switch Lite might not be that much cheaper in the end.
Don't overlook free games, either. While you have to work around free-to-play monetization, modern systems offer tons of high-quality free games you could play for hundreds of hours, including Overwatch, Rocket League, The Finals, Fall Guys, Genshin Impact and many more.
Moreover, handheld PCs are PCs. Though they're obviously gaming-focused devices, they're capable of running productivity apps when you switch out of their game launchers. The same can't be said of a Switch or PS5.

Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.
Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet's atmosphere.
"We found that we needed to include some exotic physics … physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release. "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”
On Earth, clouds usually form when water vapor creates droplets or ice crystals in the presence of tiny particles, such as dust or salt. The new study, published in Nature Geoscience, instead suggests AMEC could be forming through so-called homogeneous nucleation, where vapor changes directly into ice crystals on its own without any help from debris.
“It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window," Hernández-Bernal explained. “It’s wholly unexpected.”
This phenomenon requires extreme conditions—a sharp temperature drop of 30 degrees Celsius within 10 minutes and high relative humidity. The Arsia Mons volcano also plays a key role. When wind current hits the 65,000-foot-tall volcano, it creates a powerful wave that launches moist air high in the atmosphere in a matter of minutes.
Scientists have assumed a similar phenomenon could occur in the upper atmospheres of other planets, including Venus and even Earth, but it has never been observed. That’s not too surprising given the extreme air humidity required for this phenomenon, which is more than 100,000 times greater than any value measured on Earth.
Before this modeling, it was not known that these humidity levels existed on Mars either. “We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’ atmosphere as we do about Earth's, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success,” said Hernández-Bernal, adding, “the result is remarkable.”

Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.
The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview.
Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

Indian physicist Ashoke Sen has been awarded the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal, becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the honour, news agency PTI reported. Sen, an ICTS-Infosys Madhava Chair Professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Bengaluru, is widely regarded as one of the architects of modern string theory. His pioneering work has contributed to the understanding of gravity, black holes and the fundamental nature of matter, as per the report. The medal, established in 1988, recognises distinguished contributions to theoretical physics. It is awarded annually by Stockholm University and the Nobel Committee for Physics of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Ashoke Sen is one of India's most prominent theoretical physicists, widely recognised for his pioneering contributions to string theory and its application to some of the most fundamental questions in physics. His research has advanced scientific understanding of gravity, black holes and the underlying structure of matter. Sen serves as an ICTS-Infosys Madhava Chair Professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Bengaluru. He was previously a professor and Distinguished Professor at the Harish-Chandra Research Institute (HRI) in Prayagraj, formerly Allahabad, and has also held academic positions at TIFR in Mumbai. Sen is best known for his work on string theory, a theoretical framework that proposes that the fundamental constituents of matter are tiny, one-dimensional strings rather than point-like particles. The theory seeks to provide a unified understanding of particles and fundamental forces, including gravity. His research has made significant contributions to several areas of theoretical physics, including S-duality, black-hole entropy, string field theory and the study of unstable D-branes. He also formulated the Sen conjecture on open string tachyon condensation, an important development in the study of string theory. Sen's work on the relationship between different string theories helped establish the understanding that apparently distinct formulations could represent different limits of a deeper underlying theory. Sen delivered the Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture, titled Gravity from strings and strings from gravity, on October 22 at the AlbaNova University Centre in Stockholm. The lecture examined how string theory can provide a consistent quantum description of gravity and help address unresolved questions involving black holes and the relationship between quantum mechanics and gravity. His contributions to these areas have helped shape the development of modern string theory and earned him international recognition. Sen completed his bachelor's degree in science at Presidency College in Kolkata, followed by a master's degree from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kanpur. He subsequently earned his PhD from Stony Brook University in the United States. He later worked as a postdoctoral associate at Fermilab and the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC) before taking up academic positions in India. Sen has received several major honours for his contributions to theoretical physics. These include the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics in 2012, the Padma Shri in 2001 and the Padma Bhushan in 2013. His research helped establish the idea that different string theories can be understood as different limits of an underlying, more fundamental theory, as per PTI. Named after Swedish theoretical physicist Oskar Klein, the medal was established in 1988 to honour his scientific legacy. Every year, the organisers of the Oskar Klein Memorial Lectures invite a distinguished researcher to deliver a memorial lecture and receive the medal. The award recognises outstanding contributions to theoretical physics. Congratulating him on the latest recognition, ICTS Director Rajesh Gopakumar said, “On behalf of all of us, very warm congratulations to Ashoke. It has been no less than wonderful having Ashoke with us and setting the tone for excellence here at ICTS.” In a statement, ICTS described Sen, an ICTS-Infosys Madhava Chair Professor, as an internationally recognised researcher whose work has helped shape modern string theory, as per PTI report. Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.
Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.
The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions have been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.
“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.
“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”
The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.
Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband has been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.
“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.
“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa’.
“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway’. We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”
Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.
“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.
“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.
“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”
Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.
Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.
“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”
During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.
Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks, and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.
Advocates say Donald Trump’s massive second term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.
The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.
A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.
It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”
The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.
The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.
The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.
It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.
The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.
Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.
“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.
The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).
“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”
Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.
“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.
“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.
The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.
It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.
Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.
“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”
Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.
“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

A disability rights group has written to the Central government seeking the classification of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices and prostheses as essential assistive products under the draft Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Amendment) Rules, 2026.
Doctors with Disabilities: Agents of Change (DwDAoC), an organisation of health professionals with disabilities, said in its communication that the Centre should classify communication aids and prostheses as essential products.
In a representation to the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the group noted that these products, put in the specialised assistive products category, could create uncertainty over access to insurance coverage, public financing, replacement and maintenance.
The draft rules, issued under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, propose a framework for standards and accessibility of assistive products and technology. The notification follows a Supreme Court directive calling for clear, non-negotiable accessibility requirements under Section 40 of the Act. The draft invites objections and suggestions before finalisation.
AAC devices include picture-based communication boards, speech-generating devices and applications that convert text or symbols into speech. In its representation, DwDAoC argued that the need for specialist assessment, customisation, fitting or rehabilitation should not determine whether a product is essential. It called for the classification to reflect the role assistive products play in enabling autonomy, participation and the exercise of rights.
The group said the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, recognise augmentative and alternative modes of communication. It also cited the World Health Organisation’s Priority Assistive Products List, which it said includes communication aids and artificial limbs, and ICMR’s National List of Essential Assistive Products (NLEAP), 2023, which has prostheses among its prioritised products.
DwDAoC urged the government to align the draft rules with these frameworks and consult AAC users, prosthesis users and other persons with disabilities before finalising the rules. It has urged the government to ensure equitable access to assistive products, regardless of the complexity of the services required to provide them.

On October 6, the National Medical Commission (NMC) issued guidelines on advertising and public communication by doctors and hospitals. Intended to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, they cover hospital hoardings, social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond curbing deception, they raise another question regarding how much can doctors and hospitals say to the public about their work and achievements?
What is prohibited?
Claims of “guaranteed cures”, “100% success” or being the “best” are barred. Similarly, fake reviews, manipulated online rankings, misleading celebrity or influencer endorsements, and offers encouraging unnecessary treatment are deemed unethical practices. The guidelines rightfully prohibit AI-generated or manipulated patient images, voices and testimonials. But section 8.1(i) prohibits advertisements that create “unnecessary demand” for medical procedures or promote “fear-based marketing”. Without objective criteria, such expressions leave considerable room for subjective interpretation and inconsistent enforcement.
Hospitals may publish factual details of services, charges, accreditation and doctors’ credentials. Yet Section 8.1(iii) restricts advertising professional achievements and success rates, and Section 8.1(v) prohibits promotional “before and after” surgical photographs, except for specified scientific or educational purposes. Such blanket restrictions risk regulatory overreach, particularly when authentic, appropriately contextualised images could help patients understand surgical outcomes. Section 9.2 also restricts the use of doctors’ photographs for self-promotion, including on letterheads and signboards. These restrictions apply only to registered medical practitioners under the NMC’s jurisdiction.
Why the information asymmetry?
Patients rarely possess the same medical knowledge as those treating them. Even amid an abundance of AI-enabled health information, choosing a surgeon or assessing a hospital’s safety record remains difficult. Verifiable professional achievements, including the number of surgeries performed, years of experience and treatment outcomes, could help patients make informed choices. While such figures can be misleading without context, they are fundamentally different from unsubstantiated claims to be the “best” or to guarantee success, which the guidelines already prohibit. Rather than restricting genuine professional accomplishments, requiring their accurate and transparent disclosure could better serve patients’ right to informed choice. The answer may lie in better disclosure, rather than less information.
Is commercialisation unethical?
The guidelines seek to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, while Clause 8.1(ii) restricts promotion, suggesting commercialisation of medical practice. But in India, profit-making healthcare is lawful, as section 2(c) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, recognises privately operated hospitals, and section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, enables lawful commercial enterprises, including hospitals. Government policy also permits 100% FDI in hospitals.
Article 19(1)(g) protects citizens’ freedom to practise a profession or conduct business, subject to reasonable restrictions. In the case Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), the Supreme Court recognised commercial speech under Article 19(1)(a), including the public’s right to receive information, while permitting restrictions on misleading advertisements. The current guidelines appear to treat commercialisation itself as a problem, without clearly distinguishing legitimate business interests from practices that mislead or exploit patients.
Are government schemes exempt?
Central and State government schemes undertaken in the larger public interest are exempted, and can advertise. Flexibility for vaccination drives and other health programmes is understandable. But the exemption is broad. Safeguards should remain equally important whether a campaign is run by the government or a private hospital. Patients seeking private healthcare may independently praise or criticise doctors. But the guidelines remain silent on hospitals and practitioners using unsolicited patient testimonials for promotion. What if a patient voluntarily posts an account and a hospital subsequently shares it? The distinction remains unresolved.
Other unclear aspects
Graded penalties are intended for violators, starting with a warning and mandatory ethics training for the first violation, and increasing to a 6- to 12-month suspension for subsequent violations. At the same time, repeated offences could lead to removal from the register for one to three years. State Medical Councils will enforce these provisions after issuing show-cause notices and considering doctors’ explanations. Appeals can be made to the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board.
The guidelines remain unclear about who can initiate complaints and the evidence required. It addresses genuine concerns, but its broad and ambiguous provisions may create confusion over compliance and leave considerable room for subjective enforcement, particularly affecting smaller hospitals. Protecting patients from misleading advertisements and commercial exploitation is necessary. However, treating commercial intent itself as inherently suspect serves little purpose. Clearer distinctions between legitimate professional communication and unethical promotion would better serve both patients and healthcare providers.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari begins preparations for first Gangasagar Mela under BJP govt
Held every January on Makar Sankranti, the Gangasagar Mela draws millions of Hindu pilgrims to Sagar Island in West Bengal’s South 24 Parganas district.
With Durga Puja celebrations over, the BJP government in West Bengal has turned its attention to preparations for the 2027 Gangasagar Mela, the first edition of the annual pilgrimage since the party came to power in the state in May 2026. The government has set its sights on giving the event international recognition, in line with the BJP’s promise ahead of the Assembly elections.
Held every January on the occasion of Makar Sankranti, the Gangasagar Mela draws millions of Hindu pilgrims to Sagar Island in West Bengal’s South 24 Parganas district. Devotees take a holy dip at the confluence of the Ganga and the Bay of Bengal. The gathering is considered the second-largest congregation of Hindu pilgrims in India after the Kumbh Mela in Prayagraj.
“We have come to transform the upcoming Gangasagar Mela into an international event,” West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said at a rally in Kakdwip, the mainland gateway to Sagar Island.
Adhikari has also held an initial meeting with senior bureaucrats and top police officials to begin preparations for the event. The government is expected to convene a high-level meeting at the state secretariat in the coming weeks, after the Durga Puja holiday period ends, a senior official said.
“The chief minister held a meeting with senior bureaucrats on Saturday to prepare for the upcoming Gangasagar Mela. Plans are afoot to make it a grand event this time,” the official said.
BJP’s promise of international recognition
In its manifesto for the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, the BJP promised to develop the Gangasagar Mela into an international spiritual and cultural festival, with support from the BJP-led government at the Centre. The party also said it would pursue the event’s inclusion in UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
The proposed push comes amid a long-running debate over the development and recognition of the pilgrimage. In 2021, Kolkata’s Durga Puja received UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage recognition during the tenure of former chief minister Mamata Banerjee.
Banerjee had repeatedly sought national-level recognition for the Gangasagar Mela and criticised the BJP-led government at the Centre over what she described as inadequate financial support for infrastructure development at the pilgrimage site.
Senior officers to coordinate preparations
The state government is planning to deploy senior Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officers at Kakdwip and on Sagar Island to coordinate preparations across departments, an official said.
A senior IAS officer is expected to be designated as the “mela officer” and stationed in the area for the next two months. The officer will coordinate arrangements involving the various departments responsible for organising the annual gathering.
The chief minister also set deadlines for departments involved in the preparations during Saturday’s meeting, the official said. Further details of the arrangements are expected to emerge after the next round of meetings.
Muri Ganga bridge project in focus
Infrastructure connectivity is likely to remain a key part of preparations for the pilgrimage, particularly the proposed bridge over the Muri Ganga river connecting Sagar Island with Kakdwip on the mainland.
In January, Banerjee laid the foundation stone for the bridge, which is intended to improve access to the island. The project is significant for pilgrims travelling to the Gangasagar Mela, as reaching the island currently involves ferry services.
Adhikari, however, questioned the progress made under the previous government and alleged that the project had not been adequately prepared.
“The previous government lied about the Muri Ganga bridge. Neither land was acquired nor any detailed project report was drawn. We will inaugurate the bridge in 2029,” Adhikari said.
The bridge is expected to be a major infrastructure project for Sagar Island, although its proposed 2029 inauguration would come after the 2027 edition of the Gangasagar Mela. The state government’s immediate challenge will be to prepare the island and surrounding areas to accommodate the large number of pilgrims expected in January.

Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January 1, 2027, requiring their services to remain linked to the active SIM associated with a user’s registered mobile number. According to a Times of India report, platforms must complete implementation by December 31, 2026, ahead of the reported operational start date the following day. The requirement could affect users who access messaging apps on phones without the associated SIM. The mandate stems from directions issued by the DoT in November last year under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024. The original directions named WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh, and JioChat. The department said some app-based communication services continued to function without the SIM associated with the registered mobile number being present in the device. According to the DoT, this allowed fraudsters operating from outside India to misuse Indian mobile numbers. SIM binding requires covered services to remain continuously linked to the associated active SIM, rather than relying solely on verification when an account is first set up. The government said the measure was intended to improve traceability and curb phishing, digital arrest, impersonation, and investment scams. The original directions gave platforms 90 days to implement the measures and 120 days to submit compliance reports. However, the government subsequently specified December 31, 2026, as the compliance deadline for SIM binding. Platforms Prepare For Compliance According to a CNBC report, Apple has updated its iOS software to support the SIM-binding requirements ahead of the implementation deadline. WhatsApp and Arattai have confirmed that they are working to comply with the rules. Telegram is yet to clarify on its compliance status, while Signal has not responded to government notices, CNBC reported. Snapchat has reportedly maintained that the mandate does not apply to its service because it does not use phone numbers to identify users. Questions also remain about how individual platforms will support eSIM users. CNBC reported that WhatsApp and Telegram would require a physical SIM card to function, although the precise requirements for eSIM users have not been clarified. The mandate could affect users who access messaging apps over Wi-Fi on phones without their registered SIM, as well as those who frequently switch SIMs. Its impact on access across multiple devices will depend on individual platforms’ implementation. However, the DoT has clarified that international roaming will not be affected as long as the associated SIM remains in the handset. The implementation push comes amid concerns over cyber fraud in India. According to data sourced from the home ministry, Indians lost ₹22,495 Cr to cyber fraud in 2025 compared with ₹22,845 Cr in 2024. In June, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said Indians had lost around ₹52,976 Cr to cyber-enabled fraud over the past six years, with nearly 8% of the losses linked to digital arrest scams. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on global technology companies, financial institutions, and telecom operators to work together to build a comprehensive framework to tackle cyber fraud and deepfakes. “At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks,” Modi said, adding that trust was crucial for people using phones to communicate and make payments.

Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?
A February study found 99,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024
Sitting at his desk in a sun-filled apartment in Tel Aviv, economist Itai Ater pored over data that shows more Israelis have left the country over the past three years than ever before.
Those have been tumultuous years for the country of around 10 million people, with war, economic uncertainty and a prime minister plagued by corruption charges whose trial started in 2020 and still hasn't reached a verdict.
Ater, a professor at the Coller School of Management at Tel Aviv University, says these departures could accelerate depending on the outcome of next week's legislative elections, destabilizing the country's economy and causing ripple effects throughout the region.
"Israelis are thinking, 'do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?'" Ater said. "Unfortunately, and I understand, I sympathize with their answers, many of them realize that the answer is no. And that's why they're leaving."
In February, Ater and his colleagues published a study using data collected from the Central Bureau of Statistics that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. The study looked at Israelis who left for at least three consecutive months and stayed out of the country for more than 270 days during the first year of their departure.
Ater says he understands why people might want to leave: 'Israelis are thinking, "do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?"' (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
According to the data, 50,000 left in 2023, a year that saw Hamas militants storm southern Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and kidnapping another 250. Israel responded by embarking on a devastating military campaign in the Gaza Strip that continued until a fragile ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, though Israel still controls roughly 60 per cent of the enclave and engages in regular military activity there.
In 2024, 49,000 left. Ater says preliminary data shows the trend continued in 2025, and he believes the looming election could push those numbers even higher in 2026.
Election fuels uncertainty
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a defining figure in Israeli politics for the past three decades and is by far the country's longest serving leader, is once again vying for power.
Polls suggest his far-right bloc will fall short of the requisite 61 seats in the Knesset to form a government and that a rival bloc headed by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, is currently in position to secure the most seats. As of now, Eisenkot's coalition is expected to be short of a majority.
- Analysis Netanyahu's future uncertain as Israel starts to prepare for national election
- Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election
Israel's multiparty system, in which coalitions are often required in order to form a government, means the election results are often only just the beginning of the intrigue and lead to a jostling of parties and power in the days after the vote.
Netanyahu has long been considered a master at this process.
A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, displays a flag depicting him at Mahane Yehuda market, ahead of Israel's national election, in Jerusalem on Oct. 22. (Kevin Coombs/Reuters)
"We are really, really, really terrified in the sense that if there is no change in the patterns, then there's no change in October in the elections," Ater said. "These [emigration] numbers will go up dramatically."
Avigail Ben-Porat, 50, said she dreams of leaving but doesn't have the resources to do so.
The single mother lives in Kiryat Shmona, near the Israel-Lebanon border, where she said she still regularly hears the sound of rocket fire.
"I would go and never look back," Ben-Porat said. "Most of my friends are living abroad, some of them in Portugal, some of them moved to Canada. Some of them are in Thailand and in Goa in India. They pretty much left and fled."
Economic impact
It's not just the volume of people leaving that has Ater and others concerned — it's their jobs.
Ater's study suggests that 2023 and 2024 saw a dramatic increase in the number of doctors, Ph.D. holders and engineers leaving the country, with 2,360 net departures from Israeli engineers and 509 net departures from doctors.
"Israel's economy depends on the human capital," he said. "It's the tech industry, it's academia, it's health care. We need these best individuals to stay in Israel."
Lawyer Liam Schwartz, seen in Tel Aviv in September, says many companies, under pressure from investors, are moving chunks of their business outside Israel. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Liam Schwartz oversees the corporate immigration department at Goldfarb, Gross, Seligman, an Israeli law firm based in Tel Aviv. He said Israeli companies are also eying the exit.
"There are a good deal of Israeli companies that are just — they call it business viability," Schwartz said. "They have to answer to their shareholders who are not necessarily Israeli and investors who are not necessarily Israeli and they are concerned about the viability of business operations based in Israel. So they are more willing to move chunks of their workforce to North America or to Europe."
Schwartz believes the discontent started when the government proposed judicial reforms that would have stripped power away from the Supreme Court back in January 2023.
"People are just disappointed," he said. "They feel like the Israeli government is no longer meeting its part of the social contract."
All of this adds up to making Tuesday's elections one of the country's most consequential.
"I think that the October elections in Israel are going to be a watershed moment in whether … the rate of Israeli emigration increases or not," Schwartz said.
For Ater, the stakes could not be higher.
"I'm saying it. It's a strategic concern, strategic risk," he said. "To the future of Israel as a democracy, as a liberal country, and that's not only a concern for Israel, it's also a concern for the Middle East and also for the world."

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Delhi man arrested for uploading Siddaramaiah-targeting video, gets bail; JDS link under probe
The accused told the investigators that he uploaded the footage at the direction of a person associated with the JD(S) social media team, police said.
A Delhi man accused of uploading a video targeting former Karnataka chief minister Siddaramaiah was arrested by Bengaluru Police on Saturday. He was later granted bail by the metropolitan magistrate court, subject to the condition that he will cooperate with the investigation.
The investigators were examining whether he acted on the instructions of a person associated with the Janata Dal (Secular) social media team, according to officers in the know of the development.
The accused, 22-year-old Ritesh Pandey, was arrested in Delhi and brought to Bengaluru, where he was questioned by the Cyber Crime Wing of the Central Crime Branch. Police suspect he uploaded the video, which was circulated through “Karnataka Honey Trap” accounts on YouTube and X.
Accused says he uploaded video on direction of a JDS-linked person
According to the officer, Pandey told investigators that he uploaded the footage at the direction of a person associated with the JD(S) social media team. “The CCB is now trying to identify the person and determine whether others were involved in recording, uploading or distributing the video,” the officer said.
The arrest is the first in the case, which began with a complaint filed by Siddaramaiah over the circulation of the alleged sting operation. Police are examining electronic devices and technical material seized from Pandey, including a second hand mobile phone suspected to have been used to upload the footage. "Teams are also tracing how the video subsequently spread across social media, including Facebook,” the officer added.
The CCB has also issued notices to several people suspected of uploading or sharing the video. Some of those sought by investigators have reportedly become untraceable.
Siddaramaiah says video fabricated
Siddaramaiah has called the video fabricated and alleged that it was part of an attempt to blackmail him. Speaking to reporters in Mysuru on Friday, he said he had approached the police because he wanted the facts established.
“I have filed a complaint so that the truth comes to light. I have also obtained a stay order from a civil court to prevent further circulation,” he said.
“This is a case of blackmail. It needs to be uncovered who is behind this. I filed the complaint because I know this is a complete fabrication. I served as Chief Minister for eight years, and during that time, no such blackmail attempts were made against me. I do not have authority now,” he said.
The episode has also triggered allegations about possible involvement by people within the Congress. Siddaramaiah’s son and minister Yathindra Siddaramaiah said the woman seen in the video appeared to be a Congress worker and suggested that the purported operation may have been intended to help her obtain a Congress ticket to contest the 2023 Puttur Assembly election. He said the involvement of an individual party worker would not mean that the Congress as a whole was involved.

Iran remains open to talks with US under Pakistan-brokered deal, envoy says
Iran remains open to U.S. talks under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, according to Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad
ISLAMABAD -- Iran remains open to talks with the U.S. under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad said Saturday, accusing Washington of undermining diplomacy and prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam said that Iran recently conveyed through Pakistan that it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, but accused U.S. President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker the June agreement, which sought to restore shipping through the strait, lift the U.S. naval blockade and begin negotiations toward a broader deal addressing Iran’s nuclear program.
Moghadam, speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, said that Iranian officials had conveyed their willingness to reopen the strait during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Muni r, provided Washington ended its blockade.
Moghadam also said that Tehran would study the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement that includes Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey before deciding whether to support it, describing it as a potential instrument for unity. “We will study the Mecca Agreement, and if it is good, we will support it,” he said.
The agreement was signed following renewed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saudi Arabia. The three countries who signed it said it would strengthen collective deterrence and expand defense cooperation.
Turkey has submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification. Turkish and Pakistani officials say it is defensive and does not target Iran or any other country. Turkey has ruled out sending troops into Yemen to attack the Houthis, while Pakistan says its role would be strictly defensive.

You’re reading our ESMO in 30 Seconds newsletter. Sign up here to get updates from the major European cancer conference in your inbox.
Hello again from Madrid, where we can tell you it’s Day 2 of the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual meeting, but definitely not what day of the week it is. Perhaps some of the other nearly 40,000 people here can relate?
Enjoy today’s newsletter; we’ll be back with one more edition wrapping up the conference Monday afternoon. And on Thursday, join us for The STAT Recap, where we’ll catch you up on all the ESMO news you need to know, and answer your questions live.
In the meantime, we’re at [email protected] and [email protected].
Inside Moderna and Merck’s ‘presidential’ presentation
Adam Feuerstein/STAT
No surprise, the arena-sized room was packed with ESMO attendees eager to see Georgina Long of the Melanoma Institute Australia present the intismeran INTerpath-001 study results. The unfortunate data leak on Thursday made her talk less dramatic, but at the end, she received extended applause and a limited standing ovation.
Long summarized the intismeran results — a 42% reduction in the risk of disease recurrence and a 38% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis-free survival — as a “new benchmark for adjuvant treatment of melanoma.”
“More critically,” she added, “it establishes intismeran as a landmark advance in personalized cancer medicine.”
The full trial data will be published next month in the New England Journal of Medicine, Long also noted.
Inge Marie Svane of the University of Copenhagen, the discussant following the data presentation, was positive if not overly enthusiastic about the trial, describing the results as “compelling” and adding that they “mark a crucial moment for personalized cancer vaccines.”
But Svane also pointed to a number of outstanding questions, including whether there would be a survival benefit with intismeran, and what exactly was driving the vaccine’s benefit — was it the specific targeting of the neoantigens, or was it the general immune boost that studies have suggested mRNA vaccines provide?
She also took no position on the best way to treat the approximately 40% of higher risk melanoma patients enrolled in the study — a key debate with commercial implications. If intismeran is approved, it will compete against neoadjuvant immunotherapy, or treating patients before surgery. Svane laid out pros and cons of each approach, leaving the question of which will benefit patients more unanswered.
On mistrust and mRNA
The vast majority of the discussion about Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine centered on the quality of the data and the further application of individualized cancer therapies. But Toni Choueiri, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, raised an important point during an address in a special session all about mRNA vaccines.
Mistrust and misinformation, Choueiri said, “is a key challenge to adopting anything that is mRNA.”
It seems that many people who hold unfounded doubts about mRNA vaccines for infectious diseases separate the technology’s potential in cancer — no more so than the people running the U.S. health department. While the federal government is throwing its weight behind cancer vaccines, it’s also drastically cut funding for mRNA vaccine research for pathogens.
But Choueiri said the pandemic highlighted how widely and quickly myths can spread, citing 2022 survey data that indicated 15% of people falsely believed that the mRNA Covid-19 shots could alter human DNA.
The concern is that such misguided fears could have ripple effects to anything called a vaccine, particularly if it’s made with mRNA. Choueiri noted that some people have moved away from using “vaccine” when describing products like the Merck-Moderna treatment, instead calling it a personalized neoantigen therapy.
Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel, speaking to STAT a couple of hours before the intismeran presentation, believes showing the benefits of an mRNA-based therapy in cancer — a disease that has affected a broad swath of Americans — will go a long way towards shifting perceptions of people who might have viewed mRNA in a negative way.
“I think the cancer treatment is going to help a lot,” Bancel said. “People will realize what we already know, that mRNA is a molecule that’s already in your body.”
An expanded use for Amgen’s Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer
The combination of Amgen’s Imdelltra plus Astrazeneca’s Imfinzi used as a maintenance regimen improved overall survival in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer — a successful outcome that is expected to expand the commercial opportunity for Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer.
The presentation also drew a standing ovation from some in the room.
In the DeLLphi-305 study, the median overall survival for patients treated with Imdelltra and Imfinzi was just over 21 months compared to just under 13 months for patients receiving Imfinzi alone. Statistically, the doublet regimen reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to Imfinzi.
Cytokine release syndrome, a type of immune side effect, was reported by nearly half of the participants in the doublet arm, but the cases were mostly mild to moderate.
The 563 patients enrolled in the study had extensive-stage small cell lung cancer that had not yet progressed following first-line immunotherapy. The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The results appear to set a new survival benchmark for maintenance therapy in small cell lung cancer. A previous study that combined Jazz Pharma’s Zepzelca with Roche’s Tecentriq reduced the risk of death by 27% compared to Tecentriq alone.
“The separation of the curves that we’re seeing here is not the kind of thing that we typically see in small cell lung cancer,” Jacob Sands of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, who presented the data, told reporters. “These are extraordinary hazard ratios.”
Stephen Liu, a Georgetown University oncologist who was the study’s discussant, echoed that point.
If patients are eligible for the treatment approach, Liu said, “I can’t think of a subset where I would not want to offer this regimen.”
Astrazeneca’s bladder cancer push falls short
The neoadjuvant, or presurgical, use of Astrazeneca’s drug Imfinzi in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer reduced the risk of death by 42% compared to surgery alone. The risk of disease progression or death was reduced by 49% compared to surgery alone.
The positive results, however, don’t quite match the current standard of care.
Astrazeneca’s Phase 3 VOLGA study treated advanced bladder cancer patients with Imfinzi plus Pfizer’s Padcev before surgery, followed by Imfinzi after surgery, and compared their outcomes to patients who only underwent bladder surgery.
The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
At two years of follow up, 63% and 45% of the patients in the Imfinzi-Padcev and surgery only arms, respectively, were alive without tumor progression. Overall survival at the same time point favored the Imfinzi-Padcev group over surgery alone, with 78% and 69% of patients alive, respectively.
The VOLGA outcomes fell short of the current standard of care for the neoadjuvant treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Merck’s Keytruda plus Padcev reduced the risk of death by 50% and the risk of tumor progression by 60% compared to surgery alone.

Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.
