WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

How to extend the battery life of your Apple AirTags
Why the battery in your AirTag might die quickly, and what you can do to make it last longer.
Apple's AirTag is a must-have accessory for travelers or anyone who's forgetful, and one of the best parts about using AirTags is that you don't have to worry about recharging them. That's because the tracker runs on a standard coin-cell battery, which Apple says lasts for more than a year before you need to replace it. But in practice, you might find that your AirTags run out of battery much faster — it really depends on how you use them.
Even with the the second-generation AirTag, which released earlier this year, the battery performance remains the same. The good news is that a few simple habits can help its battery last longer. Whether you're setting up an AirTag for the first time or having trouble with an older one, here's what to know about an AirTag's battery life.
What kind of battery does the AirTag use, and what performance can you expect?
Every AirTag uses a CR2032 coin cell battery — a 3V lithium battery commonly used in car key fobs and watches. They're super easy to find, with plenty available on Amazon and likely at your nearest drugstore or supermarket. Plus, they're quite cheap, usually costing no more than $1 each.
When you buy a new AirTag, it comes with a battery already installed. Replacing the AirTag battery is very simple: just press and twist the AirTag's steel underside cover until it comes off. Remove the old battery and insert the new one with the positive side facing up, then put the steel cover back on and twist it to close. If you did everything right, the AirTag will play a short sound when it turns back on.
So how long does the AirTag's battery typically last? In most cases, Apple's estimate is accurate, and you can use one for a year or more before it runs out completely. But depending on how often you call on its features, the battery may run out sooner, lasting a few months instead of a year.
Checking the battery level of your AirTags is easy: open the Find My app on your Apple device and switch to the Items tab. If you see an orange battery icon next to an AirTag, it's time to replace the coin cell. When the battery is in good condition, the app doesn't show any icons. Older versions of Find My always showed a battery indicator, but Apple removed this because it was often inaccurate.
When an AirTag's battery is low, it will restrict some features to preserve the small amount of power left: you can't use the precision finding feature and it won't play sounds. If you're worried about the battery running low at an inopportune moment, set a reminder for a year out whenever you change one.
Tips to make your AirTag battery last longer
Your AirTag doesn't have an on/off switch because it's always sending its location via the nearest Apple device. However, certain types of use drain the battery faster, so avoiding them can help the battery last longer.
Repeatedly triggering the AirTag's sound alert is one of the actions that drains its battery quickly, since it requires the speaker to fire up all the time. Precision Finding also uses more power, as that enables the Ultra Wideband chip to communicate with your iPhone or Apple Watch in real time. The same goes for constantly opening Find My to check on a tag that's sitting in the next room. There's no problem using these features in typical situations — that's what an AirTag is designed for. But some people like to play around with these features just to see them in action, which can drain the battery faster.
This also applies when the battery is low. Depending on what you do with your AirTag on critical power, it can last a few days to weeks or even a month. If a battery becomes low during a trip and you can't replace it, try not to track or locate the tag unless absolutely necessary.
Using a good battery also helps your AirTag last longer. Generic CR2032 batteries tend to hold less charge, so choosing one from a well-known brand is recommended. Apple recommends the Duracell 2032 Lithium Coin Battery — just keep in mind that some bitterant-coated CR2032 batteries may not work in an AirTag. Temperatures can also affect how long the AirTag's battery lasts, so avoid placing them in extremely cold or hot places. Apple rates the AirTag to operate at temperatures between −4°F and 140°F (−20°C and 60°C), so throwing it in the trunk of a car isn't the best idea.
Also, an AirTag that's constantly moving tends to experience faster battery drain because it's always pinging its location. If the AirTag in your car runs out of battery before the one on your keychain, that's normal.

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and headed north toward the Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about 150km (93 miles) east of Taiwan, the CWA said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

Tesla posted the videos to showcase the official launch of the company's new Roadster model. The footage shows the car performing several mid-air stunts in front of a live audience. Attendees also posted their own videos from the event, corroborating Tesla's footage. Whether the vehicle actually "flew" during the demonstration is up to individual interpretation. It is unclear whether Tesla's final product would have the same capabilities as the "flying" car seen in the clips.
On Oct. 15, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla and social media users posted videos purportedly showing the company's new "flying" car performing a number of mid-air stunts.
The footage depicts a launch event for the automaker's long-awaited Roadster model. It shows a prototype driving up an upside-down ramp before flipping off and landing on its wheels, flipping over a row of other Tesla products and accelerating from zero to 60 mph in 0.81 seconds.
Throughout the video, Tesla's CEO, Elon Musk, and his fellow hosts made references to the vehicle being a "flying car."
Snopes readers searched our site to find out more about the vehicle.
In short, there is nothing to suggest the video is fake, meaning it was not created using artificial intelligence tools or the product of digital editing. Tesla livestreamed the footage on YouTube on Oct. 15. The event showcased the company's new Roadster model and was conducted in front of a live audience. Some of those attendees posted their own clips on social media, corroborating Tesla's footage. Therefore, we rate this claim true.
Audience members posted their own videos (archived, archived), among other content, and reputable car magazine Top Gear also said its staff attended the event and saw the demos. Reputable news media outlets also covered the event.
Though the clips excited autophiles and technology experts worldwide, some people cast doubt over Tesla's claim that the new Roadster is a true "flying" car (archived, archived).
There is nothing to suggest the demonstrations of the Roadster's abilities were fake. The event took place in front of a live audience, with Tesla CEO Elon Musk saying, "We need an audience to prove that it's not AI or SI." SI refers to Super Intelligence, U.S. President Donald Trump's new name for artificial intelligence.
But whether the Roadster is a true flying car is open to interpretation. The demonstrations showed the prototype dropping or launching off a surface and controlling its fall over shorter distances. Musk said the car could "fly like a rocket" but did not demonstrate sustained flight over a longer distance during the event.
Given the car is not in production as of this writing, it is unclear whether the final consumer product, if or when it reaches the market, would have the same capabilities as the car in the videos. The prototype did not have a human driver.
2nd Roadster nearly 10 years in the making
Tesla first announced its second-generation Roadster during an event in November 2017. The next year, Musk teased on X (archived), then Twitter, that the new Roadster could come with a "SpaceX option package" consisting of roughly "10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car."
"These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering," Musk wrote, "Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly."
SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car. These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) June 9, 2018
However, Musk soon became busy with other acquisitions, such as Twitter, and progress stalled on the Roadster.
Nearly nine years after it was announced, Musk said that, in 2028, Tesla would "enter production" of a new Roadster that would use a suction system on the bottom of the car to allow it to drive upside down and would feature SpaceX rockets to allow it to "fly like a rocket."
According to Tesla's website, the automaker would sell two versions of the Roadster. The "Thrust" would feature "a multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters" that allow the car to accelerate from zero to 60 mph in under one second. The "Rocket," which members of the public would be able to buy via invitation only, would be the flying version of the car, fitted with cold-gas thrusters that "support forward and upward acceleration as well as lateral rotational movement."
Tesla says of the "Rocket" version, "So yes, it can fly."
The company notes on its website that the "Rocket" is "not approved for public road use." It is unclear at the time of publication how a flying car would be regulated and what sort of licenses a driver or pilot might need to hold to operate it.
According to technology website The Verge and business news outlet CNBC, some early adopters placed $50,000 deposits on the Roadster in 2017. OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman reportedly had his $45,000 deposit refunded in 2025 after he wrote (archived) on X, "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays. But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
For further reading, Snopes routinely investigates claims related to Musk and Tesla.

Muskan Rastogi, Sahil Shukla challenge death sentence in Saurabh Rajput's ‘blue drum’ murder case before Allahabad HC
The court had convicted the two on September 30 for the murder of Muskan's husband Saurabh Rajput and for attempting to conceal his body.
The two convicts in the blue drum murder case - Muskan Rastogi and her partner Sahil Shukla - have approached the Allahabad High Court challenging their death sentence by a Meerut court.
A division bench of the high court is likely to hear the matter next week.
The court had convicted the two on September 30 for the murder of Muskan's husband Saurabh Rajput, a former merchant navy officer, and for attempting to conceal his body. The death penalty was given on October 14.
Senior Jail Superintendent of Meerut district jail Viresh Raj Sharma told PTI that the appeal on behalf of Sahil and Muskan was filed on Friday by senior advocate Sushil Shukla.
The lawyer said both Sahil and Muskan had consented to appoint him as their counsel, following which the lower court's verdict was challenged.
In their appeal, the two convicts described the trial court's verdict as illegal and arbitrary and urged the high court to acquit them of all charges under the relevant provisions of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Their appeal also contends that the prosecution failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, but the trial court arrived at its conclusion on the basis of speculation and conjecture while overlooking established legal principles, they claimed.
The appellants also pointed to alleged contradictions in the statements of witnesses regarding the purchase of the weapon, cement and drum.
They have argued that neither CCTV footage nor valid purchase receipts were produced to substantiate these transactions.
Other grounds raised in the appeal include the alleged absence of signatures of independent witnesses on recovery memos, violations of videography procedures and the absence of mandatory certificates required for electronic evidence.
Saurabh was murdered in the Brahmpuri police station area of Meerut on March 3, 2025. Sahil and Muskan then concealed his body in a blue plastic drum filled with cement and concrete in an attempt to dispose of it. The case had triggered widespread outrage after it came to light.
Following an investigation, police arrested Muskan and Sahil. District Judge Arvind Kumar Mishra pronounced the verdict of death sentence that came after 126 hearings and a 13-month trial.

Texas did reinstate rules that treat certain THC products as controlled substances.
Texas did not make all marijuana possession a felony; possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana remains a Class B misdemeanor, for example. In addition, the vote was a Democratic primary proposition, not a statewide legalization referendum open to all voters.
In mid-October, social media users recirculated a claim that Texas made marijuana possession a felony despite more than 70% of voters supporting legalization.
For instance, one Reddit post (archived) featured a graphic reading, "Texas just made weed a felony after over 70% of voters voted to legalize it. That's what happens when incarceration rates go down and for-profit prisons start to lose money."
(Reddit u/dude1984)
Over the months, the rumor spread on multiple social media platforms, including Instagram, LinkedIn, Bluesky, X and Facebook.
In short, it's not true that Texas voters approved marijuana legalization in a statewide referendum, as social media posts suggested. In reality, voters taking part in the Democratic primary election in March 2026 were asked whether they supported legalizing cannabis for adults. The question appeared as a "survey" on Democratic primary ballots and was a nonbinding party proposition.
Also, Texas did not make all marijuana possession a felony. The change that took effect July 31, 2026, reinstated definitions under which manufactured delta-8 THC and certain other forms of THC were designated controlled substances. Possession of some of these products can result in felony charges. However, possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana remains a Class B misdemeanor under Texas law. Moreover, the change didn't originate with the vote in 2026. The disputed THC definitions dated back to 2021 and were reinstated in 2026 after several years of court proceedings.
As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
Vote was a Democratic primary proposition
The first part of the claim referred to a proposition that appeared on Democratic primary ballots on March 3, 2026. An official Harris County sample ballot identified it as "DEM - PROPOSITION 8" and asked voters whether "Texas should legalize cannabis for adults and automatically expunge criminal records for past low-level cannabis offenses." Respondents could choose "for" or "against."
The proposition received strong support. Official statewide results showed 80.1% in favor and 19.9% against. However, this was not a statewide referendum in which Texas voters decided to legalize marijuana. The question appeared on Democratic primary ballots only, and the result did not change state law.
Under Texas law, political parties can place nonbinding propositions (such as cannabis legalization) on their primary ballots. The process is described in the Texas Election Code, which allows a political party's state executive committee to put a proposal on the primary ballot about specific legislation or another issue that could be included in the party's platform or resolutions.
In other words, the cannabis question was not a statewide legalization referendum open to all Texas voters, but a nonbinding proposition presented statewide to Democratic primary voters. As such, the vote did not legalize marijuana or change Texas criminal law.
Texas did not make all weed possession a felony
The second part of the claim referred to restrictions on certain THC products that took effect July 31, 2026. According to the Texas Department of State Health Services, the change reinstated rules treating manufactured delta-8 THC and some other forms of THC as controlled substances.
Possession of certain controlled THC substances can carry felony penalties, but this did not mean Texas made all marijuana possession a felony. Under Texas law, possession of two ounces or less of marijuana remains a Class B misdemeanor, while larger amounts can carry more-serious penalties. Texas also continues to permit up to 0.3% delta-9 THC in consumable hemp products.
THC policy at issue dated from 2021
The policy at issue actually dated back several years. According to the Texas Supreme Court's May 2026 decision, DSHS published the disputed schedules in 2021, seeking to treat manufactured delta-8 THC as a controlled substance.
Hemp businesses challenged the policy, and a court temporarily blocked it while the case continued. On May 1, 2026, the Texas Supreme Court ruled that state law did not prevent DSHS from classifying manufactured delta-8 THC as a controlled substance and reversed the injunction.
Following the ruling, DSHS reinstated the disputed definitions, effective July 31, 2026. The reinstated definitions are now facing a separate federal court challenge, as the Texas Tribune reported. On Aug. 9, a federal judge denied an emergency request to temporarily block the restrictions, while a request for a preliminary injunction remained pending. Therefore, although the Democratic primary vote happened in March and the restrictions took effect in July, the disputed policy dated back to 2021.
Bottom line
All in all, the claim had a kernel of truth. Democratic primary voters supported a nonbinding proposition calling for the legalization of cannabis, and possession of certain controlled THC products in Texas can lead to felony charges. However, Texas voters didn't legalize marijuana and Texas didn't later make all marijuana possession a felony. Finally, the THC policy at issue dated back to 2021 — several years before the 2026 vote.

If Netflix wants this, Erin Foster is ready to serve up a fourth season of her Jewish romantic-comedy.
Following the release of Nobody Wants This Season 3, the series creator recently confirmed she has “more story to tell” if the streamer gives the show a renewal, but noted she tries not to “get too attached to the outcome” in these situations.
“There’s those next steps as people who are not in their 20s, getting married and you’re starting off already kind of behind everyone else,” she told Parade. “I experienced that when I got married, I was 37, and it’s a different experience. So, yeah, I do think that there’s more story to tell.”
Foster continued, “But I’m also someone who doesn’t get too attached to the outcome and is sort of fluid about allowing sort of the market to tell us what they want from us. I never want to have a show that goes on longer than people want to see it. I’d rather people want more than want less.
Watch on Deadline
In Nobody Wants This, inspired by Foster’s relationship with her music exec husband Simon Tikhman, agnostic podcaster Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) begins an unexpected romance with Rabbi Noah Roklov (Adam Brody), which shakes both their families as Joanne immerses herself in Noah’s culture and decides to convert to Judaism.
Foster’s Season 4 comments come after she responded to Brody’s support of “Free Palestine,” which has sparked controversy among pro-Israel fans of the show. “While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s okay,” she said.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Uttarakhand helicopter carrying 6 passengers makes precautionary landing after technical snag
A Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter carrying six passengers made a precautionary landing at Tehri Garhwal’s Baurari stadium after a mid-air technical snag. No injuries were reported.
A helicopter carrying six passengers made a precautionary landing at Baurari stadium in Uttarakhand’s Tehri Garhwal district on Saturday morning after developing a technical fault mid-air, officials said. No injuries were reported, and the aircraft was cleared to resume its flight after an inspection.
The aircraft, operated by Trans Bharat Aviation, was on its way from Dehradun to Guptkashi in Rudraprayag when the pilot detected a snag mid-air around 7:15 am.
“The chopper made a precautionary landing at Baurari stadium due to a technical fault. The pilot examined the aircraft, and after a thorough inspection lasting nearly 40 minutes, it received clearance to resume its flight,” Tehri Garhwal district disaster management officer (DDMO) Brijesh Bhatt said.
Parmanand Maithani, a local resident who was out on a morning walk, said people in the area ran to safety as the chopper unexpectedly came down, while children were playing in the stadium. “We were walking when we suddenly heard the loud sound of an approaching helicopter. When it became clear that it was about to land right there, everyone panicked and ran**.”**
This is the second such incident involving the same aviation service provider in the region this year. In May, another helicopter operated by Trans Bharat Aviation made an emergency landing in Nawa Gaon village of Tehri Garhwal after encountering a technical failure while flying from Badrinath Dham to Dehradun. During that landing, the tail section of the aircraft sustained damage after coming into contact with a high-tension power line in nearby fields.

Farooq Abdullah's remarks on Pakistan, Kashmiris spark row; BJP demands apology
The former Jammu and Kashmir CM made the remarks at a party event in Baramulla district of Kashmir Valley.
Former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah set off a political row with his alleged pro-Pakistan remarks made at a rally in Baramulla district of Kashmir Valley on Saturday. The J&K unit of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) sought an apology from Abdullah, who is also the chief of J&K National Conference party, over the controversial remarks.
Without naming Pakistan, Abdullah said that the 'neighbour’ is protecting Kashmir. He said there is little hope for Kashmiris from the Centre and urged Kashmiris to have courage to confront Delhi.
"If you don't keep it, you will be erased. Even our trace and identity will disappear. Nothing will be left. They are silent today because there is noise in the world, and our neighbour is constantly behind this. Everywhere they say, 'the decision regarding Kashmir has not been made'. That is what is saving us. Otherwise, their intentions are not good," he said.
He further asserted that the people of J&K never denied being Indians.
"We never said that we are not Indians. Time and time again, we affirmed that we acceded to India - to the India of Mahatma Gandhi, the India of Jawaharlal Nehru, the India of (Maulana Abul Kalam) Azad," he said.
He alleged that Muslims and Hindus are being pitted against each other for ‘power’.
"India's fabric was destroyed; we never imagined this would happen. But this too shall end, God willing; its time will come," Abdullah was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
BJP seeks apology
The remarks kicked up a row with BJP's J&K president Sat Sharma demanding an apology from the former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister.
“Farooq Abdullah needs to understand that he has the freedom to say whatever he wishes in this country. It is precisely because of this freedom that he is able to make such statements. Had you made these remarks in Pakistan, you might not have been spared,” Sharma said, adding that Article 370 was imposed on the state.
Also read: JDU expels Mokama MLA Anant Singh from party for 6 years, days after controversial remarks spark row
“The rights of women were taken away. Today, Muslims across the country, including those in Jammu and Kashmir, understand the situation. Muslims in Jammu and Kashmir know that they are safe in the hands of India...The Bharatiya Janata Party will not tolerate such conduct. He should publicly apologise to the people of India. Otherwise, I would say that Pakistan would be a better place for him, and he should go and settle there,” he added.
Former union minister Arjun Munda also condemned Abdullah's remarks, saying that such a statement, if made by a former chief minister, was unfortunate and reflected his view of the country.
"If such a statement has come from him, then it becomes self-evident how he views this country. Today, that is clearly reflected in his statements. I did not expect his statements to take such a form, but since they have, it is not just saddening; it is condemnable,” Munda was quoted as saying by news agency ANI.
Uttar Pradesh minister Suresh Kumar Khanna accused Abdullah of exploiting Kashmiris throughout his political career. He said that the region's integration into the national mainstream under the Modi government was in the best interests of its people.
“It is people like Farooq Abdullah who have exploited Kashmir throughout their lives. Farooq Abdullah is responsible for reducing Kashmiris to second-class citizens, and he ought not to be making such statements. It is precisely because of India’s diversity that Kashmir is now integrated into the nation’s mainstream, and every citizen of Kashmir enjoys the same rights as those in the rest of India," Khanna was quoted as saying.

Q&A: Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn’t need Alberta separatists’ support
Premier sat down with CBC Radio’s West of Centre for an in-depth interview
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the matter of separatism is settled within her party and she doesn’t need the support of those who want the province to leave Canada.
Smith says she told members of her United Conservative Party on Wednesday that they should support the will of the majority of Albertans who have voted to stay in Canada, or leave the party.
But some prominent separatists like Mitch Slyvestre, the president of the UCP's Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association, have long argued that they helped oust former premier Jason Kenney and get Smith in as leader of the UCP.
CBC Radio’s West of Centre host Kathleen Petty interviewed the premier on Friday.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Jared Wesley from the University of Alberta had observed “a referendum does not just reveal your strength — it can also reveal your weakness.” Did it here?
It showed to me that certainly on the constitutional questions, there just is not the appetite to pursue it. And I think there's a couple of reasons for that.
On constitutional change, I think people are still a little fatigued from all of the different realms that were unsuccessful in previous years. So I think it's a question of how much success we could have on them. But they're also not top of mind for people.
I think what we saw is the immigration questions are certainly more important than the other ones. And so those will be the ones we'll prioritize.
But not hugely more important, because that number is still pretty skinny. So what guidance do you believe that's giving you for the legislation that you're planning for this spring?
Well, it seems to me people are very enthusiastic about the idea of having to show citizenship in order to be able to vote. So I think people need to be prepared that that is very likely going to be the first thing that we act on with enabling legislation. And our next provincial election is next October.
We're making it as easy as possible because we now have a citizenship marker on your driver's licence. So you can go through and get all of that process done. So you can just have one piece of ID.
When it comes to waiting periods for temporary workers or what the fees might be to access some of the programs, we're going to have to take a bit more time with that.
But I think we can solve a lot of the problems by focusing our newcomer population on the jobs that are available. Because when somebody comes with a high-paying job, they probably don't need to rely on social services. And when somebody makes a commitment to being a permanent taxpayer as a permanent resident, they'll get the same programs as everyone else.
So if we can fix that part, then I think it will reduce some of the stress on our health care and education and other systems.
Question 10, you say it’s settled — 75 per cent of Albertans said we want to stay in Canada. It seems it isn't settled in your party though. So how do you deal with that?
Well, it is settled in my party.
How’s it settled?
I am the leader not only of government but also of my party. I'm the chief communicator for our party, and I have said that anyone who wants to run as a candidate for us, anyone who wants to be on our provincial board, has to align with what Albertans told us.
If you're going to be in a political party and show faithfully that you're going to represent the people, then you have to listen to the message they gave you and the message that Albertans gave us — 75 per cent — that they're proud Canadians and want to stay a part of Canada.
So how will you enforce it?
Right now, I am allowing people some time to reflect on what democracy means.
And when they’re finished reflecting?
If you don't want to agree to follow the will of the people, you don't have to be a candidate for us. Don't put your name forward. You don't have to run for our provincial board.
And if they do, you don't sign their nomination papers?
Well, I guess we'll see whether or not people will rise to the occasion. I think most people do.
Most people. But I'm curious about what you do with the people who don't.
They have lots of options to continue. They can be in advocacy groups. They can set up podcasts. They can continue to be involved in other political parties.
But in our political party, we respect democracy and we respect Albertans. If you had candidates running for you who said, “You know what, vote for me and I may or may not do what you ask me to do,” it's not a very strong selling feature. I think for us to have the credibility with Albertans, that we're going to listen to them and faithfully implement what they ask us to do, we have to sign that pledge.
UCP MLA Jason Stephan announced that he would not be running for re-election. Had you told him you would not sign his nomination papers, given that he publicly said he was voting for Option 2, which is to have another referendum?
He made his own decision. He had told me last year that he wasn't sure whether or not he was going to run again, and he wanted to take some time to reflect on that. And so he obviously did that over the course of the last week or so, and he made the decision not to run again.
So you didn't influence that decision by saying anything?
He announced that, I believe, before the results came in. So he had made that decision.
I'm curious how you feel about how separatists will continue with their advocacy, because they argue you won the leadership and the election, in part because of them. Can you keep your leadership and election without them?
[Laughs] Well, that's not who was supporting me.
The people who were supporting me were the ones who were really concerned about the COVID response. The people who were supporting me were the ones who were concerned about some of the DEI ideology that was in classrooms. They were the ones who were concerned about young children being transgender … behind their parents’ backs. Those are the people who voted for me.
This new movement is actually brand new. I mean, some of the leaders of it just woke up one day in April of last year and decided to join the separatist movement.
But some of them you had relationships with. It’s not like you didn’t know them, like Mitch Sylvestre and David Parker.
But to be clear, you run your campaign on areas of common interest and common policies, and the areas of common interest and common policies were the ones I described — but also talking about autonomy within Canada.
Our position as a party and my position in running was: let's try to make Canada work by getting Canada to focus on its areas of jurisdiction so we can focus on ours. That's always been my pitch. Others think that there's another way, but that's not been my position.

If you crave a compact phone that doesn’t feel like a brick in your pocket and slips easily into a small bag, the flip style is for you. Samsung’s eighth-generation clamshell is seriously refined, and as svelte and slick as it comes. It may not offer a tablet-sized screen or the fashionable new passport shape, but it is arguably the most practical type of folding phone.
Like almost every other phone this year, the Z Flip8 offers tiny improvements over its predecessor and costs $100 more. If you’re wondering whether it’s worth updating from last year’s Z Flip7, it’s not. The Flip8 is a teeny bit lighter and slimmer with a newer processor, and that’s about it. But if you’re looking to dip a toe in folding-phone waters or just want something small, the Z Flip8 should be in the conversation.
Slimmer and More Foldable
Photograph: Simon Hill
Everyone is excited about the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8’s sexy new form factor, but Samsung continues to iterate on the flip phone format for folks who prize compact devices. The Z Flip8 shaves off 0.02 inches (0.55 millimeters) and a third of an ounce (8 grams) compared to its predecessor, making it the slimmest and lightest option in this category. The improved hinge makes the crease slightly less noticeable and a little easier to open. I still found it a bit tricky to open one-handed, but you get the knack after a while. The new hinge is also supposed to be more durable.
The Flip8 has an IP48 rating, so you don’t need to worry about dropping it in the bath, but tiny dust and dirt particles (less than 1 millimeter) can still cause damage. It comes in pink, like my review unit, as well as graphite, cream, and mint. It still has a physical SIM slot, and the power button has a fingerprint sensor in it that works pretty well.
The screens are the same as last year's. It has a sharp 4.1-inch AMOLED display on the outside with a 60- or 120-Hz refresh rate. Open it up to reveal the 6.9-inch main display, also AMOLED but with a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) that’s better for battery life. Both screens are reasonably bright (2,600 nits peak), and I never struggled to read the screen outdoors.
Powerful Performer
Photograph: Simon Hill
Flip phones used to get palmed off with lesser processors, but the Z Flip8 boasts the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy (the same cutting-edge chip that's in its two bigger siblings). It has 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. You can jump to 512 GB for an extra $200, but there’s no option to increase the RAM.
I encountered no stutters or lag and found performance to be generally excellent, whether jumping in and out of apps, firing up the camera, or gaming. The Z Flip8 can get warm, and this may throttle the processor somewhat if you’re playing a demanding game for a while (more than an hour). This is mostly down to the compact design.
The stereo speakers are better than I expected. They get quite loud without distortion, and they’ll serve you just fine for watching videos. Call quality is also solid, and slamming it shut to end a call never gets tired. I also like opening it to answer calls, but you must enable this in the Phone app settings under Flip options. Connectivity includes 5G (no mmWave), Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 5.4, but there’s no ultra-wideband (UWB) for more precise positioning. The Fold8 models have Bluetooth 6 and UWB.
While it’s very capable, the Z Flip8 is only average when it comes to battery life, another drawback of its size. Samsung put in a 4,300-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’s good enough for casual use. If you’re on your phone a lot, you’ll want a power bank handy. Charging speeds are disappointing at 25 watts wired and 15 watts wireless, and I’m annoyed by Samsung’s refusal to implement the magnetic feature of Qi2.
Snap Shot
If you’re a keen photographer, you can get many better camera systems in a range of Android phones for the same money or less. That said, the main 50-megapixel shooter is perfectly good in many situations, and most folks will be happy with the photos it captures. Some noise creeps in when it’s dark. The 12-megapixel ultrawide is useful when you want to cram a lot in or take a group selfie, but it’s a definite step down in quality. Sadly, there’s no telephoto lens, but you can emulate 2X zoom without losing detail by cropping, and it offers passable results in good lighting up to 10X.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8, main camera.
I don’t see much reason to use the 10-megapixel punch-hole selfie camera outside of video calls, since you can flip it to get a cover-screen preview and use the main camera for selfies (a big benefit of this design). I also love Samsung’s Horizon Lock, which lets you shoot video with a steady horizontal plane no matter how you turn or move the phone.
Another new AI feature from Samsung is My FanCam, which lets you pick a subject to focus on in group videos and reframes them as though your chosen subject is the star. Handy for school plays or soccer games, if you remember to use it. (You can also apply it to old videos.) Speaking of AI, Samsung offers Now Brief to float up calendar events, reminders, and useful info like local weather, and Now Nudge to suggest adding dates to your calendar from messages, sharing locations or photos, and auto-filling forms.
Compact Competition
The cover screen, or FlexWindow, has been a weakness for Samsung’s Flip line, and it’s still limited in the Flip8. On the plus side, you can use more apps with the cover screen, including most of Samsung’s apps (Health, Calendar, Browser), YouTube, Netflix, Google Maps, and Messages. But if you want other third-party apps, you still have to install Good Lock, then the MultiStar plug-in, and select the apps you want to use. It’s stupidly convoluted, and I don’t understand why it isn't preinstalled, especially since Samsung has virtually all its other apps on there, along with a few third-party apps I never asked for (Facebook, Spotify, and Instagram). This is admittedly a bugbear of mine, but it's disgraceful that Samsung is including bloatware on a phone this expensive.
Photograph: Simon Hill
I like that you can have YouTube on the cover screen, as you can prop it up and there’s a little toggle at the bottom to switch between full screen, above the camera lenses, or standard vertical format for scrolling. You’ll mostly use the inner screen, but I have sometimes used the Flip8 this way to prop up a video I’m half-watching on my desk, and it’s a nice option to have.
There’s only really one competitor for Samsung if you’re set on a flip phone, and that’s Motorola's Razr line. You can step down to a less powerful but much cheaper Razr at $800, or spend a little more to snag the superior Razr Ultra. The latter has a better camera, more RAM and storage, and charges much faster, but it costs $1,500. The awkward middle child, the Razr+ at $1,100, is a tougher sell (it has an older processor and shorter software support). You might consider last year’s Z Flip7 if you can find it discounted.
Sadly, this might be your last chance to get a Samsung flip phone. Persistent rumors suggest Samsung will sunset this form factor as the Fold8 takes off and goes head-to-head with the iPhone Duo, though Samsung hasn't officially confirmed it. If you do pull the trigger on the Flip8, you get an excellent seven years of platform and security software updates, potentially taking you all the way to 2033. Who knows, maybe small phones will be back in fashion by then.

Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing the deal is only half the battle. The real challenge comes when you integrate the business, unlock synergies, and deliver the value that justified the deal in the first place. Much of this heavy lifting falls on CFOs, who are expected to go beyond balancing the books to evaluate acquisition targets, assess financial risks, structure deals and ensure the business derives long-term value from the transaction. This is part of a broader shift in the CFO’s role, from financial oversight to strategic decision-making. Whether determining how to extract value from an acquisition or assessing if an investment in AI will deliver adequate returns, finance leaders are making critical capital-allocation decisions while ensuring the business stays on track to meet its growth ambitions. At Perfios, a B2B SaaS fintech serving more than 1,000 financial institutions across multiple geographies, Group CFO Prashant Mahagaonkar sits at the heart of these decisions. With more than 25 years of experience across traditional finance, multinational companies, M&A and venture-backed businesses, Mahagaonkar’s career has given him a front-row seat to the changing nature of the finance function. For the concluding edition of The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Mahagaonkar to discuss his experiences and learnings from decades of building finance systems, integrating acquisitions and working alongside founders and CEOs. Speaking with Inc42, Mahagaonkar broke down how his role has evolved, what he has learnt from acquisitions, why CFOs need to question technology spending, and what he believes will define the next generation of finance leaders. Walking The Tightrope Between Risk and Reward Mahagaonkar's career began in 1999 at Tata Motors, but he soon realised traditional audit and compliance work wasn't where he wanted to build his career. In 2022, Mahagaonkar joined Givaudan India, a Swiss flavour and fragrance major where he got his first real exposure to what a well-built financial system looked like. For Mahagaonkar, the experience became an education in how large organisations build systems and roll them out across markets. Mahagaonkar then shifted to Essilor India, a spectacle lens manufacturing company, where he was exposed to acquisitions and moved from traditional finance to a more M&A- and business-oriented role. He later joined venture-backed Amba Research, where he raised capital, worked with investors across geographies and eventually managed an exit. Moody’s acquired the company. Mahagaonkar moved to CitiusTech, where he became the company's first CFO and worked closely with the founder-CEO to scale revenue from roughly $60 Mn to $500 Mn. “Working with the founders to scale the team was a great learning experience for me. I realised how different a founder’s mindset is from that of a professional CEO. Their risk-taking appetite is very different, and they bring perspectives that a traditional professional may find difficult to act on,” said Mahagaonkar. As Mahagaonkar puts it, the experience taught him how to keep the company business-friendly while also protecting it financially. According to him, while founders may be willing to offer more flexibility to win a customer, the finance leader's job is to ensure the company is adequately protected. “But the solution was not always to take the most conservative position. Instead, the finance team had to establish a playbook that clearly defined what it would agree to and where it would draw the line,” said Mahagaonkar. He added that finding “the art of the possible” within an accepted compliance framework is one of the most important skills he has developed over time. Making Acquisitions Work Beyond The Deal Mahagaonkar’s M&A experience proved valuable when he joined Perfios in July 2025. By then, the company had completed three acquisitions, and his mandate was to integrate the acquired businesses into a cohesive organisation. Perfios acquired an eFRM (Enterprise Fraud Risk Management) business, a segment it had not historically operated in. In another acquisition, it added a collections company, adjacent to its existing loan origination, approval, and credit underwriting businesses. Each acquisition required a different integration strategy. Mahagaonkar shared that his task was to determine what should be fully integrated into Perfios, what should retain its independence and how each business could contribute to the broader ecosystem. All this had to be done while ensuring that every entity remained compliant with the applicable regulatory and reporting requirements. Smaller companies often lack the same level of compliance infrastructure as a private equity-backed or larger organisation. “Therefore, the integration process involved bringing acquired businesses up to Perfios’ standards across areas such as information security, contracts, insurance, risk and statutory compliance,” the CFO said. However, amid all the finance and integration of compliance functions, what generally gets understated and undermined is the integration of people and cultures. Mahagaonkar argues that people integration is also a finance responsibility because acquisitions can easily leave redundant roles and overlapping functions in place. “You need to put it together and be part of those discussions to help and make sure that we build that one organisation which is required,” he said. AI Spend Under CFO’s Scanner The expanding role of the CFO is particularly evident in capital allocation, where Mahagaonkar believes AI has fundamentally changed how technology investments are evaluated and prioritised. “Today, product life cycles have shortened so much that companies may have just six months, rather than two years, to get ahead of competitors before they develop similar products,” he said. For the CFO, this means asking harder questions about whether the company is deploying its capital into the right assets and whether its innovation engine is moving quickly enough to match the pace of competitors. But in this chase, increasing AI spend may seem like the obvious choice for almost every problem, and Mahagaonkar believes companies need to look before they leap. “Not every problem needs AI, particularly when a simple automation can do the job,” Mahagaonkar said. At Perfios, the company has built an ROI matrix around its usage that monitors productivity gains, potential changes in hiring requirements and whether a particular use case should use AI at all, instead of automation or machine learning. Becoming The CEO’s Co-Pilot With the changing relationship between finance and technology, Mahagaonkar believes the CFO has moved from being a backroom player to becoming a co-pilot to the CEO or founder. He also mentioned that being a co-pilot to the CEO does not mean becoming the de facto CEO. Mahagaonkar estimates that around 40% of a CFO’s decisions today require forward-looking judgement rather than relying solely on historical financial data. When asked about the skill sets that will matter most for the next generation of CFOs, he said, “We must accept that today’s young people often know more than we do. They have greater access to information, and they can process and apply it much faster. The real test for the next generation of leaders, not just CFOs, will be managing such high-calibre talent, helping them find meaning in their work and creating an environment where they can succeed.” According to Mahagaonkar, finance leaders of the past could succeed by knowing the numbers better than everyone else, but CFOs of the future will have to understand the numbers, the business, the technology and, increasingly, the people behind the decisions.

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.
Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.
Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.
He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.
A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.
King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.
Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.
Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”
Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

Bill Clinton is not a fan of Trump’s White House renovations
Clinton took issue with the new Rose Garden that Trump paved over and added Mar-a-Lago-style umbrellas to

Former Democratic President Bill Clinton has revealed his thoughts about Donald Trump’s White House renovations - and he’s not a fan.
The current president has painted the Oval Office gold and paved over the Rose Garden as he seeks to put his mark on Washington before the end of his second term. He has also built a new helipad and is working on constructing a ballroom that dwarfs the rest of the White House.
But Clinton is not a fan.
“I think Congress made a mistake not protesting turning the Rose Garden into what looks like the entrance to Liberace's bathroom,” Clinton said at a Democratic campaign event in Hollywood, Florida, this week.
Clinton was referring to the musician popular from the 1950s to the 1970s, known for his bedazzled costumes and glitzy pianos.
Tables with yellow-and-white striped umbrellas — reminiscent of those at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida — fill the concrete patio, a project the president undertook in the summer of 2025.
“This is really the new Rose Garden — look how beautiful it is, with the White stone that matches the White House,” Trump said at an event in July. “This used to be grass, and it was always wet…we had a lot of very upset women that stand [sic] in there with the high heels, and they’d just go down like quicksand.”
The Rose Garden has been an iconic addition to the White House since 1903. It has seen several renovations throughout the years and has been used to host press conferences and other events.
Clinton hosted the leaders of Israel and Jordan at the Rose Garden in 1994 during a trip to sign a peace agreement known as the Washington Declaration.
Clinton was in Florida this week to campaign for former Democratic congressman David Jolly, who is running for governor against Republican Congressman Byron Donalds.
Trump was in Fort Myers, Florida, stumping for Donalds Friday — part of his cross-country tour, in which he calls on his supporters to vote Republican and keep control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.
Aside from paving over the Rose Garden, Trump has also demolished the East Wing of the White House to make way for his massive, golden ballroom.
Trump has said it will cost about $400 million to build his dream ballroom and promised he and other donors would pay for it. But the project’s contractor told his administration that the ballroom would cost $600 million, with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.
The president also wants to build a 250-foot Triumphal Arch at the end of the Arlington Memorial Bridge that would be topped with a golden winged figure flanked by two gilded eagles.
He already tried renovating the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool, but days after the project was complete, blue paint started chipping off the shallow basin, and the water turned green with algae.
As Trump spends time on his first love — real estate — Americans worry about his priorities.
Seventy-three percent of U.S. adults believed he wasn’t paying enough attention to the country’s most important problems, according to a CNN poll conducted by research firm SSRS in July.

Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
- Published
On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.
Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.
Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.
Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.
The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.
Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.
The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.
Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?
Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.
D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.
In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.
Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.
Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.
But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.
"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."
That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.
Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.
Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.
Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."
The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.
In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".
The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.
Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.
After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"
There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.
Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.
Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security.
"There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates, resident tells BBC
A resident of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region, says that the atmosphere is calm but people are very stressed after fighting broke out between government troops and the party that controls the region on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to full-scale civil war.
He says that many banks have been running low on cash for months, leaving people to rely on mobile banking, with fears that could now be blocked.
An adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister accused the Tigray People's Liberation Front of launching an all-out offensive, including in the two neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. The Tigrayans say they are engaged in defensive combat.

Indian Railways suffered its third successive defeat in the FIBA-Women’s Basketball League Asia (WBLA) at the Sree Kanteerava Indoor Stadium here on Saturday, going down 86-56 to Akari Sparks (Philippines) to finish sixth and last.
As in its previous two outings, Railways started with energy and intensity in the first quarter, only to lose steam in the subsequent periods. In fact, Railways produced its best basketball in the opening quarter, defending well and shooting efficiently to trail by just six points (15-21).
As the game progressed, however, its familiar weaknesses resurfaced. Mispasses, poor shooting from inside and beyond the arc, a drop in pace and execution, and lack of coordination took their toll. Sparks increased the lead with every quarter: 42-30 in second, 72-42 in third and 86-56 in final.
However, Railways did better than Sparks in second chance points: 11-9 but lagged behind in all other aspects such as points from turnovers (17-27), points in the paint (16-36), fast break points (15-21) and fast break points from turnovers (11-13) and bench points (22-25).
“I heard that Denso Iris (Japan) plays lot more tournaments. I want to tell our National Federation (Basketball Federation of India) is we have to just not focus on the Asia Cup. We have to go for lots of invitation tournaments, exposure trips, especially in the under 16 and under 18 categories. Then only we can improve,” she said at the post-match press conference.

United States GP: How likely is pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli to win 2026 F1 Drivers' Championship on Sunday in Austin?
Kimi Antonelli starts on pole position for Sunday's race in Austin from Max Verstappen, so what are his chances of winning the championship today? Watch the United States GP live on Sky Sports F1 & Sky Sports Main Event at 8pm on Sunday, with build up from 6.30pm
Sunday 25 October 2026 01:03, UK
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff believes it is "not realistic" for Kimi Antonelli to win the 2026 F1 Drivers' Championship on Sunday at the United States Grand Prix, despite the Italian starting on pole position.
Antonelli was not expected to claim top spot in qualifying but produced a superb lap in Q3 to beat Red Bull's Max Verstappen and take his first pole position since July's Belgian Grand Prix.
Should Antonelli win Sunday's race in Austin with Lewis Hamilton finishing fifth or lower and George Russell ninth or lower, he will seal the title with five rounds remaining.
Hamilton will start fifth and Russell sixth when the lights go out at the Circuit of the Americas at 8pm (build-up from 6.30pm), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event.
However, Wolff has warned Mercedes will not have the pace to win as they did not have the pace in Friday practice's long runs.
"We are not talking about that [the championship]. It's not realistic," he told Sky Sports F1.
"I don't think we are quickest in the race, so it's about scoring points and eventually, hopefully, winning."
Antonelli is also wary of Red Bull's race pace and the possibility Verstappen in second and Isack Hadjar in third can also work together.
He admits this week has been "a bit different", knowing it is the first opportunity to become the sport's youngest world champion at 20 years old.
"The goal stays the same. I just need to keep doing my job, and actually, I feel like I can enjoy the driving and everything more," said Antonelli.
"But of course, we still have to do the race, still have to try and win, and then, of course, we'll see what happens. But, I feel like I can enjoy it a bit more because obviously I'm in a very good position. But still, the mindset is always the same."
Verstappen plans to 'keep it respectful' against Antonelli
The uphill run towards the wide Turn 1 at the start provides a good opportunity for the driver in second to steam up the inside of the pole-sitter, something Verstappen may look to do if he has a strong getaway.
Verstappen, who has won the last two races, effectively has nothing to lose but suggested he will not be excessively aggressive against championship leader Antonelli.
"Kimi wants to go for the win right? That helps his position in the championship," he told Sky Sports F1.
"We keep it respectful and try to win the race."
Tyre degradation was high in Friday's practice sessions in Austin but that has been the case at several races this season, only for the Grand Prix to turn into a one-stop race as the teams have changed the setup on their cars and the track has gripped up over the weekend.
Nevertheless, overtaking is possible and Verstappen cut a quietly confident figure to make it a hat-trick of wins and deny any chance Antonelli has of winning the title on Sunday.
"We have been happier in the long runs, and I hope that it will be the same tomorrow," he said.
As for Russell, it has been another tricky weekend and he faces a big challenge to overtake Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in front of him, who have both been quick in practice, to get into the podium fight.
Russell has been unable to get to grips with Mercedes' new upgrade package but admits he simply just did "two bad laps in Q3".
"I think I could have been in the top three. My Q2 lap was two and a half tenths quicker than what I achieved in Q3 but that obviously isn't good enough from my side," he told Sky Sports F1.
Asked about his race prospects, he said: "I think it's a long race, a lot happens here in Austin. Strategy plays a role so still opportunities."
