Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up to Half-Life 2 (after so, so many years) may remember last year’s flurry of speculation that Half-Life 3 was finally nearing completion. Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development.
That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel at GameSoundCon, an industry conference devoted to “the art, technology, and business of game audio.” In a panel devoted to Valve’s use of open audio engines (captured in this Vimeo clip), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio:
Our HDR system is basically that’s one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR. HLX has its own version, so on and so forth [emphasis added].
“HLX,” of course, has been widely reported as the internal code name for Valve’s next Half-Life project. The codename has shown up in Valve engine code since at least 2024, but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Morasky was responsible for a close call in an interview last year).

The pros and cons of using an eSIM over a physical SIM card
The conveniences of an eSIM come with a few strings attached.
First, you should know there is no quality difference between using an eSIM or physical SIM card. The difference between the two is how you activate and move your cellular service. Both identify your subscription to a mobile network and feature the same reception and data speed. A physical SIM is removable, while an eSIM uses built-in hardware and a downloadable carrier profile.
The primary advantages eSIM has over physical cards is that it's flexible and convenient. You don't have to open a side tray or transfer the SIM when you purchase a new phone. Instead, you can simply activate a supported plan via an app, QR code or the phone's settings. On compatible devices, you can even store multiple profiles, which makes it easier to separate your work and personal numbers without carrying around spare SIM cards.
If you spend a lot of time on the road, there's another useful eSIM feature to consider. With an unlocked, compatible phone, you can purchase a travel eSIM ahead of time instead of finding a retailer that sells physical SIMs once you reach your destination. Depending on your plan, that could save you some money instead of roaming with your home carrier. You can also keep the travel plan dormant on your phone until your next trip, compared to losing the SIM card at home. At the same time, an eSIM is not a guarantee of a better deal. For instance, some domestic cell plans already include international roaming, so switching is mostly a waste of time.
There are smaller pros too, like not having to wait on a SIM card to ship for a new plan. Plus, removing the SIM slot from phones broadly means manufacturers have more room for larger batteries or other improvements elsewhere.
Is there a downside to using eSIM?
There's always a drawback, and the biggest disadvantage of eSIM is compatibility and transferring service. Both the phone and carrier have to support eSIM, and that support may vary by model and the market. An eSIM also can't bypass a carrier lock; to use another provider's plan, your phone generally needs to be unlocked. Opera's free eSIM on Android is a good test before purchasing one.
Knowing that, it's always a good idea to look over the requirements before purchasing a travel plan or assuming you can move your existing number to a different device. After all, a downloadable profile is only useful if the phone and provider will activate it.
Some carriers make the business of moving service from one phone to another more complicated than it needs to be. With Apple's eSIM Quick Transfer, you can move service between compatible phones without contacting support, but some require a carrier app, a replacement QR code (as if we need more of those) or help from customer service. Fortunately, cross-platform transfers are improving. For instance, some iPhones and Android phones can now transfer eSIMs directly.
You also have to be careful with your carrier while traveling internationally, which means reading the fine print before you head out. For instance, you might still be able to utilize your normal phone number while using the travel plan for data, but your carrier may have hidden some roaming fees. Make sure your phone is set to use the travel eSIM for data upon your arrival. You can also turn off your regular line entirely, but you won't receive any cell calls or texts on that number while it's disabled.
Why are people against eSIM?
For some, the primary objection is losing the fallback simplicity of a physical SIM. For all the talk about switching from one phone to another with an eSIM, popping the tray open and physically switching a card to another phone is pretty easy, unless you have a severe case of fumble fingers. As previously stated, some carriers require in-app QR codes or switches, both of which can be a pain. So it's less about the convenience of an eSIM and more about the available tools and how efficient they are.
Physical SIMs still offer a wider degree of compatibility with older and simpler phones, which works out great for the Gen Zers going retro or the many seniors who still prefer them (though that's changing). While there's no removable card to lose or physically extract, digital activation doesn't eliminate account fraud or SIM-swap scams either.
Ultimately, it boils down to what "convenience" matters more to you. If your phone supports both formats, then you're good whichever way you go. In fact, you can do both: retaining your physical SIM while using an eSIM for another supported line.

I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”
Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”
That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.
They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?
Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”
Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …
Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.
There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”
Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.
How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees??
Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.
Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.
Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”
Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”
You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?
Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.
Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?
Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.
One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?
When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.
I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.
Berger: The economic value piece is really important, because women have long suffered from being stuck at home as domestic laborers, because we weren't seen as economically valuable in the marketplace, right? So the idea behind Aged Intelligence Society is that if anyone needs to optimize their time, it's women.
In some ways, AI is the new washing machine or the new laundry or whatever it is. It's giving women many, many hours of the day back by offering them automation.
The reason we narrowed the aperture to people 40-plus is that we feel like the product-market fit for women who are over 40 is so spot on. One, because we have very discerning taste after many decades of honing it. We know how to ask really sharp questions. We have very strong bullshit meters, so we're not going to take just the first answer. We're going to keep probing and pushing.
And so we feel like in some ways this tool was built for people who have a certain level of intelligence and accrued experience. It's not really built for young people. It's not built for people who have not already gone through the failure and the friction of life and learned for themselves what makes for a good question.

Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs
Around 110,000 march in Paris alone in challenge to Macron, before police respond with tear gas, water cannons
Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close on Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's government.
The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. Near its endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.
The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry's estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities had confined the march to the city's southeastern edge, away from the centre.
Elsewhere in France, police used tear gas in several other cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, as well as water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's end point.
The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with Saturday's demonstration and 40 placed in police custody. Those arrested included six minors.
Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offences or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.
A police officer throws a tear gas canister during a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, on Saturday. (Jeremias Gonzalez/The Associated Press)
The unrest is shaking Macron's authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes.
In Paris, an Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d'Italie early in the afternoon, but it appeared to be a smaller crowd than a week earlier. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, as authorities sought to prevent another weekend of looting, burned cars and attacks on public buildings.
More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Around 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over that weekend amid street violence not seen in years.
Museums closed, shopkeepers worried
Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris on Saturday. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."
- Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about the wave of youth-led protests across Europe? Send us your questions before our Oct. 24 show
Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some protests have been banned
Police changed the Paris protest route Friday. At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135 euro (around $210) fine.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d'Italie.
"They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters," she said. "But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools."
A protest march was also scheduled in Marseille, but in cities including Nice and Montpellier, as well as Lyon, rallies were banned by the local authorities.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as the National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend's unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.
Students and workers are angry
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $310) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron's successor.
"The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. "And it's not possible anymore."
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Organizers from the "yellow vest" protest movement called for another day of rallies Oct. 31 to defend the right to demonstrate.
Other protests rock major European cities
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations are also rocking many European cities Saturday from Madrid to Milan, Lisbon and Tirana, Albania.
The protests encompass a broad range of issues from pensions and housing to anti-war movements, education and corruption.
People march through the streets of Milan on Saturday to protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests in Italy organized by groups across the political spectrum. (Antonio Calanni/The Associated Press)
In Milan, luxury boutiques were boarded up in the Italian fashion and finance capital as protesters launched fresh demonstrations on Saturday, one week after looting and clashes with police.
Italian Prime Minister Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week.
Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A separate anti-war march took off in central Rome, and there are concerns over possible infiltration by violent groups.
Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
Aside from Rome and Milan, demonstrations have been called in at least seven other cities. The newly formed "Oct. 17 Movement" has been the main driver alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and anti-war coalitions.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 police officers are patrolling the streets Saturday.

మక్కాలోని ఒక మసీదులో “అసభ్యకరమైన” చర్యకు పాల్పడ్డారనే ఆరోపణలపై, సౌదీ అరేబియా ప్రభుత్వం 14 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఇద్దరు బంగ్లాదేశీ జాతీయులైన నజ్రుల్ ఇస్లాం అబ్దుల్ బసీర్, స్వీటీ అక్తర్ (సిటీ అక్తర్)లను ఉరితీసినట్లు మీడియా కథనాలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఆ చర్య గురించిన కచ్చితమైన వివరాలను అధికారిక ప్రకటనలో పేర్కొనలేదు. ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, అబ్దుల్ బసీర్, స్వీటీ అక్తర్ మసీదులో సన్నిహితంగా ఉన్నప్పటి దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియోలు, ఫోటోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: మక్కాలోని మసీదులో అసభ్యకరంగా ప్రవర్తించారనే ఆరోపణలతో అక్టోబర్ 2026లో సౌదీ అరేబియాలో ఉరితీయబడిన బంగ్లాదేశీ జంటను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ అవుతున్న దృశ్యాలు ఉరితీయబడిన బంగ్లాదేశీ జంటకు సంబంధించినవి కావు. మొదటి వీడియోలో ఉన్నది మక్కాలో కాబా వద్ద తమ గర్భధారణ గురించి ప్రకటించిన యూకేకు చెందిన దంపతులు (బిల్లీ రెహ్మాన్, ఖదీజా) కాగా, మొదటి ఫోటోలో ఉన్నది ఈజిప్ట్కు చెందిన ఇన్ఫ్లుయెన్సర్ దంపతులు (గెహాద్ ఎల్బానా, రామ్జీ మహమూద్). కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
వీడియో 1:
ముందుగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోను బిల్లీ రెహ్మాన్, ఖదీజా బెల్గోమ్ అనే దంపతులు 07 ఆగస్టు 2026న ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్లో పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. తాను గర్భవతినని మక్కాలో కాబా దగ్గర ఖదీజా తన భర్త రెహ్మాన్కు వెల్లడిస్తున్నప్పటి వీడియో ఇది అని వీడియో వివరణలో ఇవ్వబడింది.
అయితే, తమ వీడియోను సౌదీలో ఉరితీయబడ్డ బంగ్లాదేశీ జంటతో ముడిపెడుతూ సోషల్ మీడియాలో జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారాన్ని బిల్లీ రెహ్మాన్, ఖదీజా బెల్గోమ్లు ఖండిస్తూ ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్లో స్టేటస్ పెట్టారు. ఈ ఘటనతో తమకు ఎటువంటి సంబంధం లేదని, తమ వీడియోలను తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేయడం ఆపాలని సోషల్ మీడియా యూజర్లకు విజ్ఞప్తి చేశారు. లండన్లో నివసించే తాము సురక్షితంగానే ఉన్నామని బిల్లీ రహ్మాన్ ఆజ్ తక్కు స్పష్టం చేశారు.
ఫోటో 1:

Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power
- Published
At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation.
That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture.
Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final.
Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008, not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts.
"It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports.
"So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special."
To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two).
While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point.
In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A.
The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years.
For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare?
Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance?
Premier League sides make strong start
English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once.
In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them.
In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them.
Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21.
The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams.
But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years.
So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory?
Money talks
Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List.
It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League.
Premier League clubs earn more than £1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined.
Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30.
Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'.
Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final.
In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively.
In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League.
All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates.
The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of £3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues.
Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.
You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings.
Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent.
"With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August.
"A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer."
Europe still rules in Champions League
Despite the success of Premier League sides in the Europa League and Conference League, the Champions League is a harder nut to crack.
While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered.
Over the past two campaigns, eight of nine English teams have been knocked out by one of the Deloitte Money League's big four, according to the last report produced in January 2026.
Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Liverpool were eliminated by an aggregate score of 25-6 last season.
No English club appeared in the top four of Deloitte's Money List, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain leading the way. Three of those have won the Champions League five times between them in the last seven years.
English clubs are certainly very much in the mix for the Champions League, with Arsenal losing last season's final on penalties and Manchester City winning in 2023.
But, with just one English club in the past three finals, the Premier League elite are yet to take their European domination to the very top.
Come May, it could well be Bournemouth, Brighton, Crystal Palace or Sunderland leading the English charge in Europe.

A day before Vijayadashami, Lekh Raj, 45, a debutant vlogger, eager to go viral, stood outside a plastered but unpainted temple in Bisrakh, a village in Greater Noida, some 30 kilometres from Delhi.
He adjusted the phone on his selfie stick and rehearsed the script his teenage son had drafted. Around him, no festive crowds and no towering effigies were waiting to be set alight; none of the signs of celebration unfolding across much of the country.
In the Hindu mythological saga of the Ramayana, Vijayadashami (victory on the 10th day) is the day Lord Rama vanquished Ravana, the 10-headed demon-king of what is now Sri Lanka. The festival celebrates the triumph of good over evil.
“What you are seeing behind me is not just any village temple,” says Raj, speaking into his phone camera, turning it from his face to the entrance of the modest shrine called Prachin Shiv Mandir.
Behind him, an elderly priest, his matted locks tied around his head, is garlanding a figure of Ravana carved into the wall.
Raj continues speaking into his phone: “This temple has a legend more unusual than most. It is the birthplace of Ravana, the only place where the demon king is a son of the soil, and Dasara is not a festival.” He adds that the village derives its name from Ravana’s father, sage Vishrava.
For decades, Bisrakh had one temple, a swayambhu (self-born) Shiva shrine, which was known as Ravana’s birthplace. Then, in 2000, the Shree Mohan Divya Yog Mandir came up, barely 300 metres away and contested the claim.
For Raj and several other content creators on social media, this is gold. People have told him that beginning a video at the temple could bring him luck. The algorithm — hungry for online newness that could spiral upward into a trend — may grant him his wish to be famous.
Divine dreams and a temple’s renewal
Mahant Ramdas, caretaker of the original temple most villagers regard as Ravana’s birthplace, has expanded the shrine into a sprawling complex. Hailing from Kanpur Dehat in Uttar Pradesh, Ramdas claims to have seen the temple in a “divine dream” over four decades ago. He sought it out and found the place lying neglected in the forest, he says.
It now has three worship areas, residential quarters for 10 priests, a bathing space, a garden, and a large open ground for festival gatherings.
He also managed to get huge land donations from villagers to construct another temple, in front of the existing one, dedicated to various goddesses.
He also governs another temple in Rajasthan, he claims, as his students travel across north India to perform Bhagwat Katha (reciting the holy book Bhagwat) and Rudrabhishek (a bathing ritual associated with Lord Shiva).
Pointing towards the dimly lit sanctum, Ramdas says that the Shivalinga inside is “taller than a mountain” and no one could dig its roots out. “When we tried to (during the reconstruction process), snakes started coming out from the earth. This work was stopped, and since then we have locked the basement of the sanctum,” he shares, further emphasising the ancientness of the temple.
The priest points towards a newly constructed section of the temple, where the bust of Ravana is placed side by side with Lord Rama.
“Nowhere in the world will you find Ravana being worshipped with Ram,” he says.
For Raj, this is precisely the kind of image that might attract travellers and pilgrims. As he pans his camera across the complex, he also captures boards bearing the names of donors.
He repeats several of the claims he hears from the priest and residents before pausing to ask Ramdas a question.
“How come Ravana, who was born to a sage in Greater Noida, became the king of Lanka, situated miles away?” he asks Ramdas. The priest offers Raj’s audience a legend.
“Parvati, Shiva’s wife, was adamant about having a palace of her own. Shiva commissioned the job to Vishwakarma, the divine architect, who crafted the breathtaking city of Lanka out of solid gold. To perform the house-warming, Vishrava, Ravana’s father, was called. Deeply pleased with Vishrava’s rituals, Shiva offered him anything he wanted,” Ramdas says. Driven by ambition, the sage asked for the golden city itself, he adds.
Shiva granted it, and that is how Lanka became the inherited realm of Vishrava’s lineage. It was first passed to Kubera, the god of wealth, before Ravana seized it from his half-brother and established his reign.
The Uttar Ramayana, which talks about the lives of Lord Rama and Sita after their return to Ayodhya, describes Ravana as the son of sage Vishrava and Kaikesi, the descendant of Pulastya, who is a mind-born son of Brahma. This claim is mentioned in mythological author Devdutt Pattanaik’s article titled: What is Ravana’s Surname? The article also mentions that the presence of Sal forests in his maternal region has led scholars to question the traditional belief that the early Ramayana’s geography extended far south of the Vindhya and Narmada rivers. Keen to boast of Ravana’s lineage, Ramdas adds, “Ravana was such a wise Brahmin that even Ram had performed penance and prayers after killing him.”
A new site and claims of an old home
In the newly built temple, Acharya Ashokanand repeats the story of Ravana’s journey to Lanka, adding that it is this temple’s premises that he was born in.
Ashokanand identifies himself as Mahamandaleshwar, a title given to Hindu monks within the Dashanami tradition of Shaivite ascetics. Ashokanand, who usually wears trousers and T-shirts, changes into a saffron robe whenever a devotee arrives at the temple. He also says Bisrakh is mentioned in the Shiva Purana, one of the 18 puranas in the series of religious texts. He immediately opens a page in Kalyan, a book published by Gita Press, which mentions a river called Harnad, which he claims is today’s Hindon and describes Bisrakh as the birthplace of Ravana and his half-brother Kubera.
“I do not contest the ancientness of the Shivlinga in the other temple. It was the place where Ravana’s father used to worship. But my temple was his house. People don’t give birth in temples. They give birth in homes. So the place I own is Ravana’s real janmabhoomi (birthplace),” he says, while drawing a parallel to the Ram janmabhoomi in Ayodhya.
Here, a temple was built at the exact site where the idol of Ram Lalla was placed in 1949. Over the years, it led courts to first lock up the Babri Mosque structure, then allow Hindu worship inside, eventually turning that spot into the legal anchor of the dispute.
In his temple, spread across about 1,600 metres, statues of various Hindu gods, including Rama and Hanuman, stand. Ravana’s is absent. “In 2016, I was the first to propose the installation of a statue of Ravana in the temple. But the statue was vandalised by fringe groups that opposed it. At that time, Ramdas also objected. He said that Ravana could not be worshipped as he was a demonic figure. But later, he himself installed Ravana’s statue,” he alleges. He adds that he has now ordered a taller statue of Ravana, which will be ready in time for Vijayadashami next year.
Claiming that the Ramayana, written by Valmiki, has unnecessarily vilified Ravana, Ashokanand says that the demon-king never abducted Sita with the aim of making her his queen. “He abducted Sita to ensure his own sister Surpanakha was safe. He never touched Sita. She was kept with an all-woman army. He never met Sita in Lanka,” he claims. When asked about Ravana proposing to Sita in Valmiki’s Ramayana, he says it has many flaws.
Over 300 versions of the Ramayana exist globally, ranging from Valmiki’s Sanskrit foundational text to international adaptations like Thailand’s Ramakien. Sri Lanka uniquely preserves this legacy through its own cultural lens, honouring king Ravana as a heroic ruler.
Meanwhile, in the village
Confused between the legacy claims of two temples situated within walking distance, Raj decides to speak to the residents of Bisrakh, which has a population of around 5,000 people, including Muslims.
In the village, signboards proudly advertise Raavan DJ, Raavan Kirana Store, and Raavan Hair Salon. Sonu, a student from the village, exaggerates for the reel, as he says, “Some villagers have even named their children after him”.
Dishondhi Saifi, 90, one of the village’s oldest residents, says he has not seen a Ramlila in Bisrakh ever in his lifetime. “Some people tried to organise the Ramlila performance, followed by the effigy burning of Ravana here, but young men died in the village mysteriously. After that, no one dared to celebrate Dasara,” he says.
Mr. Saifi’s claim is supported by Ajay Bhati, the last village head of Bisrakh before it became part of an urban civic body.
“Our village holds great religious importance. Despite Ravana abducting Sita, you cannot dispute his dedication to Shiva and his wisdom. I really feel that this place needs immediate attention from the government,” Mr. Bhati says, urging both the Central and Uttar Pradesh governments to include Bisrakh in the Ramayana circuit.
The Ramayana circuit is a religious tourism initiative developed by the Government of India to connect and upgrade the infrastructure of key cities associated with Lord Rama’s life.
“I have met the MP of our area [Mahesh Sharma], who was then an MoS (Minister of State) with the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, but he never paid heed to our requests,” he says, adding that the soil from Bisrakh was sent during the construction of the Ram temple in Ayodhya.
Bisrakh is not alone in honouring Ravana. He is also worshipped in Kanpur, Jodhpur, and Kakinada, where people celebrate his intellect and devotion to Shiva.
In Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh, locals even revere Ravana as their son-in-law, believing it to be the hometown of his wife Mandodari.
Beyond the mythology and folklore lies a complex web of caste politics. Dominating the demographic landscape of Bisrakh are the Gujjars, a prominent agricultural community in western Uttar Pradesh. Many villagers believe that Brahmin-dominated socio-religious institutions have intentionally suppressed the village’s historic heritage. “We cannot deny that Brahmins claim all religious landmarks. Maybe this is the reason why a Gujjar-majority village never got its due,” Bhati says. He supports Ramdas’s temple as the original birthplace of Ravana.
A pitch for development
Not everyone in Bisrakh is interested in choosing a side. Suman Devi, 64, visits the Shiva temple to offer prayers. She lights a diya before the Shivling as the smoke from incense curls through the courtyard. She does not visit the other temple, but believes, “Both temples are ours.”
Beyond the mythology and the rivalry, Bisrakh’s immediate concerns are more practical. Neighbouring areas in Greater Noida have transformed with glass-fronted office buildings and sprawling high-rise apartments, while Bisrakh still looks like a village with broken roads and homes where people cannot afford paint.
“People may disagree over which temple marks Ravana’s birthplace, but all of us want to put Bisrakh on the national pilgrimage map. The prospect of visitors brings the promise of better infrastructure and livelihoods, even if the scale of those benefits remains uncertain,” says Devi.
As Raj looks for one more detail to make his video stand out, he returns to the question that has animated his visit.
“We all know he died on Vijaydashmi. But when was he born?” he asks the priests.
Ramdas draws a blank, waving away the question. Ashokanand offers a vague reference to an ancient divine timeline which, he says, has not been recorded.
The question remains unanswered.
As twilight settles, Raj finishes editing his short video, adds a trending soundtrack, and puts it in drafts for a final review. He pulls on the shoes he had left outside the older temple.
On one wall, a hand-painted sign displays a phone number, inviting people of any religion to call and discuss whatever is troubling them.
Raj saves the number on his phone, seeing another possible angle for future content. Then he leaves Bisrakh’s dusty lanes behind.

A multiple sclerosis treatment from Novartis cut by a third the rates of relapses that people with the condition have compared to a standard treatment, data presented Friday show. While that efficacy doesn’t match the performance of a rival drug from Roche, Novartis’ treatment has a cleaner safety profile that could give it a shot at being competitive in the market.
In two Phase 3 studies in the relapsing form of MS, the Novartis drug, called remibrutinib, reduced the so-called annualized relapse rate by 35.2% and 31.2% when tested against Sanofi’s approved drug Aubagio. That translates into about one relapse every 13 years, Heinz Wiendl, a neurologist at the University of Freiburg, said while presenting the data from the REMODEL-1 and -2 studies at an MS conference in Toronto.
In its own pivotal studies, Roche’s drug fenebrutinib cut the relapse rate by more than 50% versus Aubagio.
Some analysts had said that if remibrutinib could reduce relapses by 40%, it could be competitive with fenebrutinib, given its cleaner safety profile. Remibrutinib did not quite meet that mark.
Novartis’s U.S.-listed shares were down 3.5% on Friday.
In the Roche trials, however, there was one case of what’s known as Hy’s Law, a sign that a patient is at risk of potentially fatal drug-induced liver injury. Other patients experienced elevated liver enzymes, a potentially worrisome sign.
There were no Hy’s Law cases in the remibrutinib studies, and elevated liver enzymes occurred at very low rates.
“We haven’t really seen a liver signal at all,” Wiendl said.
Liver safety issues have tripped up similarly designed drugs with the Food and Drug Administration, and some analysts have questioned whether U.S. regulators will approve fenebrutinib, even as Roche maintains its confidence in the drug.
Novartis said last month its two pivotal trials were positive, but had not released the full data until Friday at the MSToronto conference. The results were also published in the Lancet.
The stakes for the remibrutinib, already quite high, have only increased in recent weeks as Novartis saw two major trial blow-ups — one for a common heart disease risk factor, and one for a rare neuromuscular condition — that stoked concerns about the company’s pipeline and business development strategies as it navigates a major patent cliff.
Remibrutinib and fenebrutinib are what are known as BTK inhibitors, a new class of drugs that aim to quiet the activity of both B cells and the immune cells found specifically in the nervous system, called microglia. The hope is that taming those cells can reduce the attacks people with MS experience.
The FDA previously rejected Sanofi’s BTK inhibitor tolebrutinib in MS because of liver safety concerns, but it has won approval from regulators elsewhere, including in the European Union.
Remibrutinib is approved as Rhapsido for chronic spontaneous urticaria and symptomatic dermographism.

The Delhi High Court on Friday sought a response from the makers of "Doosra," a film directed by Abhinay Deo, to cricketer Sourav Ganguly's plea alleging infringement of his personality rights. The movie was released on 23 October. A vacation bench of Justice Vinod Kumar said it would consider interim relief concerning the film only after receiving the defendants’ responses. The bench also directed them to arrange a screening of the movie, PTI reported. Justice Kumar, who held court while the Delhi High Court was closed for the Dussehra break, issued summons to the film's producers, director, and distributor after a lawsuit was filed by Ganguly and Luv Films LLP, which is producing a biopic of the former cricket captain. The senior counsel for the makers of the film stated that it was not a biopic but a fictional story of a middle-class girl hailing from Rajasthan who gets inspired by certain sporting events involving the cricketer. Justice Kumar then said, "(The defendants to make) arrangements for playing the film so that it can be decided whether the personality rights of the plaintiff are violated or not." The defendants’ lawyer said it was too late to seek interim relief because the film had already been released, but the plaintiffs’ lawyer argued that the court could still order a stay. The development came after the high court on Thursday declined to halt the film's theatrical release. The filmmakers’ senior lawyer said permission to use clips featuring Ganguly had been obtained from the relevant rights holders. According to ANI, Ganguly moved the Delhi High Court ahead of "Doosra's" release and alleged that the movie uses references associated with his identity and cricketing career in a way that infringes upon his personality and commercial rights. The plea refers to Ganguly’s captaincy during India’s dramatic chase against England in the 2002 NatWest Series final and his shirtless celebration on the Lord’s balcony afterwards, a moment that remains etched in Indian cricket’s history. Ganguly's lawyer said the cricketer had not licensed the film's production. However, counsel for the "Doosra" makers argued that a player cannot claim personality rights over footage from the 2002 NatWest series. The cricketer has asked the court to protect his rights against what he alleges is the unauthorised use of his persona for commercial gain in the film. The case highlights questions about how filmmakers can depict celebrated athletes’ lives, achievements and iconic sporting moments, and when doing so could infringe their personality rights. In recent times, personality rights disputes have become increasingly common, with more celebrities moving the courts to protect their names, images, likenesses, and other attributes associated with their identities from alleged unauthorised commercial use. The Delhi High Court has scheduled the next hearing on Ganguly's plea for 29 October. Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

This week, Snopes received emails and searches from readers asking if U.S. President Donald Trump's administration chopped down 430 trees last weekend at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., the same site where Trump planned to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links property.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration revealed visual plans to overhaul the property into a championship-style golf course. Then, Trump announced on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin in September. The DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the project, with District Court Judge Ana Reyes presiding over the case.
One reader asked us via email, "Did the Trump administration order removal of 430 trees from the East Potomac Golf Links?" People shared the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and other social media platforms.
In sum, the claim that the Trump administration cut down and planned the removal of 430 trees from the same park where planned golf course renovations will take place is true. 
A memorandum opinion that Reyes authored on Tuesday, in which she granted an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order in the DC Preservation League's case against the Interior Department, confirmed the tree cutting was taking place. That order blocked the Trump administration from continuing the work for two weeks, through Oct. 26.
Reyes' opinion, arriving one day after an emergency hearing on Monday, specifically mentioned the suddenness of crews cutting down 430 "healthy, non-invasive" trees, with the government only notifying the court minutes prior to close of business on a holiday weekend. She also noted the Trump administration argued the removals aligned with recommendations in a 2019 National Park Service report, leading Reyes to write she was "skeptical" of the timing. More about that report appears later in this article.
Snopes' email correspondence with the Interior Department, in which a department spokesperson appeared to indirectly acknowledge that crews cut down hundreds of trees with no reasonable notice to the court, also appears later in this article. We emailed the park service, an agency the Interior Department oversees, and the White House, as well as the DC Preservation League to ask for additional documentation and a statement, and will update this article if we receive further information.
430 trees cut down with very little notice
Reyes' opinion, handed down on Tuesday, laid out the timeline of events:
- Tree-cutting plans began internally within the Interior Department at least early last week.
- The government provided unreasonable notice to the court (at 4:55 p.m. last Friday) of its plans to remove "up to 529 trees" to restore the golf course's "historic links-style character."
- Tree-cutting work began 15 hours later at 8 a.m. on Saturday.
- An emergency hearing occurred the following Monday — on Columbus Day, a federal holiday.
During the Monday hearing, Reyes reportedly said she was "furious" that the government told the court they knew of the tree-cutting plans at least days earlier than they notified the court. In May, she told the government she wanted to receive notice if crews planned to remove more than 10 trees, the Associated Press reported.
An NBC4 Washington journalist reported, "In all of my years of covering court proceedings, I have never seen a judge so angry," adding Reyes was "raising her voice" at government attorneys.
Reyes wrote in the opinion:
The Government then did precisely what Plaintiffs feared. Sometime between the September 3 hearing and October 2, plans moved from removing only hazardous, dead, dying, or invasive trees to removing hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees. And then it removed them without providing meaningful notice to Plaintiffs or the Court.
Reyes wrote that Trump administration lawyers said the Interior Department "ordered, considered and approved" a plan for the park service to oversee the cutting down of hundreds of trees, as well as that the government said it knew of no reason for any urgency to complete the work. She said the administration acknowledged in court that crews cut down 430 nonhazardous trees, adding that "about 300 additional trees are on the literal chopping block" but weren't yet fallen thanks to a "rain delay." (A tally of well over 700 targeted trees exceeded the "up to 529 trees" part of the notice Reyes said the government provided.)
Journalists live-posting from Reyes' courtroom on Monday documented the administration's mention of chopping down 430 nonhazardous trees and planning to cut 299 more — out of the park's roughly 3,800 total trees.
We emailed Riverbend Tree Service in Virginia, a company with crews that appeared in a local news video report, to ask if its workers were present and when they first learned of the job, among other questions, and will update this story should we receive details.
Interior Department response, 2019 plans
In an email to Snopes, an Interior Department spokesperson chided Reyes for her involvement with the case and didn't directly respond to our request to confirm the department ordered and approved the removal of hundreds of trees with very little notice. The email appeared to only indirectly confirm the tree-removal work.
The department spokesperson described the current state of the golf course as "riddled with garbage and choked by overgrown trees" and that "the work carries out a plan, seven years in the making, to address tree overgrowth" at the park.
Reyes wrote that the government claimed the tree-cutting work, referenced as a Tree Management Plan (TMP), applied to a Cultural Landscape Report the park service authored during Trump's first term in 2019, and had "nothing to do with" Trump's golf course plans. She continued, "The Court is skeptical," and wrote:
The Government claims that the TMP implements a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report and has nothing to do with the Washington National Plan. It is a coincidence, the Government seems to suggest, that DOI cut down hundreds of trees at the Course weeks after the President asked DOI to cut down trees at the Course, and not, say, any other time in the last seven years.
That 2019 report credited golf course architect Walter J. Travis with designing "the original links-style, eighteen-hole course" in 1917 and emphasized retaining the character and history of the property. One part of the report said the early design of East Potomac Park Golf Course (EPPGC) originally largely lacked trees:
Links–style courses typically have very few trees and shrubs. Too many trees would interfere with the characteristic views and ever–present wind.
At EPPGC there were some trees originally, but overwhelmingly the property was treeless allowing for views across the golf course and to the surrounding water. Many trees have grown up within the course due to lack of maintenance, creation of dumping areas, and aggressive planting without regard to the history or function of the golf course. Trees and understory will have to be managed in order for EPPGC to return to its links character.
The Interior Department's email response to Snopes featured three attached images allegedly showing glimpses of a large garbage problem at the park. We followed up to ask if the images showed debris from Trump's White House East Wing demolition, seeing as crews reportedly began dumping debris from the construction site of Trump's ballroom project on the golf course last October. A department spokesperson denied it with a one-word answer: "No."
For further reading, we previously reported about a similar rumor alleging Trump ordered the removal of cherry trees from the same park, the site of the nation's first cherry blossom planting. Reyes' opinion didn't mention anything about the removal of cherry trees.

Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after a two-week closure following strikes from Yemen's Houthis on the Saudi capital, though the Iran-backed group warned of more to come.
The Flight Radar monitoring site showed a plane taking off from Riyadh airport early Sunday (October 25, 2026), heading to the Saudi city of Jeddah.
Saudi Arabia, along with Yemen's internationally recognised government that it backs, has faced a wave of Houthi attacks in recent weeks after a years-long truce broke down in the summer.
The fighting has shifted the focus of the wider U.S-Iran war and deepened a humanitarian disaster crippling Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries.
"Please be advised that Terminal (1) will be designated for domestic flights and Terminal (2) for international flights operated by national carriers at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, effective Sunday, October 25, 2026," King Khalid International Airport posted on X on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on Riyadh's airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional, and local airlines, as well as staff and travellers, against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said. "The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport,” he added.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said early Sunday (October 25, 2026) it had shot down two drones in the Riyadh area.

An Indian expatriate who won 100 million dirham (approximately ₹240 crore) in The UAE Lottery has spoken about how the windfall has changed his life a year after the win. Anilkumar Bolla, a 29-year-old technology professional based in Abu Dhabi, won the jackpot in October 2025. Since then, he has purchased properties in India and the UAE, bought cars for himself and his brother, gifted gold jewellery to his mother and acquired farmland for his father. Reflecting on the past year, Bolla, who hails from Telangana, said the biggest change has been the opportunity to spend more time with his family. Bolla won what was described as the largest lottery prize ever awarded in the UAE when he secured the 100 million dirham jackpot in October 2025. Speaking about the year since his win, he said spending time with his family had become a priority. “The most important thing is that I am spending quality time with my family,” he was quoted as saying by Khaleej Times. Describing the experience as “transformative”, he added: “Winning the lottery reshaped my life and my ambitions as well.” The money has also enabled him to enjoy material comforts. Over the past year, Bolla has purchased an iPhone 17 Air and four to five high-end watches. However, he said helping his family has been among the most meaningful outcomes of his lottery win. One of his early purchases was gold jewellery for his mother. “It was her dream to have a few ornaments, so I brought it all together and gifted it to her,” he said, according to Gulf News. The gift brought tears to her eyes. Bolla comes from a farming family in Telangana. Although he has purchased properties in India and the UAE since winning the jackpot, his family continues to live in the same house they occupied before his ₹240 crore lottery win. Bolla describes the house as his father's dream home. He has, however, gifted his father farmland where he can pursue his interest in organic farming. "My happiness is always linked to my family," he said. "Whatever I've done for them, those things are really special to me, and those are the things that make me the happiest, more than what I do for myself." A year after his win, Bolla says the excitement he initially felt about travelling has faded. During the past 12 months, he has travelled to several destinations and enjoyed new experiences with his family. Bali, Thailand and Amsterdam were among the places he visited. "Somehow, the excitement has faded away, but I'm really grateful for the opportunities I'm getting and the things I'm doing," he said. With many of his wishes fulfilled, Bolla has begun exploring potential business ideas and long-term financial planning. His investments include property near the airport in Abu Dhabi and at Dubai Marina. Asked what advice he would offer other lottery winners, the Indian techie said: “Welcome to the millionaires’ club. AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron has issued an open letter to New York City residents reiterating the company’s desire to continue operating its longstanding Kips Bay 15 multiplex in the Manhattan neighborhood of that name, but concedes the decision is not AMC’s to make.
Neighbors of the Kips Bay-Murray Hill section of Manhattan along Second Avenue near the East River have been vocal about the planned closure of the multiplex that’s been a central commercial hub since 1999 (AMC took over the venue in 2006). The property on which the multiplex sits was privately purchased last year by NYU Langone, one of New York’s major health care systems.
AMC announced in August that the purchase would likely mean the closure of the multiplex by the end of this year, prompting an outcry and protests from residents and other businesses in the area.
Watch on Deadline
Following “direct engagement” from Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, AMC’s Aron issued the open letter concurring with Hoylman-Sigal that the neighborhood needs such amenities as a movie theater, supermarket and housing.
Writes Aron, “Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.”
Read the entire statement below.
“AMC Theatres does not want to go,” Aron writes. “Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay….Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours. Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make.”
According to Aron, the NYU Langone Health facility “wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.”
Aron notes that AMC has “engaged” with NYU Langone to suggest various alternatives that would allow the multiplex to continue operating in some form. “Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds,” he writes, adding, “We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.”
The AMC chief warns that time is running out for the venue. “Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.”
