Can a dream help you solve a problem? Here's how to try tonight
We spend about two hours every night making home movies in our minds. Over a lifetime, that adds up to about seven years of dreaming.
For most of human history, those movies were considered sacred. Many early civilizations believed dreams were messages from the gods. In ancient Greece, people slept in temples hoping a dream would bring guidance or healing.
By the 1970s, scientists took a far less romantic view. A few psychiatrists likened dreams to the brain's attempt to make sense of random signals, and their theory threw cold water on the idea that dreams were meaningful.
Psychologist Rosalind Cartwright, known to colleagues as the "Queen of Dreams," pushed back. She believed dreamwork could be a form of therapy and made her case in books including Crisis Dreaming, co-written with Lynne Lamberg and The Twenty-Four Hour Mind. She published many studies from her lab experiments.
Today there's a resurgence of interest and new research. And one ancient practice is getting a fresh look: dream incubation, planting a question in your mind before sleep in hopes your dreams will offer insights.
It may sound mystical, but there's research behind it. In a small study from the 1990s an instructor at Harvard Medical School asked college students to focus on a problem at bedtime. About half reported a dream related to it, and many felt the dream contained a solution.
Jungian analyst Lisa Marchiano uses the practice with people navigating challenges and midlife transitions. The first step, she says, is asking a good question, and that takes time. "You want to ask a question that could be answered," Marchiano says. Skip yes-or-no questions. Instead, make it targeted but open-ended. If you're weighing a job offer, ask, "What would it look like if I took this job?" or "What would it look like if I went on another date with this person?"
Next, write down what you already know about the problem. "You're looking for the stuff you don't know," she says. "You want to invite your unconscious to fill in the gaps."
In other words, consult your inner "dream maker." As Marchiano puts it, "Instead of going to ChatGPT, try going to your dream maker."
Finally, turn it into a ritual so it doesn't feel like one more chore. You could take a bath as a way to wind down as you set an intention or "ask" for a dream. Marchiano says she writes her question in her journal, then copies it onto a slip of paper, folds it and tucks it into a small velvet bag to put under her pillow.
How to try dream incubation tonight:
- Think of a challenge, decision or problem you face. Write it down as an open-ended question.
- Review it before lights out. If you can, place a related picture or object by your bed.
- As you drift off, tell yourself you'd like to dream about it.
- Keep a pen and notebook on your nightstand.
- When you wake up, lie still before reaching for your phone. Jot down anything you remember, even a fragment or an emotion.
That last step matters. Many people say they don't remember their dreams, and the window is short. "You only have about three to five minutes to remember," says Dr. Harrison Shong-Wen Chow, a Stanford anesthesiologist. Writing a dream down or telling someone helps move it into long-term memory, he says.
Chow's own research explores something even more surprising: how dreams under anesthesia may help people process fear and trauma. There's also research into how an electronic device may help deliver dream prompts for targeted dream incubation.
Be patient. Dream incubation may not yield anything the first night, and dream recall is subjective. But over time, the practice may lead to a fresh insight, or at least a new way of listening to yourself.
To hear more about how to unlock the power of your dreams, listen to the new episode of Your Turn w/ Allison Aubrey wherever you get your podcasts and follow our Your Turn newsletter to help navigate the twists and turns of midlife.

Twenty-one-year-old Saouhum Sharma, a 4th-year History honours student at Hans Raj College, joined the October 12 rally led by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi to the Supreme Court. By the end of the day, a knife had been slashed across his throat.
The Assault
Sharma and three friends met at Barakhamba Road at 2 pm. They subsequently met more friends and made their way to Mandi House.
“It wasn’t too chaotic at first,” he told Alt News. “We got the call from some Indian Youth Congress (IYC) people who were leading the protest around the area that Rahul Gandhi and everyone was reaching the Supreme Court; we should also reach the Supreme Court. The route from Mandi House to the Supreme Court is a straight road. So we decided to just start walking there. It was two groups of IYC workers and us.”
By 5.40 pm, the group had made some headway towards the Supreme Court when they encountered police barricades. “Some of the IYC people tried to topple the barricades but could not. So we went through a cut onto Sikandra Road.”
As they walked along Sikandra Road, they came across around 15 men standing beside a jeep. Sharma said some appeared to be Hindutva workers, based on what they were wearing.
“They were donning some markers of Hindutva workers. A couple of ‘gamchas’, one in a saffron-coloured T-shirt. Nothing overt, but definitely visible,” he said.
Initially, the men were provocative rather than violent, Sharma recalled. “They were whistling at the female IYC workers — whistling and calling after them. They called a few of them ‘chikni’. They were calling them while standing 20 metres ahead on the side of the road; arms around each other’s shoulders. From afar, they did not look like they would interfere because we outnumbered them. So we didn’t really think of turning back.”
However, as the group approached, the men began taking saffron flags with long poles out of the jeep. “They still weren’t exactly being violent, just provocative.”
Asked whether the men identified themselves as members of any organisation, Sharma said they did not. The flags, too, did not name any organisation, he said. They were generic saffron flags bearing images of an angry Hanuman or the Ram Mandir.
“The men decided to swing the poles, and the IYC workers got a bit agitated, and a bit of a brawl ensued between them; the IYC workers got into an argument with the goons,” Sharma said.
Amid the confrontation, a young man, whom Sharma estimated to be 18 or 19, entered their group. He was not wearing any of the visible markers that Sharma had associated with the men beside the jeep.
“Then this one guy, he was probably 18-19 years old, made his way inside our group. He wasn’t wearing any of those identifiable markers. So we couldn’t tell that he was from the other group. He stood beside me for about five seconds and then… it happened quite quickly.”
“He pulled out a barber’s knife. My friend saw it and dragged me towards herself at which point he swung the blade. He missed my face, and it grazed my neck. He walked away after that.”
Sharma said it took him some time to realise what had happened. “I felt a sting in my neck and realised I was bleeding. At that point, we walked away from the group and decided to head home.”
Encounter with Police
After walking around 500 metres from the spot of the assault, Sharma and his friends encountered a police official on Sikandra Marg, who spotted the blood on Sharma and called out to them.
“He was drinking chai by a police vehicle, wearing a light green vest. There wasn’t a lot of police presence at that point, as we were a little far from the protest site. He offered to give us a ride after he saw the blood,” Sharma said.
As the group considered the offer, the officer turned to the driver seated in the vehicle and asked him to detain them, Sharma alleged. “We got scared, turned him down and left. He insisted at first but didn’t follow us when we left. We immediately left the vicinity of the protest site, went to the Jama Masjid metro station and left.”
According to Sharma, the police official was not wearing a name tag.
“Thankfully, the cut wasn’t that deep as he missed my face and the knife only grazed my neck. After returning, I cleaned the wound a bit and then got a tetanus shot,” he said.

Fantasy to imagine collegium isolated from political pressure: Ex-SC judge Sanjay Kaul; flags Centre’s NJAC grudge
Justice Kaul traces this dynamic to the political establishment’s inability to reconcile itself to the top court’s move striking down the NJAC in October 2015.
The collegium may be the Supreme Court’s answer to keeping political influence out of judicial appointments, but it has never been insulated from the pressures of the political establishment, former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul writes in his forthcoming memoir, arguing that the government’s lingering resentment over the scrapping of the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) in 2015 has shaped its dealings with the judiciary ever since.
“It is fantasy to imagine that the collegium is isolated from political pressures,” Justice Kaul writes in Without Fear or Favour, to be published by Juggernaut Books later this month, offering an account of the appointment process that is as much an indictment of its informal workings as it is a critique of former Chief Justice of India (CJI) Dhananjaya Y Chandrachud’s approach to the government.
Justice Kaul underlines that the problem is not consultation between the judiciary and the executive, which he considers inevitable, but the point at which consultation becomes an attempt to secure the government’s approval before judges have even deliberated on a candidate.
“There is a difference between consultation and what I came to regard as pre-approval -- seeking the government’s nod before the collegium had even formally deliberated…Any political class will always assert itself if you give them a wedge in the door,” he writes.
Justice Kaul traces this dynamic to the political establishment’s inability to reconcile itself to the Supreme Court’s decision striking down the NJAC in October 2015. The commission, created through a constitutional amendment and a companion law passed with overwhelming parliamentary support, would have included the Union law minister and two eminent persons alongside three senior judges. Any two members could have blocked a proposed appointment. A five-judge Constitution bench struck down the arrangement by a 4:1 majority, restoring the collegium system. To be sure, the collegium system resulted from Supreme Court rulings in the 1990s, giving the judiciary primacy in making recommendations for appointments to the constitutional courts.
Justice Kaul himself believes the NJAC should have been allowed to function before being rejected outright, even as he draws a distinction between disagreeing with a constitutional ruling and disregarding it.
“Once the Supreme Court has ruled on a constitutional question, that law must stand as declared, and it is incumbent upon the political branches to follow the system in letter and spirit,” he writes.
His account of the friction with Justice Chandrachud is rooted in this distinction. Justice Kaul, who joined the Supreme Court collegium in June 2022 and retired in December 2023, says he repeatedly argued that the court needed to engage the government firmly but collectively. He believed the chief justice was “too deferential” on appointments and preferred to manage the relationship with the executive himself.
Yet Justice Kaul’s criticism extends beyond the personalities involved. He acknowledges that the collegium itself is “deeply imperfect”, with opacity, excessive concentration of power and informal channels leaving the process vulnerable to pressure.
One of his most revealing accounts concerns a candidate from a minority faith whose elevation was questioned by the government. According to Justice Kaul, the government first raised the question of whether the Supreme Court needed additional representation from that faith, despite the candidate being from a state under-represented on the court. A further query concerned the caste to which the candidate’s family had belonged before converting to the faith.
The former top court judge found the question irrelevant and the reasoning troubling. He says he told Justice Chandrachud that if appointments were to be made on such considerations, the government might as well appoint judges itself. He then shut the file and walked out of the collegium meeting. The meeting was adjourned, and the government eventually relented.
“Governments assert themselves: If you give them an opening, they will grab it,” he writes, adding that the challenge is to maintain institutional integrity while navigating these pressures.
Responding to Justice Kaul’s account, former CJI Chandrachud said it would be difficult for him to comment on what Justice Kaul had written, as he had not yet read the book. “Unless I read his observations and understand the context in which they were made, I would not be in a position to offer a detailed response,” he added.
Justice Chandrachud, however, added that the collegium’s official records showed that its resolutions, along with the reasons for its recommendations, were made public on the Supreme Court’s website and that the decisions were unanimous, with Justice Kaul endorsing every recommendation.
Justice Chandrachud added there was not a single instance of Justice Kaul recording a dissent when the collegium formally proposed candidates to the government for appointment as judges. He said this was an important part of the record to consider while assessing the decision-making process.
Justice Chandrachud also emphasised that collegium decisions were not arrived at abruptly in meetings. “Judges held multiple rounds of informal and formal discussions before names were officially considered and recommendations sent to the government”, he said, adding that Justice Kaul had never walked out of any such meeting. According to Chandrachud, the meetings were conducted in a congenial atmosphere.
Meanwhile, Justice Kaul’s proposed answer to the collegium’s shortcomings was not merely to insist on a firmer line with the executive. He also wanted judges to examine the work of the candidates they were considering, according to his memoir.
When he entered the collegium under Chief Justice NV Ramana, Justice Kaul insisted that the judgments and disposal records of candidates be circulated before discussions on appointments. He argued that it was extraordinary that judges could be considered for elevation to the Supreme Court without their colleagues first examining their judicial work.
Ramana told him that this had not been the established practice and that collecting the material would take time, but Justice Kaul refused to allow the process to proceed without it.
“How could we assess a judge’s suitability for the Supreme Court without reading their prominent judgments?” he asks in the memoir, arguing that both the quality of judgments and the speed with which cases were disposed of mattered.
The practice was adopted when Justice Uday U Lalit became chief justice in August 2022. Soft copies of judgments began to be circulated before collegium meetings, allowing members to scrutinise a candidate’s judicial record before making up their minds. Justice Chandrachud continued the practice.
Justice Kaul describes this as a lasting reform that brought “a semblance of professionalism” to a system whose opacity and accountability deficit remain legitimate concerns.
Justice Kaul further recounts instances in which the government eventually accepted the collegium’s recommendations after he intervened directly, including cases involving appointments to the Delhi High Court and the proposed chief justice of a large high court. His experience, he writes, reinforced a conviction that governments are more likely to respect a judiciary that stands its ground.
“The government respects judges who respect themselves,” writes Justice Kaul, while adding: “Perhaps it is too idealistic to expect the government to not attempt to influence the process. It is unlikely that any government in independent India has risen to that standard, but at the very least, judges should be expected to stand up for their institution.”
Justice Kaul retired as a judge of the Supreme Court in December 2023. He was part of the collegium and authored several important judgments after his elevation to the Supreme Court on February 17, 2017. Prior to this, he had also served as chief justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court and the Madras High Court.

What kind of cooling system do EV batteries use and how does it work?
Most EVs pump coolant through the battery pack.
Have you ever pulled into a fast charging station on a freezing morning without notifying your EV first, and found that it charges more slowly? Turns out that if you set that same charger as a destination in the car's navigation, many EVs will use the time it takes to drive there to prepare the battery. It's something Tesla's manual tells owners to do 30 to 45 minutes before arriving, while Porsche goes so far as to warn that, without doing so, a vehicle's charging power might be lower.
This warm-up routine is part of an EV battery's thermal management system in most modern cars. Alongside it is usually a cooling loop, which uses liquid coolant pumped via tubes or metal plates pressed against the battery, collecting heat and carrying it to a radiator or into the car's air conditioning system.
Why EV batteries need cooling
Fleet management company Geotab tracked more than 22,700 EVs for a study and found that, on average, batteries lost 2.3 percent of their health each year. Cars in hot climates lost about 0.4 percentage points more a year than those in mild ones, while cars that frequently used fast chargers above 100 kW lost 3 percent a year against 1.5 percent for those that rarely did.
At the average rate, a battery would still be at roughly 77 percent after a decade, in line with research suggesting that EV batteries can last much longer than experts first predicted. When fast charging, where 300 amps or more can be pushed through the battery pack, a lot of waste heat is generated and needs to be removed. In 2021, a review in the journal Energies found that more than a 5 degree Celsius temperature difference across a cell can speed up aging by 25 percent, meaning that a good cooling system has to keep the whole pack both balanced and regulated.
In a cold battery, internal resistance climbs, and fast charging one can cause lithium plating, a buildup of metallic lithium on the cell's electrodes that can get worse as temperatures drop. Recurrent, which studied more than 30,000 US EVs, found that batteries averaged 78 percent of their ideal range at freezing temperatures, and around 70 percent at -7 degrees Celsius. Cabin heating accounts for about two-thirds of the extra energy an EV uses in the cold.
Air, liquid and refrigerant cooling
The original Nissan Leaf, from way back in 2010, used passive air cooling for its 24 kWh pack, while Tesla, GM and Ford used liquid systems. Leaf owners in Phoenix tested 12 cars from the 2011 and 2012 model years and found range losses, which Nissan said affected fewer than 0.3 percent of US models, as noted by MIT Technology Review in 2012. The third-generation Leaf Nissan unveiled in 2025 finally switched to a liquid-cooled 75 kWh battery. The benefit of liquid cooling is that it needs two to three times less energy than air to hold a pack at the same temperature, according to Energies, and most EVs now use it as a result.
The engineers behind BMW's i3 decided to skip the coolant loop entirely, and instead opted to run refrigerant from its AC straight to the battery. British automaker McLaren went a step further with its Speedtail by submerging all its cells in an electrically insulated oil, a step it called a first for a production road car. Simulations cited in the Energies review found that immersion cooling like this could move heat up to three times better than cooling plates.
Where does all the heat go?
A battery's coolant loop will usually be linked to a radiator for light loads and, through a heat exchanger, to the car's air conditioning for heavier methods like fast charging.
Let's take Nissan's thermal management system as an example: It switches between the two modes and routes heat from the charger into the battery during home charging, a feature that the newer Leaf model uses to warm it up. Tesla's Model Y, meanwhile, uses a valve nicknamed the "Octovalve" to move coolant between the motors, battery and electronics, as Jalopnik found following an engineering teardown. Tesla is also exploring a patent on running the drive motor inefficiently on purpose, so that its waste heat can warm the battery.
General Motors says that its Ultium heat pump collects waste heat from the battery, power electronics and even passengers' bodies to warm the cabin, which adds around 10 percent more range. China has recently introduced new rules that require new EVs to show that their batteries don't catch fire or blow up when a cell goes into thermal runaway. That requirement, however, depends on the pack's cooling and insulation stopping heat from spreading to other cells.

We cannot fight until the last Ukrainian – it’s time to call Putin’s bluff
The surge in civilian casualties in Ukraine shows how the West, including the UK, must defend Kyiv’s airspace or face worse in the future, explains world affairs editor Sam Kiley

A grim, expensive, choice faces Europe and the United Kingdom. Take on Russia in Ukraine or wait for the fight to come into our homes. Prepping for Armageddon by stockpiling tins of rice pudding, water and wind-up radios will mean nothing if the fight is not taken to the enemy.
Ukraine has proved this. And the suffering being endured across the country as the Trump administration has sabotaged Kyiv’s weapons systems shows how far Vladimir Putin will go to achieve his ends – a nihilistic fetish for chaos among his rivals.
As Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said this week: “Terms like hybrid warfare and grey zone threats do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as state-sponsored terrorism.
“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.”
In real muscular terms, and in the very short term, “national defence” should include the consideration of deploying Nato forces into Ukraine to protect its civilian population.
Existing anti-missile systems have been mostly exhausted. Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population, its train networks, heavy industry and data centres are all being targeted with the intent to break the will of the nation so that it will cave in to Russian demands and sue for peace.
A ceasefire or even peace deal that freezes the front lines where they are might look good for Ukraine, but it will be catastrophic for the West.
Russia will use a window of peace to rearm, retrain, and re-equip forces that are the second most proficient in the use of modern weapons on Earth. State-sponsored Russian interference and terrorism will continue.
Western democracies, already trying to cope with the crumbling economic aftermath of neoliberal economics and populations equally unrealistic about what free services they are “owed” by their states, will be unable to resist the Kremlin’s destablisation campaign.
This isn’t hyperbole, this is the reality that will unfold because the West isn’t prepared to invest in protecting the freedoms and democracy that Vladimir Putin wants to destroy in Ukraine and beyond.
There’s no case for going to war. There is a strong case for the “below the threshold” war or conflict that Russia is already prosecuting.
Nato can, and arguably should, get involved in very aggressive defence of Ukraine. Not because we are morally outraged by Russia’s murder of toddlers and children, or its massacre and hunting safaris against the elderly on the streets, but because it is in the interests of the West to do so.
Justin Bronk, an aviation expert at the Royal United Services Institute has taken a look at what could be done to protect Ukraine against Geran jet-powered missiles or drones. These are the old Shaheds but capable of flying at up to 500 kmph carrying a warhead of around 90kg, painted in black and often launched in swarms.
“A dedicated multinational Nato squadron of armed jet trainers could shoot down Russian drone incursions without burning through frontline fighters and scarce air-to-air missiles,” Bronk writes in a recent paper for Rusi, the military establishment’s think tank.
Ukrainian jets have shot down drones including Gerans and even ballistic missiles. The 11th Separate Army Aviation Brigade recently posted a video of a rear gunner, leaning out of the back seat of a Yak-52 propeller plane, to shoot down a Russian drone in flight.
Bronk argues that Nato could deploy small jet training aircraft with two seats, one for the gunner or weapons officer, to bring down Gerans and other missiles and drones, in a new anti-drone squadron.
Tasked with only defending Ukraine but legally able to protect itself, with say advanced Nato fighter jets like F-35 and Typhoon, a Nato squadron could plug the gap in Ukraine’s air defences and send a message to Putin that “we see see you and we raise you”.
Nato, without the US, easily outmatches Russia’s military capacity. Its full force is being held back by a small nation of only 40 million.
Nato, without the US, has almost twice as many aircraft in every category, as Russia. It has a bigger navy by 4.5 times and almost twice as many submarines.
Russia does not appear to be afraid of being attacked by nuclear weapons, which Putin and his flunkies have threatened to use against Nato countries or Ukraine. The Kremlin is unmoved by a nuclear threat from non-US Nato – perhaps because Russia has eight times as many nukes.
But also because the Kremlin understands the insanity of MAD, Mutually Assured Destruction. Putin knows that the West is never likely to drop The Bomb.
Current evidence, though, is that places like the UK are preparing for cyber attacks and other mayhem by hoarding baked beans and loo paper.
International Monetary Fund data shows that Russia’s GDP places it as No 8 in the world, below the UK and France. Add the UK into the European Union and it emerges that the bloc is the second-largest economy on Earth at over $27 trillion in GDP – almost 10 times the size of Russia’s.
So far all this “superiority” has amounted to projecting fear and weakness to a bully in the Kremlin, and his fellow bully in the Oval Office.
Ukraine’s parliament has long called for a no-fly zone of the kind that saved the Kurds in Iraq from Saddam Hussein and Kosovo from Serb extremism in the 1990s and early 2000s.
It is time that Europe and the UK admitted to their populations that it is time to call Putin’s bluff. Fighting to the last Ukrainian is no longer an option.

Why your Ring camera is still useful without a subscription
Patrolling your porch or pets doesn’t require a monthly fee.
Beyond serving as a fully functional doorbells, the Ring Camera lineup still offers plenty of solid use cases. Unfortunately, like most smart gadgets, whether fitness trackers or bird feeders, you'll need a monthly subscription to unlock all of its features.
With three tiers to choose from, starting at $4.99/month, keeping your home fully secure comes at an added cost that might put you off. On the bright side, you can get by without a subscription, unless you need to access saved footage for future reference. Ring cameras can still operate as a live intercom that'll come in handy whether you're home or on the go.
The company has garnered some bad press over the last year, but its security cameras still provide protection and some peace of mind for owners, with or without the monthly fee.
It's best for parents, pets and packages
The Two-Way Talk and Live Feed features help in many scenarios. Even when you're home and just waiting on someone, you can see exactly who's at the door and talk to them through the app before getting up to answer it.
Personally, whether dealing with weak water pressure or other household issues, there've been plenty of times when a maintenance technician waited outside my door and rang the bell, letting me speak with them through the Ring app so I could give an ETA for when I'd be back home. If you're a parent who wants to keep an eye on your young ones from another room, the free tier is a great choice.
Similarly, indoor Ring cameras do the trick for pet owners without a subscription. Using your phone, you can keep an eye on them when you're out for the day or ask "who's a good dog?" with Two-Way Talk. The association between pets and Ring cameras is a touchy subject, however.
If you travel often and want to make sure there's no funny business in or outside the house, or an eye on incoming packages, the free plan is a great choice. On the contrary, with porch pirates on the rise, subscribing to one of Ring's plans makes sense if you've had items stolen and want access to the footage.
What are some problems with Ring?
While they have benefits, Ring cameras also come with a fair share of privacy concerns, which both owners and disavowers have raised for years.
For starters, the Familiar Faces feature that debuted last year, which uses AI to recognize which friend, neighbor or relative is at your door, led to a recent lawsuit that suggested Ring and Amazon were collecting facial recognition information unbeknownst to plenty of people who walked by a Ring camera.
This suit follows widespread backlash of this year's Super Bowl commercial, which framed the AI-assisted Search Party feature as a way to find lost dogs. Of course, no one is complaining about seeking out missing pets, but people are worried about the mass surveillance.
The lawsuit and commercials came months after Ring partnered with Flock Safety in 2025, originally permitting law enforcement to request footage from Ring owners. Following widespread reactions to the pet-focused commercial, that deal was dismantled days after the Super Bowl.
In an effort to ward off negative reactions, the Amazon-owned company's recent TAKE software update (Throw Away the Key Encryption) asserts that "Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys," putting people in full control of who can access footage. Ring likens it to a pair of house keys, as only the owner can decide who gets a spare.

Celebrity shark returns to South Korea canal after failed rescue
- Published
A famed dusky shark in South Korea has returned to the canal where she had been stuck for a month, just one day after authorities said they had successfully guided her out, local media report.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after she was spotted lingering in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
South Korea's oceans ministry said on Wednesday evening they had led Bukangi out of the canal into an open harbour - but reports later said the shark had swum back to the mouth of the canal, having apparently broken through a barrier installed by authorities.
Another operation to relocate Bukangi has been scheduled for Thursday.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In recent weeks, more than 1.6 million visitors have descended upon a park in Busan to catch a glimpse of Bukangi, named after the canal in which she was spotted.
Her popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating. There were concerns that she would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans cheered and waved goodbye to their shark, unaware that she would still be lingering in the canal by the next day.
Before Wednesday's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

Anthony Ippolito had to do more than nail Sylvester Stallone’s signature voice to play him in “I Play Rocky.”
He also had to transform his skinny physique to one with bulging muscles.
“It had its moments for sure. I was being tested,” Ippolito told me Saturday at the AFI Fest “I Play Rocky” screening in Los Angeles. “It’s like a consistency thing, though. I had a great deal of time, so just an entire lifestyle shift and it was just one of the priorities of every day for a pretty long period.”
As Ippolito previously told Variety’s Clayton Davis, he spent nearly two years bulking up from about 150 pounds to roughly 180 while training at Gleason’s Gym in Brooklyn.
Popular on Variety
What did family and friends think?
“It happened over time, but a couple of people were like, ‘What’s going on?’” Ippolito recalled. “They didn’t necessarily know I was doing the prep, and they were like, ‘What’s going on here?’ I was like, ‘I’ve been going to the gym, been eating.’”
“I Play Rocky,” directed by Peter Farrelly, follows Stallone’s journey to get “Rocky” made in 1976. Now considered one of the greatest films ever made, the odds were way more against Stallone than with him when he first pitched the movie in Hollywood.
AnnaSophia Robb plays Stallone’s first wife, Sasha, in “I Play Rocky.” Stephan James portrays Carl Weathers. Rounding out the cast are Kiki Seto, P.J. Byrne, Matt Dillon, Tracy Letts and Jay Duplass.
If jitters on the first day of filming weren’t already enough to contend with, Ippolito’s first scenes were with a dog playing Stallone’s pooch Butkus. Stallone famously sold Butkus for $40 when before he found fame because he couldn’t afford to feed him. After selling the “Rocky” script, he bought him back for $15,000.
“I hadn’t met that specific dog until like the day prior to shooting,” Ippolito said. “He didn’t happen to take a liking to me until a couple of days in. When you give him enough treats, then he started to warm up. But at that point he was, you know, a 140-, 160-pound dog [and] wasn’t a huge fan of me, so it kind of just added to it. He just did whatever he wanted to do, and that was usually not what we were looking for him to do … In some ways they, they give you the most beautiful stuff. It’s just you gotta be patient.”
“I Play Rocky” is in limited release on Nov. 6, followed by going wide on Nov. 20.

Dalton Smith beats Alberto Puello to retain WBC light-welterweight title after split decision victory
Dalton Smith wins on his Sheffield homecoming; the 29-year-old was taken the distance in his first title defence but makes it 20 wins from 20 fights as a professional; two judges score it 115-113 in his favour and one 116-112 to Alberto Puello, who suffers just his second defeat in 27
Saturday 24 October 2026 22:59, UK
Dalton Smith retained his WBC light-welterweight title with a thrilling, split-decision victory over Alberto Puello on Saturday night.
On his homecoming at Utilita Arena, the Sheffield man was taken the distance in his first title defence, but kept his unbeaten record in tact as judges Kieran McCann of England and Spain's Jon Llona both scored the bout 115-113 in his favour, while Filipino Ray Danseco had it 116-112 to Puello.
Puello - is a former WBA and WBC champion - suffered only his second defeat in 27 fights. Smith has won 20 from 20, including beating Subriel Matias in New York in January - who inflicted Puello's only previous loss - to become world champion.
The 29-year-old had been due to fight mandatory challenger Puello four months sooner in June, but an injury to the Dominican Republic fighter resulted in a postponenment.
Smith, speaking to DAZN after retaining his title, said: "We knew what we were coming in for, he's a two-time world champion [and] look at the names he's beat.
"We knew it wasn't going to be a show, he was going to be an awkward opponent, but a champion has to do what he has to do.
"These are the best in the world and I'm proving why I'm number one now."
He added: "I got his rhythm early on. I think he respected my power, but, look, he's experienced.
"He's a lot more experienced than me, and that's what I'm gaining now. I switched off a little bit in the early rounds, but I did what a true champion did and win the last couple, so I'm very proud."

Here's how to test a CR2032 battery to see if it's good
You won't need expensive equipment or invest much time.
Your car key fob suddenly needs several presses to unlock the door. Your AirTag stops responding when you try to locate it. Before blaming either gadget, it's worth checking the battery inside. One common type is the CR2032, a 3V lithium coin cell also used in Samsung's SmartTag2 and some smart home sensors. Depending on the device and how often it's used, one can last way over a year.
A multimeter can help you check the battery's voltage, and it's a good addition to your toolbox if you don't already own one. There are cheaper ways to check, too, but don't mistake a voltage reading for a complete picture of battery health.
How to test a CR2032 battery with a multimeter
Begin by checking the battery itself. If you spot crusty residue, rust-colored patches, swelling or leakage, skip the test and replace it. Have a look at the device's contacts too, since corrosion there can cause trouble even with a good battery.
Remove the CR2032 and set your digital multimeter to DC voltage (V with a solid line over a dashed line). Plug the black lead into COM and the red lead into the V or VΩ port. If your meter doesn't automatically select a range, set it above 3V, typically 20V.
Hold the battery by its edges over a nonconductive surface. Touch the red probe to the broad face marked with a plus sign (+) and the black probe to the center of the smaller negative face underneath. Keep the probe tips from touching each other or bridging the battery's terminals. A negative reading simply means you've reversed the probes.
A fresh CR2032 typically reads around 3V, while a reading closer to 2.5V is a good reason to bring in a replacement. But don't give that 3V reading too much credit though. A multimeter draws almost no current, so a battery might look fine on the display but struggle when your key fob or tracker actually needs power. There's no single pass-or-fail reading for every device. If it keeps acting up, try a fresh CR2032 unit before assuming the device is faulty.
No multimeter? Here's how to check your AirTag or key fob battery
A dedicated coin-cell tester is another option. Some cost around $10, although certain models only measure voltage rather than how the battery performs under load. Basic multimeters can cost less than $20 and are good for checking other batteries or troubleshooting low-voltage electronics. Still, buying either just to diagnose one suspect $3 battery is a harder sell.
There's also the LED trick, assuming you have one lying around. A small red or yellow LED is a better choice than a blue or white one because it generally needs less voltage to light up. Touch its longer leg to the CR2032's positive side and the shorter leg to the negative side. If it lights up, the battery can supply some current. That's about all it proves. The LED won't tell you how much life is left, and one that stays dark doesn't necessarily mean the battery is dead.
AirTag owners can check Find My before opening anything. Select Items inside the app and tap your AirTag. If it says "Low Battery," or shows a depleted battery icon, skip the testing and replace the CR2032. Some CR2032 batteries have bitterant coatings that may prevent proper contact, even when they're brand new. Apple recommends packaging marked "Compatible with Apple AirTag" when replacing an AirTag battery, and says an AirTag's battery lasts more than a year, while Samsung rates the SmartTag2 for up to 500 days in normal mode.
After removing a CR2032, keep it out of children's reach and tape its terminals before taking them to a battery collection facility. If one is swallowed, seek emergency medical care immediately, as serious internal injuries can occur in as little as two hours.

Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
- Published
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.
"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.
Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.
The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.
Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".
This was just the start of the problems.
Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.
In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.
GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.
Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.
Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.
"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.
Hopes for the future
Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.
But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.
Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.
Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

Surprisingly, Human Torch, who remains at the bottom of the Marvel Rivals tier list, is one of the best characters to defeat Thanos in the new PvE mode. All the aerial heroes have an advantage in this mode; they can avoid minions on the ground and focus on shredding Thanos’ massive health bar.
So, Human Torch can remain in the air all the time. Before spamming his Fire Clusters, make sure to cover the area Thanos roams by creating a Pyro-prison with Blazing Blast attack. In this way, you can significantly boost damage numbers. Lastly, you can unleash hell on the battlefield with Torch’s ult, Supernova.
Jubilee
The best Strategist for Avengers: Endgame PvE mode is none other than Jubilee in Marvel Rivals. The firecracker was recently buffed in Marvel Rivals Season 10.5, and she continues to shine on the battlefield even in the new PvE mode. Jubilee can excel at both dealing damage and saving her teammates with her heals.
Make sure to keep dropping Blooming Balls and inflating them to keep nearby allies healed. The newly buffed Fireworks Finale ult also comes in handy, especially in the second phase. So, Jubilee is without a doubt the best Strategist hero for Avengers: Endgame PvE mode in Marvel Rivals.
Storm
Storm, who used to be one of the least picked heroes, has instantly become one of the most-picked characters in Marvel Rivals‘ new PvE mode. Once again, an aerial duelist has emerged as a top pick to defeat Thanos. Similar to Human Torch, Storm players can prioritize dealing damage to Thanos over his minions.
The mutant goddess can remain at a distance and keep attacking with her Wind Blades and switch between her two attacks. The Omega Hurricane is still useful to clear Thanos’ Chitauri and Chitauri Gorillas while simultaneously attacking Thanos. The only disadvantage of picking Storm is her mobility; you cannot easily escape all incoming attacks from Thanos.
Phoenix
Marvel Rivals’ Jean Phoenix is the same lethal hero in the Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. The best way to play as Phoenix in this mode is to stand in the outer arena and keep hitting Thanos with the Cosmic Flames. Since Thanos has a gigantic hitbox, it’s much easier to aim for his head even from far away.
Both Telepathic Illusion and Dark Ascent allow you to readjust your position on the arena with ease, and it is crucial, especially when Thanos begins to unleash the power of Infinity Stones. The Ultimate Ability Endsong Inferna is also capable of mass destruction if you time it and place it properly.
Iron Man
As everyone knows, Iron Man became the MVP at the end of the final Avengers movie, and he can pretty much repeat the history here in the Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. As an aerial Duelist, Iron Man gets a natural advantage and can only concentrate on nuking Thanos with his repulsor blasts and unibeam.
In case you didn’t know, his missiles received auto-tracking capabilities in Season 10.5 for the first time. So, players can keep sending out missiles in addition to his primary attacks. As Iron Man, your regular drill would be entering Armor Overdrive mode and keeping fire on Thanos to quickly charge your ultimate. Then send out the Invincible Pulse Cannon in Thanos’ way before he moves.
Moon Knight
The swarm of Chitauri, Chitauri Gorillas, and other minions on the battlefield are definitely annoying. But you can take advantage of this opportunity by picking Moon Knight in Marvel Rivals. The large number of enemies makes life easier for Moon Knight, as his Crescent Darts can easily ricochet between foes without any disturbance.
So, keep placing your Ankhs and spam your Crescent Darts to continuously attack Thanos and his mighty monstrous army at the same time. Since there isn’t any high ground here, it is a bit difficult to survive as Moon Knight. So, make sure to stay near healers or ask a friend to play a healer, if you can.
Scarlet Witch
Scarlet Witch, aka Wanda Maximoff, was a great pick for both Avengers: Age of Ultron PvE mode and Avengers: Infinity War PvP mode in Marvel Rivals. And her winning streak continues in Avengers: Endgame PvE mode.
Chaos Control, Scarlet Hex, Chthonian Burst, Sorcerer Supreme, etc., basically all the abilities in Wanda’s kit are deadly and are perfect for wiping out Chitauri squads and sucking Thanos’ life force. Although it is hard to rely only on Mystic Projection, you can surive for a long time on the battle arena if you play your cards right.
The Hood
It’s hard to survive as a Duelist or Strategist in the Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. So, the natural option is to pick a Vanguard who can withstand longer. Out of all the Vanguards in the game, The Hood remains the only solid pick for the new PvE mode. While most of the Vanguards are melee-focused, Marvel Rivals’ The Hood can obliterate with his accursed dual pistols.
Similar to how you play as The Hood in other game modes, keep dealing damage with his pistol to build up the Demonic Energy. Enter the Half-Demon state to get movement and attack boost which results in increased damage. Finally, you can easily hit your shots during The Hood’s Demon of the End ultimate ability, thanks to Thanos’ massive hitbox.
Ultron
The second-best Strategist after Jubilee in Avengers: Endgame mode is Ultron in Marvel Rivals. Ultron has all the same perks as an aerial Duelist. In addition, he can easily manage healing as he gets a better view of the battle from the top.
As Ultron, keep shifting your drones between the heroes in need of health and keep hitting Thanos with the Encephalo-Ray. Then make sure to use the Rage of Ultron ultimate ability When Thanos orders the spaceships to strike as well as when he uses the Infinity Stones to rescue the injured heroes.
Jeff the Land Shark
Last but not least, Jeff the Land Shark is one of the best characters for Marvel Rivals Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. His Joyful Splash has a great range, so you can heal your allies while also damaging the minions at the same time. Use Hide and Seek ability whenever you need to escape and you can use your Healing Bubbles to heal yourself and remain alive on the battlefield.
While you cannot use It’s Jeff, one of the best ultimate abilities in Marvel Rivals, to swallow Thanos, it is still good enough. The created healing water zone is helpful in healing allies and you can instead focus on swalling the members of Thanos army.
And these are our top 10 picks for the best heroes/characters for the ongoing Marvel Rivals Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. It is very easy to defeat Thanos by picking any one of the characters we have listed here.
That said, if you feel like any other hero deserves a spot on our list, let us know in the comments below.

Why your EV battery still loses charge while it's parked
Your vehicle doesn't truly sleep when you lock it.
It's already costly enough to leave your EV at the airport for a week without it quietly discharging electricity while you're away. You could end up with a reduced battery percentage, even if the odometer hasn't budged. The truth is that an EV will lose a bit of charge while it's parked, but the amount lost will vary depending on the EV and what it has been doing while you were away.
There are a lot of factors involved when it comes to EV energy loss. Lithium-ion cells can lose charge naturally through electrolyte oxidation and reduction via a process called self-discharge. However, that is negligible compared with the electricity used while driving. The larger loss is from systems that continue to operate after you've locked the doors. It is not usually a problem over a weekend, but if you leave an EV unplugged for a couple of weeks, those little losses can begin to add up.
A parked EV still has work to do
A locked vehicle doesn't automatically shut down every electrical system. The battery management system periodically checks battery conditions, and the high-voltage battery is sometimes called upon to recharge smaller low-voltage batteries used for the locks, computers and other electronics. Tesla says that its Model 3, when parked, routinely performs these system checks and any necessary battery maintenance. Rivian also confirms its R1T also uses the high-voltage battery to maintain its 12V battery.
Then there's the convenience tech. Connected services include the ability to check the status of your vehicle, start the climate control or prepare the cabin before getting behind the wheel. Tesla explicitly mentions app requests, climate functions and infotainment as sources of power consumption while parked.
Third-party apps that repeatedly wake a sleeping vehicle can add to the drain. If you've left cabin cooling enabled during hot weather, it's not cooling for free. That's one area where Slate's barebones electric pickup might have an advantage, with fewer connected features to keep running while parked, though its actual battery drain remains untested.
Cold weather complicates the situation further. The range estimate can decrease with battery temperature fluctuations, even if the vehicle has not used an equivalent amount of electricity. Model 3 owners can use the Energy app's Park tab to see how much energy the car consumed while parked. This is more informative than watching the range estimate move around. What drains an EV battery while driving is another story.
When parked battery drain becomes a problem
Optional features can make the biggest difference. Tesla's Sentry Mode employs cameras and sensors to keep an eye on suspicious activity, and Rivian's Gear Guard Motion Cam can capture activity around a parked vehicle. That's a fair compromise in an unknown parking lot, but an electronic lookout does require power.
How much charge can you expect to lose? Tesla's Model 3 manual says the battery can lose approximately 1 percent per day, depending on the settings and conditions. Recurrent reports that sleeping Teslas can lose just 0.1 to 0.3 percent a day, while those running energy-intensive features can lose several percent daily. These figures reflect different conditions, so neither is a guarantee.
The size of the battery is also important. A 0.5kWh loss, for example, is roughly 1.2 percent of a 42kWh battery and 0.6 percent of an 80kWh battery. That makes the same drain more noticeable in smaller city EVs.
If you are going to leave your car for a long time, turn off unneeded surveillance and climate controls, limit apps that repeatedly wake the vehicle and make sure you have enough juice to get back. Tesla actually recommends keeping the Model 3 plugged in when it's not in use, especially for several weeks, and maintaining around 50 percent charge during long-term storage.

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.
Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.
Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.
Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.
Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.
“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.
But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.
“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”
Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.
Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats
The former US president slammed his successor’s ‘corruption and incompetence’ and blamed his ‘bad decisions’ for the rising cost of living
Former US president Barack Obama delivered a scathing critique of his successor, Donald Trump, at a rally in Ohio on Saturday to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,’” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”
The 65-year-old Democrat blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices.
“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.”

Park24 has announced plans to provide a consolation payment of ¥3,000 in cash or gift cards to Times Car vehicle-sharing service users affected by a recent data breach.
The company has confirmed that about 6.62 million user accounts were compromised. Of those accounts, eligible for the payment will be about 1.46 million accounts from which images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, were externally transferred.
Park24 said Friday that it will respond appropriately on a case-by-case basis if actual damage occurs. It added that the affected images were not immediately viewable because they were encrypted.
The total cost of the consolation payment is expected to be some ¥4.4 billion. The company plans to book an extraordinary loss of ¥5.5 billion for the year ending this month, including other expenses related to the data breach.
On Friday, it was also learned that Makino Law Office plans to organize affected users and file a damages lawsuit against the Times Car service operator and others.
Yuki Makino of the law office said that the payment amount is “too low” given concerns over identity theft and the burden on affected users of dealing with potential damage.
According to Makino, more than 90,000 people have registered online to participate in the planned lawsuit.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O’Neil, in the months between Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund saying it was ending financial support and LIV filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
The payments are part of a trove of documents filed late Thursday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in New Jersey. That included 129 payments to creditors in the 90 days before LIV’s bankruptcy filing and $26 million to Jon Rahm in the year before the September 8 filing.
Another payment in the previous year was to Greg Norman, who left as LIV’s first CEO in January 2025. He was paid a $5.8 million settlement and a $3.6 million bonus on September 26, 2025.
LIV Golf is trying to emerge from bankruptcy without the financial muscle of the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, which has spent upward of $5 billion since the rival league launched in June 2022 and offered nine-figure bonuses to top PGA and European tour players.
BC Partners Credit has pledged up to $300 million to back what is being called “LIV 2.0.” Key to that is players staying with the league, and already a number of top players — Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Louis Oosthuizen, Adrian Meronk and rising Spaniard David Puig — have separated from LIV agreements or indicated they are leaving.
It’s not unusual for companies going through bankruptcy to compensate top executives to get through the process. Documents show David Phillipps, the chief financial officer, received a $3.37 million retention payment and John Ruzich, the chief legal officer, received $2.6 million, both on June 24. That’s also when O’Neil was paid his $6.375 million.
O’Neil also received a $2.7 million bonus on Feb. 13, two weeks before the start of the Iran war and two months before PIF’s board approved a new investment strategy that led to LIV Golf’s funding ending after the 2026 season.
Payment to players include Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau (nearly $13.9 million), Dustin Johnson ($10.7 million) and Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson, both around $2.5 million.
LIV’s bankruptcy proceeding has a November 5 hearing in the bankruptcy court. BC Partners originally set a Sunday deadline for players to decide if they are on board for LIV 2.0, though that deadline can be extended under an amended restructuring agreement.
The new version is aiming for prize funds of about $9 million — down from $20 million for individual purses — with at least 10 tournaments and a focus on team golf.

Another accused in Tiger Shroff shooting case arrested from Indore, supplied weapons used in attack
The accused, Pranjal Thakran, 22, a resident of Haryana's Sonipat, allegedly played a key role in the attack and supplied the weapons used in the crime.
Police on Saturday arrested another accused in connection with the Tiger Shroff shooting case from Madhya Pradesh's Indore, nearly a week after the Bollywood actor was attacked in Mumbai. His driver and a vlogger were injured in the incident on October 19.
The arrested accused, Pranjal Thakran, 22, a resident of Haryana's Sonipat, allegedly played a key role in the attack and supplied the weapons used in the crime. The arrest resulted from a joint operation by the Indore and Mumbai crime branches after the latter shared information.

However, police officials declined to disclose further details about the investigation.
Deep Dive
According to police, Pranjal had arrived in Indore around five days ago for his brother’s treatment. After establishing his involvement and tracing his location to Indore, crime branch of Mumbai Police contacted the Indore crime branch on Thursday night seeking assistance with the arrest.

A senior police officer, who wished not to be named, said, “Acting on the input, police tracked his presence in Indore and launched an operation. Four officers from the Mumbai crime branch, along with around eight personnel from the Indore crime branch, participated in the raid. The Mumbai crime branch will now interrogate him to probe the larger conspiracy behind the firing, the supply of weapons, and his links with other suspects involved in the case.”
Arrests made in the case so far
This is the first arrest made from Madhya Pradesh in connection with the case.
The three main suspects who opened fire at Shroff's vehicle were nabbed from Rajasthan's Kota on the morning of October 19. They were identified as Rehan alias Sukka (18), a resident of Sonipat in Haryana; Ritwik Kurmi alias Roshan Fighter (22), reportedly from Bihar and currently residing in Andheri West and 18-year-old-Phool Singh.

Shooting attack on Tiger Shroff
On the evening of October 18, three motorcycle-borne men fired five to six rounds at Shroff’s car in Mumbai’s Juhu area. While the actor escaped unhurt, his driver and a vlogger sustained injuries in the attack.
Soon after the attack, an individual identified as Anil Pandit later claimed responsibility for the firing through a social media post, alleging links to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.
