The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Lee Chang Dong’s seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff – 2,600 employees – after which many died by suicide. Possible Love is the latest in a long line of Lee movies that engage with themes of class or labor or religion or compressed modernity, that uniquely Korean affliction, without feeling didactic.
Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
In Possible Love, the director of Burning tackles labor struggle, human connection, and the nature of capturing others on film.
A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go.
The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English.
I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education?
As you know well, Daegu is referred to as the heartland of conservatism in Korea. I went to school there, all the way through university, so I grew up steeped in that conservative disposition and was influenced by it. But until I graduated from college, in the spring of 1980, I didn’t realize how politically conservative Daegu citizens were.
That spring, in May of 1980, I participated in protests against the Chun Doo-hwan regime as a university student. It was on the streets that I met them, the citizens, and experienced their hardline sentiments in a visceral way. It was shocking to me. Afterwards, I thought a lot about how come the people in Daegu were so politically conservative. In light of all that, the thoughts of a person I perceive as myself, that person’s attitude towards the world, could only be bound with a certain kind of tension.
I was interested in how different directors respond to similar social forces in different ways – like Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice. I imagine you know them both personally. What is the conversation between you all when working on your various projects?
We do know each other personally, but we seldom talk about our work. It might be the result of coincidence. Though of course, there might be a certain inevitability hidden within them. We lived through the same modern Korean history, and you cannot call that coincidence.
One thing does come to mind. A long time ago, I think before he made Mother, Bong Joon Ho told me over drinks that he had almost finished writing a script and wanted to show it to me. It was a story about a mother, and he was wrestling with how he could portray that person’s pain, whether he even had the right to. He said he wanted to show me the script. But once he sobered up, maybe he forgot, because he never showed it to me. Later, when I saw the film, I felt I might understand what he had been talking about.
Possible Love is concerned with similar questions: How can I portray another person’s story, another person’s pain? What position am I in? How much distance should I keep from them? You could say that these questions around the ethics of the camera are connected to the worry Bong Joon Ho had back then.
Like Ye-ji, I come from the so-called margins, and now report on that terrain, which is perhaps why watching her character pursue a near-vampiric level of access, I felt something close to repulsion. How were you able to represent the filmmaker–participant dynamic so accurately?
I can’t say how accurate it is. I don’t think Ye-ji’s attitude can be generalized. Not every documentary filmmaker has a rich husband. Nevertheless you can say Ye-Ji captures something universal about filmmakers, or those who deal in other people’s stories, directors such as myself, or reporters, in that they aren’t exactly the people they portray. Even if they came from a lower class, they are no longer of it. Their position in life has changed. And yet, in order to do their work, what do they do? When someone else’s suffering unfolds dramatically in front of them, are they to capture the moment on tape, or should they step away from the camera? Or maybe it isn’t unfolding dramatically in front of them, in which case, do they create a certain effect by producing the moment, by staging it?
I think those are basically properties of the camera. The moment you hold a camera you have power, and the camera operates according to that power.
It’s not so much that I portrayed it so precisely, but these properties of the camera are something worth thinking through together.
For us filmmakers, we don’t belong to the world of our subjects, nor are we on the side of capital either. We are in the middle where we are, it can be said, in a neutral, or perhaps cowardly position. Despite that, those who make movies, those who tell stories of others, in the end, can, through their efforts, bring about some small change.
In this film, Ho-seok ends up pouring out what’s inside of him in front of the camera, which functions as a kind of treatment, even if that isn’t what Ye-ji intended.
Possible Love is a collaboration between you and screenwriter Oh Jung-mi. How did you two come to work together, and what does that collaboration look like?
She is a student I met at Korea National University of Arts. You could say it’s a school that draws the most talented and ambitious students, and she was special even among them. By special I mean she was creative and wrote well, of course, but she also has a perspective, and the ability to take a step back and regard something, and find meaning in things.
As I get older, I grow duller and numb, and set in my ways, and she is a friend who reliably jolts me out of it, which is very precious to me.
I think I’m lucky. Not just with Oh Jung-mi but everyone around me that I work with is very precious to me, and I feel lucky to have met them.
The problem with Oh Jung-mi, though, is that while working together, I kept scrapping projects. So she suffered. But she never left. She stayed beside me, and even though she herself is someone who makes and develops films, she has given me a lot of help up to now.
Ye-ji documents in service of higher purpose. Mi-ok’s character snaps photos of the table spread for no purpose at all. The footage from the helicopter captures a moment of police brutality. How does the function of cinema compare to all the other instances in which we hit record?
Ye-ji has a desire to capture in her camera vanishing laborers [and] the value of their labor — not unlike her dry cleaner father. And yet, it is undeniable that she also regards their lives as source material for her own movie. As narrative filmmakers, stories of others in pain often is nothing but material for a commercial movie.
As for Mi-ok, she knows about the properties of the camera, but she, too, has a desire: to broadcast her pain, and her problems. She has a secondary desire, which is that she wonders if her husband’s traumas may not be healed through the camera, because she believes that his biggest issue is keeping all his problems, his despair and his anger, hidden.
So each has their own desires regarding the camera.
As a filmmaker, firstly, I had the goal of conveying the contents of the documentary Ye-ji was making, of capturing the sufferings of the laid-off laborers. I believed what Ye-ji tried to show, I had to show through my own film.
The group therapy session scene, for example, could be very long and tedious, and for some viewers it might be something that they cannot emotionally relate to, because they came to see a narrative film, not documentary. Despite that, I felt I had to convey it.
Regarding the crackdown scene, some of it appears through archival footage shot from a distance. But as someone making a fiction film, I also have a responsibility to convey Ho-seok’s subjective memory cinematically. So you could say within the narrative structure of Ye-ji’s documentary, multiple layers of roles and goals co-exist.
What are some notes you received from your American movie executives that felt unique to working in the American system versus Korean?
I didn’t feel that at all. From pre-production through post-production, Netflix, as the investor, never once interfered or offered unsolicited notes. Of course, I can’t generalize from that. I haven’t asked everyone else. But I had none of that. In that sense they absolutely guaranteed my independence and freedom as a director.
Now the film is finished and we are promoting it, and in particular part of what we call the Oscar campaign. I probably wouldn’t have gotten this kind of help without Netflix, that’s clear.
Possible Love was released in select US theaters October 23rd and will be available on Netflix globally on November 6th.

Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago.
In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it.
Frozen to the bed
“Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what’s left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base.
Most glaciers are warm-based, meaning meltwater at the bed lets them slide, and sliding ice grinds up everything beneath it, erasing the record. Barnes is cold-based, and thus frozen directly onto the bedrock beneath it, which prevents it from sliding.
“If there is an ice event where you live and you have to go and scrape off your windshield, that ice that’s plastered to the windshield of your car, that’s a good example of how cold-based ice operates. It’s sort of just stuck to what it’s on,” Young says.
This stuck ice preserves what’s beneath instead of eroding it. As the Laurentide retreated across the plateau, tundra plants colonized the newly bare ground. When the ice came back later, it simply smothered them in place and held them there, intact, for two millennia. Mumbai Indians announced Kieron Pollard as its new head coach for the IPL 2027 season on Saturday. Pollard, whose association with the franchise runs back to 2010, will take over from Sri Lanka’s Mahela Jayawardene.
Speaking about his role and expectations for next year, Pollard said his immediate focus was to bring a team-first mindset to help MI become a title-contending team again.
“I think my first task is about understanding what’s needed to be done. Again, and then when you get into that, bring that spirit and that energy. Talk about that. When you walk into the Wankhede Stadium, you are not seeing the yellows and the reds and stuff like that. You want to see that blue flag flying, and you want to see that passion and spirit from the fans. And that can only come from within us,” Pollard said.
“We recognize the fact that we have not been where we wanted to be in the last couple of years. So there’s no hiding, sort of from that.
“But what’s going to happen is that we’re going to try our best now to ensure that we continue to play for that badge, put the team above self, and then ensure that when the opposition comes, it’s something that they remembered from the past. Yes, it’s history, but sometimes in order to go forward, you have to go back a little bit and understand. And I think that’s where it’s going to start,” the West Indian added.
Mumbai Indians, the joint-most successful team in the IPL with five titles, has looked a pale shadow of its former self in recent IPL seasons.. The team failed to qualify for the Playoffs in two out of the last three seasons, and has not won the title since 2020.

Pollard also said his players would have complete freedom to express themselves, a personality trait that came to define the West Indian during his playing career.
“I think that’s very very important, and that’s something that has been leaving the game, and not true. Sometimes a lot of the guys wanted to show their personality and be free, but through the rules and regulations of the demerit points and all of these things, I think at times we have gotten a bit robotic in that sense.
“So, guys don’t actually sometimes try to show their true personality, and I think that is what is missing a little bit. So for us, as a Mumbai Indians team, I think it’s very important that we show personalities because each and every individual in our dressing room has something that people would not have seen that has gotten them to where they have got at the stage, and that is where you need bring it out,” Pollard added.
Pollard also spoke highly of Jayawardene, stating the Sri Lankan’s technical acumen has strongly influenced his understanding of the game.
“What stood out for me immediately from then was how precise he was from a tactical perspective in that in that sense.”
“Having to experience him as a coach playing under him, I think was even more fantastic for me. And then following that, being under him as an assistant, as well as a batting coach, the knowledge that I would have gained over that period of time, from someone like him, I have to say I’m blessed, to be able to be in that position, to be able to receive all that he had to bring from different perspective from opponent into the coaching setup,” Pollard said.
On how he would approach the head coach job, Pollard said it would involve player management and data driven decision-making.
“It comes down to the players. It comes down to conversations, one-on-one conversations. Yes, it comes down to the team talks and the team tactics. Also, with how much cricket has changed lately, data also becomes an important aspect, it helps with preparation.”

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday (October 23, 2026), the head of the World Health Organisation said.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.
"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work," he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the U.S.-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial "shortly", CEPI said in a statement.
"Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks," said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
'Important step'
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.
"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives," he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
"Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities," said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO, two days later, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued after the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units and about 3,000 tents and folding beds as well as torches and winter clothing arrived in the region.
The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191km (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18km.
The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10km, according to its website.
Videos posted by China’s national broadcaster CCTV said showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.
China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.
More than 300 police officers had been dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilised almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported.
Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.
The earthquake also caused rockfalls that had forced local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows were expected in the quake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, CCTV said.
China’s leader, Xi Jinping, called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.
Nagqu is more than 300km north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.
Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.
In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.
A huge tremor in Sichuan province in 2008 left approximately 90,000 people dead or missing, including about 5,000 schoolchildren.

Himesh Reshammiya had a conversation with Komal Nahta and revealed that he had a habit of storing songs and tunes in his bank even before he got a break with Pyaar Kiya To Darna Kya (1998). He said, “I have ready songs in my bank. When David Dhawan ji approached me for Dulhan Hum Le Jayenge (2000), we locked as many as 7 songs in just two hours. Chapter closed! I could even offer you 40 more songs and then you could take that many songs to people to get their feedback. However, it would only add to your confusion.”
Himesh Reshammiya reveals, “I composed 7 songs of Dulhan Hum Le Jayenge in 2 hours and ALL songs of Humraaz in 1 sitting… every day, I compose AT LEAST one song!”
He added, “Similarly, in just one sitting, we finalized each and every song of Humraaz (2002) with Abbas bhai and Mustan bhai. That’s because I gave them their whole world and setting of the film through the songs.”
Himesh Reshammiya continued, “When I wake up in the morning, the first thing I have to do is to compose a song. I get on a call with my lyric writer. As soon as we get a tune, I record it immediately and I send it to my sampled group and also to the lyricist. Aisa koi din hi nahin gaya mera jahan pe ek gaana nahin bana hain. At times, I have even created 3, 5, 8 and even 10 songs in a day. Daddy (Vipin Reshammiya) sikha ke gaye hain ki ‘Everyday, ek gaana toh banna hi hain’. Thanks to that habit, I have been able to have 10,000 songs in my discography and bank.”
He revealed, “Many of these songs were made long back and used when the time was right. The songs of Sanam Teri Kasam (2016) were made in the 90s. The sitting for that film happened only in 2014. Yet, it sounded fresh as the arrangement was modern. We have a great mix in our team – all our old musicians are there, while new people have also joined us.”

Singapore expects all parties to honour commercial gas contracts, says PM Wong after Indonesia cut exports
Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under such contracts, says Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.
SINGAPORE: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday (Oct 25) after Indonesia cut its exports.
Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Mr Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.
Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. In response to CNA’s queries, Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand.
About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia.
“The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments, and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” said Mr Wong, who is the PAP secretary-general.
Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply.
However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, added Mr Wong.
This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said.
“Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” said Mr Wong.
“But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.”
From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country's ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy.
Known as the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached in order to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme.
Mr Wong said: “Dealing with today's concerns is only part of our job. We must also prepare Singapore for tomorrow – that means looking ahead, anticipating problems and acting before they become more difficult to solve.
“Consider the economy of the future. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.”
STRENGTHENING PARTNERSHIPS
In his speech, Mr Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added.
“We remain a trusted partner, and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” said the prime minister.
In addition, Singapore is proactively strengthening partnerships across different regions of the world, with office holders travelling more frequently to build relationships and deepen cooperation.
In the past week, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam made a state visit to Sweden, while Mr Wong recently returned from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
“These countries are in different parts of the world, but they all see value in working closely with Singapore,” said Mr Wong. “That reflects the trust and goodwill we have built over many years.”
Singapore is known as a reliable partner, a trusted hub, and a country that delivers on its commitment, said Mr Wong.
“This reputation is a vital asset, especially in today’s fragmented and troubled world. It helps us attract high-quality investments,” he added. “And the investments support growth, create jobs and enable incomes to rise.”
Some challenges are harder to tackle as they cross national borders – these include online scams or haze.
Singapore is grappling with its worst haze episode since 2015. It has sent notices to 10 Singapore-based firms and 10 Indonesian firms under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
“We cannot solve these problems through our own efforts alone. We need cooperation from other countries,” Mr Wong said.
“But that does not mean we stand by and do nothing. We are doing everything we can within our power to protect Singaporeans, strengthen our own response and work with partners to tackle these problems at source.”
"BUILT WITH SINGAPOREANS"
Touching on governance, Mr Wong said that the Singapore we want cannot simply be delivered by the government to Singaporeans, and has to be “built with Singaporeans”.
“That is the partnership we strive for: a PAP Government that listens, acts and delivers. A people who step forward and contribute and a society where everyone looks out for one another,” added the prime minister.
While Singaporeans have given the PAP a strong mandate to govern for another term, this mandate is not an entitlement, said Mr Wong.
“It is a responsibility – to deliver what we promised, tackle the difficult issues facing our country and prepare Singapore for what lies ahead. That is why we must never take the trust of Singaporeans for granted. After all, no political party has a permanent claim on that trust,” said Mr Wong.
“Every generation of PAP leaders and activists must earn it afresh. We know what is expected of us. We must listen and deliver. We must hold ourselves to high standards, and we must always put Singapore and Singaporeans first.”
Mr Wong noted that while some sectors of Singapore’s economy are doing well, others are facing pressures.
Some workers are benefiting from new opportunities, but others are struggling to keep up. Lower-wage workers worry about keeping pace with rising costs, while Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s who lose their jobs worry about finding work again.
“We understand these concerns and we will respond to them. Our task is not just to keep the economy growing. It is to make sure that growth translates into better lives for all Singaporeans,” he said.
The government is also doing more to ease the burdens on parents and give families greater assurance, as seen by measures introduced at this year’s National Day Rally, he added.
Mr Wong acknowledged that the government has a “full agenda”, such as continuing to tackle the cost-of-living pressures and helping Singapore secure better jobs.
Ultimately, the government will do its part, but everybody has a part to play too, said the prime minister.
“We will create opportunities and support workers through change, but workers must be prepared to learn and adapt,” said Mr Wong.
“We will reduce the emphasis on exams and broaden education pathways, but parents must give their children space to grow at their own pace.
“We will strengthen support for families and seniors, but all of us must also look out for one another.”

Five years after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, actor Christina Applegate revealed this week that she had been misdiagnosed. Her experience puts a public face on one of the most consequential challenges in neurology: how to diagnose a complex disease early enough to prevent irreversible damage without sacrificing accuracy.
How MS is diagnosed has changed dramatically during my nearly four decades in the field. When I began my career, physicians often had to wait for symptoms to recur before they could confirm MS. Today, advances in imaging, biomarkers, and diagnostic criteria are helping us recognize the disease earlier, when treatment may have the greatest opportunity to prevent irreversible neurological damage.
But progress brings a critical responsibility. Too many people still spend years searching for an accurate diagnosis, while others are told they have MS when another condition is responsible for their symptoms. Applegate’s experience is a powerful reminder that the future of MS diagnosis cannot be about speed alone. Our goal must be both: diagnosing MS earlier and getting the diagnosis right.
The challenge is that MS does not look the same in everyone, and other neurological disorders can produce similar symptoms. Signs such as numbness, vision changes, fatigue, and difficulty walking can occur in many other neurological disorders. Even abnormalities detected on an MRI are not necessarily unique to MS.
The consequences of both misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis can be substantial.
Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may receive treatments they do not need, potentially exposing them to unnecessary risks while delaying appropriate care for the condition actually causing their symptoms.
For people whose MS goes undiagnosed, time matters enormously. While there is not yet a cure for MS, there are more than 20 therapies that can help reduce disease activity and slow worsening for many people living with MS. Research has demonstrated the importance of initiating appropriate treatment early in the course of disease, before neurological damage accumulates. Every unnecessary delay can mean a missed opportunity to protect long-term neurological health.
Fortunately, decades of research have fundamentally changed what is possible.
Today, we have better diagnostic tools, more sophisticated imaging technologies, and a deeper understanding of MS than at any point in history. Yet significant challenges remain in ensuring that these advances reach the people who need them.
One of the most significant developments has been the evolution of the McDonald Diagnostic Criteria, the internationally recognized guidelines physicians use to diagnose MS. Working in partnership with the European Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis, the National Multiple Sclerosis Society helped advance these criteria, contributing to progress that has shortened the diagnostic process from years to months in many cases. The latest revisions incorporate new imaging techniques and biomarkers designed to improve both the speed and accuracy of diagnosis.
One particularly promising example is an MRI technique that identifies the central vein sign, a feature that can help physicians distinguish lesions associated with MS from abnormalities caused by other conditions. Alongside progress in spinal fluid biomarker research, this technology offers the potential for earlier, more accurate diagnoses.
Artificial intelligence and sophisticated data analytics may eventually help clinicians recognize patterns in imaging and other clinical information, identify people who warrant further evaluation, and improve diagnostic precision.
These tools are still evolving, and they will require rigorous research and validation before they can be widely incorporated into clinical practice. But even the most sophisticated diagnostic tools cannot improve outcomes if patients cannot access the specialists and health care systems equipped to use them.
Access to neurological care across the country is uneven. Some communities face significant shortages of neurologists, particularly those with specialized expertise in MS. Patients may wait months for appointments, travel long distances to see specialists, or encounter lengthy referral processes before receiving the evaluation they need.
Clinician education is equally important. Primary care providers are often the first professionals to evaluate someone experiencing unexplained neurological symptoms. Helping them recognize potential early signs of MS and understand when to refer patients for neurological evaluation can make a meaningful difference.
Applegate’s willingness to share her experience has brought attention to an issue that extends far beyond any one person’s diagnosis. We have transformed our ability to recognize and treat MS over the past several decades, but scientific progress alone is not enough. The next challenge is ensuring that these advances translate into earlier answers, more accurate diagnoses, and better outcomes for everyone affected by the disease.
That will require continued investment in research to develop and validate better diagnostic tools, better education for the clinicians who first evaluate patients with unexplained neurological symptoms, and improved access to neurologists and MS specialists. Together, these efforts can help smooth the often difficult path from the first unexplained symptoms to an accurate diagnosis, while reducing the risk of both misdiagnosis and unnecessary delays.
The goal is not simply to diagnose MS faster. It is to get the diagnosis right, as early as possible, so that no one loses precious time, or the opportunity for appropriate treatment, while searching for answers.
Bruce Bebo, Ph.D., is chief research and medical affairs officer at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. A cellular immunologist, he has dedicated nearly four decades to advancing research into multiple sclerosis, a commitment inspired by his mother’s experience living with the disease.

A day after the company opened its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, Goldman Sachs downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “Sell”. The brokerage slashed the stock’s price target to ₹23. It foresees a challenging path for Ola Electric to become cash flow positive given the relatively high interest cost and capex needs of the cell and E2W business. It also cut the EV maker’s top line growth projections by up to 10% for the period FY27-29. The bearish momentum comes a day after Ola Electric opened its rights issue for bidding. Within hours of opening the issue, Motilal Oswal and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities — ANI Technologies and Indus Trust. Founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr. Ola Electric plans to use the proceeds from its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue primarily to reduce debt and fund business expansion as it looks to strengthen its financial position and move towards cash-flow breakeven. Of the total proceeds, ₹350 Cr has been earmarked for the repayment or prepayment of borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable penalties, while ₹400 Cr will be invested in organic growth across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
- Published
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare

The festive season, usually a time to splurge, is telling a different story this year. A smaller number of card transactions and weaker smartphone sales are hinting at consumers tightening their purse strings amid mounting pressure on household budgets. Early data from Redseer estimated that India’s online festive sales clocked $7-8 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the first leg, from October 8 to 18. Nearly 100 Mn shoppers placed more than 350 Mn orders, with consumption running at around three times the everyday rate. However, the data also pointed to a more cautious spending environment. According to Datum Intelligence, a market intelligence and consumer data analytics company, the online festive sales amounted to ₹29,800-₹30,900 Cr this year, down 7-10% from ₹33,200 Cr during the corresponding four-day period last year. Card spending, too, declined 12-15% YoY. The broader consumer picture was also subdued. LocalCircles’ ‘Mood for the Consumer 2026’ survey estimated that urban households would spend ₹1.97 Lakh Cr on festive discretionary purchases this year, down 6% from ₹2.10 Lakh Cr in 2025. The survey received more than 67,000 responses from urban consumers across 307 districts. The trends pointed to a central challenge for retailers: consumers continued to browse and buy, but rising expenses, uncertainty over earnings and jobs, and less compelling discounts made them more cautious about committing to expensive purchases. Shoppers Tune In But Spending Remains Muted Flipkart’s ‘Big Billion Days’ sale, which opened on October 8 and closed on October 19, recorded 6.3 Mn concurrent users in a minute during its opening hour. Listed Meesho’s ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’, which went live on October 9 and wrapped up on October 18, also reported a 75% YoY rise in day-one orders and 60% growth in transacting customers. Over at Amazon, the ecommerce major said that its nearly two-week long ‘Great Indian Festival’ sale (stretching between October 8 and October 20) saw the number of products ordered during the first twenty four hours more than double YoY. Redseer’s assessment also highlighted the expanding reach of online festive shopping beyond major cities. Tier II and smaller towns accounted for around two-thirds of shoppers during the first leg, while the number of first-time shoppers from these regions doubled in 2026. Gen Z made up more than 35-40% of festive shoppers, with demand across gaming devices, creator cameras,wearables, sports footwear, grooming and beauty. Around 60% of Flipkart’s festive demand came from non-metro customers, while more than 72% of Amazon’s visits came from outside the top nine metros. Meesho also reported strong growth in orders through its Meesho Mall offering. However, traffic, visitors and orders measured different aspects of shopping activity. They did not, by themselves, establish how much consumers spent or whether the average purchase value increased. Datum’s card payment data offered another view. On October 9, the first day Amazon and Flipkart opened their sales to all shoppers, card transactions stood at 83.5 Lakh against 82 Lakh on the corresponding day last year. Yet, the value of those payments fell 18% to ₹6,594 Cr from ₹8,067 Cr. The figures point to lower spending despite a similar number of card transactions. Meesho’s order growth, much of which came through cash on delivery, also illustrated why order counts alone could not establish the value of sales. The year-on-year comparison, however, comes with an important caveat. The major online sales in 2025 coincided with the September 22 GST rate cuts, which reduced prices on several consumer products. The opening of this year’s sales did not have a comparable tax-led trigger. Fashion And Select Categories Find Buyers Category-level disclosures showed that consumers spent on fashion and certain premium products, even as electronics faced pressure. A Bank of America research note (dated October 20) found that Myntra’s daily active users rose around 40% during the first six days of its ‘Big Fashion Festival’, which ran between October 8 and October 25, compared with its September average. Myntra’s monthly active users stood at around 93 Mn (up 8% YoY), while Nykaa Fashion’s monthly active users grew 24% to around 17 Mn. Flipkart also reported a 42% YoY rise in beauty sales during the first hour of its sale, while its lifestyle category grew 12.5%, according to the company’s disclosures. Meesho also reported demand for festive décor and other lower-priced products. Redseer’s category-level estimates showed that large and small appliances recorded more than 20 times their average daily GMV during the festive period. Electronics ran over seven times the everyday level, while mobiles exceeded five times. These multiple compared festive daily GMV with the January - August 2026 daily average, rather than with the previous year. Amazon’s disclosures show that some premium categories performed well. Televisions measuring 55 inches and above accounted for 65% of its TV sales, while premium Android smartphones’ sales rose 70% YoY. The company also reported that high-end home theatre sold at 100X its regular day levels, while front-load washing machines with capacities of 9 kg and above sold at 80X. Fashion and beauty also recorded strong festive demand. Redseer estimated that fashion grew 20-25% and accounted for nearly a fifth of festive GMV, making it the second largest category. However, these numbers reflected performance in specific categories and do not establish a broad recovery in big ticket demand. LocalCircles’ survey provided another indication of household priorities. Among respondents who planned festive discretionary spending, 72% intended to buy clothing, footwear or accessories. Home appliances and furniture and travel and holidays were each cited by 45%. Only 22% planned to buy mobile phones, consumer electronics or gadgets. The findings suggested that expensive electronics were not a priority for most households planning festive purchases. Household Budget Under Pressure LocalCircles estimated that urban households would spend around ₹20,000 on festive discretionary purchases in 2026. While 57% of respondents said they intended to spend, 31% planned no discretionary festive purchases. The survey’s findings on how households planned to fund their purchases were equally telling. Around 83% of households intending to spend expected to use savings to some extent. About 34% expected savings to cover at least a quarter of their festive expenditure, including 16% who said they would fund the entire amount from savings. This came as retail inflation stood at 5.54% in September and food inflation at 7.74%, according to figures cited by LocalCircles. Higher everyday expenses left households with less room for purchases. LocalCircles founder Sachin Taparia said, “Household earnings are not rising, and inflation continues to rise.” He also pointed to concerns over AI and its potential effect on white-collar jobs, along with a lack of attractive deals on online commerce platforms. Discounts may also have done less to persuade shoppers to buy. The Economic Times reported that festive discounts were 35-40% lower than last year. The report also cited price increases of 30-40% for premium electronics in recent months. Smartphone Sales Exposed The Limits of Online Traffic Smartphones provided one of the clearest indications of the pressure on high-value purchases. Counterpoint Research’s early assessment found that smartphone sales fell 16% YoY during the first three days of Amazon’s and Flipkart’s festive sales, despite strong traffic on both platforms. The research firm had initially forecast a 12% decline in festive smartphone volumes. Its early assessment suggested that the fall could be steeper, although the figures available in the supporting documents did not establish the final full-season outcome. Counterpoint’s report identified higher device prices and fewer direct discounts as factors weighing on demand. Brands relied more on no-cost EMIs, bank cashback and exchange offers to make upgrades affordable without cutting listed prices sharply. Premium Samsung models, including the Galaxy S25 Ultra and the S25 FE, found buyers, but their performance did not prevent the overall decline in smartphone sales during the opening days. Entry-level devices faced greater pressure because even discounted models were generally more expensive than a year ago. “We had projected a 12% decline in smartphone sales, but based on the first wave of festive sales, we would not be surprised if the decline deepens to around 16%. Platforms have seen strong traffic, but conversions have been weak. Premium smartphones, however, continue to sell well, which could support revenue despite pressure on volumes,” Tarun Pathak, Research Director at Counterpoint Research. Counterpoint also noted that the opening days fell during Pitru Pakha, when some consumers in North India traditionally defer purchases. Navratri began on October 11, after the initial sales period, leaving the full festive effect on offline demand to pay out later. With the online sales campaigns now over, the early figures underline the difficulty retailers faced in converting strong digital engagement into higher-value purchases. Overall, with household budgets under pressure, rising product prices and fewer compelling discounts, shoppers appear to be prioritising essentials and selective purchases over expensive upgrades this festive season. Convicted murderer who attended McGill's faculty of law now back in custody
Jeffrey George Ewert, who was out on day parole, has been arrested on a warrant, CBC confirms
A convicted murderer who has stirred controversy while attending law courses at McGill University is back in custody while authorities look more closely at his case.
The Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) confirmed to CBC News on Saturday that a suspension warrant for Jeffrey George Ewert was issued.
“The offender has returned to custody while a more thorough assessment of the situation is being conducted,” the statement said. Two sources had confirmed to CBC that Ewert had been picked up on Friday.
Ewert was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for attacks against two women in B.C. in 1984 and is serving a life sentence.
He was granted day parole in 2025 and began taking law classes and going to faculty events at the Montreal institution in August. He had not been on campus since early October, according to a statement from McGill's provost.
His parole was extended for another six months in June 2026. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”

The parole board did express concern about his interactions with and attitudes toward women.
In a statement Saturday, the federal agency that oversees adult offenders said a conditional release can be suspended in situations where there are “reasonable grounds to believe that the offender has breached a condition of release or that the risk they present can no longer be safely managed in the community.”
The case will be reviewed with the established post-release decision-making process, the agency said. That could include further consideration by the Parole Board of Canada (PBC).
The CSC says given it is an active case, it can’t comment further or provide further information about what led to the suspension as per the Privacy Act.
Presence stirs debate at McGill
But his attending McGill has created a deep divide over the presence of a convicted killer in the classroom.
One petition has circulated outlining why students feel unsafe and don’t want to be in Ewert’s presence. The petition expressed concern over his alleged behaviour while attending McGill.
However, another petition argued that excluding Ewert from campus undermines his access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.
The CSC says information about an offender's time in the community is continually gathered.
“When concerns arise regarding an offender's behaviour, compliance with release conditions, or ability to be safely managed in the community, CSC takes appropriate action,” the CSC said.
“If the risk can no longer be safely managed in the community, CSC may suspend the offender's release and return them to custody. CSC works closely with its partners to respond quickly when circumstances require intervention.”
In a statement to CBC on Friday, a spokesperson for McGill said the "safety and security of our students is paramount."
The university also promised to "actively review its admissions processes to ensure a similar situation never happens again."

Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
- Published
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.
