Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

The administrations of former US President Joe Biden and current President Donald Trump have repeatedly asked Elon Musk's SpaceX to activate or restrict its Starlink satellite internet service in different countries, highlighting Washington's growing reliance on private technology companies to implement foreign policy objectives, according to a Reuters report citing six former senior US officials.
The requests, made before the recent restrictions on Ukraine's military access to SpaceX satellite communications, included disabling Starlink to prevent Iran-backed militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using the service and activating it to provide internet access in Iran and Ukraine, Reuters reported.
During Biden's presidency, US officials sought to restrict the service's availability to certain militant groups while also requesting its activation to support internet access in Iran and military communications in Ukraine, four former officials told Reuters.
The Trump administration similarly asked Musk, SpaceX's chief executive, to
make Starlink available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026. The objective was to strengthen internet connectivity and communications for anti-government protesters, the report said.
The recent restrictions on Ukraine's access to SpaceX satellite services have renewed concerns about the relationship between the US government and Musk, whose company operates satellite communication systems considered important to the US military and its allies.
The earlier requests by both administrations illustrate how Washington has increasingly depended on a private company to support diplomatic, political and military objectives abroad.
The restrictions affecting Ukraine have also caused concern among European officials, some of whom argue that Europe needs to develop independent military satellite communication capabilities.
European governments face a significant challenge because there is currently no readily available alternative that can immediately match SpaceX's capabilities, according to the report.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that access to Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused satellite communication system, had been deliberately restricted, affecting the performance of Ukrainian military drones.
He also said that Starlink connection speeds had been reduced. Ukraine relies on the service for several military operations, including frontline communications and defence against Russian missile attacks.
Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).”
Reuters previously reported that the order to restrict Starshield's operations in Ukraine originated within the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not confirmed whether it issued the order.
The developments have raised questions about the extent to which a private technology provider can influence the communications capabilities of a country engaged in a war.
Starlink has become a vital communication network for Ukrainian forces, connecting military units operating along the frontline. Ukrainian personnel have said there is currently no rival offering comparable capabilities.
The service has helped maintain communications in areas where conventional networks have been damaged or disrupted by fighting.
Starshield receivers, designed for military applications, are also used in Ukrainian drones as guidance systems and to maintain communication links with remote pilots.
These systems support drone operations, including missions deep behind Russian lines within Ukraine. Their resistance to radio-frequency jamming has made them particularly valuable in a battlefield environment where electronic warfare is widespread.
The latest developments have intensified debate over the strategic risks of relying on privately owned satellite infrastructure for national security and military operations.
For Ukraine, any disruption to satellite connectivity could affect coordination between military units and the operation of drones. For European governments, the episode has underscored the need to strengthen independent defence communications infrastructure.
The repeated requests by successive US administrations also demonstrate how satellite internet services have become instruments of international policy, with decisions by a private company potentially carrying consequences for governments, armed forces and civilian populations.

Is indoor air safer? 7 things to know and ways to stay protected in this prolonged haze season
A test reveals worse air quality indoors than outside, while product testing shows that some expired masks still filter particles effectively. Talking Point finds out from experts why neither finding tells the whole story.
SINGAPORE: Staying indoors with the windows shut may seem the safest way to escape the haze. But just how much cleaner is the air in your home?
When CNA’s Talking Point tested the air quality in a fifth-floor flat whose windows had been closed for an hour, the PM2.5 reading of 187 micrograms per cubic metre was higher than the level outdoors, which was 169.
The finding comes as Singapore grapples with its worst haze episode since 2015, with 20 consecutive days of unhealthy air recorded as at Oct 24, surpassing the 15-day streak in 2015.
As the haze persists, there is public concern about prolonged exposure to PM2.5, the predominant pollutant during periods of transboundary haze.
PM2.5 particles, which are roughly 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair, can penetrate deep into the lungs and cause inflammation.
Prolonged exposure has been linked to increased risk of a stroke and lung cancer, among other things, highlighted respiratory physician Steve Yang from The Respiratory Practice.
So, viewers have written to Talking Point to ask how best to protect themselves. Does air-conditioning help? Do expired N95 masks still offer protection? And which air quality standards should they rely on?
Programme host Diana Ser met the experts to look at seven things that Singaporeans should know during this haze season.
WATCH: How harmful is the haze and how can we protect ourselves? (23:20)
1. WHAT IS YOUR INDOOR AIR QUALITY LIKE?
In the first flat Ser visited, where the air quality was worse than outdoors, the windows were open in the morning before the resident closed them.
“It’s entirely possible that the windows were closed … (when) the PM2.5 levels were higher, thereby trapping the polluted air,” said Nanyang Technological University (NTU) assistant professor Leonard Ng, who used a professional-grade air quality monitor to record the measurements.
In a 15th-floor flat in the same block, where the windows were also closed for an hour, the reading was lower at 149 but still elevated. When they opened the windows, it climbed to 301 as the haze worsened.
As there is stronger airflow on a high floor, haze particles get blown indoors faster even as these homes are less exposed to traffic emissions, said Ng. “If the air quality is poor outside, it’ll be poor inside as well.”
He advised opening the windows at home only when the outdoor air quality “isn’t that bad”.
2. HOW MUCH CAN AIR-CON OR AIR PURIFIERS HELP?
When the air-con in one bedroom in the 15th-floor flat was run for 10 minutes, the PM2.5 reading dropped from 131.6 to 109.8, which was still in the elevated band.
While most air-con units have built-in filters that remove some airborne particles, they are not designed to “fully clean your air”, said Ng.
When an air purifier was run for an hour in the living room, however, the PM2.5 reading dropped to 40.7, within the normal band.
While the tests were conducted under different conditions and with different durations, the findings suggest that the air-con is no substitute for an air purifier.
For those considering an air purifier, Ng advised choosing one based on room size — by checking its clean air delivery rate, which measures the volume of clean air produced and thus the purifier’s effectiveness in that space.
While high-efficiency particulate air filters will capture fine airborne particles, they are not essential, he added. A regular filter rated for removal of PM2.5 particles can also be used.
He also recommended running the air purifier for an extended period with the doors and windows closed, while keeping its vents unobstructed.
3. CAN EXPIRED N95 MASKS STILL BE USED?
One Talking Point viewer asked whether his N95 masks that expired in 2017 could still offer him protection.
Ser sent two of them to ST Engineering’s mask production facility, along with other commonly used masks. There, the company tested how effective each mask was in filtering out airborne particles, including those similar in size to PM2.5.
The viewer’s masks achieved 99 per cent filtration efficiency, exceeding the 95 per cent requirement for N95 masks. By contrast, another N95 mask that expired in 2022 was at 93 per cent, below the required standard.
ST Engineering’s head of respiratory protection, Jerome Lee, said manufacturers may design masks that exceed filtration requirements to take account of deterioration over time. Masks stored in cool, dry conditions may also retain their filtration capability even years after expiry.
But he advised against using expired masks, as their performance can no longer be guaranteed and the amount of degradation “isn’t something you can observe using your naked eye”.
Talking Point also found that a surgical mask filtered out 67 per cent of the test particles, compared with 95 per cent for a KF94 mask and 98 per cent for new N95 masks.
Even an efficient mask offers less protection, however, if it does not fit snugly, Lee cautioned. Surgical masks, in particular, are not designed to be sealed tight.
He recommended discarding masks with damaged straps, deteriorated nose pads or other signs of wear.
4. WHY DO DIFFERENT WEBSITES HAVE DIFFERENT READINGS?
Some viewers asked why air quality readings on the National Environment Agency (NEA) website differed from those on international websites.
Ser compared a one-hour PM2.5 reading of 164 on the NEA website with a reading of 214 on the World Air Quality Index (AQI) website. “That’s quite a disparity. Why is that so?” she asked.
Natasha Jamali, principal scientific officer in the NEA’s environmental quality monitoring department, said some third-party websites use different data sources, including the NEA’s readings as well as low-cost sensor data from individuals and private organisations.
These sensors may not be calibrated as frequently as NEA’s analysers, and their readings can be affected by humidity and temperature. “More data may not necessarily be better because it depends on the quality of these data sources,” she said.
Calculations based on the AQI, developed by the United States Environmental Protection Agency, are also different from Singapore’s method of calculating PM2.5 readings, so the numbers are “not directly comparable”, she added.
As for how to use the NEA readings, she advised looking at the one-hour PM2.5 reading for the most recent indication of air quality before heading out or not.
The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index, meanwhile, indicates the overall air quality over the past day. It measures six pollutants including PM2.5 and is used for health advisories and planning activities.
For next-day activities, Singaporeans can refer to the NEA’s air quality forecast, which also takes into account weather conditions and regional haze.
5. WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF EXERCISING OUTDOORS?
Despite the lingering haze, some people are exercising outdoors. One runner told Talking Point he came from an ActiveSG gym where all the treadmills were occupied. Another said: “I don’t like running on treadmills.”
A cardiopulmonary exercise test showed how much more PM2.5 particles they could be inhaling outdoors.
Riding an exercise bike at mild intensity, Ser breathed in about 50 per cent more air per minute than at rest. This rose during moderate exercise to three times her baseline and to six times with maximal exertion.
Senior consultant cardiologist Peter Ting at the Harley Street Heart and Vascular Centre said athletes could breathe in 10 to 20 times more air during vigorous exercise.
His fellow doctor, Yang, estimated that Ser would have inhaled about 1.7 micrograms of PM2.5 per minute at rest and about 7 micrograms during intense exercise if she were outdoors, based on the PM2.5 reading at the time.
PM2.5 exposure can increase the risk of heart attack, particularly among the elderly and those with existing lung and heart conditions. “After about an hour,” Ting warned, “the risk already starts to go up.”
He advised those exercising outdoors to check the one-hour PM2.5 reading, reduce workout intensity and duration and avoid busy roads, where traffic adds to the pollution.
Yang said he would move exercise indoors once air quality reaches the unhealthy range — while continuing to monitor the PM2.5 reading as there could be indoor air pollution.
6. WHEN WILL THE HAZE END?
Singaporeans can expect some relief by mid-November, according to NTU climate researcher Wang Jingyu.
The assistant professor said the arrival of the northeast monsoon will change the prevailing winds; smoke from forest fires in Indonesia will no longer be carried to Singapore.
But there is a secondary haze season, typically from March to May, when hot and dry conditions can increase the risk of wildfires in the region, he highlighted.
7. COULD IT GET WORSE IN FUTURE?
Wang said scientists also expect future climate conditions to “be more El Nino-like”. This could reduce rainfall in Southeast Asia “significantly” and make forest fires harder to extinguish, increasing the likelihood of a similar haze episode recurring.
Whether it could get worse, however, also depends on countermeasures to control the haze. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has created a roadmap aimed at achieving a haze-free region by 2030. Strengthening enforcement is one of the strategies.
In recent days, the NEA issued notices to 10 companies in Indonesia under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, followed by notices to 10 Singapore-based firms for the first time under the law.
Singapore has also offered Indonesia assistance with its firefighting efforts and in cloud seeding. For now, Singaporeans can only look ahead to the winds to change.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

To strengthen Karnataka’s organ transplantation programme and increase deceased donor transplants, the State Health Department will constitute an Organ Transplant Visionary Committee under Nagesh Hegde, who heads the State-run Institute of Gastroenterology Sciences and Organ Transplant (IGOT), Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday.
Mr. Khader said the decision was taken at a progress review meeting with the State Organ Transplant Advisory Committee, which he chaired.
The proposed committee will recommend measures to raise public awareness about organ donation and improve access to transplantation, with a focus on strengthening infrastructure and streamlining procedures across the State, he said.
Brain death certification
One of the key priorities would be to facilitate brain death certification and organ retrieval at all district hospitals and government medical colleges. The committee would also recommend measures to expand organ transplant facilities in government hospitals, Mr. Khader said.
“Most hospitals do not want to obtain licences for organ retrieval due to the long process of paperwork. To avoid this, we are proposing that all hospitals with 50–100 beds capacity should automatically become organ retrieval centres. If they do not wish to, they can apply to get it cancelled,” he said.
The early launch of a new software system for organ allocation and tracking would be another priority, aimed at improving the efficiency of the process. The government would also focus on renewing registrations of transplant centres whose approvals had lapsed, he said.
Waitlist
Mr. Khader said 6,291 patients were awaiting organ transplants in Karnataka and stressed the need to encourage more people to pledge their organs. One deceased donor could help save multiple lives, he said.
The Minister urged the public to pledge their organs through the Jeevasarthakathe portal at https://jeevasarthakathe.karnataka.gov.in.
He said the proposed measures were intended to strengthen the State’s organ donation network, expand transplant services in government hospitals and improve access to life-saving organs for patients on the waiting list.

Australia’s top federal law enforcement official has drawn a direct link between politicians’ rhetoric and threats and abuse being directed at leaders.
The safety of elected representatives at all levels has been thrown into the spotlight after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly deliberate attacked outside her Wangaratta electoral office.
Haines remains in a serious but stable condition at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne, following her double leg amputation.
The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said there was no doubt the threat environment had changed for politicians.
“When I start work every morning, one of the first things I do is read a report … [that] summarises all of the threats that have been reported to the AFP over the last 24 hours,” she told the ABC’s Insiders program.
“Now, some days that report is pages and pages long.”
The commissioner said she wasn’t interested in policing free speech or intervening in political discourse.
“But I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse,” she added.
The move from the sending of physical hate mail to online threats had played a significant role in the increasing volume of worrying material, while also highlighting the influence of inflammatory political imagery and language.
“We do see where there is particular political conflict or discourse occurring … it does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it’s very immediate,” Barrett said.
Past One Nation cartoons depicting political figures, including the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, being hit by cars or buses have resurfaced in the days since the alleged attack on Haines.
The AFP commissioner said there was “a reaction amongst the community” to material such as the cartoons.
The policing agency, which is responsible for protecting federal politicians and office-holders, has held a number of emergency safety briefings with parliamentarians since Monday.
Male and female MPs were targeted equally with threats and abuse, Barrett said, but women were more often singled out individually, often with threats of sexual violence.
“My hope is that this really causes people to pause and have a think about what’s happening in this country and the impact of that,” she said.
“And if this is not the incident, then what is?”
Federal MPs from across the political spectrum have acknowledged the difficulty in balancing their personal security and access to voters.
“As a local MP, I don’t want to stop going to community events,” Liberal frontbencher Ted O’Brien told News24 on Sunday.
“That open access is a cornerstone of democracy. We’re particularly good at it in Australia. We can’t take away grassroots politics.”
Labor minister Catherine King said she has been contending with the deteriorating safety for some time.
“It is when, not if, that something will happen to one of us and we’ve been saying that certainly for the last five years or so,” she said.
“I had a mobile caravan for almost 25 years. I don’t use that now because it doesn’t have a second exit point.
“If someone did kick off and I’m trapped in the van, it’s very hard to deal with that.”

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.
The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.
Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.
People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.
The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.
The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.
Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.
A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.
A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.
“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of these 2.75-inch sonic cubes together, should you so wish.
Now, because it’s highly unlikely any one household will ever own more than a handful of mini Bluetooth speakers, this is one of those consumer-tech statements that rarely gets tested. So we asked the good folks at Älmhult in Ikea headquarters if they’d let us do just this. To our surprise, Ikea not only agreed, but it also upped the ante, saying it might be possible to link up to 150 without breaking the connection, so that’s exactly how many it sent us. “No one has ever tried this, though,” an Ikea spokesperson said. “We haven’t.”
That is how we ended up building a literal wall of sound at our London office, stacking 150 Kallsups carefully on top of one another to test how many would chain-play from a smartphone. Sadly, one casualty during shipping from Sweden—a single Kallsup—despite lighting up correctly and looking ready to chain, made an ominous rattling sound as if its innards weren’t entirely secure. Sure enough, it refused to play ball (or anything else), so we ended up with 149 speakers.
The chain process itself is simple. Once you have paired a single Kallsup with your music device—in our case, an iPhone 16 Pro—and it’s up and running, simply power on another cube while playing and hold down the Play button until a chime tells you it’s in “multi-speaker” mode. It should then immediately start playing whatever the Bluetooth-connected Kallsup is playing.
Thanks to this near-effortless chaining process, linking up all these Kallsups took much less time than we'd expected, about 30 minutes. We stopped at 100 to test how loud the “system” sounded at that stage before resuming the build and moving on to the maximum amount. As the music continued while we chained the speakers, it would be obvious when the collective refused to add more cubes. But this didn’t happen, and the plucky Kallsups joined forces without grumbling right up to the full 149.
It Might Get Loud
It’s tempting to preface the next few paragraphs with the phrase “for a $10 speaker,” because, despite Ikea’s vast buying power, experienced research and development team, and global presence, the ability to produce a tiny speaker that doesn’t sound absolutely horrible for less than a pint of half-decent craft beer is pretty incredible.
Each Kallsup has a single 1.8-inch, full-range driver powered by a 3-watt amplifier, with Bluetooth 5.3 support. No separate tweeter or woofer, just the one tiny driver.
On its own, the Kallsup speaker sounds fine. Yes, it lacks anything resembling the deep rumbling bass people talk about in audio reviews, but did we mention it’s a $10 speaker? It is a bit tinny, and you won’t want to push the volume very hard, but as a little desktop speaker, one by the side of the bed, or to throw in a suitcase, the Kallsup does the job. It doesn’t match the performance of one of our best Bluetooth speaker recommendations, but keep the cost in mind, and it’s hard to be disappointed.
Even at low background volumes, the Kallsups worked surprisingly well together, especially playing acoustic tracks. As we paired more speakers, the sound gradually grew nicely in scale. Nothing was overpowering or dominating, just the cumulative effect of all those tiny drivers moving small amounts of air.
With 149 individual 1.8-inch drivers, the combined surface area is roughly equivalent to one enormous 22-inch driver. Each Kallsup also has its own 3-watt amplifier, giving our wall a combined rated output of 447 watts. That doesn’t mean it behaves like a giant subwoofer or a conventional 447-watt speaker, but it explains why things got so loud.
But before we turned these up, if you will, to 149, we listened at 100, and when we pushed the volume, the collective Kallsups were seriously loud. But for the record, loud like a fire alarm, not a hi-fi system. With the wall complete, we worried the collective vibrations might send the whole thing crashing down. Disappointingly for the socials, it stayed resolute. Instead, we played Trans Lunar by Twin Dimensions (WIRED director of consumer tech and culture Mike Calore’s excellent band) and slowly increased the volume to maximum.
We almost wish we hadn’t. The noise was brain-numbingly loud as we blasted, somewhat appropriately, Richard Strauss’ Also Sprach Zarathustra. We couldn’t hear each other speak, and we could feel our internal organs vibrating. Any sense of fidelity disappeared, but—all power to the Kallsups—it worked. We’d successfully linked 149 Bluetooth speakers, though sadly we’re well short of the world record of 1,500 speakers set by Majority Audio in March 2026.
At more modest, realistic volumes, everything sounded considerably more composed, even if the music lacked levels of depth and detail. The overall lack of clarity could also be due to minor timing differences between the individual drivers.
At $1,490, a wall of Kallsups is quite an investment, and not one we’re recommending, but it is extremely impressive that we managed to sync and play music wirelessly through so many small, cheap speakers.
We also tested the wall alongside WIRED’s choice for best overall party speaker, the $500 LG Xboom Stage 501. Cranked up, both reached similarly ear-splitting, frankly uncomfortable volumes. But with two 5.25-inch woofers, two 2.5-inch full-range drivers, and clever digital signal processing, the LG delivered understandably fuller, deeper bass and a considerably more musical experience, as expected.
Powering Down
What’s remarkable about this experiment is that so little went wrong. Only one of the 150 speakers shipped didn’t work, clearly broken in transit. We managed to get all 149 sound cubes chained easily and quickly. And when we weren’t blasting the wall of sound at max volume, instead keeping levels moderate, the speakers sounded surprisingly competent as a collective.
However, there were hints of the Kallsup chaining capacity reaching its limit, as Ikea suspected. As we got beyond 100 units linked together, the incidence of failing to chain on the first try increased. Still, no speaker refused more than twice as we got toward the end of the build.
We also would have preferred indentations on the tops of the speakers, which would have given us a bit more confidence that the whole stack wasn’t going to collapse in a heap as volume ramped up (which it didn’t). Such a simple design feature would help whether you’re dealing with just a couple placed on top of each other, let alone 149—but this is splitting hairs.
Lastly, although this setup was impressively loud, no one in their right mind would do this in their own home. Ikea has been a good sport letting us try this out, but the ultimate, unsurprising lesson is: If you want high-quality audio, spend your money on a better speaker. As for the Kallsup? Simple to use, easy to chain, with approachable sound and clean design. You really can’t ask much more for $10.

Delhi court orders trial of Yasin Malik, Engineer Rashid, 5 others in terror funding case
The court in September held that sufficient material existed to raise a “strong suspicion” against all accused for an offence under PMLA.
A Delhi court on Friday ordered the commencement of trial against jailed Kashmiri separatist leader Yasin Malik, Baramulla MP Sheikh Abdul Rashid, alias Engineer Rashid, and five others in an alleged ₹8.94 crore terror-funding and money laundering case linked to Pakistan-based hawala channels.
Special Judge Prashant Sharma of Rouse Avenue courts, formally framing charges against the accused, directed that the recording of prosecution evidence will begin on November 19.
Also read: Farooq Abdullah's remarks on Pakistan, Kashmiris spark row; BJP demands apology
The development came after the court on September 9 ordered framing of charges against the accused, observing that there was sufficient prima facie material on record to raise a "strong suspicion" regarding the involvement of the accused in generating, receiving, and laundering proceeds of crime to fund secessionist activities in Jammu and Kashmir.
Yasin Malik pleaded ‘not guilty’
The proceedings were conducted in an in-camera hearing. Appearing through video conferencing from Tihar Jail, Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) chief Yasin Malik pleaded not guilty to the charges under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and stated that he would contest the case.
The court had in September held that sufficient material existed to raise a “strong suspicion” against all seven accused for an offence under Section 3 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).

“I conclude that prima facie, there is sufficient material on record based upon which strong suspicion is raised against all seven accused persons,” the special judge had said.
The accused in the case are Malik, Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali, Abdul Rashid Sheikh, Shabir Ahmad Shah, Masarat Alam, Naval Kishore Kapoor and Trison Farms and Constructions Pvt Ltd.
What the Enforcement Directorate said
According to ED, the criminal activities under investigation generated proceeds of crime totalling ₹8.94 crore. The agency alleged that the money was subsequently received, transferred, concealed, possessed, acquired and used by the accused through different channels.
ED alleged that funds were allegedly moved through cash couriers from the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi to members of the Hurriyat leadership, including Malik, to promote the secessionist agenda and support subversive activities.
Also read: Demand for students' union, row over ‘slogans’ trigger tensions in Jamia Millia Islamia
The agency also relied on material recovered from Ghulam Mohd Bhat, an accountant-cum-cashier working with Watali. The documents allegedly showed that Malik, Shabir Shah and Masarat Alam received foreign contributions through Watali during the 2015-16 financial year.
The investigation further uncovered emails associated with Malik which, according to ED, indicated that he had developed a network to raise funds abroad for terrorist, secessionist and unlawful activities in J&K in the name of a “freedom struggle”. The agency alleged these funds were used to sustain the JKLF and intensify secessionist violence.
ED had further alleged that Malik received another ₹15 lakh through Watali during 2015-16, bringing the total amount allegedly received by Malik to ₹30.75 lakh.
Malik received ₹15 lakh from Saudi in 2013
The National Investigation Agency (NIA), in its second supplementary charge sheet, alleged that Malik had received ₹15.75 lakh from Saudi Arabia in 2013.
ED treated these amounts as proceeds of crime allegedly derived from criminal activity connected with the scheduled offences.
The money laundering proceedings are linked to an NIA case registered in 2017 over an alleged larger conspiracy involving terrorist and secessionist activities in J&K.
NIA invoked provisions including criminal conspiracy, 121 (waging war against the government) and 121A (criminal conspiracy against the state) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sections of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
ED registered its case on June 14, 2017, to investigate the alleged laundering of proceeds generated through those criminal activities. Its main prosecution complaint was filed in 2020, while a supplementary complaint in January 2023 arraigned Malik as an accused.
NIA had alleged that Malik was involved in terrorist and subversive activities in the Valley and in raising and receiving funds through illegal channels, including Hawala. The underlying NIA case ultimately resulted in Malik’s conviction in 2022.

Nature vs. bulldozers: The environment minister's balancing act at UN nature summit
Julie Dabrusin heads to COP17 in Armenia looking for ways for Canada to have 'leadership role'
Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major projects that put those protections in jeopardy.
Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin spoke to CBC News about the work she hopes to advance in Yerevan and responded to critics who say the government's actions on the nature file are "incoherent."
Dabrusin is heading to COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference, on Saturday.
"Canada is the second-largest country in the world. We have the longest coastline in the world. So whatever we do has a real global impact," said Dabrusin before departing to Armenia.
She said international environmental conferences are "real moments" for Canada to have a "leadership role" in "pushing the world" to protect nature and reduce global emissions.
The environment minister attends COP17 on the heels of making a series of announcements to conserve lands and waters.
In October, Dabrusin announced that Canada is conserving an area of forest and peatlands near Kapuskasing, Ont., that's 1.3 times the size of Toronto.
In 2025, the minister said Ottawa would support the conservation of an area of land that's the size of Japan. As part of the initiative Northwest Territories: Our Land for the Future, the Canadian government is funding one of the world's largest Indigenous-led projects, conserving 380,000 square kilometres of land and water.
Policy 'incoherence': Greenpeace
But Dabrusin's attendance at COP17 comes as the Carney government receives sustained criticism for changes it's making to Canada's environmental laws.
"I think the big headline specifically for Canada is policy incoherence," said Salomé Sané, the nature and biodiversity campaigner for Greenpeace Canada.
The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, is making its way through the House of Commons. The omnibus bill is proposing to amend several pieces of environmental legislation in order to fast-track pipelines, power lines, mines and other projects that fall under federal jurisdiction.
- Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment
- Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in new bill to fast-track development projects
"We have the same federal government pushing for a very destructive bill under C-39 that will allow development projects to be built by bypassing, amongst other things, environmental regulations," Sané said.
"So our question to the government is, which is it? Are we protecting nature or are we destroying nature? Because going to COP to talk about nature protection and not defending nature at home will not allow us to deliver nature recovery."
Debrusin responded to that criticism noting the government didn't move forward with some of the amendments it was contemplating due to pushback. She added the bill focuses on how projects get assessed, not weakening environmental standards.
"There's nothing in the policies we're putting forward that reduces our environmental standards," Dabrusin said.
Canada co-hosted with China the UN biodiversity conference in 2022. Countries signed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which set a target of the world conserving 30 per cent of lands and waters by 2030.
Since setting those targets, global progress has been slow according to UN Secretary General António Guterres.
"Even if current national commitments are met, only 26 per cent of terrestrial, and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030. That is well short of the promise made in Montreal," Guterres said in the Armenian capital last week.

New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
Efforts to understand how classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD summon powerful changes in consciousness tend to focus on what's happening inside our head.
That's because these compounds bind tightly to serotonin receptors that densely populate certain structures of the brain, and a growing number of studies demonstrate they can exert long-lasting changes in mental health and well-being for people with a range of psychiatric conditions. 
Increasingly researchers have started to probe how these drugs elicit other physiological changes, given that many cells and tissues beyond the brain possess those same receptors, known as 5-HT2A.
Now, new research offers some of the first evidence in humans that psychedelics may also hold potential for treating diseases characterized by inflammation and immune dysregulation throughout the body.
The data, published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA Psychiatry, draws from a small pool of patients with Parkinson's disease, but it reflects what's been observed in lab studies with animal and cell models for years. For certain diseases, psychedelics appear to combat inflammation and even help restore stressed mitochondria, the energy-producing factories of the cells.
The team at the University of California, San Francisco, who conducted the study, used blood tests to measure five different signaling molecules involved in inflammation in participants, both before and after two sessions with psilocybin.
The participants had significantly lower levels of inflammation following the treatments, compared to baseline, and those changes persisted a month after their final dose of psilocybin. The researchers also tracked a blood marker of mitochondrial stress. Here, too, there were substantial improvements immediately after participants were given psilocybin, though not during the longer-term follow up.
"This gives us an initial biological signal to investigate," says Dr. Ellen Bradley, an associate professor of psychiatry at UCSF who helped lead the analysis.
The findings were based on 12 participants in a pilot study to evaluate the feasibility and safety of giving psilocybin to people with Parkinson's disease. Patients with neurodegenerative conditions are typically excluded from trials on psychedelics and mental health for safety concerns.
The original study, which was published last year, assuaged researchers' concerns about the risks. Bradley says they found a "really promising safety profile" and that "symptoms even seemed to get a bit better."
The researchers emphasize that the study has limitations: they did not have a control group, and the participants knew they were receiving the drug. So the data on what was happening in their blood needs to be confirmed in follow-up studies before making definitive claims, says Aoife O'Donovan, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF and co-author of the paper.
Still, O'Donovan says the findings reflect "objective markers" that changed over time and that gives them confidence to pursue this line of research.
Parkinson's disease is characterized by dysregulated inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This data, Bradley notes, could help explain why the participants appeared to benefit from the drugs during the trial.
Beyond that, the results raise the proposition that psychedelics may help address others diseases that are characterized by troubles with inflammation, says D. Parker Kelley, a research scientist in the Mitochondrial PsychoBiology group at Columbia University who was a first author on the paper with Bradley.
"It's a potential jumping off point for a lot more research in this area," he says, "that may apply not only to Parkinson's, but also neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and anxiety, and even cardio-metabolic and inflammatory disorders."
While previous studies have looked at biomarkers of inflammation after psilocybin, those have generally included healthy volunteers – not people with real disease, says Charles Nichols, a professor of pharmacology, biochemistry and experimental therapeutics at LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.
"I think it's really exciting," says Nichols, who didn't work on the study, but whose lab discovered that certain psychedelics could have powerful anti-inflammatory effects about fifteen years ago.
That insight came from studying lab-grown cell culture that simulated inflammation of blood vessels and hardening of arteries, also known as atherosclerosis.
In that experiment, they found a psychedelic acting on the 5-H2TA receptors functioned as a "potent anti-inflammatory," even at doses well below what would cause a psychoactive trip, he says.
Since then, Nichols' group has run numerous experiments in animal models of disease including asthma, arthritis, and cardiovascular disease, but the field has needed to test whether these protective effects hold up in humans.
He says this new study in Parkinson's patients is a proof of principle.
"We can only draw so much from those conclusions," he says. "But I do think it validates a lot of the pharmacology that we've been doing over the last 15 years on the anti-inflammatory, the mitochondrial protective effects."

The king of ghosts lives in a haunted $4.3 million dollar mansion in the heart of New Orleans' French quarter. The dozens of paranormal tour guides who lead tourists through the neighborhood are sure to know of him and have an opinion of him. Lance Zaal is the most controversial man in America's booming ghost business, CEO of what competitors have dubbed "The Walmart of Ghost Tours."
Over the past half-decade, Zaal, 42, and his company, US Ghost Adventures, have opened ghost tours in more than 250 cities and towns, employing more than 1,000 guides, according to his company's website. He's also been buying up the country's haunted landmarks like it's the first trip around the Monopoly board — the Lizzie Borden House in Massachusetts, the Villisca Axe Murder House in Iowa, the McInteer Villa in Kansas, and two historic houses in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. "Lance has said he wants to build an empire, and that's what he's doing," says Diane Student, who hosts the industry podcast History Goes Bump.
USGA also sells ghost detection gear through the brand Ghost Daddy — products with names like the Sinister Speaker, Medusa's Net, and Devil's Marble MK2. An Ultimate Ghost Hunt Kit For Two sells for $629.99. The whole operation has made Zaal wealthy enough to buy the Lalaurie Mansion, his primary residence, which stands on the site of an infamous slaveowner's torture chamber. Previous guests have reported unexplained moaning and groaning inside, along with the sudden, putrid smell of burning flesh, and, according to New Orleans tour guide Catie Santos, passing guides stand on the opposite side of the street because of the house's dark energy. On tours, Santos, who was briefly employed by Zaal as a content creator, also warns her guests "about the real life Marvel supervillain living in that house," she says.
In assembling his dominion of the undead, Zaal has made a host of enemies among the living. I spoke with more than a dozen competitors and insiders in the industry who described him as "vindictive," "predatory," a "bully," and a "hemorrhoid." He has been accused of borrowing content from local tours, ripping off merchandise designs, redirecting negative reviews to competitors, misclassifying workers as contractors, and using names similar to local companies to confuse tourists. The allegations have resulted in a mounting pile of lawsuits against USGA. Zaal, who did not respond to repeated inquiries for this story, has consistently denied any predatory behavior and emphasizes his commitment to historic preservation.
When passing Zaal's mansion, Catie Santos warns tourists of "the real life Marvel supervillain living in that house," she says.
He has gone after his rivals, filing copyright and defamation suits and frequently threatening legal action. "This gang of competitors are the bullies. So desperate to restore their monopolies or do whatever they can to eliminate their competition," USGA wrote in the comments section of "Exposing US Ghost Adventures Corrupt and Unethical Business Practices Part 1," a recent video from the YouTube channel The Paranormal Engineer.
When Walmart surged through the country in the 1980s, it sparked fierce resistance from the mom and pop stores threatened by their expansion. Today, the rise of the Walmart of Ghost Tours has ignited a war in the ghost industry.
In the biography published on his website — which has a slapdash, early-2000s blog design — Zaal describes a hardscrabble childhood in Southern California. After his parents divorced when he was 6, he was often homeless, sometimes sleeping in the family van. He was bullied in school, he writes, and threw himself into little entrepreneurship projects like a lemonade stand, where he bumped his margins by charging extra for a "Lemon Special," which involved adding a Lemonhead candy to the drink. He says his youth was also marked by eerie experiences — mysterious footsteps, doors opening and closing without explanation — that inspired a lifelong fascination with the supernatural. "I've experienced odd things I can't explain," he said in a recent interview with Business Insider.
After 9/11, Zaal enlisted in the Marine Corps at age 17. He completed three tours, including two in Iraq, where he was stationed for a time at President Saddam Hussein's palace. Then he got an MBA at William and Mary, and worked briefly at Booz Allen Hamilton and Mythics Inc., until he was laid off in 2012. He set out on his own, developing a GPS-guided audio ghost tour app called ItourMobile. It was good timing. America was in the midst of a ghost renaissance.
In a 1978 Gallup poll, 11% of Americans said they believed in ghosts. By 2025, that number soared to 39%. Some attribute the trend to a decline in traditional religion, with non-religious people becoming more inclined to seek other supernatural answers to life's big questions. And as paranormal beliefs have risen, there has been an influx of people trying to profit from them. Reality TV shows "Ghost Hunters" and "Ghost Adventures" took off in the 2000s. By 2023, "dark tourism" — which ranges from the sites of atrocities to haunted houses — was valued at $32 billion and projected to reach $39 billion by the decade's end, according to Grand View Research.
Years after US Ghost Adventures took off, an interviewer at Authority Magazine asked Zaal what advice he wished he could give his younger self. "You're on your own," Zaal said, in a quote displayed under a photo of him in a vest, arms crossed, blue-steeling the camera. "You have no friends. The market is God."
Ting Rappa, an EMT and firefighter who runs an Orlando-based ghost tour called American Ghost Adventures met Zaal in 2015, when he was managing a tour called Colonial Ghosts in Williamsburg, Virginia. Zaal approached Rappa after she attended one of his tours with a proposal to team up. "He was a little off," Rappa says. Something about his energy made her apprehensive. "But he was a very intelligent person. I could tell he had a drive." Zaal said he would help finance her company in exchange for a share of the operation. But the deal didn't seem like an even partnership, so she turned him down.
You're on your own. You have no friends. The market is God.Lance Zaal
Three years later, she discovered that Zaal had a new name for his company that resembled hers: US Ghost Adventures. When she tried to trademark American Ghost Adventures years later, the application was denied because Zaal had registered his first. In 2024, she filed a suit asking for the USGA trademark to be cancelled, still working its way through the courts. "There's just no ethics to it," she says of Zaal's expansion. "Competition is good, but play nice. Right now, you're just being a big bully."
In the Authority Magazine story, Zaal was asked how he researches whether someone else has already had one of his ideas, a question that would become more significant as his business continued to grow.
"It's not relevant," Zaal said. "Who cares who else thought of an idea? This is fear at first thinking. What matters is creating a sustainable, strong business. Just because there are others in your market, doesn't mean you can't succeed in it, or even redefine it. What is important is ensuring you don't break the law, whether that be a trademark, patent, or whatever."
A ghost tour is a pretty simple business to set up. Most are walking tours through public spaces that require little overhead. At USGA, guides are generally contractors paid a flat rate of $40 to $50 per tour, plus tips, per its website. With a tour drawing dozens of customers paying $20 to $40 for a ticket, the money can quickly pile up.
USGA wasn't the only company to pursue ghost tours on a national scale — the rival Ghost City Tours operates 60 tours — but it was the most aggressive. During the pandemic in 2020, as other tour companies were shuttering, Zaal expanded to dozens of cities and towns, ready to put guides on the pavement once restrictions were lifted. That year, he unsuccessfully sued to reverse a COVID ban on walking tours in Massachusetts. By 2021, USGA had operations in 33 cities, each under a local name.
One of the first cities targeted was Baltimore, where Melissa Rowell had operated Baltimore Ghost Tours since 2001. Zaal came on her radar when she began receiving phone calls from irate customers. "We are trying to find out where this ghost tour is," one man complained in a voicemail shared with Business Insider. "Nobody's answering the goddamn phone … after we spent almost $100."
The man was looking for Zaal's new local affiliate of USGA, which had begun operating under the name Baltimore Ghosts. Rowell sent Zaal a letter asking him to change the name to something more distinct. Soon after, Rowell says, USGA started using the name Baltimore Ghost Tour in some materials. "Instead of trying to cause less confusion, they seemed to be trying to cause more," she says.
Rowell and Zaal have since been in a cold war, volleying terse emails and cease-and-desist letters. "I understand you actively collaborate with a confederation of other companies to disparage and damage both the company and my personal reputation," Zaal wrote Rowell in 2024. "Let us honor the spirit of Halloween this season and cease this animosity. There's enough customers for all of us."
Rowell denies that she is part of a confederation, but local tour guides have collaborated in dealing with their ascendant rival. There's a private Facebook group where guides across the country share information about USGA. Mike Carter, a tour guide from Annapolis, Maryland, bought the domain name USAghostadventures.com to build a site that urged customers to choose local ghost tours instead of Zaal's outfit. (Zaal got the site taken down and sued Carter for defamation.) Some paranormal companies, like Central New York Ghost Hunters, have rejected partnerships with USGA out of solidarity with local guides.
In Austin, Texas, USGA was sued by the owners of a local Booze and Boos Tour after Zaal opened a Boos And Booze tour. In Savannah, Georgia, the national company Ghost City Tours, which operated a Dead of Night Tour, sued USGA for opening the Savannah Terrors Ultimate Dead of Night Haunted Ghost Tour. In Charlotte, North Carolina, the local Queen City Tours sued Zaal's Queen City Ghosts. USGA generally argues in court papers and public statements that the names are too generic to own. The Austin suit was settled in 2024; the latter two lawsuits are currently making their way through the courts.
USGA was sued by the owners of the Booze and Boos Tour after it opened a Boos And Booze tour; the Dead of Night Tour for opening the Savannah Terrors Ultimate Dead of Night Haunted Ghost Tour; and Queen City Tours for opening Queen City Ghosts.
In one instance, a guide alleges that Zaal uses these similar names to trick tourists into leaving negative reviews on his competitors' tours. Angela Taverniti, who runs Colonial Ghosts of Williamsburg, said a USGA customer, Samantha Butler, accidentally left a negative review on Taverniti's tour. When she pointed out the mixup, Butler pulled up the link she got from USGA asking her to review the tour and tested it. A screen recording Butler shared with Business Insider shows that when she submitted a four-star ranking, she was directed to the Google review page of the USGA tour she took. But when she submitted a two-star rating, she was directed to the Google page for Taverniti's tour. Spooky. Reviews are a big deal for tour operators. "98 percent of our business comes from Google," Taverniti tells me. "It's a game that you have to play constantly. And he knows how to play it."
Other paranormal guides say Zaal borrows the content of the tours along with the names. Laine Johnson, a former park ranger, spent the last decade developing a tour of the supernatural happenings in Durango, Colorado, drawing from firsthand accounts of locals, newspaper archives, and out-of-print books. When a new tour called Durango Ghosts set up shop there in early 2023, Johnson took it to check out the competition. She says she was startled that they followed her exact route and told the same stories, sometimes with the same phrasing.
When she got home and did some research, she formulated a theory of what had happened. During the pandemic, she had uploaded her materials to a site called Junket, which allowed her to host virtual tours. Junket and Durango Ghosts were owned by Lance Zaal. Her content, she's convinced, had been snatched from the Junket website and co-opted by her new competitor.
USGA has meaningfully eaten into her bottom line, she says. "This is a really small town. It's ridiculous that there's now three ghost tours going here," she says.
By 2021, USGA purchased the crown jewel in its collection of haunted property, a three-story Greek Revival House in Fall River, Massachusetts, where Lizzie Borden was accused of axe-murdering her parents in 1892. It's famous for paranormal activity, and Zaal mentioned in an interview shortly after the purchase that he felt as if "someone, or something, was in the room with him," when he spent the night there alone.
This is a really small town. It's ridiculous that there's now three ghost tours going here.Laine Johnson, a ghost tour owner in Durango, Colorado
In 2023, a small cafe called Miss Lizzie's opened nearby, and Zaal sued, arguing that the name and logo — a blood-stained hatchet — infringed on his trademark. "She's a historical figure," cafe owner Joe Pereira counters. "I don't think anyone can own her." It was a strange reversal of the trademark suits that had been filed against him, and local competitors followed the case closely.
The next year, a judge sided with Pereira, saying the logos were substantially different. "Miss Lizzie's hatchet has a handle and smooth axe blade that spews blood," the judge wrote in his decision. "Ghost Adventures' hatchet is bereft of either handle or blood and features a notch halfway along the blade." But the lawsuit, which dragged on for years afterwards, has taken a financial toll on Pereira. Though a judge affirmed the initial ruling this month, Pereira was also ordered to pay $31,207 in legal fees after missing various filing deadlines.
Amid the acrimony, USGA has continued to grow. From 2019 to 2023, Zaal told Entrepreneur Magazine, USGA's revenue increased by 2,600%. To service the expansion, he contracted with writers and creators to develop tours and other content about new cities in the USGA empire.
Some guides, like Sabrina Velandry, a psychic medium who conducts tours for USGA in Salem, have had broadly positive experiences with the company. It's more professionalized than some of the local tours, she says. "It is corporate, but it's just really really well-run and organized." Others have butted heads with management, and two lawsuits have alleged misclassifying workers as independent contractors and failure to pay overtime wages. USGA has denied these claims, and one suit was settled while another is still in the courts.
In 2023, Ronald Murphy, a high school teacher outside of Pittsburgh, began picking up some extra work for USGA as an independent contractor, where he would crank out a new tour for $200, or make $40 for a 300 word blurb on the USGA website. All told, he says, he wrote tours for about 18 cities.
He says he wasn't given time for deep research and didn't like the idea of using content posted by competing local tours, so for a tour about Fort Worth, Texas, he decided to get creative. "I was going to simply make up the ghosts," he says. He thought the local Cowboy Museum was the sort of place that a ghost might frequent and wrote this fiction for the website: "Of course, no cowboy can hold a candle to The Duke himself, Mr. John Wayne. Visit the Texas Cowboy Hall of Fame where it's said the apparition of the 6 foot 4 actor has been seen admiring the cowboy memorabilia on display." The work eventually dried up. Today, USGA is recruiting an AI Creative Specialist, at $42,000 a year, "to draft, edit, and refine engaging tour scripts, website copy, and compelling marketing collateral." Even ghost jobs aren't safe from the AI revolution.
Trevor Foster didn't have much interest in ghost tours until he was ripped off, he tells me. He's a ceramics artist who specializes in dark pieces like bones, pistols, and mystical eyes. This January, he received a message informing him that USGA may have stolen one of his designs to sell on its Ghost Daddy website — an intricate skull-shaped mug with a handle like a curved bone. From initial casting to final glazing, it took Foster about about 100 hours to complete.
The skull on Ghost Daddy looked like one Foster designed in a slightly different color. Foster says the fact that it had the same sutures on the top — "almost like a fingerprint" — made it clear it was a ripoff. He also found that Zaal had recently purchased the same skull mug from him. "For someone to buy it and make a direct mold just seems kinda brazen," Foster says.
Foster sent a cease-and-desist letter, and Zaal responded that he planned to remove the item within six months. "My understanding in looking at your website is that you have your initials on the bottom (ours doesn't), each one is hand crafted and unique (ours are consistent and the same which is why yours looks better), ours is of a lighter color, and our logo is on the back," Zaal added. To Foster, it seemed Zaal was implying that replacing his initials with the USGA logo was enough to make the knockoff legal.
An Instagram video Foster posted went viral in the ghost tour community, and Zaal agreed in an email shared with Business Insider to discontinue the item immediately. He attributed the similar design to a mistake made by an overseas supplier who was given multiple examples to draw inspiration from. That wasn't good enough for Foster, who sued and settled with Zaal in September.
Foster was surprised to have found something of a community as a result of the whole debacle. After he'd posted about the situation, he was inundated with dozens of messages from people with their own grievances with US Ghost Adventures, commiserating with him. "It's just kind of incredible how many people they've angered," Foster says.
And — if you fall into the 39% of the country that believes in ghosts — you might believe that it isn't just corporeal beings that have been angered. This summer, a group of part-time ghost hunters visited Zaal's newly purchased McInteer Villa and set up K-2 meters, REM pods, and a ghost box.
But the group's leaders Dawn Lorenzen and Amy Osborn found the ghosts to be surprisingly uncommunicative. When they'd visited before Zaal's purchase, the ghost hunting had been good.
They Facetimed a medium to figure out what was going on. The ghosts were irritated, she told them, and it seemed to be related to the new ownership. "They made a circus of the place," the ghosts kept repeating, she said. "And now we are a spectacle."

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.
During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.
Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, the Wall Street Journal reported at the time.
His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.
Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments into AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.
All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”
Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. Many California companies left for Texas, Nevada, and California in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.
But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.
