‘JD(U) is finished’: Expelled MLA Anant Singh says party will be reduced to 10-12 seats, hints at own outfit
Singh, who was expelled from the JD(U) on Saturday for six years, said he had "no regrets" over the disciplinary action taken against him.
Expelled Janata Dal (United) MLA and Mokama strongman Anant Singh on Sunday claimed the party would be reduced to “10-12 seats” in the next Bihar assembly elections, and indicated he may float his own political outfit.
Singh, who was expelled from the JD(U) on Saturday for six years over alleged anti-party activities, said he had "no regrets" over the disciplinary action taken against him. He also questioned the authority of the current party brass, saying although the party originally belonged to former Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar, it has lost its political standing under the leaders who reportedly orchestrated his removal.
“The party belonged to Nitish ji. Now that he is no longer there (in an active role), what is left of the party? Who among those in the leadership — the ones who expelled me — has actually contributed anything?” he told reporters.
“Now, they will be reduced to 10-12 seats... Why will I go anywhere? I will simply build my own party. The JD(U) is finished. Once they hold elections, everything will become clear,” he added.
The JD(U) currently has 84 MLAs in the 243-member assembly. It is the second largest party in the state after its ally, the Bharatiya Janata Party, which has 88 members. In the Lok Sabha, the JD(U) has 12 members.
Singh had revolted against the JD(U) by campaigning for Jan Suraaj Party's candidate Anuj Singh for the Bihar legislative council elections. He vowed to "defeat" JD(U) MLC Neeraj Kumar in the council polls by supporting and canvassing for Anuj Singh. The JD(U) also recommended to the Bihar assembly speaker that Anant Singh's membership as an MLA be terminated under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, commonly known as the anti-defection law.
Also read | JDU expels Mokama MLA Anant Singh from party for 6 years, days after controversial remarks spark row
Besides Singh, his wife and former MLA Neelam Devi has been expelled from the party for six years over alleged anti-party activities. Reports suggested the expulsions came after Union minister and senior JD(U) leader Rajiv Ranjan alias Lallan Singh met Kumar in Patna on Saturday.
The former JD(U) leader maintained his personal equation with Kumar was cordial and that there was “no distance” between them. He said he continued to hold the former chief minister in high regard and claimed no one would have dared to act against him if Kumar retained control over the party. The current leadership, he alleged, consists of people who had no role in building the party.
Also read | Bihar Council polls turn into NDA unity test as JD(U), RLM face rebellion; rift in Oppn too
Singh, long known as ‘Chhote Sarkar’ in the Mokama-Barh belt for his local influence, has had a chequered relationship with the JD(U). He first won the seat on a JD(U) ticket in 2005 and retained it in 2010, before walking out of the party in September 2015 in protest against Kumar’s alliance with the Rashtriya Janata Dal. He contested and won that year’s assembly elections as an Independent, but later joined the RJD ahead of the 2020 polls and retained the seat.
He rejoined the JD(U) ahead of the November 2025 Bihar assembly elections, after he was acquitted by the Patna High Court in August 2024 in the arms case.
His wife earlier unsuccessfully contested the 2019 Lok Sabha elections from Munger on a Congress ticket against JD(U)’s Lalan Singh. She later won the 2022 Mokama bypoll on an RJD ticket after Anant Singh’s disqualification following his conviction in an arms case.

The SAG-AFTRA board voted Saturday to extend the contract of Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, the union’s national executive director, for four years and to add CEO to his title.
Crabtree-Ireland’s contract was set to expire in 2028, but will now run through June 20, 2032. The financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. He was paid $1.1 million for the 2026 fiscal year.
The extension will carry Crabtree-Ireland through the next round of negotiations with the major studios, with the current deal set to expire in June 2030. In a statement, the union said that the extension will offer “added stability and continuity for the union during a time of unprecedented industry disruption.”
Crabtree-Ireland has spent nearly his entire career at SAG-AFTRA, serving as general counsel and chief operating officer before being named national executive director in 2021. He has made artificial intelligence a key focus of the union’s negotiations, reaching a series of agreements that aim to allow performers to capture the upside of AI while protecting them from unauthorized uses of their likenesses. He was also a central figure in the 2023 actors’ strike.
Popular on Variety
Sean Astin, the president of SAG-AFTRA, praised Crabtree-Ireland in a statement after the vote.
“To battle giant global transnational corporations, we need expert leadership with a track record of successful bargaining and significant operational management expertise,” Astin said. “That is Duncan. He is a powerful executive who has led our union at the bargaining table, in the halls of Congress and in boardrooms and conference rooms across the industry and the world. We are thrilled to have guaranteed Duncan’s continued service to the members of SAG-AFTRA.”
The extension was approved with 98.34% of the board in favor in a weighted vote.
“Leading SAG-AFTRA’s staff is the honor of my career, and I’m grateful for the opportunity to keep doing this work,” Crabtree-Ireland said. “As we continue fighting for human creativity, the coming years will be crucial for charting the path forward. I intend to fight alongside our leadership to make sure our members control their image, likeness, voice, and destiny in the workplace, and that they are compensated fairly in the process. I thank President Astin, the national officers, and the National Board for their trust, and our extraordinary staff team for everything they make possible.”

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
For anyone navigating the healthcare system, diagnosis is only the harsh beginning. There are medicines to afford, compulsive researching, decisions to make, follow-up appointments to keep and, sometimes, conflicting advice to sort through. For people living with chronic illnesses and disabilities, these become part of everyday life. The question is not only whether medical science can offer a treatment, but whether the care is in reach and if one can understand their options and make informed decisions about their health. A few of this week’s reports look at these questions
Treatment and questions
The government has capped trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs, as Bindu Shajan Perappadan reported. The move brings the discourse on the cost of cancer treatment back into focus. For patients and their families, the price of medicines can influence how manageable treatment is over months or years. A price cap is an important policy intervention, but its real value will depend on whether patients see meaningful savings.
And in Keralam, parents of children with spinal muscular atrophy have sought political support over concerns about a generic drug. For families dealing with a rare condition, access to treatment can involve difficult decisions about affordability and the medicines available to them. These decisions need clear communication and reliable evidence on safety and effectiveness, alongside efforts to make treatment accessible.
There is also the question of the use of medication and Dr. Chandrakant Lahariya examines India’s problem of overtreatment and overmedication. Unnecessary tests and medicines can add costs and expose patients to avoidable risks. For people already managing several conditions or taking multiple medicines, knowing what is necessary and what may not be is an important part of safe care.
What new research tells us
I write about lung adenocarcinoma in the all you need to know about series, following news that Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery for the cancer. The Vatican later said his recovery was on track. The explainer looks at the disease behind the headlines and offers readers a clearer understanding of this type of lung cancer.
Other research this week looks at how differently people can experience disease. A study suggests that early-onset Alzheimer’s disease can look very different from the late-onset form. Another suggests that menopause may involve a more pronounced physiological shift around the final menstrual period than the idea of a gradual transition implies.
Long COVID remains another area where researchers are working to understand why some people continue to experience effects long after an infection. A new study suggests that the condition may affect bacteria in the mouth and lungs. It is still too early to conclude what these changes mean for persistent symptoms, but the research adds to efforts to understand the longer-term effects of COVID-19.
Science, integrity and disease detection
An analysis of more than 4,000 cancer research articles has identified suspected paper-mill activity, raising concerns about the reliability of published research. Scientific findings often become the starting point for further studies, so potentially fraudulent papers can have consequences well beyond the journals in which they appear. Trust in science depends not just on new discoveries, but also on how carefully the evidence is produced and checked.
V. Geetanath reports on a genetic toolkit developed by scientists at the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology to study the inner workings of tuberculosis. The tool could help researchers investigate the bacterium more closely. It is an example of the foundational work that often happens long before a discovery leads to a new test or treatment.
Another report looks at chemical signatures -- patterns of molecules and compounds in the body that could help identify diseases by detecting changes associated with illness. These signatures may offer clues to disease processes and support earlier diagnosis, but researchers must establish how accurately they can identify specific conditions and distinguish them from other causes of similar changes. The challenge is to validate these findings in different patient groups and develop tests that are reliable, clinically useful and accessible in routine healthcare.
Climate and community health
The health effects of climate change are not always immediately visible, but their potential scale is considerable. An analysis suggests that limiting global warming to 1.8°C could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life. The estimate puts the consequences of a warming planet in terms of human health, reminding us that the conditions in which people live are closely tied to their ability to stay well.
Closer home, Kozhikode has reported 161 confirmed measles cases and one death. C. Maya reports that a continuing mumps outbreak in Keralam has also renewed demands for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
Care also needs to continue beyond the immediate event that brings someone into the health system. Dr. Sowmya Josyula writes about why maternal health care after delivery is crucial. Once a baby is born, attention can shift almost entirely to the newborn, even though the mother may still need medical follow-up and support. Postpartum care is an essential part of maternal healthcare, not an optional extra.
Sudha Chandrashekar’s article on making Keralam age-ready takes up a related question: how can the rights of the elderly be translated into accessible care? Recognising those rights is only a starting point. Older people need services and support that work in practice and respect their needs and autonomy. In another important piece, Dr. Parth Sharma examines how doctors working with marginalised communities risk facing reprisals when they challenge the conditions that make people sick, from displacement and hunger to the denial of basic healthcare.
And more
Elysia Poggi Davis, Benjamin L. Hankin and Catherine Demers write in The Conversation about research suggesting that treating depression during pregnancy may benefit a baby’s brain development.
Preeti Zachariah examines why whey protein prices are rising in India.
Smruthi Prabhu explains what intestinal gas can tell us about gastrointestinal health.
Biju Dharmapalan looks at whether a sugar-rich diet while taking antibiotics could affect the gut microbiome, he also writes about why citizens should be research partners in science.
Zubeda Hamid’s In Focus podcast examines the plague case in Siberia, what is known about the disease and what remains uncertain.
In Say Her Name series, Ramya Kannan revisits the story of India’s first woman Surgeon General and the barriers she faced in pursuing a place in science.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study suggesting that wealthier Indians may be more prone to heart disease than poorer groups.
Anirban Mukhopadhyay explores a molecule that could help make treatments for inflammatory bowel disease more effective.
Dr. C. Aravinda examines how AI-MedTech is regulated in India.
Dr. Dinesh Arab reflects on health and ageing in The back end of 55.
Dr. Sushma Gopalan explore how too many treatment options can complicate decisions for patients and doctors.

On October 17, Saturday, even as 19 people were killed and several injured in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, a different scene of chaos unfolded a few kilometres away at Jadavpur.
A bulldozer was brought in by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Kolkata Police to demolish bookstalls of Left parties set up near 8B bus stand of Jadavpur. While locals and Left workers, including CPI(M) and AISA activists, protested through the night to thwart the attempted demolition, the authorities succeeded in bringing down certain bookstalls and damaging others.
Left book stalls have come under threat both from Right-wing fanatics and the administration after chief minister Suvendu Adhikari issued a warning. “You consider Sanatan Dharma to be merely cultural. You do not say Durga Puja; You call it ‘Sharadotsab’. I will tell all Durga Puja committees that if these so-called communists come to set up stalls and do not write Durga Puja, do not allow a single stall,” Adhikari had announced earlier.
Alt News has already reported on alleged attacks on book stalls by BJP workers in several parts of the state.
Same Stalls Set Up For Years
Left organisations, including the CPI(M), AISA, SUCI(C) and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), have historically set up bookstalls in and around the 8B bus stand area of Jadavpur. The CPI(M) has been setting up its bookstall there for over 40 years, while AISA’s stall has been set up for more than 10 years. The APDR has been setting up a bookstall for the past four to five years. This year, an RSS bookstall was set up right between the CPI(M) and AISA stalls.
Around 6 pm on Saturday, a joint team of Kolkata Police, Central Armed Police Force personnel and KMC arrived with a JCB earthmover to demolish the Left bookstalls. However, the RSS stall was left untouched.
According to the KMC personnel present at the spot, the Left stalls lacked the necessary permissions. Left parties, however, denied this allegation. Representatives of the Left parties argued that they had paid the required fees to the KMC to set up the stalls.
The administration, however, maintained that paying the fees did not necessarily mean that permission had been granted to set up the stalls. The Left parties, in turn, asked the authorities to show which documents they lacked, while also asking what documents the RSS stall possessed that made it legal. Their requests were repeatedly rejected, representatives told Alt News.
‘Authorities Passed the Buck’
“Police and the KMC workers were only passing the buck on each other. Police said the KMC had sought their help to demolish illegal structures. When confronted, KMC workers said that police had asked them to help demolish our stalls,” said DYFI Kolkata district committee member Sainik Sur.
“We asked police and KMC time and again to show the demolition order. But all they said was that there was immense pressure from higher levels to demolish all the Left stalls,” added Sur.
A similar claim was echoed by AISA state president Ritam Maji. “Police and the KMC made it very clear that the Left bookstalls were illegal, whereas the ‘Sanatani’ stall that came up this year for the first time was legal. We have paid the required fee to KMC and have the receipt of the same, yet they claimed that our stalls were illegal. When we asked them to show documents of the RSS-backed stall, to figure out what permissions we lacked, the police simply said that the top brass of the KMC had requested that the space be cleared,” said Maji.
Besides the earthmover, the administration had also brought a KMC dumper truck near the stalls, generally used to collect and dispose of garbage, allegedly to collect the debris from the stalls and the books, representatives of the Left said.
Hundreds Gather Around Bulldozer
After an APDR stall was partially demolished, nearly a hundred people — locals in the area and Left party workers — gathered near the bulldozer in the evening to prevent it from demolishing stalls. Armed with flags, books and posters, they formed human chains around the bookstalls, forcing the authorities to retreat. CPI(M) central committee member and former Jadavpur CPI(M) MLA Sujan Chakraborty also reached the spot to join the resistance.
Around 1 am on October 18, Sunday, personnel from Kolkata Police, CAPF and KMC workers started assembling near the bookstalls again. An hour later, they again started dismantling the APDR stall.
The SUCI(C) bookstall, set up near Gate 2 of Jadavpur University, was also demolished around this time. The area surrounding the stall was cordoned off by security personnel, and party workers could not prevent the demolition.
CPI(M) Kolkata district committee member Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the party’s bookstalls, documented the resistance against the demolition as scores of people stood in front of the JCB earthmover, through his Facebook Live.
After the SUCI(C) stall was brought down, the administration tried to demolish both the APDR and AISA stalls, which were interlocked in a single bamboo structure. Around 3 am, Left activists were again seen forming human chains around their stalls. A section of the activists sat inside the AISA stall as the police and central forces tried to demolish it, ultimately compelling police to retreat.
As the administration tried to bring down the APDR stall around 4:30 am, CPI(M), AISA and APDR workers tried to resist the advance in a unified manner. SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya was seen resisting the administrative forces, who tried to tear down the bamboo scaffolding of the APDR stall.
Subsequently, individuals identifying themselves as KMC workers used machetes to cut the ropes of the APDR stall and bring down the structure, despite the efforts of protesters.
After the APDR stall was demolished, protesters formed a human barricade in front of the CPI(M) stall. Actress Ushasie Chakraborty was among the protesters who held the barricade.
As the standoff continued, CRPF personnel wielded the baton briefly, but it failed to scatter the crowd. Around 5 am, the forces left the spot.
Although the CPI(M) stall was mostly left untouched, the AISA stall suffered extensive damage. AISA activists tore down a section of the stall and rebuilt it on Sunday morning. SUCI(C) and APDR also rebuilt their stalls, and books were sold through Sunday.
“The police informed us that if we dismantled our stall for repairs, they would not allow us to rebuild it. However, we repaired it nonetheless and carried on with our programme,” said Maji.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. “I have visited the 8B stall quite a few times in the past. Maybe this time I might have skipped coming here. But after what happened last night, I feel it is my duty to come here and show solidarity,” said Ghosh, with CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh standing by his side.
West Bengal Congress President Suvankar Sarkar also visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. So did CPI(M) state secretary Md Salim.
Chief Minister’s Warning
On September 10, Adhikari urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for bookstalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated his stance two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Following Adhikari’s warnings, on October 14, a division bench of the Calcutta High Court overturned the order of Justice Sougata Bhattacharya’s single bench and declined the CPI(M)’s plea to organise a bookstall in front of its party office in Bongaon in Jessore Road of North 24 Parganas district — a spot where a bookstall by the Hindu Jagran Manch had allegedly been set up.

The Keralam government will strengthen all legal measures to curb unhealthy eating habits among children and prevent excessive consumption of junk food, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said.
Keralam would approach the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) seeking clarity on the definition of HFSS (High Fat, Sugar and Salt) food and on the criteria for regulating their sale, he said in a statement in Thiruvananthapuram.
As junk food has no precise scientific definition, there is no clarity on which food items should be included in this category or how their sale should be regulated. Foods containing high levels of fat, sugar and salt can be classified as HFSS, but clear criteria and guidelines are needed to fix the upper limits. At present, it is the absence of such criteria which is hampering efforts to draw up a list of HFSS food and to regulate its sales near schools.
On August 7, 2026, the FSSAI had published a draft regulation on this. The draft proposes that if solid food contains more than 4.2 g of fat, 3 g of sugar or 0.625 g of salt per 100 g, it should be considered as high levels. For liquid food, the “high” thresholds are fixed at 1.5 g of fat, 2 g of sugar and 0.175 g of salt per 100 ml, respectively.
Mr. Muraleedharan said that only when the draft regulation was finalised and incorporated into statutory rules would States have a clear legal standing to prepare a list of HFSS food and to ban or restrict their sale near schools. He added that the State would write to the FSSAI requesting that criteria be finalised without delay.
Eat Right programme
The government was implementing the Eat Right School programme to ensure safe, balanced and nutritious food in schools and to foster healthy eating habits among children. The programme was also being implemented in Model Residential Schools. Work was also under way to ensure hygiene, food safety standards and the availability of nutritious food in canteens in schools and hostels, the Minister said.
So far, the Eat Right School programme had been implemented in 169 schools. The SNF@School (Safe and Nutritious Food at School) programme, a nationwide initiative launched by the FSSAI to build a culture of safe, healthy, and wholesome food among school-going children, had been implemented in 2,500 schools.
Under the Eat Right Campus programme, safe and nutritious food would be ensured in canteens in colleges, universities, hospitals and government institutions and 456 institutions had received certification under this initiative.
Mr. Muraleedharan also stated that inspections were being held regularly and that legal measures were being taken against those violating food safety standards.

- Unlock the Omniscient Spinecaster in Fisch by reaching Hex Stage V, completing nine previous rituals, and gathering all the required ritual offerings.

The Omniscient Spinecaster is one of the Halloween rods that was added to Fisch with the FischFright 3 update. It looks like a curved spinal column made of glowing bones and comes with high luck, infinite weight capacity, and a unique ability that boosts your fishing progress and the new Omniscient mutation. In this guide, learn how to unlock the Omniscient Spinecaster Rod in Fisch.
How to Unlock the Omniscient Spinecaster Rod in Fisch
To get your hands on this Omniscient Spinecaster Rod, you will first need to reach Hex Stage V in Fisch. You also need to complete all the rituals up to the Omniscient ritual. Here is how to complete these requirements:
Reach Hex Stage V
To reach Hex Stage V, you will need an 80% bestiary compilation and 200 Hex Energy in Fisch. You can do this by fishing and completing goblin quests. Every goblin quest gives you a random ingredient, which you can deposit into the Witch’s cauldron in Caustic Hallow.
Complete the Previous Rituals
You will also need to complete all the previous rituals in order to access the Omniscient Ritual. Head to the graveyard area inside Caustic Hallow and talk to the Frankenstein NPC. You will have to complete all these rituals:
- Hexing Ritual
- Scary Relic Ritual
- Haunted Ritual
- Jack-o-Moon Ritual
- Boglin Ritual
- Dutchman’s Blessing Ritual
- Enhanced Boglin Ritual
- Haunted Cemetery Ritual
- Eldritch Ritual
Complete all nine rituals before moving to the final step. Doing the rituals is helpful as some of them unlock special items, including the Dutchman’s Rod in Fisch.
Start the Omniscient Ritual
Now that you have completed all the previous rituals, you will need to activate the Jack-o-Lanterns and the Skeletal Hands located in the circle behind the Frankenstein NPC. Here are all the items you will need to submit:
Jack-o-Lanterns
| Required Items | How to Get It | 
|---|---|
| Grim-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Grim Relic | 
| Vile-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Vile Relic | 
| Doomed-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Doomed Relic | 
| Eldritch-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Eldritch Relic | 
| Zombie Nessie | Seal 15 bones inside the urn to summon Zombie Nessie, then catch it | 
| Plush Nessie | Reach 470 Hex Energy | 
| Dark Art Skull | Obtain it as a rare Goblin quest reward | 
You can get FischFright 3 relics by fishing, completing quests, and trick-or-treating. You can also buy them from the Dutchman Merchant using Treats.
Skeletal Hands
| Required Items | How to Get It | 
|---|---|
| Boglin-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Goblin Branch Rod; the fish must not have the Shiny or Sparkling mutation | 
| Doomsekkar-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Doomsekkar Rod | 
| Dutchman’s Curse-mutated Jagged Bone | Use the Dutchman’s Rod | 
| Omniscient Souls | Buy from the Dutchman Merchant for 10,000 Treats | 
| Omniscient Bone | Reach 350 Hex Energy | 
Once the ritual is done, you will get your new Omniscient Spinecaster Rod. If you are short on treats, make sure to learn how to farm treats in Fisch fast.
Omniscient Spinecaster Rod Stats in Fisch
The rod’s design alone makes it worth the grind. Here are the Fisch Omniscient Spinecaster Rod stats:
| Stat | Value | 
|---|---|
| Lure Speed | 120% | 
| Luck | 300% | 
| Control | 0.05 | 
| Resilience | 30% | 
| Max Kg | Infinite | 
| Progress Speed | +50% | 
It comes with high luck and an unlimited weight capacity, making it a good choice if you want to catch heavy fish. However, its low control can make it hard to catch rarer fish; you can fix it by enchanting it.
Fisch Omniscient Spinecaster Rod Passive and Ability
The Omniscient Spinecaster comes in two forms, each offering different benefits.
- Offensive Form: Gives you more progress from crow attacks but lowers your catch rate and weakens your pulls.
- Defensive Form: Improves catch frequency and strengthens your pulls but reduces the progress gained from crow attacks.
After performing several slashes, the rod activates an ability called Crown of Bones. This ability increases your chance of getting the new Omniscient mutation that increases the sell value of the fish by 10.6x, along with some other progress buffs.
The ability can reach Crown of Bones VI, which provides the following bonuses:
| Bonus | Crown of Bones VI | 
|---|---|
| Omniscient Mutation Chance | +42 | 
| Chance to Slash Fish | +36% | 
| Fish Weight | +30% | 
Now you know how to get the Omniscient Spinecaster Rod in Fisch. Reach Hex Stage V, complete the required rituals, and gather the items needed to unlock this limited-time event rod.
How much Hex Energy do you need for the Omniscient Spinecaster in Fisch?
You need 200 Hex Energy and 80% bestiary completion to reach Hex Stage V and at least 500 in order to perform the ritual.
How much does the Omniscient Spinecaster Ritual Cost in Fisch?
The ritual costs 100 treats (50 treats each); once done, you will unlock the Omniscient Spinecaster rod.
What is the Omniscient Mutation Multiplier in Fisch?
The omniscient mutation multiplies a fish’s selling value by 10.6x.

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.
Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.
Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”
Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

Citing former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul's yet-to-be-released memoir, the Congress on Sunday (October 25, 2026) flagged "serious questions" regarding the independence of the judiciary under the Modi government and asserted that the institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report which quoted the pre-publication manuscript of Justice Kaul's memoir 'Without Fear of Favour' as stating that former Chief Justice of India Justice D.Y. Chandrachud was "too deferential to the Government" when it came to appointments.
In his post in Hindi on X, Mr. Ramesh said, "A book by former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has raised serious questions regarding the independence of the judiciary during the tenure of the Modi government."
Justice Kaul highlights several concerning incidents — government interference in the appointment of judges, attempts to secure government approval prior to Collegium meetings, and the government's absurd questioning regarding the caste of a judge belonging to a minority community, Mr. Ramesh said.
Matters that many were previously hesitant to discuss openly have now been documented by Justice Kaul with measured, deliberate language, Mr. Ramesh said.
"Strikingly, a former Chief Justice of India (CJI) has not denied that discussions with the government take place prior to judicial appointments. When former CJI Justice Chandrachud acknowledges that the government engages with the CJI and plays a role in the appointment process, the concerns surrounding judicial independence become even more profound," Mr. Ramesh said.
Equally grave is Justice Kaul's revelation that, after a Bench he presided over raised the possibility of reconsidering certain aspects of a court ruling in a PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) case, the matter was reassigned to a different bench without any consultation with him, he said.
"This points to the extent of the government's day-to-day interference in the functioning of the Supreme Court," Mr. Ramesh said.
"When there is pressure to obtain government approval for judicial appointments, and when benches hearing sensitive cases are altered, one must ask — in the interest of safeguarding democracy — if this does not constitute pressure on the judiciary and an erosion of its independence, then what does?" the Congress leader said.
"The institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power. In a democracy, the independence of the judiciary is not merely an option; it is an absolute necessity," Mr. Ramesh asserted.

Suspect fired more than 800 rounds as cops arrived at his Texas home leaving one deputy dead
Deputy Ahmed 'Adam' Sherifi is survived by a wife and a newborn child

A suspect fired more than 800 rounds of ammunition at Texas police when they arrived at his home leaving one officer dead.
The suspect, who was later found dead from a gunshot wound, also injured another cop in the confrontation.
On Tuesday, a Van Zandt County Sheriff’s deputy and members of the Canton police went to the home of 42-year-old Mi Van Nguyen to serve two felony arrest warrants, according to NBC 5.
Around 10:20 p.m., Nguyen opened fire from inside the home using a semiautomatic rifle, unleashing more than 800 rounds at authorities, according to the report. Sheriff’s Deputy Ahmed 'Adam' Sherifi was killed and Canton police officer Chris Watson was injured.
“Think about that. 800 rounds shot at the men and women whose only purpose was to carry out their duties to protect this community,” Sheriff Kevin Bridger said at a Friday press conference, according to NBC 5. “This was not simply an attack on law enforcement. It was an attack on the peace and security that every family in Van Zandt County, in all counties, deserve."
Nguyen was later found dead inside the home from a gunshot wound, NBC 5 reported. The Texas Rangers are now investigating the incident.
He was wanted on two felony charges for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and aggravated assault on a peace officer, authorities said. No additional motive for firing at police Tuesday was released during the Friday press conference.
Bridger described the attack on cops as “pure evil.”
“Where one man chose violence, Adam chose a life of service,” Bridger said. “Where one man brought fear and destruction, Adam took an oath and gave his life. Providing the safety for our community.”
Sherifi is survived by a wife and a newborn and both were near the sheriff during the press conference.
“Adam represents everything that makes our community strong. He represents duty, bravery and service,” Bridger said. “Adam was a young officer with his whole life ahead of him. He was a husband. He was a father, and he was a son. A friend to all of us and a beloved member of our law enforcement family.”
Funeral services for Sherifi are expected to be held next week.
During the shooting, fellow deputy Brandon Fonteneau provided lifesaving care to Watson, Bridger stated. He fired at the suspect to protect the wounded officers and allow for other personnel to take Watson to safety. Watson continues to recover in the hospital.
“In the middle of the extraordinary, dangerous situation. Brandon did what he had been trained to do, and that saved lives and protect the community,” Bridger said. “His courage and quick decision helped save lives. And I want Brandon to know how proud I am of him, how grateful to this office and this community for what he did.”

Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.
“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.
Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.
The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”
Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.
On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday.
 
“What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.
“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”
Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.
“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.
The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debat, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria.
WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.
A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.
Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

A mother recently told me about her child’s holiday homework. She had asked the child to complete a set of maths problems, and every answer was correct. Pleased with the result, she asked the child to explain how one of the problems had been solved. The child couldn’t. When she probed further, she discovered that Alexa had supplied the answers.
The homework was done. The learning wasn’t.
Another incident stayed with me. A child took an answer generated by ChatGPT to school. The teacher pointed out that it was wrong. The child was unconvinced.
“No, ma’am. You got it wrong. ChatGPT is never wrong.”
And the teacher stood no chance.
These are small, everyday incidents, but they raise a question worth asking: what happens when children begin outsourcing not just their tasks, but the very faculties they are still developing?
AI and learning
AI can retrieve information, solve problems, generate stories and explain complicated concepts in seconds. Used thoughtfully, it can be a wonderful learning aid. But there is a difference between using a tool to strengthen a skill and allowing that tool to perform the thinking in its place.
Memory, reasoning, judgement, creativity and the ability to work through difficulty develop with practice. A child who struggles with a maths problem, tries different approaches and eventually arrives at a solution has gained more than the answer. The child has practised persistence, reasoning and problem-solving.
When the answer arrives instantly, that opportunity may disappear.
This does not mean every use of AI weakens a child’s abilities. We do not yet have enough long-term evidence to make such a sweeping claim. But it is worth asking whether, when AI repeatedly does the work for children, we are giving them fewer opportunities to practise the very skills education is meant to nurture.
Physical learning
There is another dimension to this conversation that deserves attention: learning through the hands.
Maria Montessori, the mother of the Montessori education system, believed that a child’s hands play a vital role in learning. She wrote, “The hands are the instruments of man’s intelligence.” Children learn by touching, handling, building and experimenting, gradually making sense of the world through direct experience. When AI provides ready-made answers, stories and solutions from a very young age, children may miss the valuable process of doing things for themselves—exploring, making mistakes and discovering. The concern is that if we allow convenience to replace experience, we may deprive children of opportunities to develop skills that grow through hands-on learning.
A child who builds a tower that repeatedly collapses learns about balance in a way that a screen explanation alone cannot provide. A child who mixes ingredients, plants a seed or works with physical objects is learning through observation, movement and trial and error. The finished result matters, but so does the process of getting there.
Experiencing emotions
The same principle applies to emotional development. Children need opportunities to experience frustration, uncertainty, disappointment and conflict, with a trusted adult nearby to help them make sense of these feelings. If every difficult moment gets resolved immediately by a convenient answer, children may have fewer opportunities to practise coping, reflecting and finding their own way forward.
The aim is not to leave children struggling without support; it is to offer the right support without taking away every opportunity to try.
And then there is the question of relationships.
A mother recently shared that her daughter refers to ChatGPT as her ‘boyfriend’. Whenever she faces something difficult, she says, “I’ll ask my boyfriend.” It may sound amusing at first. Children often give human qualities to toys, invent imaginary companions and engage in pretend relationships. But AI introduces a new dimension: it can respond to a child, creating the impression of a relationship that goes beyond imaginative play.
A chatbot is available on demand. It does not visibly grow impatient, interrupt with its own problems or require the compromises that real relationships do. For a young person who feels lonely, anxious or misunderstood, this accessibility may feel comforting.
But human relationships teach us things that a responsive machine cannot fully replicate: How to read another person’s expressions, how to empathise, listen when we disagree, repair a misunderstanding, respect boundaries and recognise that someone else’s feelings matter too. These are not incidental life skills. They are part of learning to live with other people. They are about being mindful of the people around us.
The concern is not that a child who talks to AI will inevitably withdraw from human relationships. It is that we should notice when a machine begins to replace conversations, connections and help-seeking that a child could otherwise experience with people.
This is no longer a hypothetical question. A February 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 American teenagers aged 13 to 17 found that 16% had used AI chatbots for casual conversation and 12% had used them for emotional support or advice. These figures do not establish harm or dependence, and they cannot automatically be applied to Indian children. They do, however, show that some teenagers are already turning to AI for more than information and schoolwork.
Preparing children
For parents and educators, the answer cannot simply be to ban AI or pretend it will disappear. Children are growing up in a world where these tools will be part of education, work and everyday life. They need to learn how to use AI, but also how to question it, verify its answers, recognise its limitations and take responsibility for their own decisions.
UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Framework for Students places a human-centred mindset among its four key dimensions, alongside AI ethics, techniques and applications, and system design. It emphasises critical judgement and preparing students to become responsible users and co-creators of AI.
That is an important distinction. AI literacy should mean more than knowing how to write a good prompt. It should include knowing when not to use AI, when to check its answer and when to put the device aside and do the work oneself.
What adults can do
A parent can ask a child to solve a problem before consulting AI, then compare the child’s reasoning with the tool’s response. A teacher can ask students to explain how they arrived at an answer, rather than evaluating only the final product. Children can be encouraged to write their own stories before asking AI for suggestions, build something with their hands before watching a digital demonstration, and attempt to resolve a difficulty before seeking an instant solution.
Most importantly, adults need to model these habits themselves. If we unquestioningly accept every AI-generated answer, we cannot reasonably expect children to approach it with discernment.
Offering support
There is one more question we must ask: when a child is distressed, lonely or overwhelmed, who do they turn to?
Every child needs at least one adult they can approach in a moment of crisis—someone who will listen without judgement, take their feelings seriously and help them find the right support. Technology may offer information or a starting point, but it should never become a substitute for making human help accessible.
The goal is not to raise children who are afraid of AI. It is to raise children who can use it without surrendering their own judgement, curiosity, resilience or relationships.
In a world where a machine is always available, let us make sure no child feels that it is the only one available to them.
(K. Sreedevi is a holistic learning specialist integrating Montessori education, remedial therapy and mindfulness to support children’s learning and emotional well-being. sreedeviarun@gmail.com)

GMO Internet has made an urgent request for the Japanese government to implement active cyberdefense operations following an unauthorized access incident, sources have said.
GMO Internet has revealed that there was unauthorized access to its servers for automated FX currency margin trading. A total of 26,739 such servers may have been affected, and user login information may have been stolen. It shut down all servers on Wednesday.
Since some users have reported losses from unauthorized transactions on their accounts following the incident, the company said Saturday that it will compensate users for these losses.
The company also plans to make a consolation payment of ¥5,000 to all users, regardless of whether they have suffered financial damage.
GMO Internet revealed that it had received a demand for money from who is believed to be responsible for the unauthorized access, and that the possible attacker is threatening to release its information if it rejects the demand.
The company indicated its intention to reject the demand, adding that it has requested a police investigation.
On Oct. 1, the government began operations under the active cyberdefense system, which involves the Self-Defense Forces and police pre-emptively breaking into an attacker’s server to neutralize it and prevent damage.
Following Saturday’s urgent request, GMO Internet said that defense measures and responses by private business operators alone can hardly eradicate highly skilled cybercrime organizations that steal people’s assets.

For Mugdha Kalra, a parent of a special needs adult, financial planning has consumed the past few years. The question for her is, who will take care of her son when she is no longer there? She is planning to set up a trust fund that will help him reside at a support home. Ms. Kalra is not alone: for parents of children of special needs, the question of ‘who after me?’ is constantly at the back of their minds, a question made difficult by the fact that there is very little in the way of State-funded support services in the country.
“Even the basic facilities cost ₹50,000/month. A parent must make a lifetime plan for their child to be able to have this support once they are old or too incapacitated to take care of their child. Many people with autism also have comorbidities or other health conditions and money is needed for this too. Parents need to start planning early and set up trust funds for the child,” says Ms. Kalra, who is also an autism advocate.
Understanding autism
Autism is a diverse group of conditions related to development of the brain. The World Health Organization estimates that as of 2021, 1 in 127 people globally had autism. Exact numbers for India are hard to come by, but up to 1.8-2 million children in India are thought to have ASD, as per figures cited in a paper published in Cureus in 2024.
Not everyone who is on the autism spectrum has the same level of needs or abilities. Some people with autism may face several difficulties in their day-to-day lives, while others may only need help with specific tasks. Those with higher needs may require assistance from a caregiver to function and live a life of dignity. In India, as in many other countries, caregiving responsibilities fall on the parents, and predominantly on mothers. But this then raises the question of long-term planning: how to ensure their child is provided for, and care for, after they are gone or unable to care for them anymore.
“My son will outlive me; a facility for neurodivergent individuals is the only option,” says Sutapa Bose, senior special educator, India Autism Center (IAC), a non-profit organisation based in Kolkata. Her son has just turned 19 and she is planning to set up a trust fund for him soon to help in his future care and living. “Financial stress is always there; care has become expensive. But his health and safety are also major concerns for us,” she adds.
Guilt, sibling and caregiver burnout
Caregiving is no easy task. It take a toll, both physically and mentally. “There is always guilt about not doing enough for our children even though our personal lives are affected,” says Ms. Bose, adding that their parents’ mental health inevitably suffered, an aspect of caregiving that is not much attention is paid to.
An unfair amount of the burden of caring for a person with autism also falls on the sibling, if there is one, who is younger and more able than the parent, so an unsaid expectation lies on them to offer lifetime care, Ms Kalra added.
This is what happened in the case of the Chatterjees. Jharna Chatterjee’s son lived and grew up during a time when she was the only breadwinner in the family and also took on caregiving responsibilities. Her son, Sanjib Chatterjee, passed away 16 years ago due to comorbidities. She did not have the financial resources to send him to a care facility.
“It hurts my soul to think that my son passed away, but in a way, as a mother I can die in peace knowing that my son led a dignified life and was cared for. How would I ensure that if he lived after I passed away? My elder son had spent half his life caring for my younger son, who was autistic. It drained our finances, we lost our house, and my elder son lost his business while taking care of his brother. Life felt unfair, but we had no choice,” said Ms. Chatterjee, who is now 87.
Little support
Parents, caregivers and experts point out that what makes their caregiving harder, is the lack of support from both the government and the society in caring for people with autism.
Ms. Kalra notes that even when support homes are available, the basic facilities are sometimes below average and may not always offer a dignified life.
“Once we are not there, we hope to ensure our children are in a place where they have a dignified and structured life and are cared for. However, the government does not do much: India has individuals and NGOs trying to make small changes. That is not enough. We need to have structural and policy-based change in the country to make the society more inclusive for people on the spectrum,” points out the parent of twin boys with autism.
The IAC, in this regard, recently brought out a white paper to seek GST exemption for disability support services. The institute argued that taxing therapy and rehabilitation increases the financial burden on families and sought a service-based approach instead of disability severity thresholds. Representatives of IAC also met with the Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and presented the paper to her and put forth their demands. According to Sakhi Singhi, a governing board member of IAC, the Finance Minister acknowledged the issue and assured them that they would look into the matter.

What can a biological age test actually tell you?
Experts weigh in on the tests’ current accuracy and usefulness.
How old are you? How old do you feel? Are those two numbers the same?
Biological age tests have validated what many of us sense intuitively: Our cells don’t always match our birth certificates.
As these tests have evolved over the past decade, longevity researchers have started using them to identify what behaviours and conditions cause people to age faster and whether there are interventions that can slow the process down.
And although the tests were intended to be used in laboratory research, more and more consumers are shelling out a few hundred dollars to wellness and longevity companies in order to reveal their “true” age.
Here’s what experts say the tests can tell you – and when, if ever, it’s worth taking one.
A PROMISING CONCEPT
Biological age tests claim to inform you about how your body is faring by telling you what age your blood test results most resemble.
“In a way, when the biological age is older than the chronological age, you are at high risk of adverse health outcomes,” said Dr Luigi Ferrucci, the scientific director of the National Institute on Aging in the US. “When your biological age is younger than the chronological age, you’re kind of protected against those health outcomes.”
The most prominent tests look for modifications to the genome – a process called DNA methylation – that influence whether a given gene is active or not. The discovery that some of these modifications occur reliably with age led to the development of the Horvath “clock” in 2013 by geneticist Steve Horvath, which is widely regarded as the first biological age test.
Today, there are three “generations” of this type of test. Generation one – the Horvath clock and others like it – are “literally predicting what your age should be based on your DNA methylation,” said Raghav Sehgal, a principal investigator at the Marcus Institute for Aging Research, which is affiliated with Harvard Medical School. “So it will tell you your DNA methylation looks like that of a 20-year-old, or it looks like that of a 40-year-old.”
The second-generation clocks, with names like PhenoAge and GrimAge, were introduced roughly five years later and look for methylation sites that are associated with a person’s relative mortality risk. The results are again given as an age, based on whether a person’s risk of death looks more like, say, the average 50-year-old’s or the average 70-year-old’s.
Third-generation clocks, like DunedinPACE, which came out in 2022, measure how fast someone is aging. Researchers have used a car analogy to describe the differences between the tests: The first- and second-generation models act like an odometer, measuring your age or proximity to death. The third-generation tests act like a speedometer.
The first-generation clocks “put this field on the map, made it famous, and remain probably the best known,” said Daniel Belsky, an associate professor of epidemiology at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health who developed DunedinPACE. But the second- and third-generation clocks have turned out to be more informative when it comes to predicting long-term health.
These newer clocks are also more sensitive to health-related behaviours and treatments, Sehgal said. In a recent study, he pitted 16 biological age tests against one another. The second- and third-generation clocks were more likely to change in response to various longevity-related interventions, like diets and medications.
SOME KINKS TO WORK OUT
Even with the best tests, there are concerns about accuracy and reliability, especially when the tests are used on a personal level.
Dr Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry and pathology at Yale School of Medicine, said factors like time of day, when you had your last meal or how well you slept the night before appear to influence the results. This isn’t a unique problem for biological age tests, but it is something that scientists need to figure out how to manage, and that people may need to take into account when taking a test.
Morgan Levine, who developed PhenoAge while she was a postdoctoral researcher at UCLA, pointed out that if you take multiple biological age tests, each one will give you a different answer. That’s in part because the tests are all measuring slightly different things. But it’s also because they were developed using different data sets to establish what the “average” for any given age looks like.
“I don’t think people should put too much emphasis on that number that they’re getting,” said Levine, who is launching an artificial intelligence biotechnology startup. (Levine developed and licensed another biological age test with Sehgal and Higgins-Chen.)
To Dr Mohammad Arfan Ikram, a professor of epidemiology at Erasmus Medical Center in Rotterdam, Netherlands, the biggest shortcoming of the tests is that they don’t tell you what might be going wrong in the body to cause a higher age, or, consequently, how to fix the problem.
Returning to the car metaphor, Ikram pointed out that just knowing a car has 100,000 miles on it doesn’t tell you whether the brakes or the engine or the clutch will fail first.
That issue partly stems from what the tests are measuring: When scientists isolate DNA from a blood sample, they’re only testing the DNA of white blood cells.
“You can measure the changes in these blood cells,” said Tony Wyss-Coray, a professor of neurology and neurological sciences at Stanford University, but “you don’t see changes that might happen in neurons in your brain, or in liver cells or in the pancreas.”
To try to solve for this, instead of looking at DNA, Wyss-Coray and other researchers have started testing blood samples for thousands of proteins that are released from different tissues. That enables them to evaluate how multiple types of cells or organs are doing, rather than inferring someone’s head-to-toe health from just their white blood cells.
Some experts think this approach will provide more valuable and actionable information, because while the idea of distilling the health of your entire body into one number is seductive, it’s probably more useful from a medical standpoint to know which organ is going to cause problems first. However, this technique is more expensive and not widely available to the public. (Wyss-Coray is a co-founder of a direct-to-consumer company that aims to sell the test in the next year or two.)
WHAT THEY'RE GOOD AT
Despite the tests’ shortcomings, the experts said they can be valuable research tools when used to evaluate large data sets. For example, scientists are utilising the tests as a new way to quantify how life experiences, like pregnancy or losing a loved one, affect people’s health.
Perhaps most promising, the tests can be used to assess, in a short period of time, whether a drug or other intervention being studied in a clinical trial is able to slow ageing. This is a major benefit for longevity research, since following someone for decades to find out whether a treatment altered their life span isn’t feasible.
The tests have already been used for this purpose in a few trials, including one that examined the potential health benefits of common supplements and another that evaluated whether calorie restriction might improve longevity in humans.
But in some cases, the tests have raised more questions than they have answered. In the supplement trial, for instance, the intervention significantly slowed some of the biological age clocks but didn’t affect more concrete health metrics, like blood pressure. Belsky, who was involved in the study, hypothesised that this discrepancy may have arisen because the tests could be detecting subtle changes that emerge before more established signs of disease.
There is also a possibility that the tests measure something related to ageing or health that doesn’t make a meaningful difference if it is changed. For example, people’s hair turns grey and their skin wrinkles as they age, but fixing either of those two things won’t make people younger or healthier.
FOR CONSUMERS, TIME WILL TELL
Several experts painted a rosy picture of a future in which people could purchase and use the tests to effectively track themselves long-term and to alert them to early warning signs that their health is declining.
“I think the biological age tests are the promised land of the preventive care version of medicine,” Sehgal said. But, he added, “that’s not where we are yet.”
Higgins-Chen said he saw a potential benefit now: Consumers could choose one test and take it periodically to track their score as they age, or after they start a new medication or health routine. “Ageing is a longitudinal process that unfolds over very long periods of time,” he said, so the real benefit of the tests is detecting when and how your health changes over the years.
In general, though, the experts agreed that the direct-to-consumer tests available today, especially when used as a one-off, aren’t really that informative.
To Ikram, people are better off taking standard doctor’s office tests, like those for cholesterol and glucose. “That already gives you a much better picture” and identifies things “you can directly intervene on,” he said.
At best, biological age tests can give you a loose understanding of your health, Levine said. “People who generally score lower on it, it signals to some degree that they’re probably healthier than people who are generally scoring high on it.”
But, she added, most people already have a rough sense of how healthy they are. If you exercise, eat a balanced diet and don’t smoke, your biological age score will likely be lower – and you probably already know that.

“Forza,” Marco Balsamo’s soccer drama shot between Bali and Milan, has been picked up for international sales by EST N8, which will take the film to the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s TIFFCOM market (Oct. 28–30). Before that, it gets its first public screening on Oct. 25 at Jakarta Film Week.
Balsamo’s first feature as director centers on Bima, an 11-year-old from Bali who hopes a career as a pro footballer will give his family a better life. A chance bond with a former AC Milan player in the last stretch of his career changes the outlook for both of them.
Newcomer Ghazi Alhabsyi heads the cast. Balsamo also appears on screen, alongside Tara Sibel Demren, AC Milan icon Alessandro Costacurta and Atiqah Hasiholan, Oka Antara and Tio Pakusadewo, all three winners at the Indonesian Film Festival (FFI).
Popular on Variety
Balsamo wrote the script and produced with Demren. Riva Studios originated the project, and its producers include Ario Sagantoro of “The Raid” franchise. Adhya Pictures has the film’s Indonesian theatrical release, set for 2027.
Interest at home is strong. Both rounds of online tickets for the Jakarta screening, at CGV Grand Indonesia, sold out inside five minutes.
“‘Forza’ follows a boy from Bali and a former pro footballer who open new doors for each other, and it bridges Indonesia and Italy the way only football can,” said Sophie Shi, head of studios at EST N8. “It’s a film for audiences around the world, with a story of family and hope that transcends language and culture. Our mission is to take bold Asian stories to audiences worldwide, and a family film told through the world’s most popular sport is built to travel. We’re proud to launch ‘Forza’ to buyers at TIFFCOM.”
Shi and Jan Paul Villanueva negotiated the deal for EST N8, with Balsamo and Demren representing Riva Studios. Villanueva, EVP of acquisitions and global distribution, will lead sales with Cathy Ni, head of sales and U.S. distribution, and Shams Pasha, global sales and marketing executive.
“We’ve spent years bringing ‘Forza’ to the screen, and Indonesia has been at the heart of it from the beginning,” Balsamo said. “This film is a labor of love and a testament to the perseverance and collaboration behind independent filmmaking. Sharing the film at Jakarta Film Week is especially meaningful. It’s a moment we’ve been looking forward to for a long time.”
Demren, who co-founded Riva Studios, said the film was designed for families to watch side by side and discuss afterward. “We hope Bima’s journey reminds audiences how much it matters to have someone believe in you, especially when your dreams feel out of reach,” she said. “Seeing both ticket releases fill so quickly is an encouraging start. We’re looking forward to hearing audiences’ reactions.”
Demren and Balsamo set up Riva Studios in 2022 as an independent outfit working in live action, animation and music. In 2024 it bought French animation house TeamTO. “Forza” is its first live-action feature.
Also on EST N8’s TIFFCOM lineup are “Tame,” a Thai horror title from B-EST Pictures; Dean Colin Marcial’s crime thriller “Jaguar,” set in Manila; “Master,” Rezwan Shahriar Sumit’s winner of IFFR’s Big Screen Award; “Pilgrims,” a Korean sci-fi animation from Heo Pyoungkang that was selected for Annecy; and “The Invisible Half,” a J-horror from Nishiyama Masaki.
The company, which brought together EST Studios and N8, has offices in Los Angeles and Bangkok and has sold and distributed more than 60 titles across over 100 territories. Its catalog includes “Hidden Letters,” which was shortlisted for the Oscars and nominated for an Emmy; “The Monk and the Gun,” Bhutan’s Oscar entry; “A Useful Ghost,” which won the Grand Prize at Cannes Critics’ Week; and “Blood Brothers,” which topped Netflix’s global chart.

The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email promising free championship rings in a test of its staff’s ability to detect scams, The New York Times reported yesterday. “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” the email sent in late September said, instructing employees to click a link to make a selection from two ring designs.
Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link “were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns,” the report said, citing team sources. Dolan is the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden.
It’s common for corporations to send phishing emails to find out which employees don’t pay attention to clues that an email is a scam. A cybersecurity-test email often appears to be from the company itself but includes telltale signs of phishing. For example, Ars Technica owner Condé Nast sends phishing-test messages from email addresses with a misspelled domain, “condenest.com.”
It’s not difficult for the typical Ars Technica reporter or editor to spot this kind of tell, but we haven’t received any offer as valuable as a free NBA championship ring. We can hardly blame a Knicks organization staffer for being fooled or at least greatly annoyed by a fake offer of a ring commemorating the basketball franchise’s first NBA championship in more than half a century.
We don’t know whether the Knicks email had any obvious signs that it was a phishing test, such as a misspelled domain name. The offer wasn’t implausible, either. “Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive,” wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization.
Phishing email and empty ring boxes
Vardon’s article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.

BJP alleges Sanjay Raut faked AI audio on ₹500 crore payout to Jarange; Sena UBT leader claims BJP MLC leaked clip
The BJP alleged that the recording was part of an attempt to advance Rahul Gandhi's agenda and create divisions within the ruling alliance.
The political row over an audio recording alleging a ₹500 crore payment to Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange intensified on Saturday, with the BJP accusing Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut of fabricating the clip using artificial intelligence (AI). The BJP alleged that the recording was part of an attempt to advance Rahul Gandhi's agenda and create divisions within the ruling alliance.
Raut rejected the charge, claiming that a BJP member of legislative council (MLC) had leaked the recording amid what he described as "cut-throat competition" within the party. Meanwhile, Jarange, who has denied receiving any money, called on Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde to ensure a thorough investigation and hold everyone involved accountable, news agency PTI reported.
The controversy escalated after Fadnavis ordered a forensic examination of the audio clip on Friday. The recording, released by Jarange on Thursday, purportedly features BJP functionaries discussing an alleged payment of ₹500 crore to the activist through Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Shinde, Eknath Shinde's son.
BJP alleges Sanjay Raut fabricated audio using AI
BJP spokesperson Navnath Ban called for a case to be registered against Raut, if required, and demanded an investigation into whether he had received money from Rahul Gandhi to carry out the alleged conspiracy.
Ban claimed that Raut had coordinated the operation from a purported war room in Vashi, Navi Mumbai, and alleged that he had taken up a task from Rahul Gandhi to discredit the BJP.
"Sanjay Raut orchestrated the conspiracy from a war room in Navi Mumbai's Vashi. The contract to defame the BJP has been taken by Raut from Rahul Gandhi. Raut has been consistently pushing Gandhi's agenda over the past few days," Ban claimed.
Raut claims BJP MLC leaked recording
Responding to the allegations, Raut said Fadnavis should first register a case before ordering a forensic examination of the recording. He, however, claimed that the investigation would not produce any results.
"The clip was leaked by a BJP MLC. He was involved in the talks with Jarange. The CM treated him with a lot of affection, which has backfired," Raut said without identifying the lawmaker.
Raut maintained that internal rivalries within the BJP had led to the leak and described the incident as evidence of a "cut-throat" contest within the party. He also alleged that the BJP had become the target of a sting operation.
"If an internal audio clip is getting leaked, then the Home Department has gone against you (the CM)," Raut said.
Fadnavis also heads the state's Home Department.
Raut further alleged that tensions between Fadnavis and Shinde had intensified, claiming that their "cold war" had reached its peak and that both leaders could go to any length to politically finish each other off.
What does the viral audio clip allegedly contain?
Jarange released the recording on Thursday, claiming that a conspiracy had been hatched to silence him and weaken the Maratha reservation movement.
The purported conversation features BJP functionaries discussing an alleged ₹500 crore payment to Jarange through Shrikant Shinde. A woman is purportedly heard claiming that the money had been delivered to the activist through the Shiv Sena MP.
The recording also allegedly contains a discussion about ways to counter Jarange's growing political influence in the Marathwada region ahead of the 2024 assembly elections.
The allegations contained in the clip have not been established, and its authenticity is the subject of the forensic probe ordered by Fadnavis.
The controversy emerged amid allegations by Shiv Sena leader Ramdas Kadam that BJP insiders were working with Jarange to politically "finish off" Shinde, the Shiv Sena chief and Deputy CM.
