The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.
Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.
To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.
Caravelle Sea Hunter
Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.
Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm
Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.
Brew Metric Lite Retro
This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.
Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound
Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.
Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”
Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.
Baltic HMS
Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).
Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.
Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”
Bulova A-11 Hack Watch
As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”
Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”
Citizen Tsuyosa
Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).
WIRED's top pick, however, is the new, more wearable 37-mm range conveniently on sale right now at just under our $400 target. If you venture above $600, park Citizen and go for the Lorier Falcon or Traska Commuter 36 instead.
Vostok Amphibia
WIRED watch expert Laura McCreddie-Doak has seen our Chinese chrono option and upped the ante with this Russian dive watch. Vostok traces back to the Soviet Union's Chistopol Watch Factory, a supplier to the USSR Ministry of Defense during World War II. This Amphibia 420269 (there are many, many other models) has a 2416B automatic movement that offers a 31-hour power reserve. Bafflingly just $151 on a steel bracelet, it's rated for 200 meters of water resistance, thanks to its unique, pressure-tightening case design. “This watch needs no other justification for inclusion on this list other than it was worn by Bill Murray as Jacques Cousteau-alike Steve Zissou in Wes Anderson’s The Life Aquatic,” says McCreddie-Doak.
Seiko 5 Sports
Finally, we come to the almost inevitable inclusion of the Seiko 5 Sports automatic. The familiar and affordable Seiko 5 Sports line began in 1968 as a tougher, sportier evolution of the 1963 Seiko Sportsmatic 5. The lineup is still going strong with dozens of variants plus a back catalog of thousands. That explains why, for the second time on this list, two of our experts chose the 5 Sports.
WIRED watch writer and author Josh Sims says the Seiko 5 Sports “is the MPV of watches: dependable, rugged, adaptable, as happy in the city as out of it. For my money—and this really is a lot of watch for, relatively, not a lot of money—it also has the cool of not being Swiss. Seiko isn’t just a giant of Japanese watchmaking; it’s a giant of watchmaking that deserves more r-e-s-p-e-c-t, and remains as relevant as ever.” Sims has gone for the SNSX Series that starts at $385.
Holly Ross, as executive editor of Vanity Fair’s On Time watch supplement, has gone for the Seiko 5 SRPE71 (pictured above), a model that's not new but still available if you look. “What is not to love about this chic, timeless, durable, and mechanical Seiko 5? And for a neat $320, it makes it even more desirable.”

Calls for change at massive rally in Tel Aviv ahead of Israel election
In short:
Tens of thousands of people have rallied in Tel Aviv in a final protest against Benjamin Netanyahu and his government.
The crowd heard calls for a commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7 attacks.
What's next?
The election for the Israeli parliament occurs on Tuesday.
For two years they came to Hostage Square in Tel Aviv each week to demand their government do more to get their loved ones and friends home from captivity in Gaza.
Last night they came in their tens of thousands to demand an independent state commission of inquiry into how the greatest security breach in Israel's history, and as a result the greatest mass slaughter, had been able to occur in the first place.
Three days before an election regarded as the most pivotal in the country's history, those attending the rally were clear that there needed to be a change of government, not just to get their long-demanded inquiry but because they say Israel's democracy is under threat.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has flatly refused to have an independent investigation into the events of October 7, 2023, after thousands of Hamas fighters surged across the border from Gaza.
Leaders of opposition parties have pledged an inquiry.
Among those leaders who attended the rally were the main rival to Mr Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, as well as Avigdor Liberman, Yair Lapid, Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan.
Mali Zender not only lost her daughter Noa on October 7, but as a head nurse at Sheba Hospital treated those hostages who did return from the tunnels of Gaza.
"Not everyone has taken responsibility and we do not have answers," she said.
"A country cannot move forward without soul-searching. Leaders cannot demand our faith without taking responsibility.
"Do not give up on the truth, and do not give up on our future."
Rabbi Elchanan Danino, whose son Uri was abducted and murdered in Hamas captivity, said an inquiry "will not bring our sons and daughters home, but it is necessary for the futures of our sons and daughters … and for the soldiers who are risking their lives for our existence here."
Repeated cries of "shame" echoed through the sweltering Tel Aviv crowd.
But it is not just the cause of getting an inquiry being demanded by many speakers who addressed the rally and many of those attending.
Members of the crowd who spoke to the ABC repeatedly spoke of how they believe Israel's longest-serving prime minister represents a threat to Israel's democracy, to say there must be a change of government when the election for the Israeli parliament occurs on Tuesday.
"Our democracy is torn down and it's ridiculous that the government that is responsible for this horrible war and for letting us down so many months before is still there," Aviva Mimouni Bloch told the ABC.
Her husband Yuval said: "Probably our greatest war now is against what is happening in our country, where people who are corrupt, incapable, cynical don't take any responsibility for what is going on."
Orr Rachlevsky said that "we've been fighting against the policies of this government who brought Israel into the worst place ever, experiencing the worst massacre of the Jewish people".
"And this is the last week that we have, the last opportunity that we have to save our beloved country as our parents and grandparents built, to be a beacon of hope and justice and love of people and human beings. And we will make this place a better place."
Asked if he was worried what would happen on Tuesday if the current government is returned to office, he said: "This will be the end of the Jewish country. It might take a day or two days or a week or a year, but this will be the end.
"It means that the country that my grandparents built is poisoned and beyond any repair. But I don't believe this will happen."
Ophir Baer said: "We have to make a change."
Ophir and his wife had regularly come to rallies at the square, driving one and a half hours each time.
"We did it for many, many months every Saturday, and today it was clear that this is like three days before our big, big chance to make a difference and to actually make a change. So that's what we're doing.
"If this criminal government, and it is the criminal government, if it would be up to me, I would put all 64 or later 68 Knesset members into jail because all of them are responsible for the people who died, for the people who were murdered, for the people who didn't come back alive when they could have rescued them a year earlier, at least.
"So I think we need a change after those years, after the failure of October 7."
Teenagers Tomer Nahir and Zoya Malka are too young to vote on Tuesday but believe Israel needs a change.
"We need to get rid of the corruption that's going around in the government," Tomer said.
"I'm going to cry if Bibi will be chosen again, because I really hate what he's doing to our country and what is happening, and that's why I'm also here today," Zoya said.
Tomar said he was worried the country would be much more divided if Mr Netanyahu was returned to government, and this would cause a lot of tension between groups in the community
Almost all others in positions of authority in the lead up to October 7 have lost their jobs or left, except the prime minister.
Many Israelis hold him culpable. He has said the only problem on October 7 was that no-one had woken him up when the attack started at 6:29am that day.
News stories have repeatedly documented instances where Mr Netanyahu was personally told of a looming threat from Hamas, threats he both ignored and did not pass on.
His long hold on power is also under threat because of a series of corruption charges, and because he attempted to circumscribe the powers of the Supreme Court, which many Israelis believe would have given the government untrammelled power.

There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself. Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot. And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life.
When AI agents run your life
Muse, organize my life. Make no mistakes.
This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout. She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools. Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift. They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’”
Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload. They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet. But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents.
Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her. She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said. “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present. And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’”
Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do. But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology?
On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out. Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT.
“I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive. It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.”
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What agents are out there right now?
At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse.
There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots. But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall.
You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote. How was that experience?
One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch. It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain. We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors. We have this specific budget. I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us.
One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace. There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me.
I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well. I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find. Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off.
Is that how this tech is typically used?
Most people are using this as part of a workflow. I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life. But people have been quite creative.
One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel. So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons.
I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me. I don’t love that concept.
That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies.
When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details. The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models.
I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize.
What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive.
Yes, especially because it’s all about automation. If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about.
There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account. And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see.
Oh no.
I would be mortified. So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make. If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing.
“You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.”
How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now. Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state. People are not loving it. How are they trying to sell this to the average person?
The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now. You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools. They’ve really, really leaned into cuteness and into adorable mascots.
Muse, if you haven’t seen its agent, looks like a mix between a Labubu and an Ewok. It’s very furry, very cuddly, very cute. OpenAI’s tools also have similar kinds of blobs with large eyes that might be a little endearing.
I feel like companies are hearing this kind of feedback that people aren’t trusting AI right now, or maybe they have moral or ethical reasons they don’t want to use these tools. You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.
Do you think AI agents are ultimately going to worm their way into our lives despite how unpopular AI companies are?
I do think so. I think in a couple months, maybe when I go home from Christmas, I would not be surprised if my mom had an agent on her phone because it does feel like it’s breaking through to average people in the way that ChatGPT had a moment a few years ago.
Even though there’s a lot of distrust for large companies like Meta, I think there are some appealing parts of this that will bring in millions of people. I do see this as the future of the internet.
When I think of the dream of the average person working in AI in Silicon Valley, it’s “We’re going to use AI. It’s going to free up the free time of so many people. Work is going to get done faster. You’re going to have more leisure time.”
Has that been the case for the people you’ve spoken with who are using this? Has it given them more free time to enjoy themselves or has it done something else?
You would think so, right? You would think that if people are automating these boring aspects of their life, that they would have more time to go touch grass, go see a movie, have some fun. But it does feel like that time just gets filled with other work, other productivity measures.
While agents may be able to take some more annoying or tedious things off of your plate, I am not as optimistic that it’s going to give us this utopia or freedom where I’m always at the beach.

A month after raising $85 Mn, e-bike maker Ultraviolette has unveiled its new motorcycle, X-47 Venom powered by its new VX-100 100V platform. The motorcycle has been launched at an introductory price of ₹2.65 Lakh, applicable to the first 5,000 customers. Bookings opened on October 22. Deliveries are expected to commence in November 2026, the startup said in a press release. The X-47 Venom is the first motorcycle built on Ultraviolette’s new VX-100 architecture. It combines the platform with its new UV LIGHTFURY electric motor and SRB-11 battery technology. It has peak power of 30 kW (39 bhp) and a 550 Nm of wheel torque. The Ultraviolette X-47 Venom is built to have a top speed of 155 kmph. The motorcycle offers a claimed Indian Driving Cycle (IDC) range of 343 km. It can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 5.9 seconds and has a kerb weight of 180 kg, making it up to 20 kg lighter than the previous-generation platform. Ultraviolette Introduces New VX-100 Platform The VX-100 is a new electrical architecture designed to improve energy efficiency, thermal management and charging speeds across Ultraviolette’s product portfolio. The platform incorporates SRB-11 battery technology, which the startup claims offers up to 20% higher energy density and twice the cooling performance. Its thermal management system is designed to dissipate heat up to 50% faster, while the battery pack features a cast-aluminium housing and IP67 protection against dust and water ingress. The motorcycle also features a new motor control unit that is twice as compact and delivers three times the power density, according to the company. “The X-47 Venom reflects our approach to engineering the entire motorcycle as one integrated system,” Ultraviolette cofounder and CTO Niraj Rajmohan said. He added that the modular architecture would allow the company to extend these technologies across future products as it expands its portfolio and global presence. The bike adds to Ultraviolette’s portfolio of high-end, speed focused EV bikes. Ultraviolette's flagship electric motorcycle lineup is currently anchored by the Ultraviolette F77 MACH 2 and F77 SuperStreet series. The startup is eyeing entry into the EV scooter segment soon, with production of e-scooter Tesseract as well as e-bike Shockwave expected to commence over the next few months. Recently, the electric two-wheeler startup raised $85 Mn (about ₹813 Cr) in a Series E round co-led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures, to expand its manufacturing capacity and product portfolio, as well as strengthen its distribution network in India and overseas. The startup is bolstering its manufacturing capabilities and plans to invest more than ₹1,000 Cr over the next five years to expand its manufacturing footprint. Its upcoming BIGGA Factory is set to take its annual production capacity to as much as 2.5 Lakh vehicles in the initial phase. Ultraviolette currently has an installed capacity of around 30,000 vehicles annually at its Bengaluru facility, which is being expanded to 50,000-60,000 units. The plant will continue to serve as a manufacturing, engineering and technology hub after the BIGGA Factory comes online. It is also targeting international markets, with exports expected to account for around 25% of revenue over the next five years.

The row over the distribution of “experimental drug” meant for “clinical trials” to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) patients assumed political dimensions in the State, with the Opposition quick to latch on to the issue, demanding that the government assuage the concerns of the parents.
All hell broke loose on Tuesday, with parents of SMA children claiming that the SMA drug given free of cost at the SMA clinic in SAT Hospital was an “experimental drug” as the marking on the carton said “physicians’ samples/ for clinical trials only.”
Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan expressed concern whether “the sick children were being treated like mere guinea pigs” as well as shock at the Health Minister’s “criminal negligence.” On Wednesday, senior CPI(M) leader K.K. Shailaja too said the government cannot “change the drug just like that merely because it is cheaper.”
However, the fact remains that the decision to shift to the generic version of SMA drug had been taken during the previous government so that uninterrupted supply of the drug can be ensured. The purchase processes were initiated in February 2026 itself.
SAT Hospital authorities had clarified on Tuesday itself that no “experimental drug” was being given to children and that only the generic version of the original molecule, approved by the Central Drugs Standards Control Organisation (CDSCO) was given to the patients.
“We had a shortfall in the supply of the drug. On Monday, rather than send SMA patients away, we procured some samples of the generic version from Natco and distributed it. There is no change in the drug and the scaremongering about “experimental drugs” is unnecessary,” sources at SAT Hospital said.
“No experimental drug was given to SMA children. What was given was the generic version of Risdiplam, the patented original formula by Roche, now manufactured by the Indian firm Natco Pharma and which has been approved by drug regulatory bodies in the country. The drug is priced at 97% less cost than its patented version and makes it possible for the government to give the drug free of cost to more patients,” a hospital statement said.
On Wednesday, SAT Hospital authorities said they too back the physician samples. “We received the government supply on Tuesday evening and, hence, we opted to replace the drug,” Superintendent of SAT I. Riaz said.
SAT Hospital has been running an SMA clinic since 2022. At the time, Roche Pharma was the only firm licensed to produce and market the drug Risdiplam for SMA. The cost of one 60 ml bottle was ₹6.3 lakh.
Keralam is the only State to utilise public funds for providing free SMA treatment to children. With more children being identified with the disease and getting registered for free treatment, sustaining the free drug supply was becoming a problem.
It was in 2025, after the patent period of Risdiplam expired, Natco obtained the licence of the Drugs Control General of India to manufacture the generic version of Risdiplam. The generic drug is priced at ₹15,900 a bottle.
According to the National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021), manufacturing and licensing of drugs for rare diseases by Indian pharma firms is an important objective so that the precious medication can be accessible to more patients at a lower cost.
“The generic version has all regulatory approvals and is being used by all premier medical institutions in the country to treat SMA patients. Keralam cannot continue to procure the original molecule at high prices when an approved generic formulation is available at a fraction of the price. The government’s decision to embrace generics is a patient-centric move and it is highly commendable because it prioritises equitable access to life-saving drugs over vested commercial interests,” public health expert B. Ekbal said.
IMA representative N. Sulphi, too, pointed out that the controversy was nothing but a fallout of the rivalries between two pharma firms.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said the generic version of Risdiplam had been approved by an expert committee and that any concerns about the quality or efficacy of the drug were misplaced. The government’s only intention was to make the drug accessible to more patients, he said.

ACT politicians share experiences of threats and abuse in the wake of Helen Haines attack
In short:
Several ACT politicians have spoken out about threats and abuse they have experienced, following the attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines.
Canberra Liberals MLA Elizabeth Lee shared how she received a hand-delivered death threat that named her daughter and partner, while Health Minister Marisa Paterson recalled being spat at during a meet-and-greet at a local shop.
Along with Greens MLA Laura Nuttall and Independent MLA Thomas Emerson, they emphasised the importance of being publicly available to constituents and said they were determined to remain visible.
A hand-delivered death threat, being spat at and misogynistic abuse are just some of the incidents ACT politicians say they've experienced.
Several members of the ACT Legislative Assembly have spoken out about the abuse they've been subjected to, following the attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines outside her Victorian electorate office on Monday.
It's not yet clear what motivated Brendan Nugent, 43, to allegedly run her down in the incident that led to both her legs being amputated.
But the incident has renewed concerns about the safety of elected representatives across Australia, and highlighted the risks that come with their jobs.
Canberra Liberals MLA and former ACT opposition leader Elizabeth Lee said she has had to contact police twice over "very serious threats" she received.
"I had a death threat that named my daughter and my partner, and it was actually dropped at my front gate, so it came to my house," Ms Lee recalled.
"That was a pretty scary moment, and it does actually question, to me, as a parent especially, whether it's worth it.
"I have got this duty to ensure that I am prosecuting the issues that are really important to the community, but does that come at the cost of safety to my family?"
The incident came on top of the many sexist and racist comments she has received online over the past decade of representing her community.
"Belittling criticism on a personal level. Criticisms on my weight and my body shape as well, what I'm wearing sometimes,"
she said.
The mother of two daughters, Ms Lee said she tried to find the balance between ignoring the comments and calling them out to show her girls that such behaviour was unacceptable.
"I try and ignore it on the whole, but at the same time I know that there are people who need to know that it's not okay," she said.
"So, every now and then I will take that and make an example out of it to call it out."
'Disturbing part of the job'
ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson has also had some "pretty horrible" encounters with constituents.
"Yelling abuse at you, names at you," Ms Paterson said.
"I've been spat at; I've had things like that happen, standing outside the front of the shops and I've had people make violent threats to me face-to-face."
Ms Paterson said she enjoyed meeting and greeting Canberrans at local shops and community events, and that "97 per cent of interactions" were "amazing".
But she said the abuse she received, both in person and online, was a "disturbing part of the job" that made her "feel very vulnerable".
"It's predominantly men. In fact, all of my examples are men," she said.
"And I don't know … why they feel they can say these things to me and speak to me like that. But that is what happens. It's really disturbing."
Online, Ms Paterson said the abuse had "ramped up" over the past 18 months "very, very significantly", particularly with misogynistic, violent and hateful comments.
"The online world is a very unhappy place at the moment, I think," she said.
"Aside from having this job and needing to be there, other than that, I would have no part of it.
"It is a pretty awful environment with the online comments."
'Tough being a woman in politics'
For Greens MLA Laura Nuttall, it's her sexuality, gender and appearance that are often targeted on social media.
"You'll get some pretty nasty comments, which are often nothing to do with the debate [of the social media post], and everything to do with your appearance, your political leanings," Ms Nuttall said.
"I have had my sexuality speculated on and then sort of taken through the mud. I've copped a bit of queerphobic abuse, which is never fun.
"It is tough … being a woman in politics, particularly right now."
Ms Nuttall said the comments she received could be demoralising and that she "would be lying" if she said the attack on Ms Haines hadn't scared her.
"I have occasionally … felt the impact of that in my personal life in terms of just a loss of confidence," she said.
"And at times, even though it's momentary, a little bit of loss of faith in humanity, that people could be so mean and so remorseless about it."
'Rage gets clicks'
Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said he had seen his female counterparts cop far more abuse, particularly online, than he and his male colleagues did.
"Some of the men get criticised as well, but I think criticism on the basis of policy or disagreeing is really critical, that's part of our democracy and that's what a good, vibrant democracy looks like," Mr Emerson said.
"We should be able to disagree and disagree respectfully, debate those ideas. But when that flips into just abuse that's got nothing to do with the issue at hand, it is concerning."
He said there was a lot more political leaders could do to lead by example.
"Every time we allow policy disagreement to devolve into denigrating the people we're disagreeing with, we're basically saying to the people we're supposed to be representing, and leading in some ways, that actually this is the right way to conduct yourself,"
he said.
"So there's some blame there for politicians.
"We know that rage gets clicks and it gets picked up in traditional media, on social media, and that can lead to some pretty perverse incentives for politicians themselves and for people out in that community."
Ms Lee agreed that "we all need to take responsibility as a society".
"Political leaders particularly have a role, but it's anyone who has a public voice including the media and the big companies that obviously are responsible for social media," she said.
"Anyone who has the opportunity and the privilege to be able to shape public discourse and debate has a responsibility."
As politicians across the country review their security measures, these ACT MLAs are determined to remain publicly available to constituents as part of a healthy democracy.
"It is absolutely the key part of my job that I love," Ms Paterson said.
"It is my job to be out and about talking to people, listening to people, listening to what their concerns are."
Ms Nuttall agreed that she did not want the pockets of aggression, venom and vitriol to detrimentally impact the way she did her job.
"The whole point of being a representative is to be as accessible as humanly possible," she said.

The world of Ramayana unfolds through another musical offering, ‘Mangal Rang’, which brings Lord Rama and Maa Sita into focus through a series of beautiful visuals capturing their journey together. The song brings together striking landscapes, majestic palace settings and glimpses of the couple’s wedding, offering a look at the beauty and emotional depth of their relationship.
Ramayana’s ‘Mangal Rang’ out now! Song brings Lord Rama and Goddess Sita’s love story in a heartfelt manner; watch
Featuring Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama and Sai Pallavi as Goddess Sita, the song is now available on the official YouTube channels of World of Ramayana and T-Series and streaming on all platforms. Released simultaneously across Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, ‘Mangal Rang’ brings the musical experience to audiences across languages. It moves through different moments in their journey, from the grandeur of the palace and the sacredness of their wedding to their life beyond Ayodhya.
Beyond the scale of its settings, ‘Mangal Rang’ also offers glimpses of the bond between Rama and Sita. Their wedding sequences capture the joy and sanctity of their union, while the visuals from their journey into Vanvas bring a different dimension to their relationship.
The song brings together an accomplished musical collaboration, with A. R. Rahman composing the music and Dr. Kumar Vishwas penning the Hindi lyrics. Arijit Singh and Shreya Ghoshal lend their voices to the Hindi version, while each language features its own vocalists and lyricist, bringing the song’s emotional core to audiences across the country. The Tamil version features Abhay Jodhpurkar and Saindhavi, with lyrics by Karthik Netha. The Telugu version features Raghav Kaushik and Vaishali Samant, with lyrics by Rakendu Mouli. Armaan Malik and Bela Shende lend their voices to the Kannada version, with lyrics by Karthik Saragur, while the Malayalam version features Naresh Iyer and Amritha Rajan, with lyrics by Vinayak Sasikumar.
Speaking about composing the music for Ramayana and bringing the love story of Rama and Sita to life through ‘Mangal Rang’, A. R. Rahman said, “Ramayana is a story that has lived in the hearts of people for generations, and approaching it through music was a very special experience for me. There is a certain purity and tenderness in the relationship between Rama and Sita that I wanted the music to hold on to. With ‘Mangal Rang’, I hope listeners feel that warmth and devotion, and find something personal in the melody. Some stories don't need to be explained; they simply need to be felt.”
Speaking about lending his voice to ‘Mangal Rang’ and being part of Ramayana, Arijit Singh said, “Ramayana is not merely a story or an epic; it is a timeless reflection of life, our inner consciousness and the connection we share with everything around us. The melody of ‘Mangal Rang’, composed by A. R. Rahman sir, took me somewhere beyond words, into a space where love blossoms in its purest form. The sincerity and tenderness of the eternal relationship between Shri Ram and Mata Sita kept reminding me of the thread of love that connects us all, beyond everything that makes us seem different. Being part of this melody has been a deeply transformative experience, and I feel blessed to have been a part of a dream that Namit sir and his team are bringing to life. I hope this song reaches every listener with the same feeling of love, gratitude and devotion that I experienced while singing it.”
Speaking about singing for ‘Mangal Rang’ and connecting with the love story of Rama and Sita in Ramayana, Shreya Ghoshal said, “What makes Rama and Sita's love so beautiful is that it goes beyond the happiness of being together. There is faith, understanding and a quiet strength in their bond that makes it deeply moving. Singing ‘Mangal Rang’ allowed me to connect with that tenderness, and I approached it with a lot of love in my heart. Being part of a story that means so much to so many people is something I feel truly grateful for. I hope the song brings listeners a sense of warmth and peace, and lets them experience the beauty of Rama and Sita's relationship in their own way.”
Speaking about being part of the musical journey of Ramayana with ‘Mangal Rang’, Abhay Jodhpurkar said, “Ramayana is a story that has been a part of our lives and our cultural memory for generations. Being able to lend my voice to ‘Mangal Rang’ was a deeply moving experience, especially because the song captures the love and togetherness between Rama and Sita. There is a certain sincerity in their relationship that makes it timeless, and I tried to bring that emotion into my singing. I feel grateful to be part of a musical offering that allows this beautiful story to reach audiences in Tamil as well.”
Speaking about the opportunity to be part of Ramayana through the Telugu version of ‘Mangal Rang’, Vaishali Samant said, “Being part of ‘Mangal Rang’ has been a very special experience. Rama and Sita’s relationship carries so much love, trust and devotion, and there is a beautiful gentleness to the way their story unfolds in this song. I approached it with a lot of emotion, hoping to do justice to the feeling at its heart. To be able to share this story with Telugu-speaking audiences through music is something I feel very fortunate about.”
Reflecting on collaborating on Ramayana and lending his voice to the Kannada version of ‘Mangal Rang’, Armaan Malik said, “Ramayana is a story that transcends generations, and being part of its musical journey is something I feel deeply grateful for. ‘Mangal Rang’ celebrates the love between Rama and Sita in a way that feels intimate and heartfelt. I wanted my singing to reflect that emotion and allow the melody to speak for itself. I hope the Kannada version connects with listeners in a personal way and brings them closer to the beauty of this timeless relationship.”
Talking about the emotional connection she found with Rama and Sita’s relationship while singing the Kannada version of ‘Mangal Rang’, Bela Shende said, “There is something incredibly moving about the love between Rama and Sita. It is rooted in trust, understanding and a bond that remains strong through every turn of their journey. Singing ‘Mangal Rang’ gave me an opportunity to connect with that emotion, and I approached the song with a great deal of love and reverence. I hope the Kannada version brings listeners the same warmth and peace that I felt while singing it.”
Dr Kumar Vishwas on penning the lyrics of ‘Mangal Rang’ for Namit Malhotra’s Ramayana: “I sat down several times to write a song celebrating the divine wedding of Shri Ram. Yet, every time I wrote a couple of lines and revisited them, I felt that the grandeur of the wedding of the ParamPita must have been a thousand times greater than anything I could express through my words. Eventually, when I found myself unable to feel satisfied with my own writing, I turned to Maa Saraswati in prayer. Whatever this composition has become, I believe it is her creation.”
Ramayana features Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Goddess Sita, Yash as Ravana, Sunny Deol as Lord Hanuman and Ravi Dubey as Lakshman. The film is set to release on November 5.

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat
- Published
Just under a year ago, Harry Brook was left wondering if he would be sacked as England white-ball captain and what damage he had done to his international career.
What a turnaround in 12 months. From whacked in Wellington to the run-fest in Rawalpindi, Brook is undeniably England's most important cricketer and probably the best multi-format batter in the world.
Brook's 202 in England's defeat against Sri Lanka was an astonishing display of stroke-making. There can be no higher praise than to compare Brook's dismantling of the Sri Lankan attack to the sort of innings once played by South African genius AB de Villiers.
It was the first double hundred scored by an Englishman in an ODI, passing England's previous best individual score of 182 by Ben Stokes against New Zealand in 2023. In reaching 200 in 114 balls, Brook registered the fastest double ton by anyone in an ODI, bettering the 117 deliveries of India's Shubman Gill against West Indies only last month.
Brook has joined one of international cricket's most exclusive clubs. In completing the set of a hundred in a T20, double hundred in an ODI and triple century in a Test, Brook has matched the previously unique treble of West Indies' legend Chris Gayle.
In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played.
For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side.
Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown.
Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook – he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades.
In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate.
Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026.
The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband.
Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter – that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January.
He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision.
There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket.
Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article".
"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said.
In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer.
As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos – he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers.
As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level".
The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament.
Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022.
Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport.
To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan.
In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won.
Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what seemed an impregnable position, their bowling and fielding falling apart amid a growing realisation they were in danger of failing to defend a target of 430.
There was some mitigation. Dew made the ball incredibly slippery, while their attack was weakened by the absence of the rested Jofra Archer and benched Adil Rashid.
Nevertheless, the bowling was awful, particularly Sam Curran, who conceded 103 from nine overs to return the worst figures by an England bowler in an ODI. It was an error by Brook to continue to show faith in the left-armer, while not using the full allocation of 10 overs from either Josh Tongue or Gus Atkinson.
It is one of the first major missteps of Brook's captaincy career and the sort of performance that shows England still have some way to go to be seen as serious World Cup contenders.
Now, England will have to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final, to be played on 31 October, exactly 12 months on from Brook's horror show in Wellington.
England need the sort of turnaround their captain has managed over the past year

Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?
A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.
Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.
Added up, that’s a lot of billions. And yet: It’s still just the cost of doing business for Meta. Reuters reports that in the most recent New Mexico trial, the state’s attorneys originally asked Judge Francis Mathew to award the state between $35 and $45 billion. That would’ve been significant for the state, but would that extra $20 billion have kneecapped Meta? Nope.
Even if Meta was forced to pay the total maximum fine of the New Mexico ruling—a whopping $219 billion, or $5,000 across 43 million violations, reduced by the judge to $25 billion—the company would have felt only a mild sting. As of writing, Meta is worth around $1.7 trillion. Its stock took a hit on Thursday, but that was due to a confluence of factors, like Meta’s earnings report on Wednesday, the company’s massive capital expenditures on AI, and AI stocks dragging overall.
At this point, with no immediate monetary damage to Meta, it would take an accumulation of events to force some kind of change, legal experts tell me. For one, Meta has a clear perception problem: Juries are ruling against it, protesters have railed against it, even its own employees have been more vocal about the company’s internal policies.
Every time Meta doesn’t settle a case, the evidence presented during trial can be scrutinized by the public and used in future cases against Meta, says Corban Rhodes, partner at DiCello Levitt, the outside law firm representing New Mexico in this case. “This trial included more than 100 exhibits that we were able to put into public record, things that had been kept secret for more than a decade since Cambridge Analytica,” Rhodes told WIRED.
One such item is a 2018 email that then COO Sheryl Sandberg sent to a few colleagues days after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. Sandberg wrote, “The single biggest issue we face—and I really need everyone to know this—is that there were a MILLION developers with access to the data. We are going to have many, many, many more moments like this in the next month and year.”
There are early signals that private insurers may start balking at having to cover the cost of a tech company’s legal defenses. Some experts are suggesting that insurance companies could even end up being de facto governance for AI, as they “inject responsibility into how AI is designed, developed, and deployed as a condition for obtaining insurance.” Meta learned this firsthand in March, when a Delaware judge ruled that insurers do not have a duty to defend Meta against the literal thousands of lawsuits being brought against it.
There’s no well-defined number at which Meta suddenly becomes vulnerable—the company is unlikely to ever fold from legal penalties alone. But problems could crop up if shareholders or board members stop seeing the company as some inanimate entity and start to focus on the individual directors or officers who have been making bad decisions, says Brian Quinn, a law professor at Boston College Law School who studies corporate law, M&A, and transaction law. Like, say, the people who keep appearing in lawsuits.
“The way that indemnification law is written right now, the fact that a person in a company was found to have violated a law doesn’t necessarily make them liable. It can be believed that they were acting in good faith, or in the best interest of their company,” Quinn says. “But problems start to arise if shareholders say, wait a minute, there’s not only evidence that this director or operator is violating the law, but it has appeared in the same set of facts seven times now.”
After a huge accumulation of these kinds of results, Quinn says, some angry shareholders might stand up and say the corporation should no longer be able to indemnify those directors. That’s when you might see change, because Meta’s executives would no longer be as protected.
Finally, since litigation is often behind the curve on society-disrupting technology, Meta’s legal woes are likely far from over—especially as it wades deeper into AI. “Regulators and courts have for a long time been focused on the impact of social media 1.0 and 2.0, and I think we’re moving on from that era,” says Rhodes. “I expect the next wave of litigation will be focused on AI.”

Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe
MILAN — Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.
The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.
In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported.
Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.
The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.
Army vehicles and boarded-up luxury stores in Milan
In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state."
A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.
The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence.
A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again.
Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.
Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square.
Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods.
The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center.
Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy.
Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalized, second-generation Italians," alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.
A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said.
Protesters try to force entry into Colosseum in Rome
Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.
A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters.
"I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association.
A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organizers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometer (mile) away.
Clashes and buildings set on fire in Albania
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets Saturday.
For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city center.
High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.
A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street.
Rama said Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties.
Pensions and housing spark Madrid and Lisbon protests
Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital Saturday to demand public pensions aren't meddled with.
"They are threatening us with privatizing pensions. It's just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68.
The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party criticized the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatizing public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.
Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday.
They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.
Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.

“He felt something yesterday in training. At the moment, he has some fluid [around the injury], so we have to do some tests to see how big is the injury is,” Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso told media ahead of the encounter.

Trump lost control and ordered me to be ‘quiet’ in the Oval Office. Then it got personal
What was supposed to be an announcement on fraud quickly devolved into Trump vs The Independent. Andrew Feinberg details how it all happened in the Oval Office

Already a member? Log in
Who could have guessed that Trump would get so spun up over a law that’s been on the books since Abraham Lincoln was president?
I certainly didn’t when I arrived at the White House this morning.
I was there as part of what the Trump administration has dubbed the “secondary print” element of the White House press pool, part of the rotating group of news outlets that it brings into the Oval Office for events. Normally, I am the designated “print pool” reporter approximately once a month, where I file short reports detailing what goes on in the Oval Office or any other event the president attends.
This time, my only function was to ask questions. I had a list that I discussed with my colleagues in New York, but I decided to call an audible when a reporter posted that Trump and Vice President JD Vance planned to unveil a new program and “tip line” to award so-called “whistleblowers” bounties of up to $30,000 for exposing what the administration believes to be “fraud.”
Then I became the focus of Trump’s attacks.
For doing my job, I became the target of Trump and his team. Soon after, Trump lectured and unleashed at me his White House rapid response, who called me a “Mongoloid Moron” – which is a slur for someone with development disabilities, a phrase I would never use – and the Vice President on his official government account labeled me an ‘imbecile.’
All for an event that started off pretty normal. White House officials were going to hand out a reward to Nick Shirley, the right-wing YouTuber whose viral videos jump-started the administration’s crusade against day-care and home health care businesses in Minnesota run or owned by Somali-Americans. For their part, Trump, Vance and even Shirley acted like the idea of rewarding whistleblowers was new and unique to this administration, with the YouTube personality claiming there has “never been an incentive for anyone to ever expose fraud” in the country’s entire history.
Because I’ve spent most of my professional life covering the federal government, I know there’s already a mechanism to reward whistleblowers on the books, I knew Shirley — and the rest — were dead wrong about that.
Since 1863, a law called the False Claims Act has allowed whistleblowers to sue on behalf of the federal government to recover funds that have been defrauded from federal programs. That law pays people more than Trump suggested through his program.
These lawsuits, called qui tam cases, often involve the exact types of Medicare and Medicaid fraud on which the administration claims to be cracking down. And unlike the relatively paltry 1 percent which Trump claimed whistleblowers can be awarded, the False Claims Act allows someone who blows the whistle and brings a qui tam case to receive as much as a quarter of whatever the government recovers.
The process is complex, onerous, and requires legal assistance, but the payout at the end can be significant. The new program Trump and Vance were touting appeared far less lucrative — and left Trump, not a federal judge, as the arbiter of who would be worthy of any rewards.
So why would anyone use the administration’s “tip line” when they could get far more cash for using the tried-and-true process that’s been around since the days of Abraham Lincoln?
I asked the president that exact question. His response? “Because it’s a lot of money.”
“At 1 percent, people will make millions and millions of dollars for turning in what actually is a somewhat routine crime of, you know, of millions of millions. But we’re talking about we’re talking about billions and actually probably trillions of dollars,” said Trump, who may not have understood the question or was unable to fathom that ten to 25 percent is far more than one percent.
Trump may not have understood the query, but Vance did — and he was eager to mix it up. Months earlier, we tangled in the briefing room when I asked him about the president’s stock trading. And it appeared that the Veep was unsatisfied with Trump’s response, so he chimed in to call the question “dishonest” and suggest there are certain frauds that fall outside the False Claims Act’s remit, which is not true.
Sensing that he had been emasculated by the VP, Trump asked me who I was, which was odd because he had definitely recognized me earlier when he winked at me as Vance delivered remarks earlier in the event.
I’ve been around him in the Oval, aboard Air Force One and elsewhere countless times over the decade I’ve covered him, and we’ve even spoken on the phone on a number of occasions.
But Vance’s interjection compelled Trump to ask: “Who are you?”
I answered him and said I’m Andrew Feinberg and I work for The Independent.
As the press gaggle went on, I attempted to ask more questions from the list I’d prepared — including one on his plans to renovate a popular D.C. golf course. But kept finding myself at the end of Trump’s fury.
Trump appeared to point to me more than once, but on each occasion he had apparently intended to call on the Agence France-Presse reporter directly behind me. Because from my vantage point he was pointing directly at my face, I started to speak up.
He didn’t like that.
“I don’t know who the hell you are, but you better be careful,” he said, an odd remark considering I’d identified myself not 10 minutes earlier.
When the same thing happened minutes later, he lost it completely, calling me a “sick person.”
He added: “I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”
For the record, I had an annual physical earlier this month, and I can report I’m in perfect health.
I was doing my job, and I’ll be right back at it tomorrow.
