Aga banned for fake prescription from family member
- Published
Ethiopian marathon runner Ruti Aga has been handed a six-year ban after she attempted to explain a positive test for a banned substance using a prescription from a non-existent clinic, issued by a doctor who turned out to be a family member.
Aga, who won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon, tested positive for methylprednisolone after winning a half marathon in China in March.
She received a two-year ban for testing positive for the prohibited steroid - used to reduce inflammation and classed as performance enhancing by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada).
The 32-year-old was given a further four-year ban for tampering with evidence and misleading investigators during an interview.
"Aga attributed her positive test to treatment for a knee injury, submitting a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a 'doctor' who turned out to be a family member with no medical registration with the relevant authority," the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday.
"When questioned, the family member claimed to have used an old prescription pad from a former workplace. But that clinic confirmed the individual had never worked there and the prescription was not theirs."
Aga, who has finished second three times at World Marathon Majors, has been provisionally suspended since 10 September and the ban will run from that date.

What Man Utd need now is stability, not more changes - Pulis
- Published
Walking into an under-achieving football club is never easy. I know, because I spent my career taking on such challenges.
That was the task Michael Carrick took on in January when he was appointed Manchester United's interim manager and took over a club that was drifting deeper and deeper into mediocrity.
Supporters talk about seeing a bounce when new managers take over and, from my own experiences, I do believe that to be the case.
Michael certainly experienced a fantastic period where results and performances improved. In his case, United's improvement to finish third and in the Champions League places was exceptional - and he also calmed the water behind the scenes.
Yet, with every bounce, there almost always comes a return to normality. You see players who raised the level of their performance return to the level they are used to, and everything often slips back to the way it was before.
That seems to be what is happening at United now but, while Carrick appears to be under increasing pressure, the club's problems are definitely not just down to who their manager is.
Here, I've tried to explain what he needs to do to sort some of his issues out.
Who would United manager have chosen as signings?
To properly judge Michael, you have to balance up everything he has inherited and consider whether United could be a successful organisation.
United have invested enormous amounts of money in recruiting a lot of players in the past five years.
Since 2021, they have had three other permanent managers - Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, who spent more than £1bn on 27 major signings and many of whom are still at the club.
This year, under Michael, they have invested another £150m, but the bulk of it was on three midfielders and if you assess his entire squad I would still seriously question how many players he would have chosen out of the group he now has.
As a manager going into troubled clubs, you have to immediately set your non-negotiable principles with your players - things like hard work and a collective spirit in the dressing room were imperative for me.
You give everyone the same opportunity to jump on board and then quickly recognise the players who are capable of going on the ride with you, and those who can't, or won't.
Michael will know all those things about his squad by now, good and bad, but what can he really do about it?
When players are assets on budget sheets
In my experience, and I am talking about Premier League clubs, my owners were keen on my views on the players I had just inherited - not just in terms of their ability on the pitch but their value as assets on budget sheets and in the transfer market.
I was always continually asked if I could make players better, and also if I could recover money from those I did not rate or want, so as to help the club's financial position.
I understood why - my position as manager was to 100% help the club and try to achieve maximum performances on and off the pitch - but it can be hard to do both.
It means when you are taking over a group of players your club has invested in, you cannot always be completely honest about certain players in that group.
You know the club has a vested interest in holding the player's value and the fact you have to portray positivity to protect that is sometimes unbelievably difficult.
Criticising them in the media can't happen, because of your loyalty to the club, so you are left hoping the people who watch your games week in, week out, understand and recognise your dilemma around your squad.
The club's recruitment strategy has been publicly questioned recently, of course, by defender Lisandro Martinez - and I am sure a lot of supporters agree with him and/or would like some clarity on that subject.
But, from a manager's perspective, Martinez's outburst also raises serious questions about the player himself.
Him saying what he did does make me wonder whether he believes he has been a success personally. If so, then how many more players in United's first-team squad also believe themselves to have been successful, rather than part of the problem?
Managing players with inflated opinions about themselves is another challenge in itself - and it certainly needs addressing.
You can add that to the list of Michael's issues right now, but he has an even bigger problem in how he deals with his captain Bruno Fernandes' comments after United were humbled by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday,
Watching Michael in his post-match press conference in Italy was really difficult for me.
I've managed games where my team has been beaten while having a right go, but having to see a manager man up to his side after a performance that, for me, questioned their attitude to compete or even run around and try, was heart-wrenching.
Listening to the way his captain spoke, after his own example typified his team's reluctance to do the above, it again showed me how difficult it must be at that club at the moment.
Michael's tactics are there to be followed, yet to do that away to Como on a very wet and windy miserable night, you need men and not boys.
Fernandes seemed to be enjoying his relationship with Carrick last season, when United were flying up the table, but they have now levelled off both as a team and individuals in the way I described in this column.
Proper captains, and I was lucky to work with some top guys, come to the fore when the team and club needs them most.
I've always judged leaders by people who follow them when things are going wrong. Unfortunately, many members of that team did follow their captain's example, but in a totally unprofessional way.
Carrick needs time and support like Arteta
I don't know Michael well, but he was a very honest player who deservedly has great standing at the club he is now managing.
I know his backroom staff better - Steve Holland, Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate - and they are all able assistants with knowledge and experience at the very top level.
Whenever United are not winning, there will be calls for things to change - and the manager is almost always at the top of that list.
So, where should they look now? I believe they should follow the blueprint of one of their great rivals, and realise that continuously changing direction is just not working.
When Mikel Arteta arrived at Arsenal in December 2019, he had an instant impact like Michael - not in terms of league position, but by winning the 2020 FA Cup.
For a couple of years after that early success, however, Arteta was taking pelters from fans and across the spectrum of media outlets because the upturn in results did not last.
Despite that, the club never flinched and gave him the opportunity to install a clear identity throughout the club and also time for it to take shape.
Look where they are now.
United have to take their medicine and do similar - they have to understand the consequences of the huge failures in recruitment they have repeatedly made and reset to find a direction and identity again.
Time is their biggest challenge there, because everyone demands instant success these days. People, though, have to realise that, while I believe Michael - when everyone is fit - has a group that can still compete for the Champions League places, they are never good enough for the prizes they really want.
To be contenders again, they need more than just talent. Ability, pace and character are the characteristics they will need in pretty much every outfield position but, from where they are now, achieving that will not happen quickly.
They definitely don't need to change their manager again to get there, however. I was all for Michael getting the job in the first place once Darren Fletcher had been overlooked, and in my humble opinion he should be backed again to do what is needed now.
At this moment, United are not capable of winning the league title, whoever is in charge, but stability is the way forward to fix that.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.
Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.
I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?
Twist and Shout
The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.
It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.
The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

In the heart of Rajasthan’s Thar desert, on the outskirts of the agro-pastoralist landscape of Bikaner, is a dumpsite of livestock carcasses where, traditionally, a feeding frenzy plays out among multiple species of beasts and birds everyday.
Importantly, every winter, a large number of migratory Himalayan and Eurasian griffon, whose numbers have dwindled catastrophically in the country, congregate at this dumpsite, located in the northwestern corner of Jorbeer Conservation Reserve of Bikaner. Other scavengers here are Egyptian vultures, steppe eagles, black ibises, cattle egrets and wild pigs, which feast on dead cattle, horses, camels, sheep and goats.
Now, a new study published in the journal Biological Conservation has found that perennially free-ranging dogs pose a serious threat to vultures here. This finding comes in the backdrop of other studies that have tracked the catastrophic decline in vulture populations in India: the raptor numbers plummeted by over 90% in the 1990s, largely due to the veterinary use of the anti-inflammatory drug diclofenac in livestock. When the cattle died, their poisonous carcasses killed the birds that fed on them in large numbers.
In several parts of India, vultures went extinct. An older study even corelated vulture decline to increased human deaths from a burgeoning feral dog population and the spread of rabies.
“As vulture recovery efforts continue, the presence of dogs at supplementary feeding sites [dumpsites] may hinder vulture access through direct competition and aggressive interference,” cautions the new paper.
Vulture restaurants
India’s vulture populations have historically been sustained by livestock carcass dumpsites, but with dogs increasingly in the mix, the scientists found that vultures spent about half as long on carcasses at the open Bikaner dumpsite than at dog-free enclosures. “Dog presence also altered their temporal feeding patterns, restricting vulture activity largely to the afternoon, whereas in the absence of dogs, feeding was distributed more evenly across daylight hours,” the paper added.
As dogs can consume large amounts of meat, it reduces food availability for vultures too; the canines also chase away the birds, reducing their access to carcasses. The paper concludes that dogs are “a major threat to vultures” here.
Dumpsites or ‘supplementary feeding sites’ are places where carcasses are regularly accessible to scavengers at a fixed location. In Europe and Africa they are usually managed “vulture restaurants” offering safe, drug-free carrion, co-author of the paper, Abi T. Vanak of Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment, told The Hindu.
“In India, traditional livestock carcass dumps were never designed for vultures, but their large and predictable carcass supply made them function as de facto feeding sites for vultures, as at Jorbeer in Bikaner,” he added.
Safe zones
While dumpsites function as a “highly predictable food resource[s]” for vultures, it is imperative that they are managed adequately, said the paper conceding that the “predictability” of such feeding sites “may promote the habituation of vultures,” diminishing their natural foraging activity across the reserve. Moreover, competitively superior species, such as large griffons, are more likely to monopolise the majority of this food resource available, thereby displacing subordinate species.
The impact of dogs on wildlife has been well documented.: the canines are known to have contributed to the extinction of 11 vertebrate species around the world. In India, they are known to prey on over 80 species, including black bucks, desert foxes and olive ridley turtles, according to a paper in the journal Animal Conservation. They have even been documented attacking snow leopards in Ladakh.
Prof. Vanak said that setting up more dispersed dog-proof feeding sites could encourage broader landscape level foraging by vultures, thus reducing their dependence on a single site. “Our study shows that conserving vulture populations will require more strategic management of food sources, including managing the populations of dogs, and creating vulture ‘safe zones’ where they can feed in peace,” he added.

82 days later, no repairs started on washed-out road dividing small Quebec town
L’Ascension, Que., mayor blames delays on bureaucracy of different levels of government
Mayor Jacques Allard stands in front of the 70-foot gap that now divides his town of L’Ascension.
Spray painted white lines on the ground track the ongoing erosion that continues with every rainfall.
It's been 82 days since heavy rain washed away parts of Principale Street and de L’Ascension Road that connects the small municipality to the city of Rivière-Rouge on Aug. 3.
The mayor says on its end, L’Ascension is ready to start work to repair the road.
They have their contractor, the engineer plans are in place and the replacement culvert — twice the diameter of the previous one — is sitting idly by the protective fencing that surrounds the giant crater.
So what's the delay?
The municipality says it's waiting for the green light from the Quebec government to begin the repair, which their contractor expects to take five weeks and cost roughly $3 million.
A report of the required work also had to be sent to Fisheries and Oceans Canada for approval — a report that took 70 days to be approved and was then sent to the government.
The washout is directly in front of the fire hall, impacting emergency services. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
L’Ascension is now awaiting confirmation that they will receive the subsidy from the program that provides financial support to municipalities affected by natural disasters.
Allard says the bureaucracy slowing down this work is unacceptable.
“Normally they have a protocol to fast track. Now it is a very slow track," he said.
300 people cut off
The crater left behind by the rushing water that ripped up sections of asphalt and collapsed culverts is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide.
Thirty per cent of the small population lives on the other side of the gap, meaning around 300 people are cut off from their community.
Nicolas Côté owns a small grocery store in town. He says business is already down 15 per cent compared to last year due to its inaccessibility.
Residents on the other side of the gap must either take their business to the nearby town of Rivière-Rouge or make a detour of more than an hour to reach their local grocery store.
The gap is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide and sits where the road used to connect in L’Ascension. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
Côté says when you live in a small town where the population is just shy of 1,000 people, it's more like a family.
He says many people have sent him messages saying they hope the repairs happen soon so they will see him again and be able to shop at their local store.
“Maybe it's tough to fix, but to wait so much time … and we still don't know what will happen," Côté said.
The local grocery store in L’Ascension has already seen a 15 per cent drop in business compared to last year due to the lack of access for residents. (Andie Bennett/CBC)
With winter coming, Allard says there is a lot of anxiety within the community. He is also concerned about the financial impact if the repairs are not completed as soon as possible.
“On the other side, it takes five minutes to get here. Now it's 50 minutes. How will we pay to remove the snow in the winter? The trucks will have to make this detour. We will have a big expense for fuel," he said.
CBC News reached out to the Domestic Security Ministry for comment. It said it is currently reviewing the file and will confirm, as soon as possible, whether the work is eligible for financial assistance.

Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
- Published
A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports.
The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region as on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured.
Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet.
Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

When my husband and I first met back in 2014, we had what many would consider a whirlwind romance. We met, fell in love almost instantly, moved in together after a year, got engaged six months later, married a month after that, and a little over a year later, welcomed our first child.
It was all very exciting, rushed, and filled with emotion and love.
I'm also a very rational person who doesn't get easily swept up in the moment. So we talked about a lot of the "hard" decisions that couples so often neglect to discuss at the beginning of a relationship. We talked about children, our future, and what we wanted our lives to look like. That's why, now, more than 12 years later, it's surprising to find myself struggling with something I thought I had already made peace with: our age gap.
He is 23 years older than me
My husband and I have a 23-year age difference. Yes, I was always aware of it. And, to be honest, it never really made a difference to me.
Especially when it came to the big life decisions, including having children, we had those conversations before we even got engaged. I knew exactly how old he was. I knew there would be things about growing older together that would be different for us.
But I guess there's a big difference between being aware of something that could eventually happen and actually living it.
Our age difference has been showing up in more ways than one lately, and there's a part of me that's angry with myself for being surprised by it.
It's not like my husband was always going to be the 48-year-old I met when I was 25. I knew he would age. I knew things would change as he got older. I knew there would eventually be a point when the difference between us became more noticeable.
I just don't think I ever wanted to admit to myself exactly how much.
He's in his 60s now
I knew he was going to be an older father. I knew all of this. But knowing something and seeing it firsthand are two very different things. Lately, I've seen just how much his 61 years are catching up to him, and it's been putting me in a strange place.
I keep a lot of things together for my family. We have two young children, and I have my own business. There is already a lot that weighs on me. But what I've noticed recently is my husband's physical health beginning to catch up with his age.
Don't get me wrong — my husband is in great shape for a 61-year-old. But at the same time, most 61-year-olds aren't running after toddlers or handling the daily insanity of school drop-off and pick-up.
And that difference is becoming harder for me to ignore. What bothers me most is how naive I feel. I knew this was a possibility. Quite frankly, my husband knew it, too. When we discussed having children, we were always on the same page, but he expressed his concerns about being an "old" dad. I heard him. We talked about it. We made the decision together.
And yet, now that I'm watching the reality unfold in front of me, I'm beginning to feel guilty. As though I've been selfish. As though somehow this isn't fair to my kids.
I see how much fatherhood — and, frankly, being a husband — can weigh on him.
The everyday insanity of being part of a household with a high-maintenance 8-year-old and a very independent 3-year-old is a lot for anyone, myself included. But it's especially a lot for a 61-year-old.
Sometimes he physically can't keep up with our 3-year-old, who runs at a pace that could outrun the best of us. Sometimes he mentally can't keep up with our eight-year-old, who talks at about a million miles a minute.
And those moments make the age difference feel very real.
It's not just the fatherhood aspect
I feel his patience with me beginning to waver, too, and I wonder how much of that is because we're simply in such different phases of life.
I have a thriving public relations firm, and I feel like I'm just getting started. I have energy and ambition and a feeling that there is still so much ahead of me.
He had a contracting firm for many years, but that chapter of his life is well behind him now. At his age, he should be enjoying retirement. Instead, he's a stay-at-home dad and handles a huge amount for our family. But he's far from retired.
He's the only one who drives, so he's the family's chauffeur. He makes appointments and handles logistical things. He oversees the renovations on our house. He does the grocery shopping. He does so, so much.
And the truth is, at this age, maybe he shouldn't have to.
Our relationship itself hasn't really changed. We are still very lucky to have an incredibly open and loving relationship. We talk about these things. We try to give each other space and understand where one another is coming from. We each do what we can mentally and physically for each other, for our children, and, just as importantly, for ourselves.
I think what we're realizing is that neither of us has ever been here before.
We knew there was an age gap when we met. We knew what it meant on paper. We talked about the difficult possibilities before we got married and before we had children.
At 25, I could understand that my husband was 23 years older than me. At 38, I can feel it.

I set up a digital wall calendar at a friend’s house a couple of months ago. Her first question was one I’ve constantly asked myself as I test these devices in my own home: “Does it have a voice assistant?”
It feels like the one thing missing from these devices. Digital wall calendars have been on the rise in popularity this year, driven by the popularity of the Skylight Calendar. After testing multiple models in my own home, I can see why. These devices take any and all of the digital calendars you already have (Google Calendar, iCalendar, Outlook Calendar—you name it) and put them onto a single device in your home.
It’s great if you’re like my husband and me, who live by our Google Calendars but don’t want to be tied to our phones when discussing plans. These devices can also double as household management tools with meal planning, chore trackers, to-do lists, photo screen savers that double as a digital photo frame, and even financial management for your kids if you go with the Greenlight Family Hub.
The Greenlight Family Hub has been an interesting device in the world of digital calendars because of how many features it offers. It not only adds financial management, as the company was originally a banking tool for parents and their teens, but family location tracking, which uses the Greenlight app on a family member’s phone to show their location, or a GPS tracker that you can separately purchase for younger children.
But there’s one feature behind the paywall (a $10-a-month membership) that finally satisfies the thing I’ve always wanted: a voice assistant.
Greenlight’s proprietary voice assistant has been both easy to use and has given smart, thoughtful answers. So why isn’t there a voice assistant in every digital wall calendar? And conversely, why haven’t smart displays that do have smart voice assistants gained features like full-page calendars and chore charts?
Not Just a Calendar
Part of what makes Greenlight’s hub different from other digital calendars is that the company is using the calendar as a starting point for the offerings it already has. That’s also why it’s called the Family Hub instead of just a calendar like most other devices I’ve tested. Greenlight grew from a banking tool to a way to manage chores and money for kids and teens, and has now become a full family management platform where you can track your family’s calendars, chores, kids’ spending, and even family locations.
Greenlight says it noticed the lack of voice support among competitors’ offerings and baked that into its hub intentionally. “Voice assistants have been around for over a decade, yet when building the specs for Family Hub, we noticed that voice support was absent in the digital calendar market," says Sushil Sharma, chief product officer at Greenlight. "Our goal with Hub was to create an all-in-one command center for busy families to engage with technology in a way that feels natural and seamless. By combining a voice assistant feature with a centralized home display, we are able to limit the number of devices families need in their home.”
It’s also smart for families with younger children—Sharma pointed out that not all kids can read and type fluently, and voice support makes it more accessible for them and the rest of the family. But it’s also a way people are expecting to interact with their home devices after years of smart speakers and smartphones offering voice support.
Voice Report
Greenlight’s assistant reminds me of the modern, AI-powered iterations of Alexa and Google because it’s also powered by AI. Greenlight says its family AI assistant uses frontier large language models with Greenlight’s own proprietary safety tools that it designed with family safety in mind. That means the assistant shouldn’t get into sensitive or inappropriate topics (or accidentally tell your child Santa isn’t real) but will both schedule a timer and answer day-to-day questions. You’ll also see a conversation appear on the right-hand side, reminding me a lot of the Alexa+ experience on an Echo Show device.
Greenlight’s Hub is supposed to only wake at its wake phrase, “Hey Greenlight,” but in the days I’ve been testing it, I’ve found it to be a little sensitive and likely to wake at random. It also tends to keep listening, waiting to see if you’ll continue the conversation or give a new command, so if my family is having a general conversation after asking a question, Greenlight will try to pick up a question from that and answer it. I find myself often ordering Greenlight to stop.
That isn’t an issue just for Greenlight. My Google Gemini-powered smart speaker does the same thing, and both my son and I are quick to yell, “Google, stop!” to get it to stop trying to answer a question we didn’t ask. It’s a problem with these AI-powered voice assistants overall, but I’m finding I’d rather say the wake word multiple times than get interrupted.
Big Brother Energy
When I described to my editor the laundry list of features that the Greenlight Family Hub has, she said it sounded like a “Big Brother machine.” I see why, of course—tracking your location and financial information in a device that sounds like a simple calendar might come as a surprise to most people. It was certainly a surprise to me when I went to set up the hub through the app and ended up stuck on the financial pathway (Greenlight says it’s fixing this issue in the app but I had to have support clear my information so I could set up the hub without setting up a bank card for my child).
Still, I like how much it has to offer, even if it might feel a tad Big Brother-y for some. And while it does have a microphone, it doesn’t have a camera like most smart displays have, so in that sense it feels less creepy to me than other devices I’ve had in my home.
I also really like that most of the features are accessible without needing a premium subscription—notably the photo screen saver feature, which Skylight will charge you for. (Skylight’s business model in general has become charging for storage, for both its calendars and digital photo frames.) Greenlight charges instead for its AI assistant and voice interaction, along with family location sharing. If you’re less voice-inclined than I am, you’d be plenty happy with this hub without the premium subscription.
I am hoping we see more digital wall calendars add at least some kind of voice assistance, as well as offering some control of your smart home devices. Maybe I’m biased coming from a background in smart home technology, but it feels like a huge missed opportunity. Smart displays have existed for years (and Apple just announced its first one) but have lacked the key feature that digital wall calendars have to really make them a touch point in the home beyond your voice. I reached out to both Amazon and Skylight to ask why neither has introduced any such model yet, but both companies declined to comment.
Maybe, for a company like Skylight, it’s the cost of creating an assistant that would work with its platform and needing to change its hardware to include a microphone, but Amazon is well positioned to bring something like this to the market (especially since the newest version of Alexa, Alexa+, is already paywalled). I’m hopeful we’ll see the next generation of smart displays at least make some kind of calendar mode an option; I’d certainly rather see my calendar than another ad or piece of screen clutter on my Echo Show.

1. What is the project about?

A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.
Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.
Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.
The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)
Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press releaseAsked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.
“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.
“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”
Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.
Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.
Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.

Doomsday predictions of artificial intelligence causing massive white-collar job losses haven’t come to pass. At least not yet.
There is, however, evidence that AI tools, while helping experts become more productive, are hollowing out the skills that young people acquire early in their careers. This divergence may be showing up as a big jump in “quiet quitting” — a lack of meaningful workplace connection — even in an economy like India’s, where youth are starved of decent employment.
A wave of emotional detachment is sweeping corporations. According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace survey, employee engagement declined for a second year in 2025 to its lowest level since 2020. India is mimicking the trend, with barely 23% of staff feeling invested in their roles. A staggering 59% are doing just enough to survive. The rest have switched off entirely.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.

Philippines investigates laptop found at Thomas Markle's former home

MANILA: Philippine police are investigating a laptop found alongside images of child abuse at the former home of Meghan Markle's estranged father, with "full results" expected in a week, the country's interior minister told AFP.
Thomas Markle, whose daughter is married to Britain's Prince Harry, had been living in Cebu in the Philippines until reportedly returning to the United States earlier this year.
Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla told AFP the country planned to take "appropriate legal actions" against Markle - who has denied all claims of alleged offending - if sufficient evidence was found.
"The Philippine National Police (PNP), upon the reports of the son, inspected the former home of a certain Mr Thomas Markle," Remulla said in a text message sent late on Saturday (Oct 24). "Found were a trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop."
"The laptop is currently going under forensic investigation and we will have the full results in one week," Remulla said.
"The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him."
British tabloid the Sun first reported last week that Markle's son, Thomas Markle Jr, had discovered the child abuse images while going through boxes found in his father's former home.
On Friday, Meghan Markle said she was "deeply distressed" by accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations.
After the reports, Meghan said that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London's Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection making similar accusations.
"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement.
London's Metropolitan police said it had passed on the information to the royal couple but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
Meghan Markle and Prince Harry left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud.
They made an unexpected return with their children to live in the United Kingdom in August.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Leaders in the US Space Force would like to have a new spaceport up and running in four years, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure from bases in Florida and California that have shot rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years.
The obvious problem with that ambition is 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink first mentioned the service’s search for a third launch base in May. A congressionally mandated study of the Space Force’s launch infrastructure identified the need for “another site that’s capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability,” Meink said in a House Armed Services Committee hearing.
The Trump administration released a space transportation policy in August that endorsed the construction of more launch and reentry sites for commercial and military missions. This week, the Space Force general responsible for procuring launch services for the military laid out an “aspirational” timeline for a new launch site.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.”

A time-critical investigation into the death of a British man whose body was found in a ransacked property on the Caribbean island of Grenada has stalled because of diplomatic delays between the two countries.
Charity workers supporting the family of Andrew Frederick are demanding immediate government intervention to clear the path for a full investigation to begin almost 10 months after his death, which has been ruled a homicide by a pathologist.
The Murdered Abroad charity has called on the foreign affairs select committee to step in after Grenadian police found there was “no basis … that any homicide has occurred” and closed the case.
This was despite a report from an autopsy, done in the week he died, saying Frederick, 47, had suffered “blunt force trauma”, was tortured, including by removal of his toenail, and ruling the death a homicide.
Frederick’s body was found on 4 January. Since then, the family say they have been forced to focus on their fight for justice instead of coming to terms with their loss.
Murdered Abroad’s founder, Eve Henderson, said:“We understand there are challenges but [almost 10 months] on, this family is still being met with obfuscation. If a family this determined cannot get the FCDO [Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office] to put their diplomatic powers to good use, what hope is there for the 60 to 80 families bereaved by murder abroad each year?
“A minister must look urgently at how consular services treat these traumatised families or the foreign affairs select committee must step in,” she added.
A former Scotland Yard homicide commander who is supporting the family described Grenada’s actions as “incredible”.
“In the autopsy report … the pathologist, who is a qualified medical examiner, categorically states that he believes this is a case of homicide and that Andrew was tortured before he was killed,” David Johnston said. “And yet the police just choose to ignore that because it didn’t fit with their model. I mean, it’s incredible.”
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK in August, where a second autopsy was carried out, during which it was discovered his organs were missing.
The family described this discovery as “shocking and devastating”.
In a statement, they said: “We were already heartbroken that Andrew’s life was cruelly taken, but nothing could have prepared us for what we would learn afterwards. For six weeks after his death, Andrew’s body was held under the control of the Grenadian authorities. When he was later examined in the UK, parts of his neck and all of his organs, including his brain, heart, and lungs, were missing.
“That discovery has been shocking and absolutely devastating for our family; we are still struggling to process it. It has added pain upon pain and left us with deep hurt with so many unanswered questions. Despite our multiple inquiries, no one has told us where they are, what happened to them, or why we were never told. No family should ever have to ask these questions.”
Last month a UK coroner asked the Metropolitan police to conduct an investigation. Weeks later a communication from UK authorities, seen by the Guardian, said a British high commissioner had raised Frederick’s case with officials at the highest levels of government in Grenada, and indicated that authorities there had agreed to cooperate with any forthcoming formal request for the UK to assist with the investigation.
That formal request was sent weeks ago but the family say they are still waiting for Grenada “to honour their verbal commitment to the British high commissioner and approve the request to cooperate”.
“Every day for almost 10 months we have had to live without Andrew and without answers. A formal request from the UK, asking Grenada to cooperate with its investigation into Andrew’s death, still sits unsigned. It is the best chance we have of finding the truth,” the family statement said.
Johnston said the initial handling of Frederick’s case and the further delays could have a detrimental effect on the investigation.
“In a homicide investigation we have a phrase that we refer to as the golden hours, which are the first real 24 hours from the notification, or the discovery, of a homicide [which] are the most important and crucial … because evidence diminishes and can be lost if a crime scene is not properly noted and properly managed.
“In the case of the death of [Frederick] that’s exactly what happened … the police, in my view, failed to properly identify and preserve the crime scene and to treat the crime scene in the manner it should have been treated,” he said.
Johnston added that cooperation between British and Grenadian police could help to “bring some stability to that investigation”.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British man who died in Grenada, and are in contact with the local authorities.”
The Guardian has approached the Royal Grenada Police Force for comment but has not had a reply.
The family said: “With each passing day, our family’s heartbreak deepens. We need closure, and Grenada’s prime minister, who is also the minister of national security, can help make this possible. We appeal to him, with humanity and compassion, to sign the request without further delay.”
Additional reporting by Calistra Farrier

Doctors are urging Americans aged 6 months and older to get vaccinated against the flu after an unusual early rise in cases on the West Coast that virologists are still working to understand.
It could be the strain itself. The predominant flu strain this year is H1N1, which caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic and is now a standard part of the flu shot. But this year’s version of the virus has a new mutation called G155E.
People who have been previously exposed to H1N1, either through infection or vaccination, would only have some residual protection from the older versions, scientists say.
"What people are a bit worried about is that the H1N1 strain this year hasn't been seen by a lot of younger folk, so it may be more severe in them," said Dr. Jennifer Duchon, a paediatric infectious disease expert at Mount Sinai Children's Hospital in New York, adding that her hospital has started to see some flu cases.
The 2026-2027 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, target H1N1, H3N2 — the dominant strain last flu season — and one influenza B virus.
While most children recover, flu can be deadly, especially for the very youngest and those with underlying health conditions.
Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.
The American Medical Association recommends the shot for all people 6 months and older.
The vaccine's effectiveness fluctuates depending on how well it is matched months in advance to circulating flu strains. Over the past 10 years, it has been between 30% and 60% effective in reducing flu hospitalisations and deaths. Last year, an estimated 32 million Americans had the flu, 390,000 were hospitalised and 24,000 died.
Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year's vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.
However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, "it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early," Hensley said via email.
Geography changes
Typically, flu cases start in Southern states and move north. This year, it's coming from the west, said Caitlin Rivers, a Johns Hopkins epidemiologist who tracks pathogens in a weekly newsletter called Force of Infection.
“There's no clear reason to me why this would be the case,”Rivers said.
As last year was dominated by the H3N2, there could be an "immunological gap" because immunity to H1N1 virus is not as fresh. Or, it could be the new mutation, she said.
Jeanne Marrazzo, chief executive of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said studies of antibodies from people exposed to the flu last year found they did not recognize this new mutation. That was especially true of antibodies from teens and young adults.
Marrazzo said the small studies were something to be aware of but not cause for alarm.
Falling shots, rising flu cases
Some 58 million American adults received a flu shot last season, according to data firm IQVIA, down more than 20% from the nearly 75 million in the 2019-20 season, the last season before the COVID-19 pandemic changed U.S. vaccination patterns.
Around half of U.S. children got flu shots last year, according to CDC data, compared with more than 60% in 2019-20.
Standard flu shots are made by GSK, Sanofi, and CSL's Seqirus unit. AstraZeneca makes a nasal spray inoculation called FluMist. A new mRNA vaccine from Moderna is also available.
Vaccine manufacturers say demand has been consistent with last year. Two pharmacists told Reuters vaccination rates have not picked up significantly.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention dropped its recommendation for the shot for most children at the beginning of 2025, a move a court put on hold.
CDC also pulled its ad campaign to promote flu vaccination in 2025, according to press reports.
Paul Offit, a pediatric infectious disease expert at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, said he believes immunisation rates have been hurt by HHS' decision to cut back on promoting flu shots, as well as by statements from Kennedy himself.
"He has done what he can to discourage flu vaccination," Offit said.
When asked about public health messaging on flu shots this season, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard pointed to the CDC's "Respiratory Illness Season Toolkit" on the agency's website. It says vaccination is the most effective tool to prevent serious illness.
Flu activity is low but has been on the rise since late August, CDC data show.
Positive tests reported to the CDC by clinical labs last week hit a 10-year high for this time of year at 5%. On the West Coast, that figure was 10.7%, compared with 0.5% a year earlier. At peak flu, the rates are around 30%.
Numbers are also elevated in eight Southern states including Florida and South Carolina, according to Hopkins' Rivers.

Nigerian president launches reelection bid during a cost-of-living crisis and a fractured opposition
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has launched his reelection campaign during a cost-of-living crisis and a fractured opposition
ABUJA, Nigeria -- Nigerian President Bola Tinubu launched his reelection bid Saturday, campaigning at a rally for a second presidential term during a cost-of-living crisis and a fractured opposition.
The presidential election will be held in January against the backdrop of a worsening economy that has caused anger among voters against Tinubu’s government, but which Tinubu blamed on opposition parties.
“I hear my opponents talking about hunger and poverty. Who created it? They did,” he said at a rally in the northwestern state of Kaduna. “They created the hunger, they created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."
Tinubu is being challenged by over a dozen opposition candidates, but analysts predict a three-man race between Tinubu and the two contenders he defeated in 2023. They are former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress, or ADC, a serial presidential candidate, and Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, or NDC, a former state governor who blew the last race wide open with his mass appeal to Nigeria’s youth.
In 2023, Tinubu scrapped a decades-long government-funded subsidy on gasoline moments after his inauguration as president. The move has been touted as a bold economic reform but it contributed to the naira’s devaluation and widespread hardship.
“We have prosperity and consistency, growth, recovery and opportunity, I assure you. Your prosperity is here. Fuel subsidy is in the past, no more corruption, no more lies,” he said.
Political analyst Majeed Dahiru told The Associated Press that Tinubu’s chances of winning a second term are challenged by public discontent over his economic policies.
“It is a tough one. But one thing is certain that is not going to be a walkover for any of the contending parties at all in this election. It is one that you can’t predict,” he said.
The 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu win with over 8.7 million votes. Abubakar followed with over 6.9 million votes and Obi with 6.1 million, according to the Independent National Electoral Commission.
Although Tinubu won the most votes, he recorded one of the lowest vote percentages ever for an elected president, showing how unpopular he was.
The split opposition could give Tinubu a higher chance of winning in 2027 as was the case in 2023.
Opposition candidates Atiku and Obi, among others, formed an alliance in 2025 to unseat Tinubu, but it collapsed before it took off.

Srinagar, Oct 25: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Sunday said the Kashmir Marathon was creating new opportunities for local sporting talent and expressed confidence that runners from Jammu and Kashmir would soon make their mark on national and international platforms.
Addressing the prize distribution ceremony of the Kashmir Marathon 2026 at Polo View Ground in Srinagar, LG Sinha said talent exists across Jammu and Kashmir but often lacks adequate opportunities to showcase itself.
He said a champion marathon runner could emerge from any district of the Union Territory, including Anantnag, Pulwama or Budgam.
Congratulating the winners, the Lieutenant Governor also praised participants who completed the race without securing medals, saying their determination and perseverance deserved equal recognition.
“I would also like to say something to those who did not receive a medal. You are not merely participants; you are also winners. Those who keep running and cross the finish line after several hours deserve our salute,” he said.
Sinha said the Kashmir Marathon had helped bridge the gap between talent and opportunity by providing aspiring runners with a platform to showcase their abilities.
He expressed confidence that Jammu and Kashmir would produce athletes capable of competing at the highest levels of marathon running. “I am confident that the next big name in marathon running will emerge from Jammu and Kashmir,” he said.
The Lieutenant Governor urged the winners to guide and mentor aspiring runners, saying their achievements could inspire more young people to take up sports and pursue their ambitions.
He said several young participants had described the marathon as the beginning of a new journey and expressed hope that the event would continue to nurture sporting talent in the region.
“Flowers are about to bloom and they will bloom (Phool khilne wale hain, khilenge),” Sinha said, expressing optimism about the future of young talent.
Sinha said he was pleased that the Kashmir Marathon had secured a place in the calendar of international marathons and races, describing it as an encouraging development for Jammu and Kashmir.
He congratulated the Tourism Department, police, medical teams, volunteers and all other stakeholders for their contribution to the successful conduct of the event.
The Lieutenant Governor also acknowledged the contribution of the person from Ladakh associated with the idea of the marathon, saying the event had evolved into a platform that brought people together through sports.
Sinha said the marathon was not merely a sporting event but also an opportunity to promote fitness, healthier lifestyles and greater public participation in physical activities. Expressing concern over the increasing time people spend on mobile phones and screens, he stressed the need to make physical activity part of everyday life.
He said participating in a marathon was not necessary for everyone, but people should incorporate sports and exercise into their daily routines. He expressed hope that the Kashmir Marathon would motivate people across age groups, including those above 50, to become more physically active.
Addressing the youth, Sinha said a marathon teaches important lessons about determination, patience and overcoming challenges that could be applied to life.
He said runners often experience exhaustion and difficulties during a race but continue moving towards the finish line, adding that young people should adopt the same approach when faced with setbacks. “There are no shortcuts in a marathon, and there are no shortcuts in life either,” he said.
Sinha urged young people to recognise opportunities, take responsibility and turn challenges into opportunities to achieve their goals.
He said the youth had an important role in shaping the future of Jammu and Kashmir and called upon them to contribute towards building a society marked by confidence, energy and a strong sporting culture.
The Lieutenant Governor expressed hope that the Kashmir Marathon would continue to attract runners from different parts of the country and abroad while promoting Jammu and Kashmir as a destination for sports and tourism. The Kashmir Marathon 2026 brought together local, domestic and international runners, with the event aimed at promoting fitness, sporting talent and tourism in the Union Territory.—(KNO)

“You Can See Everything” might be the buzziest film of the moment, but before the Elizabeth Holmes-focused documentary made it to theaters, co-director Lance Oppenheim has admitted that fellow director Nathan Fielder was so skeptical about being able to weave a unique enough narrative that he negotiated a “kill switch” with A24 before they began filming.
In an interview with IndieWire, Oppenheim detailed Fielder’s kill-switch idea and how it helped the project. While Fielder wanted to pursue the documentary with Oppenheim, he worried that “the story had been told so many times already.” (Before the documentary even began production, Holmes’ scandal was already the subject of a popular podcast, best-selling book, an Alex Gibney doc and “The Dropout,” the Hulu scripted series.)
“Nathan [said to A24], ‘Well, do you think if Lance and I were to go and see if there was something there, would you be comfortable with giving us money and essentially just leaving us alone, and giving us a provision in our deal, whatever the money was, that we could just kill it at any time? If we didn’t find something, we could just throw it all away, we could throw it in the garbage can,’” said Oppenheim. “And they thankfully agreed.”
Popular on Variety
Oppenheim continued, saying that the “kill switch” negotiation “changed everything,” especially as Fielder remained hesitant about how the doc would come to fruition with just 34 days left before Holmes was set to go to prison. The provision also gave them freedom with the project, he said.
“This was the first time where I’ve ever been like, ‘Oh, we actually have room to explore something without any pressure of anyone looking [over us],” said Oppenheim. “ I wish I could have that for every project, because then it really feels like you’re just operating purely out of curiosity. You can essentially fish.”
In another interview with Wired Magazine, Fielder also touched on why he wanted such a provision in the contract.
“I told A24, ‘I don’t really know what the angle is, but there is something tickling in my brain,’” he said. “She was about to go to prison, so we didn’t know what was gonna happen. I was like, ‘If you guys want, I’m down to go down and start filming and see what emerges. But we need the ability to deliver nothing to you guys if it doesn’t work out.’ And they said ‘Sure.’”
He continued: “It really meant I didn’t have to hold back with her or with them. Making a film, or any project, is very stressful. So if we had to pull the plug because it didn’t work out, it would sort of be a relief to me. It’s a very nice zone to operate in. Lance and I both thought, ‘Well, at the very least, this will be an interesting week or two that we’ll have as a story.’”

Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
- Published
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.
Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.
He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.
The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.
- What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election 
  - Published1 day ago
Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
"It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," Srdanović told the BBC.
The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.
Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.
He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.
Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.
Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.
Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.
Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."
The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.
"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.
"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.
At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people.
Vučić has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions".
But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago.
The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project – the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for Vučić to distance himself from the disaster.
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.
Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."
The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."
