Ai+ Nova 2 Power Review Verdict: A Decent Newcomer With Tough Competition
Ai+ Nova 2 Power comes in two variants. The 6GB + 128 GB is priced at Rs 16,999/- and 8 GB + 128 GB is priced at 17,999/-. Overall, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power is a good package for people who prioritize battery life and performance for everyday use without spending too much. The Dimensity 7100 handles most everyday tasks and gaming well, although it can get even better with software optimization. The colorful reflective glass back will appeal to most users, and the huge 7000 mAh battery gets you through your day. Cameras also did a decent job of handling everyday photography and videos.
But the HD+ resolution display is a real letdown, especially when so much more is available; AMOLED displays and a more polished software experience could have been better. But overall, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power gets most of the basics right, but the display and unpolished software experience hold it back, especially if you compare it with established rivals.

If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess three terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini-powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.
While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the last ten days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.
Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices, and that they've rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”
Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the last week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the last week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.
If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for what device could be at fault.
How to Check Your Device Usage
You have a couple of different options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app still lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.
There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router, and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:
- Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in.
- Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour).
- You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab.
- You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone.
Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:
- Open the Deco or Tether app.
- Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage.
- What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information.
Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter, you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface (it usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app). If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.
But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the last seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or my over the last three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home.
But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.
Why Should You Check?
It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the two terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a three-terabyte bug slowing down your whole network.

Srinagar , Oct 25: In a landmark triumph for sustainable agriculture and ecological preservation, the Union Territory of Ladakh has officially transitioned into India’s first fully certified 100% organic Union Territory.
The achievement follows a phased, multi-year initiative designed to phase out synthetic fertilizers, chemical pesticides, and toxic soil additives across both Leh and Kargil districts. Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Sunday declared the Union Territory of Ladakh India’s first 100% Organic Union Territory, recognising its farmers' dedication and the Administration’s sustained efforts to promote chemical-free farming.
The achievement marks a significant step towards protecting Ladakh’s fragile Himalayan ecosystem, improving soil and water health, enhancing farmers’ incomes and ensuring a healthier future for generations to come. Building on its traditional farming practices and unique agro-ecological conditions, Ladakh is positioning itself as a model for sustainable high-altitude agriculture.
"A proud moment for Ladakh as it becomes India’s first 100% Organic Union Territory, thanks to the dedication and hard work of our farmers. This milestone reflects our commitment to fulfilling Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji’s vision of chemical-free farming, environmental conservation and sustainable livelihoods.
Our strict prohibition on chemical fertilisers and continued efforts towards organic certification will protect Ladakh’s fragile Himalayan ecosystem, improve soil and water health, and enhance the value of local produce. This would further strengthen market linkages, improve farmers’ incomes and establish Ladakh as a model for sustainable high-altitude agriculture. My congratulations to all farmers and stakeholders on this historic achievement!" LG Ladakh posts on X .
Congratulating the farmers and all stakeholders, the Lieutenant Governor said, “This is a moment of immense pride for Ladakh and the entire nation. Our farmers have demonstrated that environmentally responsible agriculture can flourish even in the most challenging geographical conditions. Becoming a fully organic Union Territory is not merely a milestone; it is a commitment to protecting our fragile Himalayan ecosystem, preserving our traditional farming practices and ensuring better livelihoods for our farmers.”
Notably, in a major policy intervention in July 2026, the Lieutenant Governor has ordered a complete prohibition on the procurement, distribution, sale, marketing and use of chemical and synthetic fertilisers for agricultural practices across Ladakh. The move is aimed at safeguarding organic certification, protecting soil and water resources and strengthening the long-term sustainability of the agricultural sector.
The Administration has also taken steps to support farmers during the transition. In March 2026, consignments of organic fertiliser were flagged off for distribution among farmers across villages of Ladakh to ensure timely availability before the sowing season.
The organic transition is expected to create new opportunities for Ladakh’s farmers by improving the value of locally grown organic produce, including apricots, sea buckthorn, buckwheat, barley and vegetables. Organic certification, better post-harvest management, value addition, branding and stronger market linkages can help farmers access consumers who increasingly seek authentic, traceable and organically produced food.

Andhra Pradesh, Odisha on alert as IMD warns of possible cyclone over Bay of Bengal by October 26
The IMD has issued a pre-cyclone watch for Andhra Pradesh and adjoining South Odisha coasts amid the impending cyclone.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned about a well marked low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal region that will likely develop into a cyclonic storm by October 26 morning.
As per IMD’s latest bulletin, this low-pressure area is expected to persist over the same region and intensify into a depression on Saturday. Thereafter, it is very likely to move and intensify further into a deep depression on October 25 and into a cyclonic storm over the Westcentral Bay of Bengal by October 26 morning.
It would continue to intensify further and reach over Westcentral Bay of Bengal near Andhra Pradesh coast around morning of October 28, the weather department added.
IMD has issued a pre-cyclone watch for Andhra Pradesh and adjoining South Odisha coasts in this regard.

Extremely heavy to heavy rain to hit Andhra, Odisha between October 27-29
The IMD has forecast extremely heavy to heavy rainfall for coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha between October 27 and 29.
According to the roster that lists names of cyclonic storms, the next cyclone that forms in the North Indian Ocean will be named Arnab.
The name Arnab (which means "ocean" in Bengali) was contributed by Bangladesh to the regional tropical cyclone naming list maintained by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the IMD.
A weather system last month also triggered cyclone watch but ended up not intensifying into a cyclonic storm. It, however, crossed Andhra Pradesh-Odisha coast as a deep depression and brought heavy rain. The system had intensified into a deep depression over westcentral and adjoining northwest Bay of Bengal on September 23.
Classification for depressions, cyclones
According to IMD website, the weather department classifies low-pressure systems based on their intensity, using pressure patterns over land and maximum sustained wind speed over the sea. A system is classified as a low-pressure area when it has one closed isobar, while a depression has two and a deep depression has three. A system with four or more closed isobars is classified as a cyclonic storm.
Based on wind speed, a system with maximum sustained three-minute surface winds of 17-27 knots (31-50 kmph) is called a depression, while 28-33 knots (52-61 kmph) is classified as a deep depression. Once maximum sustained winds reach 34 knots (63 kmph) or more, the system is classified as a cyclonic storm. Thus, a low-pressure area does not automatically mean a cyclone; it must intensify and cross the prescribed thresholds to be classified as one.

With heavy rain, waterlogging and flooded streets becoming familiar sights during the monsoon, the risk of leptospirosis, a bacterial infection spread through water or soil contaminated by the urine of infected animals, becomes an important public health concern. India is estimated to record between 100,000 and one million cases annually. The infection can cause fever and muscle pain, but in severe cases, it can damage the kidneys, liver and lungs. Recognising the symptoms early and seeking timely treatment can help prevent serious complications.
What is leptospirosis?
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease , an infection that spreads from animals to humans, caused by bacteria belonging to the genus Leptospira. The bacteria can infect several animals, including rats, cattle, dogs and pigs. Infected animals may shed the bacteria in their urine, contaminating water and soil.
Humans can acquire the infection when contaminated water or soil comes into contact with broken skin or the mucous membranes of the eyes, nose and mouth. Drinking water contaminated with the bacteria can also transmit the infection. The bacteria can survive in moist soil and water for weeks or months under favourable conditions.
The disease occurs worldwide, but its burden is greater in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with heavy rainfall, flooding, inadequate sanitation and limited access to safe water.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that about one million cases and nearly 60,000 deaths occur globally each year. The actual burden may be higher because the disease is often underdiagnosed and surveillance systems differ between countries.
In India, leptospirosis is a recognised public health concern, particularly in coastal regions and other areas where environmental conditions favour transmission. The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), under the Union Health Ministry, identifies Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka among the States where the disease has been a concern. The Government’s Programme for Prevention and Control of Leptospirosis has expanded to cover 181 districts across 12 States and two Union Territories, according to the NCDC.
What are the signs and symptoms?
Symptoms usually develop between two and 30 days after exposure, most commonly within five to 14 days. Some infected people may not develop symptoms, while others experience an illness that resembles dengue, influenza or other infections that cause fever.
Common symptoms include-- fever and chills, headache, muscle pain - particularly in the calves and lower back, redness of the eyes, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fatigue.
The symptoms are not specific to leptospirosis, making it difficult to identify the infection on clinical grounds alone. A history of exposure to floodwater, contaminated soil or potentially infected animals can help a doctor assess the likelihood of infection.
In some patients, the illness progresses to a severe form, sometimes called Weil’s disease. This can involve kidney damage, liver dysfunction, jaundice, bleeding and respiratory complications. In severe cases, patients may develop meningitis, shock or failure of multiple organs.
Who is most at risk?
The risk of infection is higher among people who have frequent contact with contaminated water, wet soil or animals.
Agricultural workers, particularly those working in flooded paddy fields, are among the groups at risk. Other vulnerable groups include sanitation workers, sewer and drainage workers, waste handlers, flood-relief personnel and people involved in cleaning waterlogged homes and public spaces.
People living in areas with poor drainage, inadequate sanitation, rodent infestation or recurrent flooding may also face increased exposure. Those who walk barefoot through contaminated water or have cuts and abrasions on their skin may be more vulnerable.
Exposure does not necessarily lead to infection, and not everyone who contracts the bacteria develops severe disease. However, the risk of complications makes early recognition important.
The disease is not generally spread directly from one person to another. Its transmission is primarily associated with contact with infected animals or environments contaminated by their urine.
What are the treatment options?
Anyone who develops a fever after exposure to floodwater or potentially contaminated water or soil should seek medical assessment and mention the exposure to the treating doctor. Urgent care is particularly important if there is jaundice, reduced urine output, breathing difficulty, bleeding, confusion or persistent vomiting.
It is important not to assume that every fever during the monsoon is dengue or another common seasonal infection. Leptospirosis may initially present similarly, but the treatment and potential complications differ.
It is treated with antibiotics. Early treatment is important, and doctors may begin treatment when the clinical suspicion is high rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation.
For mild illness, doctors may prescribe oral antibiotics such as doxycycline, amoxicillin or azithromycin, depending on the patient’s circumstances and clinical assessment. The choice of antibiotic and duration of treatment depend on factors such as age, pregnancy, allergies and the severity of the illness.
Patients with severe disease may require hospitalisation and intravenous antibiotics, such as penicillin or ceftriaxone. They may also need supportive treatment for complications, including intravenous fluids when appropriate, monitoring of kidney and liver function, oxygen or ventilatory support, and dialysis if kidney failure develops.
Diagnosis involves tests such as PCR, which detects the bacteria’s genetic material, and IgM ELISA, which detects antibodies produced in response to the infection. The choice of test depends on the stage of illness, and doctors may also test for other infections that cause similar symptoms.
It is important to not self-medicate with antibiotics or wait for symptoms to become severe before seeking care. Antibiotics should be taken under medical supervision, and suspected severe leptospirosis requires urgent assessment.
How can leptospirosis be prevented?
Reducing contact with potentially contaminated water and soil is central to prevention, particularly during the monsoon and after floods.
Avoid wading through floodwater whenever possible. Those who must work in waterlogged areas should use waterproof boots and protective clothing, and cover cuts and abrasions with waterproof dressings. Hands and exposed skin should be washed thoroughly after contact with potentially contaminated water or soil.
Drinking water should be safe. Water that may have been contaminated during flooding should be boiled or treated using an appropriate method before consumption. Food that has come into contact with floodwater should be discarded.
Improved drainage, proper waste disposal, rodent control and measures to reduce animal exposure are important at the community level. Local health authorities should also strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnosis and public awareness in areas where cases are regularly reported.

El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
- Published
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.
Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.
He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.
Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.
Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.
The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.
It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.
The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.
Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
- Published
Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

US-based HR tech startup Firstwork has raised $15 Mn (over ₹142 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Earlybird Venture Capital, as it looks to expand its AI-led workforce automation platform across the US and Europe. The round also saw participation from Legion VC and Deel Ventures, along with existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The latest fundraise takes Firstwork’s total funding to $20 Mn since its launch in 2024. The San Francisco-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its teams across applied AI, AI research, engineering and go-to-market functions. Important to highlight that about 80% of the startup’s workforce operates from Bengaluru. It also plans to deepen its presence in the US and Europe and extend its AI agents to more workforce operations. Founded by ex-Deel executives Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary, Firstwork uses AI agents to automate HR operations pertaining to frontline workers. These include document verification, background and right-to-work checks, onboarding, training coordination, compliance management and worker follow-ups. The startup’s platform integrates within existing HR systems, allowing employers to automate workflows without replacing their existing software. According to Firstwork, more than 1.50 Lakh frontline workers start work through its platform every month. It claims that its platform has helped these customers cut the time spent by workers and HR teams on each new hire by up to 90%. Its clients include Swiggy, Zepto, Croma, Starbucks and Dr Lal PathLabs. Ravi Tamta is an innovator from Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham in Almora, Uttarakhand. He spent 13 years developing an electric flying car called HAPIDA SKYNeX. His aim is to make travel easier across mountains, especially during medical emergencies. Growing up in the hills, Tamta understood the difficulties caused by winding roads. Reaching a hospital could take hours, even when the distance seemed short. He wondered whether people could travel through the air without depending on roads, The Better India reported. This question encouraged him to develop a vehicle needing neither an airport nor a runway. HAPIDA SKYNeX can take off and land vertically, much like a drone. The prototype completed its first test flight in August from an army helipad in Almora. It remained airborne for nearly one minute, marking an important achievement for Tamta. Tamta had no engineering degree or access to an advanced laboratory. He learnt through the internet, through repeated experiments, and with support from his parents. Over the years, these efforts helped turn his idea into a working prototype. He developed the vehicle through his venture, Hapida Sky Private Limited, according to The Better India. The vehicle uses several electric motors and propellers mounted on arms extending from its body. Together, they lift it, keep it hovering, and help control movement. It has a lightweight frame, space for one pilot, and a transparent cover. Batteries power its motors, so it produces no direct exhaust emissions during operation. Tamta hopes the vehicle could eventually shorten journeys across difficult mountain routes. A 40-km road journey that takes around 90 minutes could take 10-15 minutes by air, The Better India reported. However, this remains a goal and has not been demonstrated during regular travel. Its actual flying distance will depend on battery capacity, weight and power requirements. The successful test does not mean the vehicle is ready for passenger services. More testing is needed to check control, battery performance, strength and safety during failures. Mountain weather, strong winds, landing spaces and emergency arrangements will also need attention. Ravi Tamta’s achievements extend beyond his flying car project. His earlier inventions include shoes that charge mobile phones while someone walks. He also developed a smart walking stick for people with visual disabilities. Other creations include a bamboo-splitting machine and fire-fighting equipment. These inventions reflect his interest in finding practical answers to everyday problems. For now, HAPIDA SKYNeX represents an early step towards Tamta’s larger dream. It could eventually help people reach hospitals and remote places faster. Further work remains essential. I still remember losing my mind when Captain Price slid me a pistol on a burning bridge in 2007. That iconic moment cemented my lifelong love for this series, leading me straight to this Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 campaign review.
Because I care so deeply, the rebooted COD Modern Warfare 3 broke my heart as the worst of the franchise. I gave that lazy, Warzone-padded disaster bad numbers and worried my favorite tactical shooter would never recover its soul.
Thankfully, I booted up this fourth chapter and felt an immediate wave of relief wash over my cynical doubts. Infinity Ward clearly listened to heartbroken fans like me and built a tightly scripted, single-player thriller from the ground up.
Over the weekend, I played through all sixteen missions twice to soak in every ounce of this redemptive finale. Stepping back into the muddy boots of a Rogue Price and some fresh characters finally feels like coming home to the classic glory days.
Modern Warfare 4 Has Its Own Rules of Engagement Now
The narrative picks up three years after the previous game, and I watched Captain Price spiral into a ruthless outlaw. Losing John “Soap” MacTavish shattered the squad’s moral compass, turning Price into a vengeful lone wolf hunting down Makarov’s network. I mean, at this point, Soap’s death is the plot of Modern Warfare (just like in the original trilogy).
To reach a Russian mastermind called The Archer, Price enters into a desperate alliance with cartel boss Valeria Garza. Mads Mikkelsen plays the main villain in MW4, called The Archer, with icy menace, making for a brilliant villain with personal motives to hate our heroes.
What shocked me most about this plot is how it treats beloved veterans like an episode of Game of Thrones. My favorite characters started dying out of nowhere, proving that war is brutal and nobody is an invincible superhero here.
I felt a heavy knot in my stomach during “Gone Dark,” where I played as Gaz hunting a rogue Price. Watching Ghost and Gaz clash with their former mentor in a dark hotel set up a truly devastating series conclusion. And boy, that knife fight between the top dawgs was worth every cut through my virtual veins.
Old Guard and New Fronts Show the Dual Perspectives in the Korean War
While Price wages his shadow war in flashbacks, I spent the present-day missions fighting through a sudden North Korean invasion. I stepped into the boots of Private Park Hyun-Jun, a terrified South Korean conscript just trying to survive compulsory service.
Alongside charming Sierra-1 squadmates like Corporal Dunn and Lieutenant West, I fought to hold the crumbling streets of Hajin City. Playing as an ordinary soldier rather than an elite superhero brought back the grounded tension I missed for years. It felt like COD 4 all over again.
Infinity Ward also surprised me by letting me play as the high-ranking North Korean officer questioning his ruthless orders. During a harrowing village sweep filled with public executions, I used optional dialogue prompts to calm down terrified civilians.
Having the choice to show empathy or pull my weapon added rich moral weight to the opposing side of war. When they eventually defected to help Park’s surviving marines, I felt a genuine bond between these unlikely battlefield brothers.
You Know Who They Are Purely by Their Acting
None of these tragic deaths or shifting alliances would hit so hard without the phenomenal voice actors driving every scene. Barry Sloane delivers a career-best performance as the rogue Captain Price in Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4, channeling a raspy, exhausted fury that gave me constant chills.
When he trades threats with Samuel Roukin’s Ghost and Elliot Knight’s Gaz, the raw betrayal in their British accents hurts. Their heavy breath work and sharp vocal inflections turned a standard military script into an intimate, heartbreaking family tragedy. And for someone who follows military stories so closely, this felt like an epic.
I was equally blown away by how Mads Mikkelsen and Young Mazino elevated the new faces in the cast. Mikkelsen, being a veteran on the screen, brings a quiet, calculating dread to The Archer, stealing every cutscene with his chilling delivery during brutal interrogations.
Meanwhile, Mazino grounds Private Park with a trembling, relatable vulnerability that contrasts perfectly against Price’s hardened, gravelly roars. Maria Elisa Camargo also shines as Valeria, taunting Price with playful venom that keeps their twisted partnership electric.
Linear Gameplay Variety and Open-World Pacing Finally Find the Balance
From a mechanical standpoint, my playthroughs for the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 campaign review delivered pure blockbuster variety at breakneck speed. In Manhattan, I brawled through a neon-lit nightclub as Price, using a slick new parry-and-counter melee system like John Wick.
A few missions later, I tossed plastic explosives out of a speeding van during an uncertain Paris highway chase. As Park, I even stormed a heavily fortified beach in “Counter Attack,” which played like a modern, explosive answer to D-Day.
On top of that, you get to do plenty of parkour, classic scripted objectives, and switching between characters in some missions. The perspectives of different soldiers on the field feel fresh and are a welcome move.
That relentless momentum only stumbles once during the tenth mission, “Stranded,” which drops you into a snowy Far Cry sandbox. After crashing behind enemy lines, you scavenge supplies, solve keypad puzzles, and raid outposts to craft suppressed sniper rifles.
While I appreciated the freedom to upgrade my gear at a basement hideout, the slow pacing killed the story’s urgency. Thankfully, the developers let me fast-travel straight to the three main objectives on my second run to skip the chores. But what I can keep on my screen on repeat is the…
Hollywood Cinematography and Thematic Dissonance
Beyond the gunplay, I marveled at the Hollywood cinematography that seamlessly blends sweeping wide-angle cutscenes into claustrophobic first-person combat. The camera work uses anamorphic lenses, shallow depth of field, and dirty framing to make every conversation feel like a movie.
You notice lifelike catchlights shimmering in the actors’ eyes, which amplify the dread during quiet, low-key night-vision ambushes. Even the volumetric smoke impresses, letting you punch realistic holes through the fog with rifle fire.
However, there is some awkward thematic dissonance noticeable between the serious narrative cutscenes and actual gameplay actions. Price constantly lectures Valeria about minimizing collateral damage right before blowing up dozens of cars on a crowded highway.
Meanwhile, accidentally shooting a sprinting civilian during the chaotic street battles in Korea triggers an instant mission fail screen. These are quite realistic (thanks to war crimes existing).
What is not at all realistic is the annoying armor plates. The constantly stuffing armor plates into vests around every corner instead of relying on classic health regeneration gets tiring. Infinity Ward, can we remove multiplayer mechanics from the campaign, please?
Some Fidelity Gets Dirty, and the Performance Stays Clean
Before reaching my final score in this Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 campaign review, I must address technical performance. On console, I enjoyed a locked sixty frames per second with zero noticeable drops during massive building collapses and explosions.
On my high-end PC, however, enabling ray-traced reflections and global illumination tanked my frame rate and washed out dark rooms. I disabled ray tracing completely for my second playthrough, which eliminated input delay and visual ghosting for buttery-smooth aiming.
My Setup:
CPU: Intel i7 14700K 3.40 GHz
CPU Cooler: CORSAIR H150 RGB 360mm
Motherboard: MSI Z790 Pro Wifi
GPU: Nvidia RTX 5080 Founder’s Edition 16 GB
RAM: Crucial (2x16GB) 5200MHz DDR5
SSD: Kingston 3 TB NVMe SSD
Monitor: 1440p @ 160Hz
At 4K Extreme settings with DLAA, I averaged 62 FPS with 46 FPS lows while drawing 251 watts. Switching to DLSS Quality boosted my average to 92 FPS, and DLSS Performance hit 144 FPS inside neon corridors.
When I enabled 4x Frame Generation with DLSS Quality at 4K, my counter skyrocketed to 237 FPS using 15.7 GB VRAM. However, that setting pushed render latency to 43.8ms, so I dropped to 1440p Extreme with DLAA for 121 native FPS.
Across all tests, my RTX 5080 stayed cool between 55 and 58 degrees Celsius while boosting around 2775 MHz. Despite a spinning bomb drone and one frozen pause menu, the core gunplay and sliding mechanics felt remarkably responsive. So yes, the optimization on COD MW4 is way more reliable than some of the previous entries.
Verdict: Get on That Gun and Rain Some Hell!
As the credits rolled after Price’s bloody sacrifice in the snow, I breathed a massive sigh of relief for Simon Riley. Seeing Kate Laswell welcome a surviving Ghost into the Watcher program gave me goosebumps and hope for the future.
I would love it if Infinity Ward used his survival to launch a sequel to the long-forgotten Call of Duty: Ghosts. That classic cliffhanger deserves a proper modern continuation, and Ghost is the ultimate badass icon to lead that charge.
Ultimately, the campaign deserves the flowers for putting effort into the story writing and stitching it with the gameplay. I am cutting one point solely for the brief runtime. Finishing all sixteen missions in just seven hours left me craving at least two more chapters on the Korean peninsula.
Even so, this Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 campaign celebrates a triumphant return to form for single-player fans. Infinity Ward buried the embarrassing memories of the last entry and delivered a brutal, emotional masterpiece that honors this franchise.
Now, load up your gear, silence your static, and remember that when the lines blur beyond recognition, you must draw your own line in the dirt. After all, you must “Hold the Line.”

Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
Domestic politics appear poised to trigger a new phase of war with Iran
The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.
"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.
Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."
Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.
The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Worst round yet
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.
"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."
Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)
Midterm dynamics
While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.
Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.
A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.
"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
Iran's demands
Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.
- Iran says 7 ships have been struck in Strait of Hormuz, Saudis intercept drones in airspace
- Iran's president says country won't surrender after Trump threat to 'annihilate' Islamic republic
The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.
"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Nuclear timeline?
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.
At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
'Finishing the job'
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.
Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.
"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.
"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

'We cannot remain helpless spectators': Jaishankar presses for 'dialogue and diplomacy' amid Ukraine, West Asia conflicts
Speaking in Delhi on the occasion of UN Day, Jaishankar reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only way to resolve conflicts.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said that a "war anywhere is threat to peace everywhere", raising concerns over the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia and their far-reaching impact on people and economies across the world.
Speaking at the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan in Delhi on the occasion of UN Day, Jaishankar reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only way to resolve conflicts, as he referred to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran in West Asia.
“There are today two major conflicts going on in the world: in Ukraine and in West Asia or the Middle East. Societies and economies, peoples far away, who have little say in the matter, are actually paying the cost,” the minister said.
Stressing that the international community could not afford to remain a silent spectator, Jaishankar said India was making its own efforts towards resolving the conflicts and was willing to work with other countries to restore peace.
“We cannot remain helpless spectators. India expresses global sentiment when we urge that dialogue and diplomacy are the only solution. We are making efforts ourselves and are open to working with other partners to that end,” he added.
‘Terrorism can never be justified’
The external affairs minister also flagged terrorism as another major threat to global peace, saying its use as an “instrument of statecraft” was "simply unacceptable" and could neither be justified nor rationalised.
"Terrorism is another deadly threat to peace," he said, adding that the threat continued because not all countries displayed zero tolerance towards it.
"Despite history holding so many lessons, some still allow political calculations to take precedence," Jaishankar said, calling for greater global awareness and stronger collective action to counter terrorism in all its forms.
Linking global peace to economic development, Jaishankar said progress and prosperity were equally interconnected, particularly in a world dependent on global supply chains, markets and shared resources.
“Progress and prosperity are the flip side of conflict and violence,” the minister added.
"The world cannot advance half prosperous and half denied in an era of intricate supply chains, of globalized markets, and of common resources. This is simply a prescription for continuous instability," he added.

A Chinese dissident falsely claims Kim Jong Un is dead - why is this rumour back?
- Published
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.
Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.
The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.
For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.
In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.
This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.
He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.
Yet the photographs tell a different story.
Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.
While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.
There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.
China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened.
South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.
The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.
So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.
North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.
Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.
Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader.
Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.
Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.
But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.
All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.
The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.
Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.
If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.
Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.
Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.
Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.
The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.
So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it.
He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.
Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

Man Utd not an unmanageable club - Carrick
- Published
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick has dismissed a theory the Old Trafford club are unmanageable.
Carrick is clinging on to his job after a desperate run of seven games without a win before Sunday's Premier League home game against Bournemouth (14:00 GMT).
The pressure on him has been heightened by controversial comments from senior players Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes attacking the club's recruitment and his tactics.
If Carrick were to lose his job, it would be the third change of manager in as many seasons and mean eight long-term bosses, including Ralf Rangnick, have lost their jobs after failing to get close to the heights of Sir Alex Ferguson, who retired in 2013.
Given the pressure on the club is heightened by the number of prominent ex-players who have their own media outlets, and the proliferation of fan channels that attract large numbers of viewers, there is an argument it makes United an impossible club to manage.
Carrick had a one-word answer to that notion: "No."
However, Carrick does take issue with some of the claims made about his team by former professionals and casual observers.
He is vexed at the sense his team do not run enough, and do not press the opposition when they are out of possession.
Carrick has accepted the general performance of his team in a 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como on Wednesday was "unacceptable".
However, he does not see how claims his team do not press stand up to much scrutiny.
"You've got to be careful with just saying 'not running'," he said.
"We've won a lot of games over a period of time and this pressing thing; pressing is one small part of football.
"There are all sorts of different ways that are classed as a press. What actually is it? What are you doing it for? Is it to your strength? Is it covering up other spaces?
"It's just thrown about as a bit of a word at the minute. You don't necessarily need to press to win games of football. Sometimes you do, sometimes you don't.
"It's not necessarily just running stats that define football games either.
"We've just got to get back to doing a lot of the things that we were doing last season and for certain parts of this season."
Carrick close to Sir Alex and Solskjaer
Although Carrick was appointed ahead of his former boss and team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer as Ruben Amorim's replacement in January, the pair remain close.
Solskjaer drove up to United's base in Trondheim before the pre-season victory over Rosenborg in July to spend time with Carrick and his backroom team.
They have been in touch this week, with Carrick also confirming he had spoken to Ferguson, who is a regular at matches as he approaches his 85th birthday.
Ferguson signed Carrick from Tottenham in 2006 and also managed the midfielder's Manchester United team in his testimonial game at Old Trafford in 2017.
"I speak to both of them quite regularly," he said. "There's nothing particular in that. I'm close to both of them. It's nothing different this week."
Carrick is convinced he can turn the situation around but knows he needs his underperforming squad to deliver against Bournemouth.
"I definitely trust them, 100%," he said.
"We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."

When a schoolteacher in eastern Congo learned that five of her family members had been diagnosed with Ebola, she was “deeply shaken,” fearing the worst from a disease that carries stigma and is seen by some in her community as evil.
Two of her relatives — her brother and his wife — died of Ebola in July at a treatment center in Ituri province, the epicenter of the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history.
The 34-year-old teacher, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity for fear of being stigmatized, said grief and stress over the loss of her relatives led her to seek treatment at a mental health clinic.
After two months at the clinic, the teacher said she was feeling better but worried about her future. “Will these people still be there for me?” she said of her relatives in Bunia, capital of Ituri.
Her experience highlights a burden rarely talked about in the fast-moving Ebola outbreak: the psychological toll on relatives coping with loss, fear and rejection in communities already scarred by years of rebel violence.
The outbreak is spreading at an unprecedented rate under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, fueled by mass population movements, violence, mistrust and poor working conditions for frontline health workers. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there's no approved vaccine or drug, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people infected. The World Health Organization has said that it continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it.
Losing relatives to disease outbreaks is always difficult, but responders say grief can be especially severe with Ebola in a country where the disease is viewed by many as evil due to rumors and misconceptions. The risk of transmission also limits contact with the patients even after death, depriving families of closure and the opportunity to observe their preferred burial rites.
The psychological effects of past Ebola outbreaks can persist long after the immediate crisis, according to WHO, often taking the form of anxiety and mood disorders, exacerbated by prolonged grief and discrimination.
This is Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak and has spread to eight provinces, coinciding with an escalation of decades-long conflict in the east between government forces and rebels.
Experts say the outbreak has compounded the trauma for many across the region. The medical response has focused largely on treating and containing the disease, with little to no attention to the mental health of those affected.
“There are so many areas (in eastern Congo) already devastated by war, crisis and severe malnutrition" and Ebola has worsened the condition of vulnerable populations and their mental health conditions, said Mirella Riccardi, a mental health specialist with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French name Médecins Sans Frontières.
The Congolese teacher recalled that her family felt abandoned by neighbors when her relatives began showing symptoms consistent with Ebola, including fever, vomiting, diarrhea and muscle pain.
Neighbors stayed away until Ebola responders came to take the sick to a clinic and disinfect their house afterward.
“It felt as though we were living all alone because of the illness,” said the teacher, who did not contract the disease. “It has caused severe trauma within our family.”
She also lost someone she had regarded as a father and said many others in their Bunia neighborhood have also died.
“Many people initially assumed that their symptoms were due to poisoning or malaria. Only later did they realize that they could be Ebola,” she said.
The Samelo mental health facility in Bunia, where she was admitted, said it had received up to 350 patients, a surge it attributed to the Ebola outbreak.
“Grief, fear of infection, social isolation and a succession of deaths can leave families and communities lastingly vulnerable,” said Katembo Vyaluva Anicet, the head nurse at the facility.
Five months into the outbreak, health authorities remain alarmed. More than 70% of new cases involved people who were not among known contacts, while at least 60% of deaths occurred outside treatment centers as of early October, government data showed.
The teacher has been discharged from the mental health facility but returns often for follow-up checks. Her three other infected relatives survived, and her husband said she feels much better.
But fear of Ebola persists within her family and among her neighbors.
“This has reignited fear and tension within the community,” she said. “Now, everyone is wondering how this disease will end.”

The moment in question takes place at the 19:40 mark in the C-SPAN video. In the middle of praising South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, he brought up appointing then-Gov. Nikki Haley as ambassador to the United Nations in 2017 "because I wanted this guy to become governor" (emphasis ours):
They allowed 25 million people to pour across our borders from all over the world. And if they ever won, they are going to do it all again, they're going to do it again. A page of schoolwork is hardly an unusual thing to find circulating online. But when photographs of Prakriti Malla’s handwriting began spreading across social media in 2017, people struggled to believe that the words had been written by hand.
Malla was just 14 years old and studying in Grade 8 at Birendra Sainik Awasiya Mahavidyalaya, a school in Nepal, when her exceptionally neat English handwriting attracted widespread attention. The letters were remarkably consistent, the spacing was precise, and each line appeared so uniform that many viewers mistook the page for digitally printed text.
What began as an ordinary school assignment soon became an international talking point. Images of the work circulated on Facebook, Twitter and Reddit, with users expressing disbelief at the precision of her writing. Some even suggested that her handwriting could be converted into a computer font.
Malla had already received recognition in Nepal in 2016, before the photographs introduced her work to a much larger international audience. Her achievement was a reminder that an everyday classroom skill could attract attention well beyond the school in which it was developed.
The striking feature of Malla’s handwriting is its consistency. Individual letters retain their shape throughout the page, while the distance between words and the alignment of sentences remain remarkably even.
Her writing does not depend on elaborate calligraphic flourishes. Instead, its appeal lies in the clarity of each letter and the discipline visible across the page. That is what made the photographs so compelling: the work looked typeset, yet it had been produced with a pen.
In a 2017 report, Study International noted that her writing had attracted widespread praise online, with some social media users suggesting that it should be adopted as a digital font.
The label ‘world’s most beautiful handwriting’ subsequently became closely associated with her name. However, reports do not establish a universally recognised international competition that formally awarded her that title.
Malla’s handwriting received renewed international attention in December 2022, when she wrote a congratulatory letter to the leadership and people of the United Arab Emirates for the country's 51st Spirit of the Union celebrations.
She presented the letter to the UAE Embassy in Nepal, which publicly acknowledged her work on social media. The embassy described her in connection with having the world's best handwriting, bringing her distinctive penmanship to the attention of another international audience.

Britain's Smith retains title in split-decision win over Puello
- Published
Britain's Dalton Smith defended his WBC light-welterweight world title with a split-decision victory over Alberto Puello in a triumphant homecoming in Sheffield.
The 29-year-old extended his unbeaten professional record in a high-class tactical contest at the Utilita Arena, with both fighters displaying sharp counter-punching skills.
The result hung in the balance as the judges' scorecards were read out, with victory for either man, or a draw, seemingly possible.
But Smith edged it, with two judges scoring the contest 115-113 in his favour and the third awarding it 116-112 to Dominican fighter Puello.
It was Smith's first title defence after his stunning fifth-round knockout of Subriel Matias in Brooklyn in January.
"We knew it wasn't going to be a show, he was going to be an awkward opponent, but a champion has to do what he has to do," Smith said post-fight. "These are the best in the world and I'm proving why I'm number one now."
The Sheffield fighter passes another stern test against two-time world champion Puello to extend his record to 20 wins.
With his mandatory challenger out of the way, Smith keeps his dream of headlining Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough Stadium alive and will target some of the biggest names in boxing, including unbeaten American Shakur Stevenson.
"I have a lot of respect for Shakur - he's one hell of a fighter," Smith added. "But this takes me back to the Ricky Hatton and Mayweather days. We can build something good."
Promoter Eddie Hearn added: "Dalton Smith is a legacy guy. I know that money plays a big part in boxing, and we want to make sure that this guy lives a wonderful life.
"First and foremost this guy is a real fighter, who wants belts, legacy, and to make his city proud."
Smith edges high-quality contest
Sheffield has a rich boxing history, having produced world champions including Prince Naseem Hamed, Johnny Nelson and Kell Brook, and those in attendance gave their latest champion a hero's welcome.
Wearing the blue and white of his beloved Sheffield Wednesday, he made his ring walk to AC/DC's Thunderstruck.
The contest began cagily, with neither fighter willing to overcommit as both showed sharp defensive skills.
Smith had beaten the fearsome puncher Matias by standing and trading, but Puello posed a different challenge - a slick southpaw relying on movement and counter-punching.
The champion dictated the pace in the early rounds. He landed a right in the fourth, but Puello, 32, found his range with his left before Smith connected again just before the bell.
Puello - whose only career loss came against Matias last year - came alive in the sixth, landing a series of straight lefts to take the round. The challenger then slipped to the canvas, briefly raising hopes of a knockdown among the home crowd.
The atmosphere resembled a football terrace, with a drummer and trumpeter accompanying fans singing Sheffield Wednesday songs.
A superb double jab and right hook from Smith in the ninth was answered by an uppercut and hook to the body from Puello, showcasing the quality of both fighters.
With the contest - originally scheduled for June before an elbow injury forced Smith to withdraw - finely poised, both men had everything to fight for heading into the championship rounds.
Cut below his right eye, Smith traded blows with Puello, perhaps edging the exchanges through his higher work-rate.
Smith played to the crowd in the final 20 seconds, before leaping into his father's arms at the final bell.
Is Stevenson next - and could Smith headline Hillsborough?
Smith's breakthrough year has established him among the leading fighters at light-welterweight. He had already won British, Commonwealth and European honours, and a successful first world-title defence further strengthens his credentials.
"Tonight, for me, Dalton Smith cemented himself as the number one pound-for-pound fighter in Britain," Hearn added.
The biggest challenge could come against Stevenson, the unbeaten WBO world champion and a four-weight world title-holder. The American is widely regarded as one of boxing's most gifted technicians.
Stevenson's recent departure from Zuffa Boxing could open up opportunities for negotiations, while another potential unification opponent is WBA champion Gary Antuanne Russell.
Closer to home, a meeting with unbeaten British rival Adam Azim has been discussed for several years. The pair have exchanged words throughout their rise and Smith has indicated he would welcome the contest at Hillsborough in 2027, although he believes Azim still has work to do before challenging for his world title.
"Number one goal in my life was to become world champion and make history, the second was to sell out Hillsborough stadium," Smith added.
The prospect of Smith defending his title in front of tens of thousands of supporters at the home of his boyhood football club would be another remarkable milestone.
He is not one for trash talk or the theatrics that often help fighters build their profiles, preferring to let his performances do the talking.
But the challenge now is turning world-title success into high-profile fights that could catapult him into the mainstream.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
